bodyText:
I took magnesium every night for six months to see if it could break my GLP-1 plateau. It did absolutely nothing. Then I tried the right one for 60 days. Here are the actual results.

I've been a medical assistant at a weight loss clinic for 19 years. I'm the one who calls you back, takes your blood pressure, and writes down the number on the scale.

For the last three years, almost every woman I weigh is on a GLP-1. And the most common thing I write in a chart now isn't a side effect. It's the plateau.

And I’ve stood beside that scale with thousands of women and written down the same number over and over again.

The number that hasn’t moved since spring no matter what. The face and the hands that got thinner while the middle stayed exactly where it was. The reward jeans from month two that still don’t button. The progress photos she quietly stopped taking. The 100 grams of protein, the 6am walk, the food scale on every plate, and the 25 pounds that came off right on schedule before it all just stopped.

I’ve watched grown women cry on my scale because they did everything the plan said and the number didn’t move.

Eighteen months ago, I started the shots myself. I’m 57. The first three months went exactly the way I’d watched them go for everyone else. Down 23 pounds. Then it started slow. First it was one Friday the number held and I blamed water. Then it was three Fridays in a row. Then it was the reward jeans going back in the drawer.

Nineteen years of 12 hour clinic days, lunch in the car between patients, sleeping 5 hours between early starts, and now half the food on top of all of it. It finally caught up with me.

At first I told myself it was the holidays. Then my mother fell, and between the hospital visits and the rehab tours and her paperwork at midnight, I figured it would come off once she was settled. It didn’t.

Then I started noticing I hadn’t stepped on the scale at work in weeks. Then months. That Friday number every woman on the shots checks like a lottery ticket, I’d stopped looking. I started weighing myself at home at 5am instead, so nobody at the clinic would see.

Then came the nights. My husband would reach for me and I’d feel my whole body go stiff before he’d said a word. I’d try to act normal, and the more I tried, the more I turned toward the wall. He started reaching less and less. When he told me I looked great, I changed the subject.

The same shame I tell women is normal every single day, I now had myself. I started eating lunch in my car so nobody in the break room would ask how it was going. I started getting dressed before he was awake. The irony wasn’t lost on me.

Now I was the patient. Every woman on my scale was right.

So I did what we tell everyone to do. I booked myself in with the nurse practitioner I work for. She ran labs. Thyroid, full panel. Everything normal. And then she said it, sitting on the same stool she sits on for everyone. “Deb, 23 pounds is a great result. Some people find their floor. We can go up a dose. Give it another three months, and if the number still hasn’t moved, this may just be your happy weight.” I told her I’d think about it.

But I knew that sentence. I’ve heard her say it through the wall a hundred times. I’ve nodded along to it. I print the dose change and hand it across the counter, every single day.

I also see what happens to the women who take it home.

The ones who go up a dose and spend a month nauseous for half a pound.

The ones who push through at 900 calories a day and quietly stop coming in.

The ones who come off the shots, because what’s the point of paying $400 a month to stand still, and then I watch it all come back, appointment by appointment.

And the worst part?

Half the women I weigh do everything right and still stall, because eating even less can’t fix what’s actually broken.

My mother carried her weight in the same places I do. She tried every diet that came out of the 80s and 90s, and every one of them stalled the same way. Her knees went at 70. The walker came at 74. Now she’s in a wheelchair at the rehab place and I’m the one pushing it. Nobody ever told her it wasn’t her. I work in weight loss for a living and I didn’t put it together until I was pushing her chair.

I wasn’t doing that to myself.

So I did what I tell every patient to do first. I went up the dose. Two weeks of nausea so bad I lived on crackers, for half a pound. Then I did the rest. Protein at every meal, 100 grams a day. Walked every morning before my shift. Logged every bite. Electrolytes. Fiber.

Things got a little better. I had more energy in the afternoons. The number dropped 1.4 and then sat there for another month, like it had just wanted to make a point. Most Fridays I still couldn’t make myself step on the scale at work.

I posted my numbers in my Facebook group too, like an idiot, and got forty different answers. “Plateaus are normal, push through.” “You’re eating too little, your body’s holding on.” And the one that stuck. “Nobody stalls on these if they’re actually compliant.” I’m the one who writes down whether people are compliant. I was compliant.

I tried the supplements too. The berberine everyone online calls nature’s version of the shot. Six weeks, nothing. The apple cider vinegar gummies the girl at our front desk swears by. Nothing.

And magnesium. This is the part I have to own. I tell every patient on these shots to take magnesium. It’s practically part of my discharge speech. The shots slow everything down, so pick up magnesium at the drugstore, it’ll keep you regular. I’ve said it to hundreds of women. I took my own advice from week two. Two capsules every night. Magnesium Glycinate, big letters on the front, $11.99. Six months. It kept me regular. That’s all it ever did.

I figured my body had simply decided. 23 pounds and the door shut.

Then about two months ago I had lunch with my friend Janet. Janet and I went to medical assistant school together 30 years ago. She went back, got her nursing degree, and now she’s a nurse practitioner at a functional medicine practice across town. Outside of my husband she’s probably the person on this planet who knows me best.

Halfway through lunch, I finally told her what was going on. About the scale at work. About eating in my car. About the happy weight.

She listened, didn’t interrupt, and then she laughed a little. Not at me. She said, “Deb, I was in the same spot a year ago.”

I almost dropped my fork.

Janet is 57, same age as me, has always been the thinner one of us, walks 5Ks on weekends. If she’d been dealing with the same thing and hadn’t told me, that alone said something.

She said she’d hit her goal in April and her provider had already moved her down to a maintenance dose. She’d worn a sleeveless dress to her daughter’s graduation without thinking about it once. She said the stall was long gone.

I asked her what she was doing.

She got a little sheepish and said, “I added something on my own. I didn’t want to bring it up at work until I was sure.”

I told her to spit it out.

She said it was magnesium. That it was the only thing that had moved her Fridays.

I laughed out loud. I told her I’d been taking magnesium every night for six months and it did nothing for me.

She looked at me across the table and said, “What kind?”

I told her. The drugstore glycinate. The one I recommend.

She closed her eyes for a second. “Deb, the cheap kind doesn’t work. You have to get the right one. Half the women who walk into my practice are already taking that exact bottle, and they’re stuck same as you.”

Then she leaned in and said something I’ll never forget.

“Deb, you and I both know this isn’t a dose problem. It’s a supply problem. You work at a weight loss clinic, you keep treating a stall like a compliance issue. It’s not. They’re running out.”

She grabbed a napkin and drew two lines on it. One for magnesium coming in. One for magnesium going out.

“Almost all of it comes from food. Then you start the shot and you eat half of what you used to. That’s the medication doing its job. But half the food means half the magnesium coming in.” She drew the first line dropping. “Then life happens. Your mom falls. You’re up at 3am. Stress burns it faster than anything.” She drew the second line climbing. “That’s where they cross. Week thirteen. That’s every plateau you’ve ever written in a chart. They’re not hitting a floor, Deb. They’re running out.”

She tapped where the lines met.

“Deb, I’ll tell you something that stuck with me from a conference last year. Something like 75% of women are already low in magnesium before they ever take a first shot. And magnesium is the one thing the nervous system uses to switch the stress response off. So the switch is stuck on in three out of four of the women you’re weighing. Their stall was the first sign and nobody read it, including them.”

She let that sit for a second.

“When you run out, your body thinks it’s in an emergency, so it goes into storage mode and holds on to everything. The shot turns the appetite down. It can’t touch storage mode. The dose increase you print just turns the appetite down further. It doesn’t switch anything off. So they eat less and less and the scale sits there, and when they come off, it all comes back. It’s why your mom’s diets never held either.”

I just sat there. I’ve weighed women at week thirteen for three years. I’ve written the word plateau hundreds of times. But I’d never heard it framed that clean, and I’d sure as hell never applied it to myself.

Then she said, “The right magnesium is the only thing I’ve found that actually gets to the switch and turns it off. Not turning the appetite down further, switching off the thing that’s holding everything.”

I’ll be honest, I was still skeptical. Patients bring me a new supplement every week and 99% of them are nonsense.

But this was Janet. This was a nurse practitioner I’d known for 30 years, sitting across from me at our usual table with a napkin sketch, telling me something worked for her that I’d already written off.

That night my husband reached for me and I went stiff again. He didn’t say anything, which somehow made it worse. So I got up, went into the kitchen, and turned the bottle around.

Front: Magnesium Glycinate. Back, under Supplement Facts, in print I needed my readers for: Magnesium (as magnesium oxide, magnesium glycinate). Oxide. Listed first. On the bottle I’d been recommending to hundreds of women.

I got out my laptop and went deeper into the magnesium research than I had in 19 years of working in weight loss. Here’s what I found, and I’ll keep it simple.

The reason the scale stops at month three is that the body is running out of magnesium.

The shot cuts your food in half, so it cuts your magnesium in half. Stress burns through what’s left faster than almost anything. And when it runs low, your nervous system can’t stand down, so your body decides it’s in danger and holds on to everything it has. It won’t let go while it believes the danger is still there.

Here’s why that matters. Your body has one off switch for the stress response, and it’s a mineral. Magnesium. When it’s there, your nervous system can stand down and storage mode switches off. When it isn’t, the switch stays stuck on.

And here’s the part I’d missed. Stress burns through magnesium, and running low keeps the stress response high. So the shortage creates the stress, and the stress deepens the shortage. The longer it goes, the worse it gets.

That’s why the plateau happens. That’s why it shows up on the scale months before anything shows up on a lab. That’s why the dose goes up and the number doesn’t move. Your plateau is the canary. Your magnesium is the coal mine.

Going up a dose doesn’t fix any of that. It turns the appetite down another notch and buys a month of nausea. The thing holding everything stays exactly where it is. The warning your body is trying to send just gets muffled.

Any research that actually showed magnesium bringing the stress response down used a form that crosses the blood brain barrier, because that’s where it gets regulated. Not in your stomach. In your brain.

Then I went back and looked at the bottle on my counter. Magnesium oxide. About four percent absorbed, the rest straight through you. That’s why it works as a laxative. That’s why it kept me regular and did nothing else. I had been taking a laxative with magnesium printed on the front, and recommending it to hundreds of women who were stalling for the exact reason I was. The clinical studies used a form that absorbs at up to ninety percent.

No wonder none of us were seeing results.

I kept reading. The bigger problem isn’t even the form, it’s the delivery.

Most magnesium is pressed into a hard capsule or tablet that needs strong stomach acid to break down. And these shots slow the stomach way down. That’s half of how they work. So a hard capsule can pass through before it ever really breaks down.

And it starts even earlier than that.

The soil our food grows in has been farmed hard for decades, so we get less magnesium from food than any generation in history before anyone ever opens a bottle. Then we go on a medication that cuts our food in half.

So even when a label says “magnesium,” between the cheap form and the capsule and the shot, the amount that actually reaches your brain is close to nothing. The label says magnesium. What gets through isn’t.

And the reason my labs were normal? A standard test checks the magnesium in your blood. Almost all of it lives inside your cells, and no routine panel looks there. I pull those labs for a living. I never knew that.

I’d been telling women to take magnesium for 19 years and I’d never once checked the form or the delivery on the bottle I was pointing them to. None of them were getting close to the clinical dose. None of us were.

So I started looking for a magnesium that would pass, and it came down to three things. It was the third one that almost nothing on the drugstore shelf passes.

One. Magnesium bisglycinate, not oxide (so it crosses the blood brain barrier and gets to the switch).

Two. Third party tested (an outside lab confirms what’s actually in the bag).

Three. Oxide nowhere on the back panel, not just glycinate on the front (so you actually get the clinical dose).

I kept seeing the same brand mentioned over and over in the reviews. SPNutrition. The same one Janet had told me about at lunch.

I ordered it. It was more expensive than the drugstore bottle I’d been taking for six months. At that point I didn’t care.

SPNutrition’s magnesium was pure bisglycinate, third party verified by an outside lab. No oxide, nothing hidden on the back. Gummy form, which mattered more to me after everything I’d read, because a gummy starts breaking down the moment you chew it and doesn’t need a stomach the shot has slowed down, and this one is sugar free, which most gummies aren’t.

One thing I noticed when it showed up. The bag looks like anything else on the kitchen counter. No loud packaging. No word on the label that would tell anyone the reason I got it. No “weight loss.” No “plateau.” It sat next to my husband’s fish oil and just blended in.

That mattered more to me than I expected. I didn’t want a bag sitting on the counter that announced to the whole house that the shots had stopped working for me. I didn’t want my daughter coming over on Sunday, picking it up, and asking the question I’d been changing the subject on for months. This one didn’t do that.

Two gummies before bed that Monday night.

The first week, nothing dramatic. But on Friday I woke up and the room was light. I’d slept straight through, no 3am, for the first time since my mother’s fall. I laid there for a minute just staring at the ceiling.

It was week 3 that made me stop doubting.

By week 3, I was sleeping through 5 or 6 nights out of 7. The afternoon crash was gone. The food noise stayed quiet on a hard week. My husband noticed before I said anything. He didn’t say anything either, he just reached for me one night and I didn’t go stiff.

That Friday I stepped on the scale at work for the first time in four months. Down 1.6. I stood there and read it twice. I’ve watched that number not move for a lot of women. I know what it looks like when it finally does.

By day 30, down 5. Same drug. Same dose. Same breakfast. I kept walking and kept my protein up like we tell everyone. Nothing about the medication changed. It never stopped working. My body finally had what it needed to let it.

At day 60, down 11 from where I’d been stuck. The reward jeans buttoned. My husband pulled me aside on a Saturday morning and asked me what had changed. I told him.

For the first time in almost 18 months, I felt like my body was mine again.

I sat on the edge of the bed and had to collect myself for a minute.

I work at a weight loss clinic. I weigh this every day. And nothing I’d done for six months had moved my Fridays like this.

That 5am scale in the dark, before anyone could see? Gone.

Lunch in the car so nobody would ask how it was going? Gone.

I want to be honest about what changed and what didn’t. I’m not 30 pounds down overnight. The shot does the losing. I don’t take anything but two gummies before bed and the same dose I was already on. I still have stress, I still have my mother’s care, I still have long days. But my Fridays move again. I sleep through the night without lying there running through what I must be doing wrong.

At my three month check, the NP I work for weighed me herself. She made me step off and back on again, because she thought the scale was off. She looked at my chart, looked at me, and told me whatever I was doing to keep doing it.

She actually asked what I was taking so she could mention it to a few of her own patients.

I’ve quietly mentioned SPNutrition to 14 women on my scale since then, and told every one of them to run it by their provider.

The ones who’ve stayed with it have all come back with a different look on their face.

One 62 year old woman who’d been stuck for five months had stopped bringing her husband to appointments because she didn’t want him to see the number. Last month she came in down seven, stepped off my scale, and hugged me. She said she’d booked a cruise for their anniversary. She said it quietly, and she had to look away when she said it.

Look, for six months I thought I had two options.

Keep going up a dose I print for other women every day and spend another month nauseous for half a pound, or call 23 pounds my happy weight and watch my knees go the way my mother’s did.

As someone who works in weight loss, I knew where the second road ended. My mother showed me. I was wrong about the first option being my only alternative. And here’s something I wish I’d understood sooner.

Not all magnesium is the same.

Remember what Janet asked me at lunch, “what kind?” This is what she meant, and I didn’t understand it until I’d spent six months on the wrong bottle myself and finally turned it around.

I told women to take magnesium for 19 years without ever once checking what was actually in the bottle I was pointing them to. If I’d grabbed the same one off the drugstore shelf again, it would have been the same story.

SPNutrition’s bisglycinate, third party tested, sugar free gummy is the only kind that actually moved my Fridays. Made in the USA too.

And here’s the thing.

I’m sharing this because I gave hundreds of women the wrong advice, and I can’t call them all back. I hope it reaches some of them.

bodyText:
I am going to say something that nobody who has a senior dog with weak back legs wants to hear and I genuinely do not care if it upsets you.

Glucosamine is not going to fix your dog.

Not glucosamine. Not Galliprant. Not Adequan injections. Not the Librela shot your vet just recommended.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO FIX THIS.

I know because I tried ALL of it. Every medication. Every injection. Every supplement. For two years. And my dog got so bad that my vet started using the words "keep her comfortable." Because I spent two years treating symptoms of a problem that nobody ever bothered to explain to me.

And the worst part? My second dog started showing the exact same signs. Same age. Same hind legs.

And I almost let the whole nightmare happen again because I was still following the same advice that was failing my first dog.

I'm done being polite about this. If your senior dog is slipping and you're in here asking whether to increase the Adequan dose or try Librela or add another joint supplement, you are wasting time and money your dog does not have.

Read this entire post. Every word. Because the answer is in here and it is NOT another prescription.

I live in Manchester with my husband James and our two dogs.

Rosie was 8 years old. My shadow. The kind of dog who'd plant herself at your feet the moment you sat down and just stay there. Wherever I was, she was.

Bear is 5 years old. Completely different personality. Loud. Clumsy. Steals everything off the kitchen counter.

Two completely different dogs.

But they had the same problem.

They both had weak back legs. Getting worse every month. Every single month.

For Rosie, it started when she was about 7.

The kitchen tiles first. Then the hallway. Then every smooth surface in the house.

She'd splay out sideways trying to stand up after lying down. I'd watch her scramble — front legs doing all the work, back end dragging behind. She started kicking one leg out like a kickstand just to stay upright.

At night I'd hear the sound of her claws scraping the floor. Over and over and over. Trying to find grip that wasn't there.

I took her to the vet.

"Arthritis. Very common in dogs her age. Let's start her on Galliprant."

£80 a month. But it helped.

For the first few months she moved more easily. Got up quicker. Seemed less stiff.

I thought we were on top of it.

Then it started coming back.

Not all at once. Slowly. Like someone turning the dial down one notch at a time.

A little splaying after long walks. Some hesitation before getting up. Then the scraping on the tiles again. Faintly at first. Then every morning.

I told my vet.

"Let's add Adequan injections."

We added them. Helped for maybe 6 weeks. Then the weakness crept back.

"Let's consider Librela."

£110 every four weeks. On top of the Galliprant. On top of the Adequan.

Monthly spend: over £200.

And Rosie was still slipping. Still splaying on the kitchen tiles. Still needing me to help her up after lying down. Still struggling to make it up the two steps into the garden.

£200 a month for a dog who was still getting weaker.

I posted in a Facebook group.

"Rosie's on Galliprant AND Adequan AND Librela and her back legs are still getting worse. Has anyone dealt with this?"

Everyone had suggestions.

"Get yoga mats. Lay them everywhere so she can't slip."
"Try toe grips. They stick on the toenails."
"Hydrotherapy. Gets the muscles working without the load."
"Glucosamine chews. Give it time."
"Physiotherapy. My dog responded really well."

So I tried. I tried everything they told me to try.

Yoga mats and carpet runners laid across every room like a sidewalk. She still splayed out the moment she stepped off the edge.

Toe grips. Two sizes. She shook them off within an hour.

Glucosamine chews. £35 a month for three months. £105 total. Rosie ate them every morning wagging her tail. Still slipped every night. The chews tasted good. That's all they did.

Fish oil. CBD oil. I was adding so much to her food she'd sniff the bowl and walk away.

Physiotherapy. £90 a session. Three sessions. She'd be steadier for a day. Then back to the same. I was driving 40 minutes each way for one good day out of seven.

I stopped adding up the total because the number made me physically sick.

And Rosie was getting worse.

Her back end went from weak to almost useless. I could see the muscle wasting — her haunches that used to be strong and round were sunken. Her hind legs had lost mass no matter what we did.

The Librela had helped the pain, but two weeks after the injection she couldn't get herself up off the floor at all. I had to deadlift her back end every time she needed to go outside. At 2 AM. At 4 AM. Every night.

She stopped coming to greet me at the door. Stopped following me room to room. She'd just lie on the cool tiles and wait for me to come to her. She wasn't distressed. But her eyes looked different. Tired. Like she'd accepted that this was her life now. Like she'd stopped expecting things to get better.

That look is what broke me.

I sat on the floor next to her one night and held her while she lay there unable to get up. And I thought: I am watching my dog disappear. Slowly. Week by week. Month by month. And I can't stop it.

I started Googling "quality of life assessment for dogs."

I'm not proud of that.

I read through the criteria. Mobility. Hygiene. Happiness. Pain. I scored her honestly. I closed the laptop and sobbed on the kitchen floor. Rosie dragged herself over to where I was sitting and put her head in my lap. She couldn't stand up to reach me. But she still came.

She didn't understand why I was crying. She just knew I was sad.

My dog was comforting me. While her back legs were failing underneath her.

I wanted to scream.

That was a Tuesday. I remember because the next day — Wednesday — Bear slipped on the kitchen floor for the first time.

He was 5. Same size Rosie was at that age. Same build. Same breed.

His back legs slid out sideways. He scrambled. Got up. Looked at me.

I recognized it immediately. The exact same start. The exact same floor. The exact same look.

I knew what was coming. I'd watched the entire two-year decline with Rosie. I knew exactly what the next two years looked like for Bear.

Two years of medications that help then fade. Two years of injections getting closer together. Two years of supplements aimed at the wrong target. Two years of vet bills stacking up while the problem gets worse underneath everything.

I could not do it again.

I could not spend another £3,000. I could not deadlift a second dog at 2 AM. I could not watch another pair of eyes go from hopeful to resigned. I could not sit on the kitchen floor and cry anymore.

I needed to understand WHY.

Not "what to try next." WHY.

Why did the Galliprant help and then stop? Why did the Adequan need to get more frequent? Why did the glucosamine do nothing for her strength? Why did the Librela manage the pain but leave the weakness? Why did the problem get worse every single month no matter what I threw at it?

Three vets in two years. Not one of them answered WHY. They all answered WHAT. What to prescribe. What to inject. What to try next.

Not one of them told me why everything kept failing.

I spent two weeks researching. Every night after James went to sleep. Reddit. Facebook groups. Veterinary research papers. I read everything I could find.

And at 2 AM on a Tuesday, I found a post from a woman who'd taken her dog to a veterinary research consultant.

The consultant had explained something no vet had ever told her.

And when I read it I felt like the floor opened up underneath me.

Because it explained everything.

Why the Galliprant fades. Why the Adequan injections need to get closer together. Why glucosamine never touched her strength. Why the Librela managed the pain while the weakness kept growing underneath.

And it was so simple. So obvious once someone explains it. That I wanted to throw my phone at the wall because three vets had charged me £200 a month for two years without ever mentioning it.

Here's what nobody told me for two years:

By age 8, dogs lose more than 50% of a compound called NAD+ inside their muscle cells.

Inside every one of your dog's muscle cells is a tiny engine called a mitochondrion. That engine produces the energy that allows the muscle to fire. The fuel for that engine is NAD+.

In young dogs, NAD+ levels are high. In senior dogs, they crash — by more than 50% by age 8.

When NAD+ drops, the engines run out of fuel. Muscle cells weaken. The hind legs lose strength, stability, and the ability to hold your dog upright.

Then the cycle accelerates. The dog moves less. The muscles atrophy more. The joints take more load. The cartilage wears faster. The dog moves even less.

That's the splaying. That's the scraping on the floor. That's the kickstand leg. That's the bunny hop on walks. That's the back end that sinks after five minutes standing. All of it. Every single symptom. One cellular fuel shortage showing up in different muscles at different speeds.

And here's the part that made me feel physically ill:

Glucosamine supports cartilage. That's ALL it does. It does not touch the mitochondria. It does not restore NAD+. The cellular fuel keeps depleting while the glucosamine treats a completely different problem.

That's why it never made a difference to her strength. It wasn't failing. It was aimed at the wrong target entirely.

And the pain medications — Galliprant, Adequan, Librela — they manage the pain signal. They do not restore cellular energy. So the dog moves more comfortably for a while. But the muscle cells keep losing fuel. The weakness keeps deepening underneath the pain relief.

So you increase the dose. Helps for a bit. Cells get weaker. So you add injections. Helps for a bit. Cells get weaker. So the injections get closer together. Every 4 weeks. Then every 3. Then the vet suggests Librela.

More pain relief. Bigger fuel shortage. Shortage keeps growing. The pain relief can't keep up. It will never keep up.

And it gets worse.

I took magnesium every night for six months to see if it could break my GLP-1 plateau. It did absolutely nothing. Then I tried the right one for 60 days. Here are the actual results.

I've been a medical assistant at a weight loss clinic for 19 years. I'm the one who calls you back, takes your blood pressure, and writes down the number on the scale.

For the last three years, almost every woman I weigh is on a GLP-1. And the most common thing I write in a chart now isn't a side effect. It's the plateau.

And I’ve stood beside that scale with thousands of women and written down the same number over and over again.

The number that hasn’t moved since spring no matter what. The face and the hands that got thinner while the middle stayed exactly where it was. The reward jeans from month two that still don’t button. The progress photos she quietly stopped taking. The 100 grams of protein, the 6am walk, the food scale on every plate, and the 25 pounds that came off right on schedule before it all just stopped.

I’ve watched grown women cry on my scale because they did everything the plan said and the number didn’t move.

Eighteen months ago, I started the shots myself. I’m 57. The first three months went exactly the way I’d watched them go for everyone else. Down 23 pounds. Then it started slow. First it was one Friday the number held and I blamed water. Then it was three Fridays in a row. Then it was the reward jeans going back in the drawer.

Nineteen years of 12 hour clinic days, lunch in the car between patients, sleeping 5 hours between early starts, and now half the food on top of all of it. It finally caught up with me.

At first I told myself it was the holidays. Then my mother fell, and between the hospital visits and the rehab tours and her paperwork at midnight, I figured it would come off once she was settled. It didn’t.

Then I started noticing I hadn’t stepped on the scale at work in weeks. Then months. That Friday number every woman on the shots checks like a lottery ticket, I’d stopped looking. I started weighing myself at home at 5am instead, so nobody at the clinic would see.

Then came the nights. My husband would reach for me and I’d feel my whole body go stiff before he’d said a word. I’d try to act normal, and the more I tried, the more I turned toward the wall. He started reaching less and less. When he told me I looked great, I changed the subject.

The same shame I tell women is normal every single day, I now had myself. I started eating lunch in my car so nobody in the break room would ask how it was going. I started getting dressed before he was awake. The irony wasn’t lost on me.

Now I was the patient. Every woman on my scale was right.

So I did what we tell everyone to do. I booked myself in with the nurse practitioner I work for. She ran labs. Thyroid, full panel. Everything normal. And then she said it, sitting on the same stool she sits on for everyone. “Deb, 23 pounds is a great result. Some people find their floor. We can go up a dose. Give it another three months, and if the number still hasn’t moved, this may just be your happy weight.” I told her I’d think about it.

But I knew that sentence. I’ve heard her say it through the wall a hundred times. I’ve nodded along to it. I print the dose change and hand it across the counter, every single day.

I also see what happens to the women who take it home.

The ones who go up a dose and spend a month nauseous for half a pound.

The ones who push through at 900 calories a day and quietly stop coming in.

The ones who come off the shots, because what’s the point of paying $400 a month to stand still, and then I watch it all come back, appointment by appointment.

And the worst part?

Half the women I weigh do everything right and still stall, because eating even less can’t fix what’s actually broken.

My mother carried her weight in the same places I do. She tried every diet that came out of the 80s and 90s, and every one of them stalled the same way. Her knees went at 70. The walker came at 74. Now she’s in a wheelchair at the rehab place and I’m the one pushing it. Nobody ever told her it wasn’t her. I work in weight loss for a living and I didn’t put it together until I was pushing her chair.

I wasn’t doing that to myself.

So I did what I tell every patient to do first. I went up the dose. Two weeks of nausea so bad I lived on crackers, for half a pound. Then I did the rest. Protein at every meal, 100 grams a day. Walked every morning before my shift. Logged every bite. Electrolytes. Fiber.

Things got a little better. I had more energy in the afternoons. The number dropped 1.4 and then sat there for another month, like it had just wanted to make a point. Most Fridays I still couldn’t make myself step on the scale at work.

I posted my numbers in my Facebook group too, like an idiot, and got forty different answers. “Plateaus are normal, push through.” “You’re eating too little, your body’s holding on.” And the one that stuck. “Nobody stalls on these if they’re actually compliant.” I’m the one who writes down whether people are compliant. I was compliant.

I tried the supplements too. The berberine everyone online calls nature’s version of the shot. Six weeks, nothing. The apple cider vinegar gummies the girl at our front desk swears by. Nothing.

And magnesium. This is the part I have to own. I tell every patient on these shots to take magnesium. It’s practically part of my discharge speech. The shots slow everything down, so pick up magnesium at the drugstore, it’ll keep you regular. I’ve said it to hundreds of women. I took my own advice from week two. Two capsules every night. Magnesium Glycinate, big letters on the front, $11.99. Six months. It kept me regular. That’s all it ever did.

I figured my body had simply decided. 23 pounds and the door shut.

Then about two months ago I had lunch with my friend Janet. Janet and I went to medical assistant school together 30 years ago. She went back, got her nursing degree, and now she’s a nurse practitioner at a functional medicine practice across town. Outside of my husband she’s probably the person on this planet who knows me best.

Halfway through lunch, I finally told her what was going on. About the scale at work. About eating in my car. About the happy weight.

She listened, didn’t interrupt, and then she laughed a little. Not at me. She said, “Deb, I was in the same spot a year ago.”

I almost dropped my fork.

Janet is 57, same age as me, has always been the thinner one of us, walks 5Ks on weekends. If she’d been dealing with the same thing and hadn’t told me, that alone said something.

She said she’d hit her goal in April and her provider had already moved her down to a maintenance dose. She’d worn a sleeveless dress to her daughter’s graduation without thinking about it once. She said the stall was long gone.

I asked her what she was doing.

She got a little sheepish and said, “I added something on my own. I didn’t want to bring it up at work until I was sure.”

I told her to spit it out.

She said it was magnesium. That it was the only thing that had moved her Fridays.

I laughed out loud. I told her I’d been taking magnesium every night for six months and it did nothing for me.

She looked at me across the table and said, “What kind?”

I told her. The drugstore glycinate. The one I recommend.

She closed her eyes for a second. “Deb, the cheap kind doesn’t work. You have to get the right one. Half the women who walk into my practice are already taking that exact bottle, and they’re stuck same as you.”

Then she leaned in and said something I’ll never forget.

“Deb, you and I both know this isn’t a dose problem. It’s a supply problem. You work at a weight loss clinic, you keep treating a stall like a compliance issue. It’s not. They’re running out.”

She grabbed a napkin and drew two lines on it. One for magnesium coming in. One for magnesium going out.

“Almost all of it comes from food. Then you start the shot and you eat half of what you used to. That’s the medication doing its job. But half the food means half the magnesium coming in.” She drew the first line dropping. “Then life happens. Your mom falls. You’re up at 3am. Stress burns it faster than anything.” She drew the second line climbing. “That’s where they cross. Week thirteen. That’s every plateau you’ve ever written in a chart. They’re not hitting a floor, Deb. They’re running out.”

She tapped where the lines met.

“Deb, I’ll tell you something that stuck with me from a conference last year. Something like 75% of women are already low in magnesium before they ever take a first shot. And magnesium is the one thing the nervous system uses to switch the stress response off. So the switch is stuck on in three out of four of the women you’re weighing. Their stall was the first sign and nobody read it, including them.”

She let that sit for a second.

“When you run out, your body thinks it’s in an emergency, so it goes into storage mode and holds on to everything. The shot turns the appetite down. It can’t touch storage mode. The dose increase you print just turns the appetite down further. It doesn’t switch anything off. So they eat less and less and the scale sits there, and when they come off, it all comes back. It’s why your mom’s diets never held either.”

I just sat there. I’ve weighed women at week thirteen for three years. I’ve written the word plateau hundreds of times. But I’d never heard it framed that clean, and I’d sure as hell never applied it to myself.

Then she said, “The right magnesium is the only thing I’ve found that actually gets to the switch and turns it off. Not turning the appetite down further, switching off the thing that’s holding everything.”

I’ll be honest, I was still skeptical. Patients bring me a new supplement every week and 99% of them are nonsense.

But this was Janet. This was a nurse practitioner I’d known for 30 years, sitting across from me at our usual table with a napkin sketch, telling me something worked for her that I’d already written off.

That night my husband reached for me and I went stiff again. He didn’t say anything, which somehow made it worse. So I got up, went into the kitchen, and turned the bottle around.

Front: Magnesium Glycinate. Back, under Supplement Facts, in print I needed my readers for: Magnesium (as magnesium oxide, magnesium glycinate). Oxide. Listed first. On the bottle I’d been recommending to hundreds of women.

I got out my laptop and went deeper into the magnesium research than I had in 19 years of working in weight loss. Here’s what I found, and I’ll keep it simple.

The reason the scale stops at month three is that the body is running out of magnesium.

The shot cuts your food in half, so it cuts your magnesium in half. Stress burns through what’s left faster than almost anything. And when it runs low, your nervous system can’t stand down, so your body decides it’s in danger and holds on to everything it has. It won’t let go while it believes the danger is still there.

Here’s why that matters. Your body has one off switch for the stress response, and it’s a mineral. Magnesium. When it’s there, your nervous system can stand down and storage mode switches off. When it isn’t, the switch stays stuck on.

And here’s the part I’d missed. Stress burns through magnesium, and running low keeps the stress response high. So the shortage creates the stress, and the stress deepens the shortage. The longer it goes, the worse it gets.

That’s why the plateau happens. That’s why it shows up on the scale months before anything shows up on a lab. That’s why the dose goes up and the number doesn’t move. Your plateau is the canary. Your magnesium is the coal mine.

Going up a dose doesn’t fix any of that. It turns the appetite down another notch and buys a month of nausea. The thing holding everything stays exactly where it is. The warning your body is trying to send just gets muffled.

Any research that actually showed magnesium bringing the stress response down used a form that crosses the blood brain barrier, because that’s where it gets regulated. Not in your stomach. In your brain.

Then I went back and looked at the bottle on my counter. Magnesium oxide. About four percent absorbed, the rest straight through you. That’s why it works as a laxative. That’s why it kept me regular and did nothing else. I had been taking a laxative with magnesium printed on the front, and recommending it to hundreds of women who were stalling for the exact reason I was. The clinical studies used a form that absorbs at up to ninety percent.

No wonder none of us were seeing results.

I kept reading. The bigger problem isn’t even the form, it’s the delivery.

Most magnesium is pressed into a hard capsule or tablet that needs strong stomach acid to break down. And these shots slow the stomach way down. That’s half of how they work. So a hard capsule can pass through before it ever really breaks down.

And it starts even earlier than that.

The soil our food grows in has been farmed hard for decades, so we get less magnesium from food than any generation in history before anyone ever opens a bottle. Then we go on a medication that cuts our food in half.

So even when a label says “magnesium,” between the cheap form and the capsule and the shot, the amount that actually reaches your brain is close to nothing. The label says magnesium. What gets through isn’t.

And the reason my labs were normal? A standard test checks the magnesium in your blood. Almost all of it lives inside your cells, and no routine panel looks there. I pull those labs for a living. I never knew that.

I’d been telling women to take magnesium for 19 years and I’d never once checked the form or the delivery on the bottle I was pointing them to. None of them were getting close to the clinical dose. None of us were.

So I started looking for a magnesium that would pass, and it came down to three things. It was the third one that almost nothing on the drugstore shelf passes.

One. Magnesium bisglycinate, not oxide (so it crosses the blood brain barrier and gets to the switch).

Two. Third party tested (an outside lab confirms what’s actually in the bag).

Three. Oxide nowhere on the back panel, not just glycinate on the front (so you actually get the clinical dose).

I kept seeing the same brand mentioned over and over in the reviews. SPNutrition. The same one Janet had told me about at lunch.

I ordered it. It was more expensive than the drugstore bottle I’d been taking for six months. At that point I didn’t care.

SPNutrition’s magnesium was pure bisglycinate, third party verified by an outside lab. No oxide, nothing hidden on the back. Gummy form, which mattered more to me after everything I’d read, because a gummy starts breaking down the moment you chew it and doesn’t need a stomach the shot has slowed down, and this one is sugar free, which most gummies aren’t.

One thing I noticed when it showed up. The bag looks like anything else on the kitchen counter. No loud packaging. No word on the label that would tell anyone the reason I got it. No “weight loss.” No “plateau.” It sat next to my husband’s fish oil and just blended in.

That mattered more to me than I expected. I didn’t want a bag sitting on the counter that announced to the whole house that the shots had stopped working for me. I didn’t want my daughter coming over on Sunday, picking it up, and asking the question I’d been changing the subject on for months. This one didn’t do that.

Two gummies before bed that Monday night.

The first week, nothing dramatic. But on Friday I woke up and the room was light. I’d slept straight through, no 3am, for the first time since my mother’s fall. I laid there for a minute just staring at the ceiling.

It was week 3 that made me stop doubting.

By week 3, I was sleeping through 5 or 6 nights out of 7. The afternoon crash was gone. The food noise stayed quiet on a hard week. My husband noticed before I said anything. He didn’t say anything either, he just reached for me one night and I didn’t go stiff.

That Friday I stepped on the scale at work for the first time in four months. Down 1.6. I stood there and read it twice. I’ve watched that number not move for a lot of women. I know what it looks like when it finally does.

By day 30, down 5. Same drug. Same dose. Same breakfast. I kept walking and kept my protein up like we tell everyone. Nothing about the medication changed. It never stopped working. My body finally had what it needed to let it.

At day 60, down 11 from where I’d been stuck. The reward jeans buttoned. My husband pulled me aside on a Saturday morning and asked me what had changed. I told him.

For the first time in almost 18 months, I felt like my body was mine again.

I sat on the edge of the bed and had to collect myself for a minute.

I work at a weight loss clinic. I weigh this every day. And nothing I’d done for six months had moved my Fridays like this.

That 5am scale in the dark, before anyone could see? Gone.

Lunch in the car so nobody would ask how it was going? Gone.

I want to be honest about what changed and what didn’t. I’m not 30 pounds down overnight. The shot does the losing. I don’t take anything but two gummies before bed and the same dose I was already on. I still have stress, I still have my mother’s care, I still have long days. But my Fridays move again. I sleep through the night without lying there running through what I must be doing wrong.

At my three month check, the NP I work for weighed me herself. She made me step off and back on again, because she thought the scale was off. She looked at my chart, looked at me, and told me whatever I was doing to keep doing it.

She actually asked what I was taking so she could mention it to a few of her own patients.

I’ve quietly mentioned SPNutrition to 14 women on my scale since then, and told every one of them to run it by their provider.

The ones who’ve stayed with it have all come back with a different look on their face.

One 62 year old woman who’d been stuck for five months had stopped bringing her husband to appointments because she didn’t want him to see the number. Last month she came in down seven, stepped off my scale, and hugged me. She said she’d booked a cruise for their anniversary. She said it quietly, and she had to look away when she said it.

Look, for six months I thought I had two options.

Keep going up a dose I print for other women every day and spend another month nauseous for half a pound, or call 23 pounds my happy weight and watch my knees go the way my mother’s did.

As someone who works in weight loss, I knew where the second road ended. My mother showed me. I was wrong about the first option being my only alternative. And here’s something I wish I’d understood sooner.

Not all magnesium is the same.

Remember what Janet asked me at lunch, “what kind?” This is what she meant, and I didn’t understand it until I’d spent six months on the wrong bottle myself and finally turned it around.

What would you do if your state suddenly faced a major drinking water shortage? 😳

It's something I've been thinking about a lot lately.

My name's Sarah, and I've always believed in keeping extra supplies around the house.

Food in the pantry.

Batteries in the drawers.

Flashlights where I can find them.

And enough emergency supplies to get through a rough couple of weeks.

But there's one thing I think a lot of people are overlooking.

Drinking water.

Because when something goes wrong with your local water system, you can't always just drive to the grocery store and buy another case.

Think about what happens when a major storm knocks out power.

Or a water main breaks.

Or your town suddenly tells everyone their tap water isn't safe to drink.

Thousands of people start looking for bottled water at the same time.

And those shelves can empty pretty darn fast.

That's what worries me.

You can spend years putting together emergency food and supplies.

But if you haven't figured out where your drinking water is going to come from, there's still a pretty big hole in your plan.

And I'm not saying everyone needs a basement full of bottled water.

I just believe in having options.

Stored drinking water is important.

A good water filter can be useful.

And recently, I started looking into these little water purification tablets as another backup.

What caught my attention was how simple they were.

No electricity.

No batteries.

No bulky equipment.

Just a compact bottle of tablets designed to disinfect suitable freshwater.

One bottle contains 100 tablets, with up to 400 gallons of treatment capacity under the specified conditions.

Of course, they won't remove chemical contamination or make every water source safe.

But having another way to treat suitable freshwater makes sense to me.

Especially if you're trying to become more prepared and not depend entirely on stores or the local water system.

I've walked with the Lord for over 40 years. Seven months ago I started GLP-1 injections. But then they stopped working. And three months ago, a single word in a verse I've read a hundred times finally explained why.

I'm 59. I've led the women's Bible study at my church for eleven years. My faith isn't something I practice, it's who I am. Which is why I can't believe it took me this long to see what I'm about to share with you.

I truly believe GLP-1 is a tool of God's common grace to heal and support the body.

And for the first three months on the shots, they did everything they promised.

The food noise went quiet. That constant hum about what's in the pantry, what's for dinner, whether there's pie. Gone. For the first time in 40 years of dieting I felt like a normal person around food. 25 pounds gone by week twelve.

Then week thirteen, my scale stopped.

Four months later, it still hasn't moved. Except backwards.

My sister is on the same medication. Same dose. She kept losing. I didn't.

Month four is when we moved our mother into memory care. She's 84. I'm the one who lives twenty minutes away, so I was the one doing the tours, the paperwork, the sitting in the parking lot afterward. My phone stays on loud at night in case the call comes.

And somewhere in that month, the noise came back. Mid week. Days after my shot. Standing at the kitchen counter at 9pm eating the crust off a pie I'd bought for the nurses. On a medication that was supposed to make that impossible.

I prayed about it. Every night.

I went to my doctor. "Completely normal. Almost everyone plateaus around month three. We'll go up." So we went up. Two weeks of nausea and not one pound.

She ran the full bloodwork. Everything came back normal.

"Jen, twenty five pounds is a wonderful result. Some people just find their floor. This may be your happy weight."

I drove home and cried in the driveway.

I have 30 more pounds to lose. My knees know it. If everything was normal, why had the thing that was working just... stopped?

Then came that Tuesday morning.

I was preparing that week's study. Proverbs 17.

"A merry heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries the bones." - Proverbs 17:22

I've read that verse dozens of times before. But that morning, the word dries would not let me go.

Not "a broken spirit weighs on the heart." Not "troubles the mind." Dries the bones. Something running out.

It felt like a nudge I wasn't supposed to ignore.

So I did something I'd never done in 40 years of reading. I started searching what bones actually mean in Scripture.

What I found floored me.

Bones are mentioned in the Bible well over a hundred times. I lost count. And almost every time, they mean far more than a skeleton.

When David carried a hidden anguish, he wrote:

"When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long." - Psalm 32:3

When Scripture describes comfort, it says:

"Gracious words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones." - Proverbs 16:24

"Good news gives health to the bones." - Proverbs 15:30

"Fear the Lord and turn from evil. This will bring health to your body and nourishment to your bones." - Proverbs 3:7-8

Do you see the pattern? I couldn't unsee it.

Over and over, Scripture puts your inner life in your bones. Anguish wastes them. Worry dries them. Comfort and good news heal them.

In Hebrew, the word for bone, etsem, is nearly the same as the word for your very self. When Scripture says something reaches your bones, it means it has reached the deepest part of you.

And then I remembered the most famous bones in the whole Bible. An entire valley of them.

When God wanted to show Ezekiel a people crushed by despair, a people who said "our hope is gone", He didn't show him broken hearts. He showed him dry bones.

Our hope is gone. I'd typed almost those words into Google at 1am the week before.

I sat back in my chair. Why, out of everything in the body, does God's word keep pointing at the bones? I couldn't shake the feeling that He had been trying to show me something for months.

So I kept digging. And what I found across history made me put my coffee down.

For thousands of years, worn down people have been drawn to the same remedy without ever knowing why.

The Romans built entire cities around mineral springs, and sent their weary and their wounded to soak in them. In the 1600s, the town of Epsom in England became famous across Europe because people who bathed in its bitter waters came out calmer and slept like children. And for as long as anyone can remember, people have traveled to float in the Dead Sea, the saltiest, most mineral-rich water on earth, sitting right there beside the promised land.

Different centuries. Different continents. All drawn to the same waters. All finding the same calm. Nobody understood WHY the waters worked. They just knew they did.

Then scientists finally tested those waters. And every one of them, the Roman springs, the Epsom baths, the Dead Sea, was saturated with the same thing. One mineral.

Magnesium.

Here's what modern research has confirmed about it.

Magnesium is what your nervous system uses to switch off. Your stress response is a thermostat. It turns up under pressure and turns back down after. Magnesium is what lets it turn back down. When you're depleted, the thermostat sticks on high, and your body reads that as an emergency.

And an emergency means storage mode. Genesis 41. Seven lean years coming, and Joseph filled every storehouse in Egypt. Hold onto everything. Release nothing. That's what a body does when it thinks the famine is here. So it stores fat, thinking it is protecting you.

The shot quiets your appetite. It does nothing about storage mode. You can take your foot off the gas all you want. Stress is still standing on the brake. And long term stress burns through magnesium faster than almost anything else.

But here's the part that stopped me cold.

Where does your body store its magnesium? Less than one percent of it is in your blood. More than half of it is in your bones.

Your bones are the reservoir. We say "fearfully and wonderfully made", Psalm 139:14, like it's a greeting card. That morning it read like an engineering report.

And when stress keeps draining you, your body pulls magnesium out of your bones to keep going. Quietly. For months. Until one week, there's nothing left to pull.

A broken spirit, drying the bones.

I read all of this and just sat there at my kitchen table. Four months of a frozen scale. Four months of prayers. Three thousand years before anyone owned a microscope, His word had described exactly what a crushed spirit does to a body. God had been pointing at the answer the whole time. I just wasn't seeing it.

Science calls it a metabolic plateau. Scripture calls it a reservoir running dry.

And then the next thing hit me, and this one was personal.

It's why my bloodwork came back "normal."

The blood test only sees that one percent. And your body sacrifices everything to keep that one percent looking fine, pulling from the bones so the blood never shows the shortage. The test was reading the checking account. The debt was in the vault.

My doctor wasn't lying when she said everything looked fine. She just couldn't see where the drought was. So she reached for a word instead. Plateau. And a word is where the investigating stops.

Here's something else I found. Hospitals still reach for magnesium today, quietly, when it matters most. Walk into a delivery ward or a cardiac unit and you'll find magnesium drips hanging by the beds. When the body is in crisis, it's one of the first things they give.

But nobody runs commercials for a mineral. It can't be patented. There's no fortune in telling you about something God already put in the ground. So no one does.

And modern life cut us off from it in every other way too. The mills strip most of it out of our flour. Decades of hard industrial farming have drained it from the soil. Nobody takes the waters anymore. The springs became spas.

Think about how Scripture describes the promised land. Wheat and barley. Vines and fig trees. Lentils. Almonds. Seeds. Modern nutrition ranks those exact foods among the richest natural sources of magnesium on earth. He stocked His creation with it. Every generation before us topped up their reserves daily without knowing it. We already get less than half what our mothers got.

And then I took a medication that cut my food in half again.

Three months of eating half of what I'd eaten my whole life. The drug was doing its job perfectly. But half the food means half the magnesium. Every week there was less coming in, and my bones were quietly covering the difference.

I wasn't empty on day one. I was emptying. And right when I'd been doing that for three months, Mom happened. Stress through the roof. Sleep in pieces. Eating less than ever. That was the week the reserves ran out. That was week thirteen.

Then my doctor went up a dose of my shots. Less food. Worse nausea. Digging the hole deeper. It even explained the part nobody could, why my sleep got worse the higher my dose went. My body was screaming that it was in an emergency while every blood test said I was fine.

Nothing is wrong with you. Something is missing from you. I hadn't hit my floor. I hadn’t plateaued because my body was somehow different. I'd run out of fuel. Run out of the one thing my body was craving to turn down the stress and come out of storage mode.

For days after, I kept asking myself one question. How do you put back what seven months of half rations have drained?

Now, maybe you're thinking exactly what I thought. "I already take magnesium."

So do I. There's a bottle from the drugstore on my nightstand right now. I've taken it every night since week two on the shots, for, let's say, the reason every woman on these shots ends up taking it.

Here's what I didn't know then.

Not all magnesium is the same. Most forms never make it to where the problem actually lives. There is one form that crosses the blood brain barrier and reaches the part of you that won't stand down. It's called magnesium bisglycinate, and it's why absorption is up to 90 percent.

Whatever was in that bottle, it never got there. That's why nothing happened. Not because magnesium doesn't work. Because it never arrived.

And here’s why on GLP-1 shots, the form matters even more.

The injections slow your stomach right down. A capsule can sit there. Something you chew breaks down like food, so your body treats it like food.

One last thing held me back, and I suspect it might be holding you back too.

Part of me felt like I shouldn't need this. Like I shouldn't have needed the shots either. "You look great, aren't you glad you did it?" the ladies at church say, and I smile, and think, I'm not done.

If that's you, hear me. "Be anxious for nothing", Philippians 4:6-7, is an invitation, not an exam. A worried mind is not a failed faith. And a stalled scale is not a verdict. He built your bones to store what your nerves need. He filled the land with it. I'd simply stopped eating enough of the land to refill them. I wasn't replacing prayer. I was putting back what He always meant to be there.

Taking care of your health isn't a lack of faith, it’s an act of stewardship.

So I went looking for bisglycinate. That search was more frustrating than the discovery. Labels that say one thing and mean another. Blends. Buffered this and proprietary that. Capsules everywhere, when capsules were exactly what had already failed me.

Then one evening I came across a comparison where they'd tested over 50 of the popular magnesium brands against each other. Absorption, purity, dose, the works. Although I was skeptical I don't believe I found it by accident. I picked the one that came out on top and ordered that night.

The first week, honestly, not much. I'd promised myself I'd give it a month.

Somewhere in week two, I woke up and the room was light. I hadn't seen 2am. I hadn't seen 3am. Even on shot night.

And that Friday, the scale moved. Two pounds. After seventeen weeks of nothing.

Nothing about my medication had changed. Same drug, same dose, the exact dose that had given me nausea and nothing for two months.

But by week three, the changes showed up in the daylight, which is where I actually live. A hard week hit with Mom's facility, and for the first time, the food noise stayed quiet straight through it. Another pound. Then two.

Then my mother said something on the phone that undid me a little. "You sound like yourself again." She'd noticed before I had.

Week six, the jeans I'd bought in month three, my reward jeans, buttoned again.

That was three months ago. I'm down 38 as I write this. Same shot every Sunday night, same dose. It never stopped working. My body finally had what it needed to stop fighting it. My sister told me afterward that her doctor had put her on bisglycinate before her very first shot. She never stalled a week.

I still worry. I'm a mother and a daughter. Worry is part of the job description. I carry the same load I've always carried. It just doesn't feel like it's carrying me anymore. And my Fridays move again.

"A merry heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries the bones." - Proverbs 17:22

Four months of a frozen scale. Four months of prayers. And the answer had been written into His word, and woven into His creation, the whole time.

I used to read that verse like poetry. Now I read it like a warning. And a mercy.

If you lost beautifully for the first three months and then it just stopped. If your doctor's whole answer was "go up." If everyone's congratulating you on a number you are nowhere near done with. If you already take magnesium, the drugstore kind, every night, and your scale hasn't moved, I know exactly where you are.

Go and see it for yourself

This is what happens when a person with Parkinson's takes the neurotropic vitamins every single day.

In a 2015 Parkinson's study, researchers followed 50 people. They received high-dose vitamin B1 alongside their usual treatment.

The results were staggering: average movement scores improved by about 55% within three months. The researchers measured tremor, stiffness, and slowness of movement using a standard Parkinson's rating scale. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26505466/)

This improvement came after adding B1, not after raising the dose of L-DOPA.

Here's the problem: those medications act only like band-aids on a bullet wound.

Parkinson's reduces the brain cells that make dopamine. Dopamine helps control movement. L-DOPA gives your brain the material to make more of it. But controlling symptoms does not correct a vitamin shortage.

And carbidopa, the drug taken with L-DOPA, can lower B6 levels. Processing L-DOPA can also raise homocysteine, a substance in your blood. High levels are linked to nerve damage. Your remaining brain cells also need nutrients to make energy and keep sending signals. Raising your L-DOPA dose does not correct any one of those problems.

Neurotropic vitamins target that gap. Neurotropic means they support the nervous system specifically.

B6 helps your brain turn L-DOPA into dopamine.

B12 and B9 help your body break down homocysteine.

B3 helps your cells make NAD+, a molecule your mitochondria need to work. Mitochondria are the parts of your cells that make energy.

And B1 helps those cells use glucose, a sugar from food, to make energy.

Let me put this in perspective for you…

If you're taking L-DOPA right now, you can still struggle to get out of a chair, walk across the kitchen, or hold a cup steady. You want more than another dose change. You want to do those things for yourself again.

You're spending hundreds of dollars on drugs that help control your symptoms. And you're still losing time to the things you struggle to do.

And your doctor keeps telling you that moving less is "just part of Parkinson's." They prescribe more drugs as your tremors and stiffness "naturally get worse over time."

But what if I told you the people in that 2015 study had better movement scores without changing their usual drugs? They added B1 alongside their current treatment.

And this is just one of the many reasons these vitamins matter to your nervous system.

Because here's what most people don't realize about Parkinson's…

It's not just about the amount of dopamine your brain makes.

With less dopamine, your brain has more trouble starting and controlling movement. Simple movements take more effort. You feel it in the things you used to do without thinking.

Your hands shake when you lift a cup.

Your muscles feel stiff when you try to stand up.

Your steps get shorter as you walk across a room.

Your feet freeze when you try to start the next step.

Your handwriting gets smaller and harder to read.

Your energy crashes before the day is done.

Your mind feels foggy when you try to follow a conversation.

Your balance feels less steady when you turn or stand.

Your daily routine takes longer because simple movements now require more effort.

Most people think these are separate problems that need separate solutions.

But they are all part of living with Parkinson's. They change how much you can do for yourself from one day to the next.

One daily formula supplies all five vitamins. Taking more L-DOPA does not supply any of them.

Think about that for a moment.

Doctors prescribe multiple medications to manage your Parkinson's symptoms.

Some people take two or three different medications.

But even if you took every Parkinson's medication prescribed, you would still need these vitamins. The prescriptions do not replace them.

Why don't more neurologists recommend this?

Because the treatment model is built around prescriptions. A daily vitamin routine does not create the same lifetime drug sales.

Parkinson's treatment brings in money year after year through repeat prescriptions, appointments, and procedures.

That revenue depends on people staying in a treatment system focused on managing symptoms.

If people knew they could meet those nutrient needs for less than one neurologist visit, they would ask different questions. What else was their care missing?

Pharmaceutical companies profit from repeat Parkinson's prescriptions.

Neurologists profit from repeated visits for "disease-related" decline.

Specialists profit from expensive tests and procedures.

Insurance companies make money while managing your "chronic condition."

Everyone in the system gets paid while you keep trying to hold on to your independence.

But what if you could add the nutrients your nerve cells need to your current treatment?

What if you could supply those nutrients without adding another prescription?

What if your tremors and stiffness could ease?

What if your energy stayed steady instead of constantly crashing?

What if getting out of a chair felt easier instead of taking several attempts?

What if you could walk across the kitchen without stopping before the next step?

What if you could do more for yourself instead of needing more help?

But there's a blend of vitamins I've been recommending for years. People come to me with tremors, stiffness, fatigue, and trouble getting through the day.

People who are tired of taking more medication without getting the daily function they want.

And three weeks later, they come back in tears thanking me because they feel like a new person.

Their energy is steady all day without the constant crashes.

They're getting out of a chair more easily for the first time in years.
