I tried magnesium for 60 days to see if it could get my weight loss shots working again after four months of nothing. Here are the actual results.

I'm a physician, and for 19 years I've run a weight loss clinic. For the last three of those, most of what I do is put women on the weight loss shots. And the stall is the most common thing that walks through my door. I've sat across the desk from thousands of women and explained the same things over and over again.

The Friday weigh-in that stopped moving in month three. The food scale and the notebook, every bite, same as week one. The reward jeans bought in month two that don't button anymore. The group that says push through. The daughter who says you look great. The 25 pounds that came off like a miracle and the 30 that won't budge no matter what. I've watched women cry in my exam room because they did everything I told them to do and the number didn't move.

Around 7 months ago, it happened to me.

I'm 54. For three months, the shots did for me exactly what I'd promised my patients they'd do. The food noise went quiet. 24 pounds by week twelve. Then it started slow. First it was one flat Friday I blamed on a hard week. Then it was the next Friday. Then it was the number going the wrong way. All those years of 12 hour clinic days, hospital cafeteria lunches, five hours of sleep between early starts, and then my mother's move into memory care on top of it. It finally caught up with me.

At first I told myself it was a normal plateau. I figured it would break on its own after a week or two. It didn't.

Then I started noticing I'd skipped my Friday weigh-in. Then two. Then a month. That private little check every woman does when she steps on the scale before her shower, gone. I'd stopped looking.

Then came the congratulations. My husband would put his arm around me in the kitchen and tell me I looked great, and I'd feel my whole body tense up before he'd finished the sentence. Patients asked how much I'd lost and I said 24, cheerfully, for four months straight, while the real number crept the other way. The same shame I tell my patients is normal, I now had myself.

I started changing in the bathroom with the door shut. I started keeping the scale in the closet so I wouldn't have to walk past it.

The irony wasn't lost on me. Now I was the patient. Every single one of them was right.

My own physician looked at my bloodwork, said everything was normal, and told me most women find their floor somewhere. 24 pounds is a wonderful result. This may be your body's happy weight. Keep logging. Come back in three months, and if the number hasn't moved, we'll talk about adjusting.

I told her I'd think about it. But I knew exactly how that conversation goes. I have it with women every day. I write the same plan she gave me, every single day. Keep logging. Push through.

I also see what happens to the women who follow it. The ones who push through for four months and gain three back. The ones who cut their food so low they can't get through an afternoon, and the number still doesn't move. The ones who quit, because nothing they did ever showed up on a Friday.

And the worst part?

Half my patients do everything right and still stall, because the shot can only fix what it was built to fix.

My own mother carried the same 40 pounds. Called it her build. Blood pressure pills at 58, the knee at 63, the stroke at 71. Nobody ever told her the weight was telling her something. I treat this for a living and I didn't put it together until years after we buried her.

I wasn't doing that to myself.

So I did what I told every patient to do first. I took my protein up, my steps up to 10,000 a day, tightened the logging to the gram, and cut out the glass of wine on Fridays. Things got a little better. I slept a bit more. My waistband felt looser for a week. The number moved maybe half a pound, then went right back. The stall stayed exactly where it was, and most Fridays I still couldn't look.

I tried the supplements too. I bought ashwagandha from Amazon, the one with all the 5 star reviews. Took it every day for 6 weeks. Nothing moved. I tried one of the cortisol supplements my nurse half jokingly sent me from Instagram. Same result. I tried an electrolyte powder because a patient swore by it. Nothing.

I even tried magnesium. The literature on magnesium and stress is solid, I've read the studies for years. I'd already been taking the drugstore bottle every night since week two on the shots, for, let's say, the reason every woman on the shots ends up taking it. So I bought the capsules from Amazon on top of it, took them for 6 weeks, and got nothing except more trips to the bathroom. Then I tried the powder from the health store. Same result.

I figured my own metabolism must just be too far gone for any of this to make a difference.

Then about 2 months ago, I met up with my friend Diane for dinner on a Thursday night. Diane and I went to med school together back in the early 90s. She's an endocrinologist now, 30 years into her own practice, and outside of my husband she's probably the person on this planet who knows me best.

One glass of wine in, I finally told her what was going on. About the scale in the closet. About saying 24. About the three month follow up I was dreading.

She listened, didn't interrupt, and then she laughed a little. Not at me.

She said, "Deb, I was in the same spot a year ago."

I almost dropped my glass. Diane is 54, same age as me, and she was sitting across from me in a dress I'd have needed to be unzipped to get into. If she'd been dealing with the same thing and hadn't told me, that alone said something.

She said she'd started the shots the spring before I did. Lost beautifully for three months, stalled cold at week thirteen, same as me. Said the stall had been gone for nine months now. Said her Friday number hadn't sat still once since.

I asked her what she was doing.

She got a little sheepish and said, "I added something on my own. I didn't want to bring it up until I was sure."

I told her to spit it out.

She said it was magnesium. That it was the only thing that had broken the stall.

I laughed out loud. I told her I'd been taking magnesium every night for six months and it had done nothing for me.

She looked at me across the table and said, "Deb, the cheap kind doesn't work. You have to get the right one. I tried to tell my sister in law about it and she grabbed the first bottle off Amazon and got nothing, same as you."

Then she leaned in and said something I'll never forget.

"Deb, you and I both know this isn't a shot problem. It's a stress problem. You run a weight loss clinic, you keep treating a stall like the shot quit on you. It didn't. It's cortisol."

She grabbed a napkin and drew two things on it. A stomach with a line through it. And a little vault with a lock on it.

"That's what the shot does. It quiets this. Turns the appetite down, and it does it beautifully. This one," she tapped the vault, "it never touches. When cortisol's been high for months, your body thinks it's in danger, so it locks everything it's got in here and guards it. You can eat half of what you used to. The lock doesn't care. That's why every woman who walks into my office lost 25 pounds and then watched the number sit there."

She tapped the vault again. "Deb, I'll tell you something that stuck with me from a conference last year. Something like 75% of women over 50 are low in magnesium and don't know it. And magnesium is the one thing the nervous system uses to switch cortisol off. So the lock is stuck shut in three out of four of the women you're putting on the shots. And here's the part nobody tells them. The shot cuts what they eat in half. Half the food is half the magnesium. They weren't empty on day one. They ran out somewhere around month three. That's your patients. The flat Friday was the first sign, and nobody read it, including them."

She let that sit for a second.

"The shot you prescribe takes their foot off the gas. It doesn't unlock anything. Cortisol stays high. That's why they stall, that's why they gain it back, and it's why your mom's weight never moved no matter what she ate."

I just sat there. I'm a weight loss doctor. I've known cortisol holds onto fat for decades. But I'd never heard it framed that clean, and I'd sure as hell never applied it to myself.

Then she said, "The right magnesium is the only thing I've found that actually gets to the switch and turns it off. Not eating less. Switching off the thing that's guarding it."

I'll be honest, I was still skeptical. I hear about supplements every week and 99% of them are nonsense. But this was Diane. This was an endocrinologist I'd known for 30 years, sitting across from me at our usual table with a napkin sketch, telling me something worked for her that I'd already written off.

That night my husband put his arm around me in the kitchen and said I looked great, and I tensed up again. He didn't say anything else, which somehow made it worse. So I got out my laptop and went deeper into the magnesium research than I had in my entire career.

Here's what I found, and I'll keep it simple.

The reason the number stops is cortisol. When it stays high for too long, it tells your body to hold onto everything it has. It locks it down on purpose, because your body thinks it's in danger, and it won't let go while it believes the danger is still there. The shot quiets your appetite. It has no say over the lock.

Here's why that matters. Your body has one off switch for cortisol, and it's a mineral. Magnesium. When it's there, your nervous system can stand down and cortisol comes down with it. When it isn't, the switch stays stuck on.

And here's the part I'd missed. Cortisol burns through magnesium faster than almost anything. So the stress creates the shortage, and the shortage keeps the cortisol high. Then you start the shots and eat half of what you used to, and the one thing refilling the tank gets cut in half too. The longer you're on them, the worse it gets.

That's why the stall happens. That's why it shows up at month three and not day one. That's why it shows up years before anything on your bloodwork, because a blood panel only sees the magnesium in your blood, and almost all of it lives inside your cells. Your flat Friday is the canary. Your cortisol is the coal mine.

Pushing through doesn't fix any of that. It gets you eating even less for 12 weeks and asks the shot to finish a job your body won't let it finish. The warning your body is trying to send just gets muffled.

Any research that actually showed magnesium bringing cortisol down used a form that crosses the blood brain barrier, because that's where cortisol gets regulated. Not in your stomach. In your brain.

Then I went and looked at the magnesium on my nightstand. Magnesium oxide. About four percent absorbed, the rest straight through you. No wonder it did what it did for my bathroom and nothing else. The capsules I'd tried? The same oxide with glycinate printed on the front. The clinical studies used a form that absorbs at up to ninety percent. No wonder no one was seeing results.

I kept reading. The bigger problem isn't even the form, it's the delivery. Most magnesium is pressed into a capsule or a tablet that needs a stomach that's moving to break it down. And the shots slow your stomach way down. That's half of how they work. The magnesium passes through before it ever gets absorbed.

And it starts even earlier than that. The soil our food grows in has been farmed hard for decades, and the mills strip most of the magnesium out of our flour, so we get less of it than any generation in history before anyone ever opens a bottle.

So even when a label says "magnesium", between the cheap form and the capsule and a stomach that's barely moving, the amount that actually reaches your brain is close to nothing. The Amazon capsules are the same cheap oxide with no verification of what's inside. The label says magnesium. What gets through isn't.

I'd been reading about magnesium and cortisol for years and I'd never actually checked the form or the delivery on the brands my patients were buying. None of them were getting close to the clinical dose. None of us were.

I started looking for any magnesium that was, and it came down to three things. It was the third one that almost no brand will actually pass.

One. Magnesium bisglycinate, not oxide (so it crosses the blood brain barrier and gets to the switch)

Two. Third party tested (an outside lab confirms what's actually in the bag)

Three. Oxide nowhere on the back panel, not just glycinate on the front (so you actually get the clinical dose)

I kept seeing the same brand mentioned over and over in the reviews. SPNutrition. The same one Diane had told me about at dinner.

I ordered it. It was more expensive than the capsules and the drugstore bottle I'd tried. At that point I didn't care.

SPNutrition's magnesium was pure bisglycinate, third party verified by an outside lab. No oxide, nothing hidden on the back. Gummy form, which I appreciated, because a gummy starts breaking down the moment you chew it and doesn't need a stomach that's moving, and this one is sugar free, which most gummies aren't.

One thing I noticed when it showed up. The bag looks like anything else on the kitchen counter. No loud packaging. No word on the label that would tell anyone the reason I got it. No "weight loss." No "cortisol." It sat next to my husband's fish oil and just blended in. That mattered more to me than I expected. I didn't want a bag sitting on the counter that announced to the whole house what I was struggling with. I didn't want my daughter coming over for Sunday dinner and spotting a label that spelled it out. This one didn't do that.

Two gummies before bed that Monday night.

The first week, nothing dramatic. But on Friday I woke up and the room was light. I'd slept straight through for the first time in months. I laid there for a minute just staring at the ceiling.

It was week 3 that made me stop doubting. By week 3, I was sleeping through 5 or 6 nights out of 7. The afternoon crash was gone. My husband noticed before I said anything. He didn't say anything either, he just put his arm around me in the kitchen one night and I didn't tense up.

By day 30, the Friday number moved. Two pounds, then another the week after, the way it had in month one. The sugar cravings after dinner just stopped showing up. I stopped needing the third cup of coffee at 2pm. And I want to be precise about this, because I'm a doctor. Nothing about my shots changed. Same shot, same Sunday night. It never stopped working. My body stopped fighting it.

At day 60, my husband pulled me aside on a Saturday morning and asked me what had changed. I told him. For the first time in almost 5 months, I felt like my body was mine again. I sat on the edge of the bed and had to collect myself for a minute.

I run a weight loss clinic. I treat this every day. And nothing I'd done for 4 months had moved my Fridays like this.

That scale check, wondering if it was going to be another Friday I couldn't look? Gone. Saying 24 with a smile to patients? Gone. I don't take anything but my shot and two gummies before bed. I sleep through the night without lying there running through what's wrong with me.

When I went back to my physician at the 3 month mark, she had me on the scale before I'd sat down. She weighed me twice, because she thought she'd read it wrong. She looked at my chart, looked at me, and told me whatever I was doing to keep doing it. She actually asked what I was taking so she could mention it to a few of her own patients.

I've quietly mentioned SPNutrition to 14 of my own patients since then. The ones who stalled at month three. The ones who've stayed with it have all come back with a different look on their face. One 61 year old woman who'd been stuck for five months and been told she'd found her floor told me last month her number has moved every Friday for six weeks, and her husband has started reaching for her again for the first time since their son's wedding. She said that quietly, sitting in the chair across from my desk, and she had to look away when she said it.

Look, for almost 5 months I thought I had two options. Keep pushing through the way I tell my patients to and watch the number sit there while everyone told me I looked great, or call it my floor and watch my body quietly take it all back until my blood pressure caught up with my mother's. As a weight loss doctor, I knew where the second road ended. My own mother showed me.

I was wrong about the first option being my only alternative.

And here's something I wish I'd understood sooner. Not all magnesium is the same. Remember what Diane said at dinner, that the cheap kind doesn't work? This is what she meant, and I didn't understand it until I'd wasted 6 weeks on the wrong stuff myself and finally read the research. I half recommended magnesium to women on the shots for years without ever checking what was actually in the bottles they were buying. If I'd grabbed the first magnesium off Amazon again it would have been the same story. SPNutrition's bisglycinate, third party tested, sugar free gummy is the only kind that actually got my Fridays moving again. Made in the USA too.

I still take my shot every Sunday night, same as before, and I'd tell any patient to do exactly what her own doctor tells her. I just stopped running on empty.

They offer a 30 day money back guarantee. If nothing changes for you, you get a full refund. No questions asked. In 19 years of running a weight loss clinic, I have never seen a diet program, a meal plan or a clinic offer to give your money back if it doesn't work. Think about that for a second.

And here's the thing. If Diane hadn't finally told me over that dinner, I'd still be keeping the scale in the closet, still saying 24, still dreading a three month follow up I knew I was going to fail.

I'm sharing this because I hope it helps someone else. After 19 years treating women's weight for a living, I thought I knew every option. Turns out, my oldest friend knew something I didn't.

I let my dog die because I trusted the wrong people. I'm writing this so you don't make the same mistake. 

My dog Rosie was put to sleep fourteen months ago. I held her on the floor of the vet's office while it happened. She was 9 years old.

I had spent £3,530 over two years trying to stop her back legs from failing.

It wasn't enough.

I have a second dog. Bear. He's 5. And right now, his back legs are starting to do the exact same thing Rosie's did.

And I'm terrified.

I'm not a vet. I'm just a regular person who thought I was doing everything right. And I want to tell you what happened because I see so many of you posting the same exact things I posted two years ago, and it makes me sick to my stomach.

If your senior dog is slipping on the floor — or their back legs are getting weaker every month — and you're still on the same prescriptions and supplements that stopped working, please, PLEASE read this whole thing.

I know it's long. I know you're busy. But two years ago I would have given anything for someone to tell me what I'm about to tell you.

Here's what happened.

Two years before Rosie was put to sleep, she started slipping on the kitchen floor. Just occasionally at first. She'd plant her back legs wrong after lying down and scramble to get up. I'd watch her front legs do all the work while her back end dragged behind.

I bought non-slip socks. Then toe grips. Then yoga mats and carpet runners laid across every room.

At first I thought it was just the tiles. Lots of dogs slip on tiles.

I actually posted in my Facebook group: "Rosie keeps slipping on the kitchen floor — has anyone dealt with this? Is it just the surface?"

Everyone said yes. "Get yoga mats." "Try toe grips." "Some dogs just have trouble with hard floors."

So I didn't think anything of it.

But then it got worse with Rosie.

By month 3, the slipping was every day. And the muscle loss was visible.

Her haunches that used to be strong and round were sunken. Her back legs were losing mass. She started kicking one leg out sideways just to stay upright — like a kickstand.

Bear was starting to slow down too, but not as bad. Maybe just age, I told myself.

I posted about it again. "Rosie's back legs are getting weaker every month, we've tried the yoga mats and nothing's helping. Anyone dealt with this?"

Someone said it was probably just arthritis. "Try a joint supplement — glucosamine chews — give it time." Someone else said fish oil helped their dog. Another person said to get a ramp for the sofa.

My vet confirmed it at her checkup. "Arthritis. Very common at her age. Let's start her on a joint supplement and see how she goes."

So I kept following the advice.

The glucosamine helped for about six weeks. Then it stopped.

Not all at once. Slowly. Like someone turning a dial down one notch at a time.

A little more splaying after walks. Some hesitation before getting up. Then the sound of her claws scraping the tiles at night. Faintly at first. Then every morning.

I went back to the vet.

"Let's add Galliprant. It's an anti-inflammatory — should help with the pain and stiffness."

£80 a month. But it helped.

For a few months she moved more easily. Got up quicker. Seemed less stiff.

I thought we were on top of it.

Then it started coming back.

I told my vet the Galliprant was fading.

"Let's add Adequan injections. They help lubricate the joint and slow cartilage breakdown."

We added them. Helped for maybe six weeks. Then the weakness crept back.

"Let's consider Librela."

£110 every four weeks. On top of the Galliprant. On top of the Adequan. Monthly spend: over £200.

And I found out later that long-term Galliprant and Librela carry real risks to the liver and kidneys. I even saw a comment in a Facebook group: "My dog was walking until the vet gave him this injection and hasn't walked since without a sling." I was paying £200 a month to potentially damage her while she kept declining.

I drove home from the vet one afternoon and sat in the car in the driveway and didn't go inside for ten minutes.

And I couldn't stop thinking: I tried everything. I TRIED EVERYTHING. For two years I watched her get weaker every month. I gave her every supplement. I filled every prescription. I posted about it. I asked people.

And everyone told me to try the next thing.

But here's what made everything worse.

One morning Rosie couldn't get up off the floor at all.

I had to deadlift her back end just to get her outside. At 2 AM. At 4 AM. Every night.

She stopped coming to greet me at the door. Stopped following me room to room. She'd just lie on the cool tiles and wait for me to come to her. Her eyes looked different. Tired. Like she'd accepted that this was her life now.

That look is what broke me.

I sat on the floor next to her one night and held her while she lay there unable to get up. And I thought: I am watching my dog disappear. Slowly. Week by week. And I can't stop it.

I started Googling "quality of life assessment for dogs." I read through the criteria. Mobility. Hygiene. Happiness. Pain. I scored her honestly. I closed the laptop and sobbed on the kitchen floor.

Rosie dragged herself over to where I was sitting and put her head in my lap. She couldn't stand up to reach me. But she still came.

My dog was comforting me. While her back legs were failing underneath her.

I couldn't sleep that night.

I couldn't sleep for weeks.

Two weeks later, I made the decision. I held her on the floor of the vet's office and I told her she was a good girl. The vet said she wasn't in pain anymore. I drove home alone.

I kept thinking: there has to be something. There has to be SOMETHING that could save Bear.

I was not going to let it happen again.

So I started researching.

And I mean OBSESSIVELY researching.

I joined every senior dog Facebook group. I read every Reddit thread about hind leg weakness. I watched videos from veterinary specialists. I read medical journals that I barely understood.

And I started seeing a pattern.

SO MANY people with the exact same story as mine.

"My dog started slipping on the floor around age 7." "Glucosamine helped for a bit then stopped working." "Vet kept adding prescriptions." "Monthly cost got to £200 and she was still getting weaker." "Eventually couldn't get up on her own." "Had to make the decision."

Over and over and over.

I found a thread on Reddit from two years ago. A woman whose dog went through the exact same spiral. Same timeline. Same prescriptions. Same escalation. Same outcome.

Someone in the comments said: "The medications don't fail because vets don't know what they're doing. They fail because they're all aimed at the same thing — the joints. Not the actual cause."

That destroyed me.

Because I knew something was wrong underneath. I just didn't know what it was.

bodyText:
For nineteen years I was Mark's wife. Two years after the divorce, our daughter called to tell me he was marrying a woman seventeen years younger.

She begged me to come to the wedding. I went. And I made sure everyone in that room saw exactly what he'd traded away.

Mark and I married at twenty-six. We built a life — the house on Kirkwood, the kids, Christmas mornings, the same four couples at every barbecue for a decade. Nineteen years of being "the Rileys."

Then he met someone through work. Younger. She was thirty-four when it started. I was fifty-one, and in the middle of menopause, and I'd started to feel like my body was being taken away from me a piece at a time.

The divorce was quiet and brutal. He got the narrative and the quiet loyalty of all our friends. I got the house and the silence.

For the first year, people checked in. Then it thinned. By the second year it had mostly stopped.

Then Sophie called. Our daughter. Twenty-five, caught between two parents, trying to love everybody equally.

"Mom, I need to tell you something. Dad's getting married. To Bree. It's in October."

A pause.

"I want you to come. I know how that sounds. But his entire side is going to be there and I don't want to stand in that room alone feeling like I have to choose. You're my mom. I want you there."

I said I'd think about it.

I hung up, and I went and stood in front of my bathroom mirror for a long time.

Here's the part I have to explain properly, or none of the rest of this makes sense.

I had lost fifty-two pounds that year.

On a GLP-1, and I want to say right now, before anything else — I would do it again tomorrow. It did what thirty years of dieting never did, and what menopause had made completely impossible. My blood pressure came down. My knees stopped hurting on the stairs. The constant noise about food went quiet for the first time in my adult life.

And I should have been standing in front of that mirror at the best I'd looked since my thirties.

Instead I looked ten years older than I was.

I turned sideways and my backside had gone completely flat. A straight line from my lower back all the way down to the back of my thigh. The jeans I'd bought two sizes down as a reward fit my waist perfectly and hung completely empty in the back.

The skin on my arms and my chest had gone thin and crepey — not a little, a lot. My neck. The backs of my hands. My hair was thinner all over, not just at the part.

And there were the things I hadn't told anyone. That I'd started holding the rail going upstairs. That I was taking two trips in from the car with the shopping. That I'd asked my son-in-law to open a jar in July and made a joke about it so nobody would notice.

The mirror was what I'd admit to. The jar was what actually frightened me.

Fifty-two pounds down. Everyone told me I looked incredible.

And I was about to walk into a room where my ex-husband was marrying a gorgeous thirty-six-year-old.

Every person there would look at me, and then look at her, and do the math on why he left.

Translation: she got thin, and she got old anyway. That one's the upgrade.

"I'll think about it," I'd said to Sophie.

I sat at my kitchen table in the dark for an hour. The invitation sat on my counter for three days. I couldn't look at it and I couldn't throw it away.

Then I got angry.

The next morning I called Denise.

She's been my person since we were twenty-two. The one who turned up with wine and didn't say a single stupid thing the night Mark left.

She's fifty-four. Went through menopause the same years I did — we used to compare hot flushes on the phone. She's been on the same shot as me for slightly longer. And she looks like a woman who has lost fifty pounds and kept her body. Strong. Upright. Carries her own shopping in. Not because of work — she's never had anything done. I'd know. She tells me everything.

"Sophie told me about the wedding," she said before I could even start. "And you're going. End of discussion."

Then she stopped.

"Before October, I want you to do one thing for me. How much are you spending on that counter of yours right now?"

"I don't know. The collagen, the protein powder I can't finish, the electrolyte packets, the biotin, the magnesium, the calcium, the creatine — maybe a hundred and fifty a month?"

"Stop. All of it. Because none of it is doing a single thing and I've been able to tell since June."

That stung. But she wasn't wrong. She's always been a tough-love friend and I have loved her for it for thirty years.

"Nancy, what did your doctor say about all of it?"

"That it's my age. That it's what happens after menopause, and what happens with rapid weight loss, and I should expect some of it at fifty-three."

"That's the sentence I want you to stop believing."

"Listen to me. You've had two things happen to you, one on top of the other, and nobody's explained either of them."

"The first one was menopause. When your oestrogen dropped, your muscle started going, your skin started losing its collagen, your bones started thinning. That's real. You noticed. And you were told it was your age, and you accepted it, because what else do you do."

"Then you went on the shot. And you started eating a third of what you used to — and drinking less, because it switches your thirst off the same way it switches your appetite off."

"When did you last actually feel thirsty? Not knew you should have some water. Felt it."

I stood in my kitchen with the phone against my ear and I could not remember. And Denise said that's half the problem — thirst gets quieter with age on its own, and then the shot turns it down further.

"So your body went into shortage. And when a body's short, it doesn't cut everything evenly. It picks."

"Your heart. Your brain. Your blood. Your organs. Those get protected, no matter what."

"And everything that isn't keeping you alive gets taken from to pay for it. Your muscle. Your skin. Your hair. Your nails."

"Because your body doesn't care what you look like, Nancy. It cares that you're alive."

"And here's the part nobody tells women our age. It wasn't raiding a full tank. Menopause had already emptied half of it. So you went from half a tank to nothing — and a thirty-eight-year-old on the same dose went from a full tank to three-quarters and looks fine."

"That's the difference. And here's the part that explains why nothing on your counter has fixed it."

"All of it — the protein, the collagen, the creatine — it goes through your liver first. Your liver is your body's routing system. It takes what comes in and sends it where it needs to go. To your muscles. To your skin. To your hormones. But your liver has been backed up for years. Menopause hormones. Divorce stress. Every supplement you've been cycling through trying to patch the problem. A backed-up liver doesn't alarm you — your tests come back normal because those tests catch damage, not sluggishness. Sluggishness shows up on your face, your arms, the back of your jeans."

"So the protein shakes do nothing. The creatine goes nowhere useful. You're putting clean fuel into a clogged engine. Fix the engine, and your body can finally use what's coming in."

And I said the thing I'd been waiting to say for five minutes.

"Denise, I tried milk thistle. Six weeks, two different brands. Nothing. If anything, week three was worse than when I started."

"What percentage silymarin?"

I stood in my kitchen with the phone against my ear and I did not know what that meant.

"What's on every shelf is twenty, maybe thirty percent silymarin at best. Silymarin is the only part of milk thistle that actually helps liver cells repair themselves. The level that works is eighty percent. You've been taking a fraction of what matters."

"And even at eighty percent," she said, "milk thistle on its own is only half of it."

"What's the other half?"

"The cleanse. Your liver isn't just slow. It has buildup — from years of stress hormones, medications, the supplements it couldn't fully process. Milk thistle repairs the cells. But if the buildup is still there, repaired cells still can't move anything through. That's why week three crashed — the cells got a little stronger, but the clog was still there, and it reasserted itself. You need something that clears the inside at the same time. That's wormwood and clove. Together. One repairs. One clears. Without both, you're back at week three every time."

She texted me a link while we were still on the phone.

"Gevilo. Milk thistle standardized to eighty percent silymarin — the dose that actually matters, not the diluted versions sitting in every health store. Wormwood and clove in the same capsule, because the repair and the cleanse have to happen together or neither of them holds. Plus turmeric and vitamin C to support the liver as it works through the clearing. One capsule, taken in the morning. That's all."

"I've been taking it for two years," she said. "Since before the shot. That's it. That's the difference between us."

To be completely honest, I was sceptical. I didn't believe anything could put back what I'd lost at fifty-three. But what did I have to lose at that point?

I ordered it that night.

The wedding was fourteen weeks away.

It came three days later.

I took it into my kitchen and looked at the counter. The collagen powder. The protein I gagged on. The electrolyte sachets. The biotin gummies. The magnesium. The calcium. The creatine tub with the dust still on the lid, because I'd thrown the scoop out and kept the tub, which tells you something about where I was.

Seven containers. A hundred and fifty dollars a month.

Gone. One capsule every morning in their place.

Thirty seconds, next to the coffee pot.

The first week I kept waiting to feel something dramatic the way you do with a new product. It was quieter than that. The wall that had been taking me at nine every night stopped taking me. I was awake at half past ten reading a book, and I didn't connect it to anything yet.

By the end of week three, I carried the shopping in from the car in one trip. All of it. I stood in the kitchen with the bags on the counter and realised I hadn't done that since the spring.

The next day I stood up out of my own low armchair without putting my hands down. I did it twice more to make sure.

To be frank, I was shocked. I still put it down to wishful thinking.

Week five, I went upstairs without reaching for the rail, and I only noticed at the top.

But by week six, I turned sideways in my bathroom mirror on purpose. First time since April.

And there was a curve there.

Not bigger. Fuller. Like something had been put back into it.

I stood there with my hand over my mouth like an idiot.

By week nine, the seat of my jeans stopped sagging. The crepey look on my arms had softened enough that I stopped pulling my sleeves down in photographs.

And by week eleven, Sophie came over for dinner and stopped in the doorway.

"Mom. What did you do?"

"Nothing."

"You look — I don't know. You look like you. Like before Dad left. What is happening?"

I smiled. A real one, for the first time since the divorce. "I'll tell you later."

And here's the thing I need to put in writing, because it's the part that still gets me.

The scale did not move one single pound. Same weight in October as I was in June. I measured my hips with a tape because I wanted something that wasn't my own eyes — up two and a half inches, waist exactly where it was.

I hadn't lost anything more. I'd just stopped running on empty.

I bought a dress. Deep green. Fitted. Sleeveless — which I had not worn in six years, because of my arms.

October came.

I walked into that venue alone.

Conversations stopped.

Mark's sister Carol was at the welcome table directing guests. She looked up and went still.

"Nancy." A glance down at the seating chart. "We didn't — I wasn't expecting you."

"Sophie invited me," I said. "I'm at table seven."

Sophie came across the foyer and hugged me so hard she lifted me. Then she stepped back, held me at arm's length, and said — loud enough for the welcome table — "Mom. Look at you. You look unbelievable."

Carol looked at the dress. At my arms. Then back at me.

"You look — what have you been doing? You've lost the weight, obviously, we all knew that, but you look..." She couldn't finish it.

"One thing," I said. "That's all I've been doing."

One of the bridesmaids — Mark's niece Hailey, twenty-eight, does fitness content — had been half-listening on the steps. She came over.

"Okay, Aunt Nancy, I have to ask. Everyone I know your age who's lost weight on the shot looks — sorry — older. Like, it takes it out of them. You don't. Are you training?"

"I was," I said. "Four months, and it did nothing."

"Then what?"

"Menopause took some of it. The shot took the rest. But the reason nothing worked is that everything — the protein, the collagen, the creatine I was taking — it all goes through your liver first. And when your liver is backed up from years of hormone processing and stress, it can't route any of it to your muscles or your skin. You're putting clean fuel into a clogged engine. Nothing gets where it needs to go."

"So what unclogged it?"

"Milk thistle — but standardized to eighty percent silymarin, not the twenty or thirty percent in every bottle at the drugstore. And wormwood and clove in the same capsule, because milk thistle only repairs the cells. If there's buildup blocking the system, repaired cells still can't move anything through. You need the cleanse and the repair together, every day."

"Wait — milk thistle?" She already had her phone out. "My mum tried milk thistle for her joints and she said it did absolutely—"

"Most of it doesn't. The silymarin content is the whole difference. And without the cleansing side paired with it, even the right milk thistle just tries to repair an engine that's still clogged. You need both together. Send her the link."

Carol was standing four feet away and heard every word of it.

The reception went long. I danced with Sophie. I talked to people I hadn't spoken to in two years. I ate, I had champagne, and I moved around that room with my arms bare without once thinking about them.

Around the third glass, a woman about my age came and sat beside me. Expensive, careful, the kind of maintenance that costs money. I didn't place her at first.

Then I realised: the bride's mother.

"Forgive me for being forward," she said. "I've been watching you all evening trying to work out what you've had done. Because I'm fifty-seven, I'm on the same medication you are, and my surgeon has quoted me nine thousand dollars to do something about my backside and another six for my arms."

"Don't," I said. "Nothing's been done."

She looked at me the way you look at somebody you're certain is lying.

"I'm serious. One capsule a day. Everything you're describing — the muscle, the skin — it's not a surgery problem. Your liver is backed up. Menopause gave it years of hormones to process. The shot put you on a third of what you used to eat, and what little comes in can't be routed properly by a system that's still clogged. The surgeon is treating what your liver left behind. Fix the liver and your body can use what's already coming in."

She was quiet a second.

"Write it down for me. I would rather hear that from a real woman at a wedding than from a surgeon who's trying to book a theatre."

Carol was one table over. She heard all of that too.

At one point I caught Mark looking at me from across the room. Just for a second. Then he looked away.

Sophie leaned over during the last song. "Mom. Dad's cousin asked me if you'd had work done. Everyone keeps looking at you." She squeezed my hand. "I'm so glad you came."

I had to look at the dance floor for a moment so she wouldn't see my face.

Carol found me by the coat check at the end of the night.

She stood beside me for a moment.

"The bride's mother hasn't stopped talking about you," she said. "Neither has Hailey."

Then, quieter: "I'm fifty-five. Eight months in. Down forty-one pounds. And I haven't let my husband see me undressed since February."

I did not say anything, because there is nothing to say to that except I know.

"What is it?"

I looked at her.

"It's called Gevilo. Milk thistle standardized to eighty percent silymarin — not the diluted versions filling every shelf. Wormwood and clove in the same capsule, because you cannot repair a backed-up liver without clearing what's blocking it first. One capsule in the morning, with water. That's it."

"Where?"

"I'll text you the link. Order from the official page. There are cheap bottles everywhere with a fraction of the silymarin and nothing for the cleanse — and all they'll do is convince you that milk thistle doesn't work on women. That's what happened to me."

The valet brought my car around.

"Goodnight, Carol," I said, and walked out into the October air.

Here's what I learned.

For nineteen years I was Mark's wife. When he left me for a younger woman, everybody did the math. She got old. She got replaced. She's the before picture now.

And then I lost fifty-two pounds and I was still the before picture — and a doctor told me that was my age.

It wasn't my age. Menopause took some of me, and I was told it was my age. The shot took more, and I was told it was the rapid weight loss. The real reason neither of us could fix it — his sister, the bride's mother, every woman in my GLP-1 group comparing notes — is that the body puts what little comes in through the same filter first. And when that filter is backed up, none of it gets where it's supposed to go. Not the protein. Not the collagen. Not the creatine. The filter was the problem the whole time.

His sister wrapped it in politeness. His friends disappeared. The story wrote itself.

She didn't think I was grieving. She thought I was finished.

So I had two choices. Skip that wedding, the way everyone expected, and confirm I'd faded the day Mark left. Or walk into it alone in a sleeveless dress with a body I recognised — and prove I was never just his wife.

The capsule didn't make me who I am.

It just unclogged what two things had been blocking, so the rest of them could see it.

And here's the part that made me actually click buy.

It's called Gevilo. Milk thistle standardized to eighty percent silymarin — the concentration the research uses, not the twenty to thirty percent sitting in every bottle at the drugstore. Not the fraction that convinces women the whole category doesn't work. Wormwood extract and clove in the same capsule — one clears what the other then repairs, and they have to work together for either to hold past week three. Plus turmeric, vitamin C, and a few more that support the liver through the process. One capsule a day. That's all.

I did the arithmetic on what I'd been spending across seven containers on my counter and it was genuinely embarrassing — over a hundred and fifty dollars a month on things that couldn't work, because each one was one item going into a system that couldn't route any of them.

Made in the USA, third-party tested every batch, every amount printed on the label. Ninety-day money-back guarantee — take it for three months, and if nothing's changed, full refund, no questions.

Before you order, do two things.

Stand up out of a low chair without using your hands. If you can't, or it's a struggle — that isn't just your age. That's what happens when what you're eating can't reach your muscles because the routing system is backed up.

And take the sideways photograph, even though you'll hate it. Measure your hips and write the number down. In six weeks you'll want something to check it against — and it'll be you deciding, not anybody else.

Order from the official page rather than a marketplace listing — gevilo.com/pages/milk-thistle — so you're getting the eighty percent silymarin, the wormwood and clove actually in it, and the guarantee actually applies.

And stay on your shot. I did. I'm still on it, still losing. You should not have to choose between the weight and your body, and this is the entire reason you don't.

In 2020, when the pandemic hit and grocery shelves started going bare, millions of Americans had the same thought at the same time.

I need to grow my own food.

They went online to order seeds. And they couldn't get them.

Baker Creek — one of the biggest heirloom seed suppliers in the country — shut down online ordering completely. Burpee was backordered for weeks. Smaller companies sold out overnight.

But here's the part that should concern you most.

Even the people who had leftover seeds from last year couldn't use them. Because most retail seeds are hybrids.

They grow one harvest and that's it. Save them and replant? The second generation breaks down. Stunted. Deformed. Useless.

Scientists call it F2 breakdown, and it's built into the design.

So when the supply chain broke, those families had nothing. No seeds on the shelf. No saved seeds from last year. No way to feed themselves outside of a grocery store that might not restock for weeks.

That was five years ago. It already happened once in our lifetime. And almost nobody is more prepared now than they were then.

But it wasn't the first time the supply chain broke.
In 1943, it broke even worse. World War II. Food rationed. Shelves unreliable. The government told American families to grow their own food. And 22 million of them did.

The difference? They had seeds that actually worked. Heirloom seeds. Open-pollinated. Seeds you could save and replant every year. One purchase, and a family could feed itself indefinitely.

Eleanor Roosevelt planted one at the White House.
Burpee couldn't keep up with demand. One seed breeder in Pennsylvania created a tomato before shipping off to fight in Europe. He was killed in Germany in 1944. But his tomato made the cover of Burpee's 1945 catalogue — and it's still grown today, eighty years later, because families saved those seeds generation after generation.

Nobody was dependent on the next shipment. Those seeds renewed themselves the way seeds had worked for ten thousand years.

Then the war ended. Supermarkets opened. And the seed industry quietly replaced everything with hybrids — seeds that grow once and can't be saved. Seeds designed to bring you back to the store every spring.

They turned gardeners into subscribers. And nobody told them.

The deeper I looked, the worse it got.

A study from the University of Texas found that the fruits and vegetables we grow today contain up to 38% less nutrition than what our grandparents were eating. The industry bred for shelf life — not for what goes into your body.

Then there's the Svalbard Global Seed Vault. Built into a mountain near the North Pole. Funded by governments worldwide. Designed to survive the end of civilization. And what are they storing inside? Not hybrids. Open-pollinated heirloom seeds. The exact kind your great-grandparents used.

Governments are protecting heirloom seeds in an Arctic vault. While selling you hybrids that expire after one season.

I started looking for a real heirloom source. Most of what I found was disappointing — tiny packets, single varieties, no guidance.

Then I found Nuvera.

A full heirloom seed vault. 16,000+ seeds. 35 varieties. Every one non-GMO, non-hybrid, open-pollinated. The same type of seeds that fed 22 million families through WWII.

The math is what got me. Over 16,000 seeds for roughly what you'd spend on a few dinners out.

They include two free bonuses — a Beginner's Planting Guide that walks you through every variety step by step, even if you've never grown anything. And a Garden Planner that tracks planting dates, harvest windows, and seed-saving schedules.

The vault. The guide. The planner. Everything your great-grandparents knew, in one kit.

And they back it with a 60-day guarantee. Plant them. Test the germination. Watch them grow. If you're not satisfied, full refund. Keep the ebooks either way.

bodyText:
I've walked with the Lord for over 40 years. Three months ago, a single word in a verse I've read a hundred times stopped me cold.

I'm 59. I've led the women's Bible study at my church for eleven years. My faith isn't something I practice, it's who I am.

Which is why I can't believe it took me this long to see what I'm about to share with you.

For the last two years, I'd been quietly suffering.

Not an illness. Nothing I could point to.

Just a body wound tighter and tighter by the life I carry.

My mother is 84. I manage her appointments, her medications, her moods. My phone stays on loud at night in case the call comes. My kids are grown, but a mother never clocks out. I'm the one everybody in my family casts their cares on.

And I cast mine on the Lord. Every morning. Every night.

But somewhere along the way, my body stopped getting the message.

Jaw tight by ten in the morning. Shoulders up around my ears. A chest that never fully unclenched, even on good days.

Snapping at people I love over nothing, then hating myself for it.

Tired but wired all day, then wide awake at 2am with my mind running laps.

I prayed about it. Every night, I asked God to quiet my mind.

I even went to my doctor. She ran the full bloodwork. Everything came back normal.

"You're just carrying a lot of stress. Try to relax more."

I drove home and cried in the driveway. If everything was normal, why didn't I feel normal?

Then came that Tuesday morning.

I was preparing that week's study. Proverbs 17.

"A merry heart is good medicine, but a broken spirit dries the bones." - Proverbs 17:22.

I've read that verse dozens of times before.

But that morning, the word bones would not let me go.

Not "a broken spirit weighs on the heart." Not "troubles the mind."

Dries the bones.

It felt like a nudge I wasn't supposed to ignore.

So I did something I'd never done in 40 years of reading.

I started searching what bones actually mean in Scripture.

What I found floored me.

Bones are mentioned in the Bible well over a hundred times. I lost count.

And almost every time, they mean far more than a skeleton.

When David carried a hidden anguish, he wrote: "When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long." - Psalm 32:3

When Scripture describes comfort, it says: "Gracious words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones." - Proverbs 16:24

"Good news gives health to the bones." - Proverbs 15:30

"Fear the Lord and turn from evil. This will bring health to your body and nourishment to your bones." - Proverbs 3:7-8

Do you see the pattern? I couldn't unsee it.

Over and over, Scripture puts your inner life in your bones.

Anguish wastes them. Worry dries them. Comfort and good news heal them.

In Hebrew, the word for bone, etsem, is nearly the same as the word for your very self. When Scripture says something reaches your bones, it means it has reached the deepest part of you.

And then I remembered the most famous bones in the whole Bible.

An entire valley of them.

Magnesium.

More than half of it is in your bones.

"Why does my Diarrhea run down my legs before I can get to the bathroom?" Is the #1 question I get asked everyday on my home visits. Here are the 7 exact reasons why, and what you can do right now to fix it.

I'm a home-health nurse.

The woman who asks me that is almost always retired and over 65.

Let's call her Barbara. She's 72.

She's had diarrhea for twenty years. The accidents started three years ago.

She didn't feel the last two coming.

There's a box of Depends in her bathroom and a bag in her car with wipes, a trash bag and a second pair of pants.

She takes two Imodium before she leaves the house, and on those days she doesn't eat.

She stopped going to church two years ago. Now she watches it on TV.

Four gastroenterologists, every test normal, and the last one wrote her a prescription for pads.

If that sounds like you, I wrote this for you.

You know where the nearest bathroom is right now. You checked before you sat down.

A visit with a doctor lasts about fifteen minutes. The real answer takes longer than that, so it gets skipped.

I sit at kitchen tables for a living, so I won't skip it here.

Here are the seven questions Barbara asks me, in her own words. Each answer is one of the seven reasons.

After that I'll tell you what you can do about it today.

Question 1: "Why can't I feel it coming anymore? I used to get a warning."

Because your warning is the time between your colon noticing and your colon acting, and watery food leaves no time.

I hear that question in every house, and I believe you.

Your small intestine is supposed to finish breaking down your food. It does that with enzymes. There's one for protein, one for fat, one for the sugar in milk, and a few for beans and vegetables.

When you make enough of them, your colon only gets waste. Waste arrives slowly and formed.

Your colon fills over hours, the wall stretches, and you feel it. That stretch is your warning. It used to give you twenty minutes.

When you run short, your colon gets food. It treats that food the way it treats food poisoning. It pulls in water, squeezes hard, and gets everything out fast.

Water arrives all at once. There's no slow stretch. The squeeze and the warning happen in the same second.

That's why you don't feel it coming.

That's why it's so liquidy.

And that's why the muscle that holds the door can't hold it. No muscle can hold water.

Question 2: "Why does it happen when I stand up?"

Because a formed stool sits still, and water moves the moment you do.

A formed stool sits in the last part of your colon like a stone in a bowl. You can stand, turn and walk, and it stays put until you decide.

Water doesn't sit. When you stand up from the pew or the restaurant chair, the muscles in your belly tighten to lift you. That tightening presses on your colon.

A stone doesn't care. Water goes where the pressure sends it.

That's why it happens getting up from dinner, turning in the grocery aisle, or climbing out of the car.

Nothing you did was wrong. You moved, and water moved with you.

Question 3: "Why does it happen when I haven't eaten all day?"

Because what leaves you today is the meal before it, and a worn lining leaks water on its own.

You've stopped eating before you leave the house. Some of you stop two days before. It helps less than it should, and here's why.

Your colon is still holding the last meal. It arrived half-digested and full of water, and it waits there for the next signal.

Eating sends that signal, so skipping meals does buy you a little time. But standing up sends a smaller one, and so does a cup of coffee, and so does nerves in the checkout line.

There's a second reason. Years of half-digested food wear on the lining of your gut, like a rug that wears thin where everyone walks. A worn lining breaks food down even worse. It also leaks water into your colon all day, food or no food.

So an empty stomach doesn't give you an empty colon. It gives you a hungry, shaky day and the same accident at the bank.

Question 4: "Why do I wake up to it at night?"

Because dinner reaches your colon while you sleep, and the muscle that holds the door rests when you do.

It has nothing to do with what you picked for dinner.

Dinner is the biggest meal of your day, and it takes hours to travel. It lands in your colon in the middle of the night, half-digested and full of water.

Your colon slows down while you sleep. So that dinner sits there for hours, pulling in more water.

And the muscle that holds the door relaxes in deep sleep. It's supposed to. It was built to hold a formed stool at rest, and a formed stool waits until morning.

Water doesn't wait. Some nights the pressure wakes you. Other nights you find out in the morning.

Question 5: "Why doesn't the Imodium hold it anymore?"

Because Imodium slows the muscles of your gut, and it never touches what arrives in your colon.

Imodium does one thing. It slows the muscle that moves food along. It was built for a stomach bug that lasts three days.

Your half-digested food still arrives, only later. The water is still in it. So one pill became two, and two became four before every errand.

Then it swings. You're plugged for two days, and everything that was waiting comes at once. One woman told me, "If I take an Imodium, I will be constipated for up to a week."

Imodium was never designed to fix this, and nobody told you that. Keep it for the days you need it. Just know it was built for the muscle, and your trouble starts one step before the muscle.

Question 6: "Why did every test come back normal when it's this bad?"

Because everything they checked works on your colon, and the trouble starts one step before it.

A colonoscopy looks at the wall of your colon. A CT scan looks at the shape of your organs. Bloodwork looks for inflammation and celiac.

Those tests matter, because they rule out the dangerous things. If you haven't had them, have them.

Not one of them checks whether your food got broken down.

Doctors at Augusta University in Georgia looked at 120 adults who'd had gut symptoms for over a year. Most were women. Their scans and scopes had all come back normal.

Then the doctors measured the digestive enzymes in the lining of the small intestine. 56 of the 120 were short on at least one.

That test isn't one of the standard ones. So your chart says normal, and you go home with a prescription for pads.

Your doctor didn't tell you for three plain reasons. No drug treats an everyday enzyme shortage, so no company teaches doctors about it. The test isn't standard. And the visit is fifteen minutes long.

"IBS-D" is the name you get when the tests find nothing else. It describes what your body does, and it has never told you why.

You always suspected that label wasn't a real answer. You were right.

Question 7: "Is this just my life now? The doctor wrote me a prescription for pads."

Because a pad catches the water, and nothing you were given stops the water from coming.

I'm not going to tell you to throw the pads away today. They're the reason you made it to the bank.

But here's what I see in the houses I visit. The women who wear pads this year are buying pull-ups next year, at fifty dollars a week. Their warning went from twenty minutes to ten to none, and their life went from the restaurant to the grocery store to the kitchen table.

I'm not telling you this to scare you. Your lining can heal. It just can't heal while half-digested food passes over it every day.

Researchers in Finland and Poland tested 106 healthy adults over 60. None of them had been diagnosed with a gut disease. About 1 in 5 were making too few digestive enzymes.

The older the group, the lower the numbers ran.

So the shortage is common at your age, nothing hurts while it happens, and nobody is testing for it. That's the whole reason it looks like fate.

Your husband eats the same dinner and feels fine. His body still makes enough to break that dinner down. Yours makes less than it used to.

You did nothing to cause this.

Two, your lining needs help to recover. Three probiotic strains do that job: L. plantarum, L. acidophilus and L. casei.

Three, the enzymes have to be waiting when your food arrives. That means taking them before you eat.

Researchers have put enzymes to the test.

In Maryland, 49 people whose IBS-D hit after meals took a prescription enzyme with some meals and a dummy pill with others. Most were women, the average age was 52, and most had lived with it for over ten years. Nobody knew which pill was which.

At the end, 30 of the 49 picked the enzyme.

Those 19 got enzymes with their meals. They went less, their stools firmed up, and their symptoms relieved.

Many people start trusting their body again — leaving the house without the "just in case" routine.

I'm a gastroenterologist.

The man who says that to me is almost always retired and over 65.

Let's call him James. He's 69.

He drove a route for thirty years, and he knew every bathroom and port-a-potty on it.

He takes two Imodium before any drive over an hour.

He skips breakfast on the days he has somewhere to be.

He's had the scope and the bloodwork, and every result came back normal.

One doctor wrote IBS-D on his chart. Another told him to live with it.

So he did. He stopped bringing it up, and he doesn't talk about it with anybody.

If that sounds like you, I wrote this for you.

You know where the nearest bathroom is right now. You checked before you sat down.

A visit with a doctor like me lasts about fifteen minutes. The real answer takes longer than that, so it gets skipped.

I won't skip it here.

Here are the seven questions James asks me, in his own words. He asks most of them in one sentence, and then he waits.

Each answer is one of the seven reasons. After that I'll tell you what you can do about it today.

Question 1: "I've had this for 20 years. Isn't this just how I am now?"

No. You were told to live with it, so you did. That's a different thing.

Here's what was going on the whole time.

Your small intestine is supposed to finish breaking down your food. It does that with enzymes. There's one for protein, one for fat, one for the sugar in milk, and a few for beans and vegetables.

When you make enough of them, your colon only gets waste.

When you run short, your colon gets food.

Your body makes fewer enzymes than it did at 45. It happens a little at a time, and nothing hurts while it happens.

Researchers in Finland and Poland tested 106 healthy adults over 60. None of them had been diagnosed with a gut disease. About 1 in 5 were making too few digestive enzymes.

The older the group, the lower the numbers ran.

Nobody checked yours. So twenty years went by, and you called it normal.

Question 2: "Every test came back fine. So why does my doctor just tell me to live with it?"

Because the tests you had can't see this.

You've sat across from a doctor who looked at your chart, nodded, and said everything looks fine. Then he said the word IBS-D and reached for the Imodium pad.

A colonoscopy looks at the wall of your colon. A CT scan looks at the shape of your organs. Bloodwork looks for inflammation and celiac.

Those tests matter, because they rule out the dangerous things. If you haven't had them, have them.

Not one of them checks whether your food got broken down.

Doctors at Augusta University in Georgia looked at 120 adults who'd had gut symptoms for over a year. Their scans and scopes had all come back normal.

Then the doctors measured the digestive enzymes in the lining of the small intestine. 56 of the 120 were short on at least one.

"IBS-D" is the name you get when the tests find nothing else. It describes what your body does, and it has never told you why.

You always figured that label wasn't a real answer. You were right.

Because your food reaches your colon before it's broken down.

You know every bathroom and port-a-potty between your house and anywhere you go. You planned your routes around them for years.

Here's what you were planning around.

When half-digested food lands in your colon, your colon treats it the way it treats food poisoning. It pulls in water, squeezes hard, and gets everything out fast.

That's why you get the cramping.

That's why your diarrhea is so liquidy.

And that's why it comes with no warning.

Eating makes it worse, and here's the part nobody told you. Your first few bites send a signal down to your colon to make room. Everybody has it, and doctors call it the gastrocolic reflex.

In a healthy gut that signal is a nudge. Your colon is holding your last meal, though, and that meal arrived half-digested and full of water. A nudge is all it takes.

It's also why skipping breakfast gets you through the morning. An empty stomach never sends the signal. You've been going hungry so you can leave the house.

Question 4: "Why am I in the bathroom five, six, seven times every morning before I can leave the house?"

Because supper reaches your colon while you sleep.

It has nothing to do with what you picked for supper.

Supper is the biggest meal of your day, and it takes hours to travel. It lands in your colon in the middle of the night.

Your colon slows down while you sleep. So a half-digested supper sits there for hours, pulling in water.

Some nights the pressure wakes you at 4 a.m. Most mornings it waits until your feet touch the floor, when your colon wakes up too.

Then it clears in rounds. That's trip one, and trip three, and trip six, before you can get in the truck.

Because your body made fewer enzymes than hers did that day.

Your wife's body still makes enough to break that supper down. Yours makes less than it used to. The same plate gives the two of you two different mornings.

And the amount you make changes from one day to the next.

Chicken and potatoes goes down fine on Tuesday. Thursday, the same plate sends you running.

The food didn't change between Tuesday and Thursday. What changed was how many enzymes your body made that day.

There's no way to feel the difference while you're eating. You find out later, in the car.

You did nothing to cause this. You cut foods because nobody told you to look anywhere else.

Because Imodium works on the muscle of your gut. It never touches what's arriving.

Imodium slows the muscles of your gut. Your half-digested food still arrives, only later.

All of it is a bucket under a leak. It catches some of the water, and the pipe stays broken.
