The same Bible that told you the Euphrates River would dry up also tells you that Jesus spent 40 days teaching His apostles about the signs of the end times after He rose from the dead. But it never tells you what He said.

I have read that verse in Acts my whole life and never once stopped to ask where those 40 days went, until my brother drove 6 hours to my house on a Wednesday morning, set a Bible on my kitchen table that was twice the weight of mine, and said, "Open it to the page I marked and read what Jesus told them."

I am not one of those end times people. I have never once stood in a grocery store and thought about the book of Revelation.

I am a grandmother who has read her Bible her whole life and who mostly reads the Psalms. I do not have a prophecy board on my wall.

I do not watch those channels. I go to Sunday school and I make casseroles and I pray for my grandchildren before bed.

That is who I am.

I have sat beside the same women in the same Sunday school class for 20 years. We have buried husbands together, prayed over grandbabies together, and passed the same casserole dishes back and forth so many times nobody remembers whose dish is whose.

When the lesson turned to Revelation, our teacher would read a few verses, say nobody knows the day or the hour, and we would move on to the prayer list.

I was happy with that. I believed the Bible on my end table was the whole thing, and I believed if God wanted me to know more, He would have put more in it.

So when I tell you what my brother put on my kitchen table, I need you to understand it is not coming from someone who was looking for it. I am the one in our family who changes the subject when somebody starts talking about the end of the world at Thanksgiving.

I am the one who says, Let us just pray and pass the potatoes.

But I need to tell you about my brother before I go any further, because if you do not know what kind of man he is, nothing I say after this will land the way it should. Because if a woman like me had told you this, you would have smiled and changed the subject.

I would have too. It took a man like David.

David has been reading the Bible every single morning since 1978. Not most mornings.

Every morning. He reads it the way some men read the newspaper, with a cup of coffee and a pencil, and he has worn through 3 Bibles that I know of.

I have seen those Bibles. The first one fell apart at Genesis and he taped it back together with packing tape.

The second one he gave to a man at a truck stop in Tennessee who asked him what he was reading. The third one sits on his nightstand with notes in the margin so small you need a magnifying glass to read them.

He is not a pastor. He is not a preacher.

He drives a truck for a living and has done it for 31 years. He goes to a small Baptist church in North Carolina where he has sat in the same seat since before my children were born.

He has never missed a Sunday unless he was on the road, and when he is on the road he finds a church wherever he parks the truck. He has sat in the back of churches in 40 states.

He told me once that every one of them read the same 66 books, and that was proof enough for him.

In my whole life I have never heard David say one word about missing books or hidden scriptures. Not one.

He thought that kind of talk was for people on the internet who had too much time and not enough church. He used to say, "The 66 is enough if you actually read it."

When the Ethiopian Bible started showing up on Facebook, David was the one who rolled his eyes. He told me once on the phone that anybody selling a Bible with extra books in it was selling a Bible with somebody else's words in it.

He said it like it was settled, and in our family, when David says a thing like that, it is settled.

That is the man who drove 6 hours on a Wednesday and set a Bible on my table that had 88 books in it. I want you to understand what it took for that man to put that Bible on my table.

David does not change his mind. He did not change his mind about his truck when the company offered him a new one.

He has not changed his mind about anything since 1978.

But for you to understand why I did not sleep that night.

I need to back up.

David called me on a Monday evening about 3 months ago, which was strange because David does not call on weeknights. He calls Sunday after church and that has been the routine since our mother passed.

Our mother taught both of us to read out of the same black King James. She read it at the kitchen table every morning with her coffee, and David is the one who picked up the habit.

I got the Psalms from her. He got everything else.

So when the phone rang on a Monday night and it was David, my first thought was that somebody had died. He said, "I need to ask you something and I need you to actually answer me."

I said okay.

He said, "Have you ever read Acts 1:3?"

I almost laughed. It is the first chapter of Acts.

Every Christian on earth has read Acts 1. I told him I had read it more times than I could count.

I said I was sure I had.

He said, "You have not. You have read past it.

There is a difference. Go get your Bible right now."

He said it the way our father used to talk to us when we were children and he knew we were about to lie. I knew that voice.

I had not heard it in 50 years.

I got up from the couch and got my Bible off the end table and sat back down. My Bible is a red leather King James my late husband gave me for our 30th anniversary.

My name is pressed in gold on the front. The ribbon has been sitting in Psalm 91 for so long it has left a mark on the page.

He said, "Turn to Acts chapter 1 and read me verse 3 out loud."

I read it.

"To whom also he showed himself alive after his passion by many infallible proofs, being seen of them forty days, and speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God." I knew that verse.

I had read it in Sunday school. I had underlined it once, years ago, in blue pen.

I had never read the words forty days and stopped.

He said, "Read it again."

I read it again.

He said, "Forty days. After He rose from the dead.

Speaking of the things pertaining to the kingdom of God. That is not a greeting.

That is not small talk over fish on the beach. The risen Son of God sat with His apostles for 40 days and taught them."

He said, "Luke wrote that. The same Luke who wrote down the shepherds, the manger, the boy Jesus in the temple and every parable you learned in Sunday school.

A doctor who checked everything twice. And when he gets to the 40 most important days in human history, he gives you one sentence and walks away."

I said I knew that.

He said, "Then tell me what He said."

I sat there with the phone against my ear and the Bible open on my knees and I realized I could tell you what Jesus said on the mountain, what He said at the well, what He said at the supper and what He said on the cross. And I could not tell you one single thing He said in the 40 days after He rose.

I did not have an answer.

He said, "Turn the page. Read chapter 2.

Read chapter 3. Keep going.

Tell me where Luke writes down what Jesus taught them in those 40 days."

He said, "And while you are looking, look at what the apostles do. Before the 40 days, they run away.

Peter denies Him three times. Thomas will not believe.

They are hiding in a locked room. Then after the 40 days, those same men walk into the temple and preach to the faces of the men who killed Him, and they are not afraid of anything for the rest of their lives.

Something happened in those 40 days that turned scared men into men who died singing."

I flipped through Acts sitting on my couch with the phone on my shoulder and I could not find it. I went all the way to the end of Acts.

Peter in prison. Paul shipwrecked.

Paul in Rome. Twenty-eight chapters of the apostles preaching everywhere they went.

And not once does any of them say, This is what He told us in the forty days.

He said, "That is because it is not there. 40 days of the risen Christ teaching His closest followers about the kingdom of God and the signs of the end, and your Bible gives you one verse about it and moves on to Pentecost."

Then he said, "It is not only Acts. Turn to Luke 24, verse 27."

I turned to it. The two men on the road to Emmaus, walking with Jesus and not knowing it was Him.

And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, He expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning Himself.

He said, "The risen Christ walked seven miles explaining every scripture about Himself, from Moses to the last prophet. The greatest Bible study that ever happened on this earth.

And Luke does not write down one word of it."

He said, "Now read verse 45."

Then opened He their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures. He said, "He opened their understanding.

Opened it. Whatever He told them changed how they read every page they already had.

That is what you and I never got."

Then he told me to turn to the very end of John. Chapter 21, verse 25.

And there are also many other things which Jesus did, the which, if they should be written every one, I suppose that even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written.

He said, "John tells you to your face there was more. He tells you there were books.

Plural."

I said maybe it was not meant to be recorded.

And he said, "Then why did somebody record it?" He said, "The early church did not throw those 40 days away.

Men who sat with the apostles wrote down what the apostles said Jesus told them after He rose. It was read in churches.

It was copied by hand. And then one day it was not in your Bible anymore."

I did not know what he meant.

He said, "I am driving to your house on Wednesday. I will be there by noon.

I am bringing something and I need you to sit with me at your kitchen table and read it."

He said, "I would tell you on the phone, but you would not believe me. I did not believe the man who told me.

You have to hold it."

I asked him what he was bringing.

He would not tell me. He said, "You will see it when I get there."

He said, "The forty days."

I did not know what to do with that so I said okay and we hung up. I sat on that couch for an hour after he hung up.

I read Acts 1:3 maybe 10 more times. And for the first time in my life I asked myself a question I had never thought to ask.

If the Son of God came back from the dead and spent 40 days telling His friends what was coming, why had nobody ever told me what He said?

I did not sleep much Monday night. I did not sleep much Tuesday night either.

He got there at 11:40. I know because I looked at the clock on the stove when I heard his truck.

I had made a pot of coffee and set out two cups and the lemon pound cake I make for funerals and new babies. I did not know which one this was going to be.

He came in carrying a Bible, but it was not his Bible. His Bible is a brown leather King James that I have seen in his hands for 20 years.

This one was heavier. I could tell by how he set it down.

It was not leather. It was a thick cream book with gold on the corners, and the spine was so wide he carried it with both hands, the way you carry a cake to a church supper.

There were little strips of tape sticking out of the pages like feathers.

He put it on the table and sat across from me and said, "Before I open this, I need to show you something in your Bible first. Not this one.

Yours."

He said, "Everything I am going to show you today starts in the Bible you have trusted your whole life. If I cannot show it to you there first, I will put this one back in the truck."

He told me to turn to the book of Jude.

I turned to it.

He said, "Read verse 14 and 15 out loud."

I read them.

"And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all." My voice went funny on the word Enoch.

I do not know why. I had read it a hundred times.

But I had never read it with somebody across from me waiting for me to notice it.

He said, "Stop. What book is that quoting?"

I looked at it. It says Enoch.

Right there in the verse. Enoch prophesied, saying.

I had read that verse out loud in Sunday school. I had heard my pastor read it from the pulpit.

And not one time did I stop on the name in the middle of it.

He said, "Now find the Book of Enoch in your Bible." I turned to the table of contents.

I went through it twice.

I went slow the second time. Genesis.

Exodus. All the way down to Revelation, with my finger on every line, like I was looking for a grandchild's name in a church directory.

No Enoch.

It is not there.

He said, "Your Bible is quoting a book it does not contain. Jude, a book that every Christian church on earth accepts as scripture, directly quotes the Book of Enoch by name, word for word, and then the Bible that Jude is in does not include the book he is quoting."

He said, "And it is not a little quote. Jude is warning the church about men who crept in unawares, and to prove his point he does not go to Isaiah.

He does not go to Moses. He goes to Enoch.

That is the book an apostle's own brother trusted most when he needed the church to listen."

He said, "Now turn to 2 Peter chapter 2, verse 4." I turned to it.

For if God spared not the angels that sinned, but cast them down to hell, and delivered them into chains of darkness, to be reserved unto judgment.

He said, "Angels in chains. Where does Peter get that?

Your Bible never tells you which angels, or what they did, or why God chained them. The Book of Enoch tells you all of it.

Peter was reading the same book Jude was reading."

I sat there with my finger on the verse and I did not know what to say. It was like finding out a letter you had kept your whole life had a second page, and somebody had torn it off before it ever got to you.

He said, "I want you to feel what that is before I show you anything else. Your Bible points you toward a book and then does not let you read it."

He said, "Your mother read that verse in Jude to us when we were kids. So did your Sunday school teacher.

So did your pastor. And every single one of them read the name Enoch out loud and kept going like it was nothing."

I said maybe there was a reason it was left out. He said, "There was.

I am going to tell you what it was. But first I need to show you one more thing in your Bible.

Turn to Revelation chapter 9."

He said, "And Enoch is not some stranger. Genesis 5 says Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him.

He never died. God took him up alive.

Hebrews 11 puts him in the hall of faith right next to Noah and Abraham. The man your Bible honors that much wrote a book, and your Bible quotes the book, and then hands you nothing."

I turned to it.

He said, "Read verses 7 through 10. Read them slow."

I said I did not like Revelation 9. He said, "Nobody does.

That is why nobody reads it slow."

I read them.

Locusts with shapes like horses prepared for battle. Crowns of gold on their heads.

Faces of men. Breastplates of iron.

The sound of their wings like the sound of chariots of many horses running to battle. Tails like scorpions, with stings.

I had read that passage maybe a hundred times in my life. Every time I pictured bugs.

Big gold bugs with people faces, the kind of thing that gives children nightmares. I always read it fast and turned the page.

He said, "Now tell me who wrote that."

I said John.

The one Jesus loved. The one who leaned on His chest at the last supper.

The one who was there at the cross when everybody else ran.

He said, "And when did John live?"

I said the first century.

He said, "On an island called Patmos. An old man, an exile, the last of the twelve still alive.

Everybody he had walked with was dead. And God showed him the end of the world."

He said, "First century. No planes.

No engines. No machines.

The fastest thing John had ever seen was a horse. The only things that flew in his world were birds and insects.

Now read it again, but this time, read it as a man from the first century describing something he has never seen before and does not have a word for."

He said, "God showed that man the future. Two thousand years of it.

And John did what any of us would do if somebody dropped us into the year 4000 and handed us a pen. He wrote down what it looked like."

I read it again.

This time I did not picture bugs. I pictured an old man on a rocky island, an old prisoner the Romans had sent there to die, watching something tear across the sky that he did not have a word for, and writing down the closest thing he could find.

And this time it hit me like a truck.

He said, "Locusts with crowns on their heads and the faces of men. That is a helicopter.

The spinning propeller looks like the crowns the Romans wore in John's own time. The pilot's face is right there through the cockpit glass.

Faces of men, inside a flying machine that John has no word for. He called it a locust because that is the closest thing in his world."

I had seen those helicopters on the news. Every time there is a war, they show them flying low over the desert in rows, black against the sand.

I had never once in my life put one next to Revelation 9.

I said David.

He said, "Breastplates of iron. Steel.

Sound of their wings like chariots of many horses running. That is a rotor blade.

You have heard that sound. Tell me there is a better way a man from the first century could describe it."

He said, "Verse 9 says they had breastplates, as it were breastplates of iron. As it were.

John keeps saying that. Like.

As it were. As it were the faces of men.

He is telling you over and over, I do not have the word for this, so I am giving you the closest thing I know."

I could not.

He said, "Tails like scorpions, with stings. A scorpion's weapon is in the middle of its back.

A helicopter's missiles are mounted underneath its belly. When they fire, the smoke trail behind them looks exactly like a stinger."

He said, "Verse 10. They had power to hurt men five months.

Hurt. Not kill.

A weapon designed to leave men suffering. Men have built exactly that, and they sell it to each other at trade shows."

He let me sit there.

He said, "John did not stop at the locusts. Go back three chapters.

He saw the sky itself."

Then he said, "Now read Revelation 6, verse 13." I read it.

Stars falling from heaven.

He said, "A missile coming down through the atmosphere at night." He said, "John says they fell like a fig tree casting her untimely figs when she is shaken of a mighty wind.

Hundreds of them at once, coming down out of the black sky. Turn on the news on any night in the last two years and tell me you have not seen that."

Verse 14. The sky departed as a scroll when it is rolled together.

He said, "A nuclear detonation. The mushroom cloud pulls the atmosphere in on itself exactly like a scroll being rolled from both ends."

I sat there thinking about every picture of that mushroom cloud I had ever seen in a history book. The ring of it, rolling up from the bottom and rolling down from the top at the same time.

A scroll rolled together. A man in the first century had no other way to say it.

Verse 15. The kings of the earth and the great men and the rich men hid themselves in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains.

He said, "Nuclear bunkers. Built into mountains.

The same ones governments are building right now."

He said, "Read verse 16. They said to the mountains and rocks, Fall on us, and hide us.

That is men in a hole in the side of a mountain, waiting for what is coming over their heads to stop."

I put my Bible down on the table.

He said, "John was not writing symbols. He was not writing poetry.

He was watching real weapons and real armies through the eyes of a man who had never seen a machine, and he described exactly what he saw the only way he knew how. And every single thing he described is sitting in military arsenals right now."

He said, "And Daniel was told the same thing six hundred years before John. Turn to Daniel 12, verse 4."

I turned to it. But thou, O Daniel, shut up the words, and seal the book, even to the time of the end: many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.

He said, "Seal the book until the time of the end. Then knowledge shall be increased.

You are living in the first generation in history that can read Revelation 9 and recognize every single thing in it. That is not an accident.

That is the seal coming off."

Then he said, "Now let me show you what he saw next. Because that is the part you are not prepared for."

He said, "Go back to Revelation 9, verse 14."

He said, "Because everything John saw so far was the weapons. Now he shows you what lets them loose."

I went back.

4 angels, bound in the great river Euphrates. Their assignment when they are released is to kill a third of mankind.

Not a third of a country. A third of every breathing soul on this planet.

Over 2.6 billion people.

I did the math in my head while I sat there. A third of every person I have ever loved.

A third of my Sunday school class. A third of my grandchildren.

I asked him why angels would be bound in a river. He said, "Because God put them there and told the river to hold them.

And the river is the thing you can watch disappearing."

He said, "The same river that Iraq's own government says will be completely gone by 2040. You can watch it disappearing on satellite images right now.

Year after year, pulling back from the banks."

He said, "Turkey has built dams up the river for decades, one after another, holding the water back before it ever reaches Syria or Iraq. Back in 1990 they shut the flow almost completely for a month to fill one of them.

The Euphrates below that dam dropped to a trickle while the whole world watched."

He said, "Verse 16. 200 million mounted troops.

The creatures they ride breathe fire and smoke and sulfur. Now you know what those creatures actually are."

He said, "And turn to Revelation 16, verse 12. The sixth angel poured out his vial upon the great river Euphrates; and the water thereof was dried up, that the way of the kings of the east might be prepared."

I read it twice. Dried up.

Not low. Dried up.

He said, "Two different chapters. Two different judgments.

Both of them come back to the same river. God does not mention a river twice in the last book of the Bible by accident."

I did.

I had seen the tanks with the fire coming out of their mouths. I had seen the smoke.

I had seen the rockets. I just never knew I had been reading about them in my own Bible since I was a girl.

He said, "And the only thing between those weapons and that assignment is a river that is almost gone." Then he said, "That river is older than any nation on earth.

It flowed out of the Garden of Eden. Genesis 2:14.

It is one of the four rivers God made on the first week of the world. It was the border of the land He promised Abraham.

And the last time it was turned aside, a kingdom fell in one night."

I asked him what he meant.

He said, "Daniel 5. Belshazzar threw a feast and drank out of the gold cups stolen from God's temple.

A hand came out of nowhere and wrote on the wall while he watched. That same night the army outside Babylon turned the Euphrates out of its bed, and marched in under the walls on the dry riverbed.

Belshazzar was dead by morning. The river went down, and the kingdom ended."

He let that sit for a long time.

I could hear the clock on the stove. I could hear my own heart.

I thought about every news report I had half listened to about droughts and dams in the Middle East while I was drying dishes. I had never once thought any of it had anything to do with me.

Then he put his hand on the heavy Bible on the table and said, "Now I am going to show you the forty days." But before he opened it, he said, "I need to do one more thing in your Bible first.

Turn to Exodus 24, verse 7."

I did not want to turn any more pages. I felt like I had seen enough for one day, enough for a whole year.

But I turned to it, because by then I knew he was not going to show me anything that was not already in my own Bible.

I turned to it.

He said, "Read it out loud."

I read it. "And he took the Book of the Covenant, and read in the audience of the people."

He said, "Now go back to verse 4. And Moses wrote all the words of the Lord.

Moses wrote them down. Then he read them to the people, and the people said all that the Lord hath said will we do.

Then Moses took the blood and sprinkled it on the people and said, Behold the blood of the covenant. A whole nation stood in blood that morning over what was in that book."

He said, "Stop. What is Moses holding?"

I looked at the verse. The Book of the Covenant.

He said, "Now turn to 2 Kings 23, verse 2."

He said, "Moses is not holding the Ten Commandments in that verse. Those are on stone.

Moses is holding a book. A book of words God gave him, read out loud to the whole nation, and sealed in blood."

I turned to it. King Josiah standing in the temple, reading to all the people of Judah, every word of the Book of the Covenant, which had been found in the house of the Lord.

I read it slowly. And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the Lord, to walk after the Lord, and to keep His commandments with all their heart and all their soul.

The whole nation stood to it. Every person from the smallest to the greatest.

He said, "Found. That word should stop you cold.

The Book of the Covenant had been lost. It was missing from the temple for so long that when a priest found it buried in a wall during renovations, the king tore his robes and wept because nobody alive had heard what was in it.

The most important document Moses ever wrote, the covenant between God and His people, and it had disappeared for an entire generation. Read 2 Chronicles 34:30 if you want the same story told twice."

He said, "Read 2 Kings 22 if you want the whole scene. Hilkiah the priest finds it.

Shaphan the scribe reads it to the king. And the king hears it and tears his clothes in front of everybody, because he realizes his whole nation has been living without the words God gave them, and the wrath of God was already burning because of it."

He let me sit with that.

I thought about Josiah. Eight years old when he became king.

Raised his whole life in a nation that thought it was serving God. And then a priest walks in with dust on his hands and a book nobody had read in his lifetime, and the king finds out in one afternoon that everything he had been taught was missing the most important part.

He did not argue with it. He did not say, We have done fine without it.

He tore his clothes and he wept, and then he gathered the whole nation and read every word of it to them out loud.

Then he said, "Your Bible mentions the Book of the Covenant by name at least 3 times. Moses wrote it.

Josiah wept when they found it. God sealed an entire covenant in blood over it.

And right now, tonight, if you go to your table of contents and try to find the Book of the Covenant, you will not find it. Because it is not there.

Your Bible names it, quotes from it, records kings tearing their clothes over it, and then does not include it."

He said, "And this is the part nobody wants to say out loud. If a book that important could be lost once, inside the temple, with priests walking past it every single day, it could be lost again.

And it was. Only this time, nobody tore down a wall to look for it."

I did not know what to say.

I sat there thinking about all the times I had heard a preacher say the Bible we have is exactly the Bible God gave. And my own Bible was telling me, in three different books, that a book God gave His people had been lost, and that when they found it, a king wept and a whole nation repented.

He opened the heavy Bible to a page he had marked with a piece of tape. The tape was the blue painter's tape he keeps in his truck.

He had marked so many pages in it that the book looked like a porcupine on my table.

He said, "This is it. This is the Book of the Covenant.

It has not been in any western Bible for over a thousand years. But it was preserved, word for word, in the same place this Bible comes from."

He said, "Your Bible says the book was lost and found. It never says the book was lost a second time.

That part they did not have to write down. They only had to leave it out."

I said, "Where?"

I did not say it like a question. I said it like I was afraid of the answer.

He said, "Ethiopia."

I said it back to him like I was not sure I had heard it. Ethiopia.

I had seen it on the news when I was young, pictures of hungry children. I had never once in my life heard anybody connect that country to my Bible.

He told me Ethiopia became the first Christian nation on earth. They received the complete scriptures before any council decided what to cut.

Before the burnings. Before the politics.

By the time the rest of the world started arguing over which books belonged and which ones to remove, Ethiopia had already been guarding them for generations in monasteries carved into the sides of mountains, copied by hand in a language the rest of the world could not read.

He said, "Ethiopia had the scriptures from the first generation of the church. And while every empire around them was conquered, burned, divided and rewritten, Ethiopia was never conquered.

Not by Rome, not by the armies that took the rest of Africa, not by anybody. So nobody ever walked into their churches and told them which books to throw out."

He said, "When the first King James Bible was printed in 1611, it still had 80 books in it. Tobit was in it.

Judith was in it. Both books of Esdras were in it.

Over the next two hundred years, publishers kept printing it thinner and thinner until they stopped printing those books at all. Ethiopia never printed theirs thinner.

Not once."

He said, "And the Book of Enoch, the one Jude is quoting, was lost to the western world for over a thousand years. When men finally went looking for it, they found it in one place.

Ethiopia. They had been reading it in church the whole time."

He said, "That is why this Bible has 88 books and yours has 66." He said, "And here is what should settle it for you.

When they found the Dead Sea Scrolls in those caves in 1947, older than any Bible anybody had ever held, Enoch was in there. Jubilees was in there.

Copied by hand before Jesus was born. The people who say these books were made up later have to explain what they were doing in a cave a hundred years before Christ."

Then he said, "Now read what is on the page I marked." He had his hand flat on the cover for a second before he slid it across the table to me.

The way you hand somebody a baby.

I read the opening line of the Book of the Covenant out loud. My hands were shaking a little.

I am not ashamed to tell you. I had my reading glasses on and the type was big and clear, and I put my finger under the first line the way our mother taught us to when we were small.

"In the time when I was in the world, I spoke unto you before I should be glorified, of signs that the end is near." I read it a second time out loud, slower.

Of signs that the end is near. The same signs my Sunday school teacher said nobody could know.

Jesus Himself was sitting with His apostles telling them what they were.

That is Jesus speaking. After the resurrection.

To His apostles. Telling them about the signs of the end.

He turned the pages slowly and showed me where Jesus tells them the signs before the end. Rulers who love money and hate the truth.

A king rising from the West. Signs in the sky.

Shepherds who love gain more than their sheep. Then he showed me where Jesus describes the face of the man who comes at the very end, the Son of Perdition, so plainly that I could have drawn him.

His eyes. His mouth.

What he does when he comes.

I sat there and thought about the evening news. Every one of those signs I had seen that same week.

The forty days.

And it was not only the warnings. He turned to a page where Jesus tells them that His Father chose holy vessels out of the very last generation, the latest generation, the ones who would be alive at the end.

And that He was telling the apostles exactly what was coming so those people would know it.

I read that line three times. The latest generation.

That is us. That is my grandchildren.

Jesus was thinking about my grandchildren on the other side of the resurrection and He told His apostles what they would need to know.

Then David showed me the place where Jesus says that His private words, the things He spoke to them alone, are given to the faithful ones who have the desire to know. That from the day His people want to know, He will make His home with them and give them understanding.

I put my hand flat on the page. I had wanted to know my whole life.

I just never knew there was anything left to know.

I said, "This is what He taught them?"

I did not say it loud. I think I whispered it.

I felt like I had walked into a room where Jesus had just been talking, and He had stepped out, and His words were still in the air.

David said, "This is what He taught them."

He said, "And at the end of it, it tells you who wrote it down. John and Peter and Matthew.

They wrote it and sent copies to every church. Three of the twelve.

Men who ate fish on that beach with Him after He rose. That is whose handwriting your Bible left out."

I read for about 20 minutes without saying a word. David drank his coffee and did not interrupt me once.

I read the prayer the apostles prayed, asking God to drive out every proud thought by His Name, the Name that makes the grave itself shake and drives the spirits away. I read where Jesus tells them that the ones who keep His words will be delivered from the evil days that are about to come, and that He will be with them, showing them His ways.

Delivered from the evil days that are about to come. I had spent the last 40 minutes staring at helicopters and bunkers and a river going dry, and here was Jesus, in His own words, telling me what to do about it.

I read where He tells them to pray at midnight and at the dawn, because that is when the angels visit the church. I thought about how many nights I have lain awake at 3 in the morning thinking about my children.

I never once knew the angels were awake too.

When I looked up he said, "Now you understand why I drove 6 hours." He said, "I drove 6 hours because I could not stand the thought of you reading Revelation one more time with no idea what Jesus told His own men about it.

You are my sister. You are the last one left in this family who reads every day.

I was not going to tell you over the phone."

I said I was not sure I understood any of this. I was not.

I felt like a woman who had been living in the same house for 53 years and had just found a door in the hallway that she had walked past every single day.

He said, "You understand more than you think. You have been reading a Bible your whole life that quotes books it does not contain, describes modern weapons in ancient language, and skips over the most important conversation Jesus ever had with His apostles.

And nobody ever told you to ask why."

He said, "And it is not just the Covenant. In the Book of Enoch there is a vision of the very end of the world.

Most of the sheep are blind and deaf. But some lambs are born, and they begin to open their eyes and see, and they cry out to the others.

And at the very end, the eyes of all of them are opened."

He said, "You are one of those lambs right now. You are sitting at your kitchen table with your eyes coming open.

Enoch saw you coming."

I said, "David, this sounds like something off the internet." I said it because that is what I tell my grandchildren when they show me something on their phones.

I said it because I was scared that if I let myself believe it, I would have to change something.

He said, "Then check it. Tonight.

After I leave. Open your Bible to Jude 14 and see whose words your Bible is quoting.

Then try to find that book in your table of contents. You will not find it, because it was removed.

Then read Revelation 9 again and tell me those are not helicopters and missiles. Then come back to this Bible and read what Jesus said during those 40 days.

And if any of it does not line up with scripture, you call me and I will drive back down here and take this Bible off your table myself."

He said, "I am not asking you to trust me. I am asking you to trust the Bible you already have.

It is the one sending you to this one."

I asked him why he had not told me sooner.

He said he had not known sooner. Three months ago he did not know any more than I did.

He had read the same verses for 46 years and never stopped either.

He said, "Because I did not believe it until I held it. Somebody can tell you about it all day long and it sounds like a theory.

But when you sit at a table and read the words of Christ that your Bible does not contain, and every word lines up with the 66 books you already trust, that is not a theory. That is a missing piece."

He said, "I tried for two weeks to find something in it that went against the Bible I have read since 1978. I read it with a pencil.

I could not find one thing. What I found was the other half of a hundred verses I had read past my whole life."

I asked him where he found it.

I had to know. If it had come from a website, I was going to give it back to him.

I am not going to put something on my table next to my Bible that came from some man in a basement.

He said a man at a job site told him about a group called Faith Made. Small group of believers who went directly to Ethiopia and brought back the complete ancient Bible exactly as the Ethiopian church preserved it.

All 88 books. Nothing added.

Nothing rewritten. Nothing softened by a committee.

He said the man had a Faith Made Bible on the dashboard of his truck, the pages so full of pencil marks they were gray. David asked him what it was, the way you ask a man about his tools.

The man said, Brother, it is the rest of the Bible, and you are going to think I am crazy until you read the first page.

David said over 200,000 people have one now. He said they have more than 120,000 reviews, people telling what it did to the way they pray and the way they read.

He said the people who made it come with an app where thousands of believers read and pray together every single day.

He said he ordered one expecting to prove the man wrong and he read it for 4 days straight. He said he read it in his truck at the loading docks, at truck stops, at his kitchen table until two in the morning.

He said he missed church one Sunday for the first time in 20 years because he fell asleep at 4 a.m. with it on his chest. He said that was the only Sunday the pastor ever called to check on him.

I asked him what it felt like.

I asked it because David does not talk about feelings. I have known him 70 years and I have heard him say the word feel maybe twice.

He said, "It felt like putting on glasses for the first time. Everything I had read for 46 years was still there.

Nothing contradicted. But the parts that never quite made sense, the verses that felt like they were pointing at something I could not see, suddenly I could see what they were pointing at."

He said, "For 46 years I read about the angels that sinned and never knew what they did. I read about the giants and never knew where they came from.

I read Acts 1:3 and never asked what He said. I was reading a letter with half the pages missing, and I was so used to the gaps I thought they were part of the letter."

Then he said the thing I think about every night before I fall asleep. It is the thing I have told my daughter, my son, my sister and half my Sunday school class since.

I will tell it to you exactly the way he said it to me.

He said, "The Euphrates is drying up right now. The weapons John described already exist.

The 4 angels are in that water. And the one set of instructions Jesus gave for how to understand what is coming next is in a book that was taken off your shelf before you were born."

He said, "And there is a book in there called 2 Esdras. Ezra sees a vision of the end, and in it God stops the springs of the Euphrates so His people can cross over on dry ground.

And when they come back at the end, He stops the river again. That river is a door, and God is the one who opens it."

He said, "I am not willing to watch my sister walk into what is coming without the full Word of God in her hands. That is why I am here."

He said, "When the Lord comes, I want Him to find you with your eyes open. I do not want Him to find you with half a Bible and your eyes closed, saying nobody told me."

I did not say anything for a while.

I looked at his hands on the table. Big trucker's hands, cracked from 31 years of cold mornings and tarps and chains.

Those hands had held a Bible every morning since 1978. And they were shaking.

He said, "One more thing, and this is the part that should bother you the most." He said it quietly.

David never raises his voice. That is how I knew it mattered.

He told me to turn to the front of the Ethiopian Bible and count the books. I counted them out loud like a child, moving my finger down the contents page.

It took a long time. I lost count once and started over.

88 books. The 66 I already know, plus 22 that most Bibles leave out.

He said, "Not 22 strange books. 22 books the early church read.

More than half of them were printed in the first King James. They were not added to this Bible.

They were taken out of yours."

He said, "Those 22 books include the Book of Enoch, which Jude is quoting in your own Bible. They include Jubilees, where God dictates history directly to Moses.

They include the Book of Judith, which describes armies crossing the Euphrates and burning through the same geography you see on the news every single night."

He said, "They include the Book of Judith, the woman who walked into an enemy camp with nothing in her hands but a prayer. The night before, she prayed that God's power does not stand in numbers or strong men, that He is the God of the afflicted, the helper of the oppressed, the protector of the forsaken and the savior of those without hope.

Her whole city was surrounded and dying of thirst. And God used one widow to save every one of them."

He said, "The enemy knew exactly which books to remove, the ones that name the demons, describe what is coming, and tell you how to survive it. And the men he worked through made sure you never saw them."

He said, "Enoch tells you where demons come from. Peter and Jude point at it and your Bible goes quiet.

Enoch tells you God sets holy angels as guardians over the righteous, to guard them like the apple of His eye, until He makes an end of all wickedness. Who do you think wanted that page out of your hands?

Not God."

Then he said, "But God does not lose."

He said it the way our mother used to say it when the doctors had bad news for our father. She would put her hand on the table and say, God does not lose, and then she would get up and make supper.

He said, "Everything they stripped out, He preserved. Every page.

Every word. Waiting in Ethiopia for over a thousand years until somebody brought it into English."

He said, "The same God who kept the Book of the Covenant behind a wall in the temple kept these books in a nation that was never conquered. He hid His word in the one place the enemy could not reach.

That is not a story about men. That is a story about God."

I sat at my kitchen table after David left and I did not move for a long time. His truck pulled out at a quarter to five.

I watched it go down the road from the front window. Then I came back and sat in his chair, across from where I had been sitting, and looked at the two Bibles side by side.

My red one with my name in gold. And the big cream one with tape sticking out of it like feathers.

Then I picked up the Ethiopian Bible and turned back to the Book of the Covenant and read what Jesus said to His apostles during those 40 days. I read about the signs again, and this time I was not scared of them.

Jesus was not telling His men those things to frighten them. He was telling them so they would not be caught by surprise.

So they would know Him when everything else was falling apart.

I read where Jesus tells them that the ones who know His sufferings and keep His words will be made holy, and that He will be with them in the evil days. I read where He promises that if their sins were as many as the sand of the sea, and they understood these words and did them, every one of those sins would be forgiven.

I read the widow's night prayer, asking God to strengthen her heart until it is made perfect, because He gave her a great name, the name of a Christian.

I am a widow. I prayed that prayer out loud in my empty kitchen that night, and it was the first time since my husband died that I did not feel alone in that house.

And I cried at my kitchen table, not because I was scared, but because I had been reading my Bible for 53 years and I had never once been allowed to read that page. 53 years.

Every Sunday school lesson. Every sermon.

Every morning in the Psalms. And the words Jesus spoke to His own apostles after He walked out of the grave had been sitting in a church in Ethiopia the whole time, waiting for somebody to bring them to me.

I was not angry at God. I was angry at whoever decided I did not need it.

And then I was just grateful, because God had not let it go.

I ordered one for my daughter that night.

My daughter has three little boys and a husband who works nights. She reads her Bible on her phone in the school pickup line.

I thought about her reading Revelation 9 in that car line one day and seeing exactly what I saw, without anybody next to her to show her the rest.

Not because David told me to. Not because I am the kind of woman who buys things off the internet at 10 o'clock at night.

I ordered it because I sat at my table and read the words of Christ that I had never been given, and every single word lined up with the 66 books I already trust, and I could not in good conscience keep that to myself.

I ordered it because I have prayed for my children every night of their lives that God would protect them, and I never once thought to give them what He told His own apostles about the days that are coming. Then I ordered one for my son.

Then one for my sister.

My son called me the day his came. He is 48 years old and he called me crying in his truck in the parking lot at his work.

He had read the first page of the Book of the Covenant sitting in the driver's seat before he went in. He said, Mama, why did nobody ever show us this?

Then one for the woman in my Sunday school class who lost her husband in March and has been reading her Bible on her back porch every morning since, looking for something she could not name. I wrote her a note and put it in the package so it would be the first thing she saw.

I wrote, Start in the Book of the Covenant. It is what He told them after He rose.

You will see why when you get there.

I think she was looking for the rest of it.

I think a lot of us are. We read every morning and we pray every night and there is a place in us that keeps asking, is this all of it?

I asked that question for 53 years without knowing I was asking it.

You get the audiobook and the digital version free with it, which matters to me because I started listening that same night while I was lying in bed staring at the ceiling trying to process what David had put on my table. I was not going to sleep anyway.

It is 300 hours of it. I have been listening to the Book of Enoch with my coffee in the morning and the Book of the Covenant in the car on the way to the grocery store.

There is something about hearing Jesus' words out loud, in a room by yourself, that I do not know how to explain to you. You will have to hear it.

If you order 2 they ship free, which is how I ended up ordering 4 in one night, because once you start thinking about the people in your life who are reading an incomplete Bible, you cannot stop at one. I also joined the app the first week.

bodyText:
The last book of the Bible was not written to you.

It was written to seven churches. Real churches, in real cities, with real problems and real addresses.

And those cities are still standing. Archaeologists have excavated every single one of them.

Most Christians read Revelation as a coded prediction of the future. A timeline of events that have not happened yet. They look for helicopters in the locusts. They look for nuclear war in the fire. They look for modern nations in the beasts.

But the very first verse of the book says something that almost everyone skips right past.

"The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place."

Soon.

Not in two thousand years. Soon.

And then, three verses later, it names the recipients.

"John to the seven churches that are in Asia: To Ephesus, and to Smyrna, and to Pergamum, and to Thyatira, and to Sardis, and to Philadelphia, and to Laodicea."

Seven real cities. Seven real congregations. Seven letters written to people who were living under Roman persecution and needed to hear from God before they perished.

Every one of those cities has been found. Every one has been dug up by archaeologists. And when you read the letters alongside the archaeology, something happens to this book that most Christians have never once experienced.

It starts making sense.

Take Laodicea.

Every Christian knows the verse. "Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth."

For centuries, pastors have preached this as a warning about passion. Be on fire for God or be completely cold. Just do not be somewhere in the middle.

But that is not what the text is saying. And the congregation in Laodicea would have recognized it instantly.

Laodicea had no water source.

The neighboring city of Hierapolis had famous hot springs, mineral-rich, medicinal, used for healing. The neighboring city of Colossae had cold mountain springs, clean, crisp, and refreshing.

Laodicea had neither. Its water was piped in through a stone aqueduct from miles away. By the time it arrived, it was lukewarm. Mineral-crusted. Useless. Not hot enough to heal. Not cold enough to refresh.

Jesus was not talking about passion. He was talking about usefulness.

Hot water heals. Cold water refreshes. Lukewarm water does nothing for anyone.

The church at Laodicea had become useless to the people around them. And every person in that congregation, drinking that same tepid water every single day of their lives, understood precisely what He meant.

Now look at Sardis.

"I will come like a thief." Another verse every Christian has heard. Another verse almost nobody reads in context.

Sardis was built on top of a cliff. The city was considered unassailable. Its walls were so high and its position so secure that the guards grew complacent. They stopped watching.

Twice in its history, once under the Persians and once under the Greeks, enemy soldiers scaled the unguarded cliffs at night and seized the city while it slept.

When Jesus told the church at Sardis "I will come like a thief," He was not issuing a general warning about the end times. He was pointing to the most infamous military disaster in their city's own history and saying: You are doing exactly what your ancestors did. You stopped watching.

They would have felt that in their bones.

Now look at Pergamum.

"I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is."

For centuries, theologians argued about what this meant. Was it metaphorical? Spiritual? Symbolic?

Then archaeologists uncovered the Great Altar of Zeus at Pergamum. A massive, towering stone throne, one of the largest pagan religious monuments ever constructed in the ancient world. It dominated the city skyline. Every Christian living in Pergamum would have seen it from their front door.

That altar was excavated in the 1800s. It was transported to Germany. It now sits reassembled in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. You can walk up to it and touch it.

Satan's throne was not a metaphor.

It was a street address.

This is what happens to Revelation when you give people the context that was stripped away by two thousand years of distance. The book most Christians avoid because it frightens them becomes the book that shows how precisely God speaks to real people in real places.

Every detail was composed for a specific city. Every warning pointed to a situation those believers were living through. Every promise answered a genuine fear carried by real people who were watching their friends be arrested, tortured, and executed for refusing to bow to the emperor.

Revelation was never a code about the future.

It was a letter to people who were not sure they would survive the week. And every word was written so they would hold on.

That is the realization I came to sitting across from a woman named Sarah two years ago.

Sarah had been a Christian for over forty years. She tithed. She volunteered. She came to every Wednesday night study our church offered. And she had never once opened the book of Revelation.

"I was told it was about the end of the world," she said. "I was told there were beasts and plagues and a mark you could accidentally receive. I spent my whole life frightened of the last book of my own Bible."

I opened to Revelation 2 and asked her to read the letter to the church at Smyrna.

She read it slowly.

"Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life."

She looked up. "That is not about the end of the world. That is about right now. That is about holding on."

I told her about the Crown of Smyrna, a famous ring of ancient buildings encircling the hilltop of that city, known throughout the Roman Empire. When Jesus promised the crown of life to believers in Smyrna, He was speaking in their own architectural language. Their city wore a crown of stone. He was offering one that would never crumble.

She sat quietly for a long moment.

"Forty years," she said. "Forty years I was afraid of this book. And it was written for people exactly like me. People who were frightened. People who needed to hear that it was going to be worth it."

She could not see it. And it was not her fault.

Nobody had ever given her the roots.

The next morning I started writing. And I quickly understood this was bigger than me.

So I reached out to a group of Bible teachers and pastors I had trusted for years, people who have spent their lives teaching Scripture in plain language.

Together, we began with Genesis. Everything a person needs to know before they read each book. Who wrote it. When. Why. What was happening in that city, in that empire, in that century. The central themes. How it connects to the larger story.

Not a commentary. Not a devotional. Just the roots.

Every page was written, reviewed, and rewritten by multiple teachers until my teenage son could read it and understand it completely on his own.

Sixty-six pages. One page per book. Four months of combined decades of study distilled into plain language any believer could work through on their own.

No pastor required.

When we finished, I brought a copy to Sarah.

She called me four days later. "I finished Revelation last night. The whole book. For the first time in my life. And I was not afraid once."

I started passing copies to others in my church quietly. One at a time. Every single person said the same thing.

"This is the first time I have ever understood what I was reading."

Not because we are gifted teachers. But because we finally gave them what they actually needed.

The roots.

Did you know that when Jesus said "It is finished," the Greek word tetelestai was the same word stamped on receipts in the Roman Empire to mean "paid in full"? His final breath was not a cry of defeat. It was a declaration of completion.

Did you know that the prophet Hosea, writing eight centuries before the empty tomb, wrote "After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live before Him"? The resurrection timeline was planted in the Old Testament hundreds of years before it happened.

Context changes everything. Every single time.

I call it The 66 Roots Journey. It has 66 pages. One for every book of the Bible. Each page gives you what you need before you open to the first verse. Who wrote it. When. Why. What was happening. The key themes. The symbolism. And how it connects to your actual life today.

Written in plain language. No seminary terms. No complicated theology.

Just the roots that make everything you have already read suddenly land with the full weight God intended.

Revelation was not written as a puzzle for scholars to decode in the distant future. It was written as a letter to frightened believers in seven real cities who needed to know that their suffering was seen, their faithfulness mattered, and their King was coming.

Two thousand years later, those cities are still there. The archaeology confirms every detail. And the letter still says the same thing it said the day it was written.

Hold on. It is going to be worth it.

If you have ever skipped the last book of your Bible because someone told you it was too complex or too frightening.

If you have ever read a verse you have heard your whole life and wondered what it actually meant to the people who first received it.

If you have ever wondered what you would find in God's Word if someone just gave you the context first.

This is what you have been looking for.

Get closer to God by actually understanding His Word.

Not just the familiar parts. All of it. The whole story.

That is what The 66 Roots Journey was created for.

And you can start yours today. I'll link it right down below.

God bless you and your journey through His Word. 🤍
title: Read This If You Read the Bible ☝️

The first DAY ZERO novel now has more than 500 reader ratings on Amazon. One reader described the experience this way: “I was at times feeling that this was really happening.”

Russia’s war against Ukraine has already changed Europe’s sense of its own security. European capitals are now openly discussing the risk of Russian attacks on NATO countries, while the Alliance strengthens its defenses. Behind these headlines lies a question that runs through DAY ZERO: what happens when one side sees its next move as an act of deterrence, while the other sees it as the beginning of an attack? Each believes it understands its adversary and has the situation under control. Between those convictions are millions of people who will learn what has been decided only when the consequences reach them.

Perhaps the most unsettling part of a story like this is recognizing the world you live in. Familiar capitals. Familiar talk of security, deterrence, and red lines. The familiar conviction that, at the last moment, someone will stop, pick up the phone, and find the right words.

But what if everyone is waiting for the other side to stop first?

My DAY ZERO series begins with that question.

In the first book, NUCLEAR WAR: THE LAST FLASH WE EVER SAW, a tactical nuclear strike on Iran is described as “limited.” Behind that word lie calculations, military plans, and the belief that the consequences can still be controlled. Behind closed doors, people believe they understand their adversary. They know where the other side will back down. They have anticipated the response.

Then the response comes—and demands another decision.

Washington calls emergency meetings. Moscow places its strategic forces on alert. Beijing tracks missile movements. European capitals try to buy time. Every new order is intended to protect one country, yet to someone on the other side, it becomes a signal to prepare for the worst.

As you read, you step inside that chain of decisions. You see the information people rely on and the gaps they fill with assumptions. You understand the fear of someone who cannot bring themselves to back down, and the reasoning of someone else who believes that waiting has become more dangerous than striking. And it grows harder to answer a simple question: who can still stop this?

These were the people who interested me as I wrote the book. Presidents, commanders, and analysts, with their experience, their mistakes, and responsibilities no one can fully prepare for. Alongside them are millions of people whose day began with ordinary things.

Someone is driving to work. Someone is taking a child to school. Someone puts down their phone because they have had enough of the news. Each has plans for the evening and someone they mean to call later.

The decisions that will shape that “later” are already being made.

Today, DAY ZERO spans 18 books. The story moves through nuclear escalation, the collapse of familiar life, and the struggle for a future—for food, medicine, trust, and the chance to rebuild. Its world expands as the consequences of those first decisions unfold.

And it all begins with Book One.

My stories now have a home of their own at samnyxon.com. There you can explore the books, discover the series, and find the reading order, so you know where to begin and where the story leads next.

If you enjoy thrillers that keep you weighing every decision and stay with you long after you have put them down, I invite you into DAY ZERO.

On Thursday, November 5th, just before 3 p.m., America's Doomsday Plane flew over Ohio at 31,000 feet, headed for Washington. If a Nuclear War ever starts, that's the plane the President runs the country from.

Nobody told you about it. Nobody said why.

Then, on Friday, November 6th, American forces struck Iran again.

On Saturday, November 7th, Iran's army declared it will retaliate against these attacks without geographical limits. And now I want you to ask yourself what they are getting ready for?

I've been briefed on things that would have every family in America hiding in their basement tonight if they were made public. I can't share the briefings. But I can share what I've done for my own family since receiving them. And what a retired three-star general started doing quietly every Saturday morning six months ago should tell you more than any headline you've scrolled past this year.

My daughter lives in Ohio. Married. Two kids. Three states away from me. She calls every Sunday. We talk about the grandkids. About her job. Normal things.

In September I started a different kind of call.

I can't brief her the way I was briefed. I can't show her the files. I can't explain what I know using the words I heard it in. Thirty-one years in uniform and the thing I can't do with what I've learned is SAY it.

But I can tell her what to DO.

So I wrote her a list. Not an emergency checklist from a website. A list from her father. Specific. Ordered. With dates. Each item an instruction I can give without explaining the intelligence behind it.

I mailed it in a plain envelope. No letterhead. No subject line. Just the list. And a note at the top that said: "Do these before December 24th. Don't ask me why on the phone. Just do them. Trust me the way you trusted me when I told you to wear your seatbelt before you understood what a car accident was."

She called me the night she opened it.

"Dad. What is this?"

"A list."

"I can see it's a list. Why does it have DATES on it?"

"Because the things on it need to be done before specific dates. And the most important date is December 24th."

"Why December 24th?"

"I can't tell you why. I can tell you that every person I served with who's been briefed at the level I was briefed has done every item on that list already. Most of them before summer."

She was quiet.

"Dad, you're scaring me."

"Good. Scared people prepare. Comfortable people scroll."

Let me show you the list. The same list. Item by item. Because what a three-star general wrote for his daughter is what I'd write for every family in this country if I could mail it to 100 million houses.

ITEM 1: Find every freshwater source within two miles of your house. Creek. River. Stream. Rain collection point. Map them. Walk to each one. Measure the distance. Time the walk.

She called about this one first.

"Why do I need to know where the creeks are?"

"Because someday the thing you turn on in your kitchen every morning might not give you what it's supposed to. And when that day comes, the answer isn't in your garage. It's in the landscape around your house that you've driven past for twelve years without thinking about."

"When is 'someday'?"

"The list has a date on it."

"But Dad, we have food. Flashlights. Batteries. Generator. We're prepared."

"You're prepared for everything that LASTS. Food lasts months. Batteries last years. Generator fuel, you can fill a tank. First aid sits in a cabinet. You can stockpile almost everything your family needs. But your generator runs the fridge. It can't run the pumps that push water to your tap."

"There is ONE thing you cannot stockpile enough of. The one thing your body can't go three days without. A case lasts less than a day for your family. bodyText:
One hundred and seventy-five years after a nuclear war wiped out ninety-two percent of humanity, the survivors live in Underground Cities. The Surface is a radioactive wasteland crawling with mutated monsters. When a thirty-man Vanguard scout team goes dark up top, the government wakes its best soldier — Caden Foster, call-sign Silver Wolf — and sends him up alone to find them.

Caden is a pragmatist and a lone wolf. He goes without backup. His only company is Zoe, a tactical AI in his ear. On the Surface he quickly finds the Vanguard dead or scattered, killed by the hostile lifeforms they were sent to document. He kills the monster that cornered the survivors — a sound-hunting, eight-limbed creature the survivors call the Walker — and saves the nine men still alive. Then he walks away. Finding them was his job. Leading them home is theirs.

What follows is a two-year mission on a dead Earth. Caden hunts mutated creatures, documents them, and survives on nutrient paste and salvaged fuel. He raids a pre-war Tactical Doll outpost — a compound of combat androids frozen without a commander — and wakes a five-star sniper android he names Ivy. She becomes his partner. She is smarter than most humans, loyal to a fault, and slowly becomes the one person he actually lets matter to him.

Together they fight through hostile human shelters, a predatory faction called the Beast Clan, and the broken politics of a world where the government in exile is losing its grip. Caden trades guns for food, negotiates with surface settlers, and gradually gets pulled into the larger war between the new government and a renegade force called the Chaos Insurgency — defectors who stole military hardware and want the government destroyed.

By the back half of the story, Caden is no longer a lone scout. He commands a strike unit called the Wolf Pack, runs helicopter assaults, and fights a sustained campaign against the Insurgency. The monsters that defined the opening become background hazards. The show that began as one man against a mutated world becomes a military faction serial, with Ivy as the warm emotional thread running underneath all of it.

bodyText:
The last book of the Bible was not written to you.

It was written to seven churches. Real churches, in real cities, with real problems and real addresses.

And those cities are still standing. Archaeologists have excavated every single one of them.

Most Christians read Revelation as a coded prediction of the future. A timeline of events that have not happened yet. They look for helicopters in the locusts. They look for nuclear war in the fire. They look for modern nations in the beasts.

But the very first verse of the book says something that almost everyone skips right past.

"The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his servants the things that must soon take place."

Soon.

Not in two thousand years. Soon.

And then, three verses later, it names the recipients.

"John to the seven churches that are in Asia: To Ephesus, and to Smyrna, and to Pergamum, and to Thyatira, and to Sardis, and to Philadelphia, and to Laodicea."

Seven real cities. Seven real congregations. Seven letters written to people who were living under Roman persecution and needed to hear from God before they perished.

Every one of those cities has been found. Every one has been dug up by archaeologists. And when you read the letters alongside the archaeology, something happens to this book that most Christians have never once experienced.

It starts making sense.

Take Laodicea.

Every Christian knows the verse. "Because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth."

For centuries, pastors have preached this as a warning about passion. Be on fire for God or be completely cold. Just do not be somewhere in the middle.

But that is not what the text is saying. And the congregation in Laodicea would have recognized it instantly.

Laodicea had no water source.

The neighboring city of Hierapolis had famous hot springs, mineral-rich, medicinal, used for healing. The neighboring city of Colossae had cold mountain springs, clean, crisp, and refreshing.

Laodicea had neither. Its water was piped in through a stone aqueduct from miles away. By the time it arrived, it was lukewarm. Mineral-crusted. Useless. Not hot enough to heal. Not cold enough to refresh.

Jesus was not talking about passion. He was talking about usefulness.

Hot water heals. Cold water refreshes. Lukewarm water does nothing for anyone.

The church at Laodicea had become useless to the people around them. And every person in that congregation, drinking that same tepid water every single day of their lives, understood precisely what He meant.

Now look at Sardis.

"I will come like a thief." Another verse every Christian has heard. Another verse almost nobody reads in context.

Sardis was built on top of a cliff. The city was considered unassailable. Its walls were so high and its position so secure that the guards grew complacent. They stopped watching.

Twice in its history, once under the Persians and once under the Greeks, enemy soldiers scaled the unguarded cliffs at night and seized the city while it slept.

When Jesus told the church at Sardis "I will come like a thief," He was not issuing a general warning about the end times. He was pointing to the most infamous military disaster in their city's own history and saying: You are doing exactly what your ancestors did. You stopped watching.

They would have felt that in their bones.

Now look at Pergamum.

"I know where you dwell, where Satan's throne is."

For centuries, theologians argued about what this meant. Was it metaphorical? Spiritual? Symbolic?

Then archaeologists uncovered the Great Altar of Zeus at Pergamum. A massive, towering stone throne, one of the largest pagan religious monuments ever constructed in the ancient world. It dominated the city skyline. Every Christian living in Pergamum would have seen it from their front door.

That altar was excavated in the 1800s. It was transported to Germany. It now sits reassembled in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. You can walk up to it and touch it.

Satan's throne was not a metaphor.

It was a street address.

This is what happens to Revelation when you give people the context that was stripped away by two thousand years of distance. The book most Christians avoid because it frightens them becomes the book that shows how precisely God speaks to real people in real places.

Every detail was composed for a specific city. Every warning pointed to a situation those believers were living through. Every promise answered a genuine fear carried by real people who were watching their friends be arrested, tortured, and executed for refusing to bow to the emperor.

Revelation was never a code about the future.

It was a letter to people who were not sure they would survive the week. And every word was written so they would hold on.

That is the realization I came to sitting across from a woman named Sarah two years ago.

Sarah had been a Christian for over forty years. She tithed. She volunteered. She came to every Wednesday night study our church offered. And she had never once opened the book of Revelation.

"I was told it was about the end of the world," she said. "I was told there were beasts and plagues and a mark you could accidentally receive. I spent my whole life frightened of the last book of my own Bible."

I opened to Revelation 2 and asked her to read the letter to the church at Smyrna.

She read it slowly.

"Do not fear what you are about to suffer. Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life."

She looked up. "That is not about the end of the world. That is about right now. That is about holding on."

I told her about the Crown of Smyrna, a famous ring of ancient buildings encircling the hilltop of that city, known throughout the Roman Empire. When Jesus promised the crown of life to believers in Smyrna, He was speaking in their own architectural language. Their city wore a crown of stone. He was offering one that would never crumble.

She sat quietly for a long moment.

"Forty years," she said. "Forty years I was afraid of this book. And it was written for people exactly like me. People who were frightened. People who needed to hear that it was going to be worth it."

She could not see it. And it was not her fault.

Nobody had ever given her the roots.

The next morning I started writing. And I quickly understood this was bigger than me.

So I reached out to a group of Bible teachers and pastors I had trusted for years, people who have spent their lives teaching Scripture in plain language.

Together, we began with Genesis. Everything a person needs to know before they read each book. Who wrote it. When. Why. What was happening in that city, in that empire, in that century. The central themes. How it connects to the larger story.

Not a commentary. Not a devotional. Just the roots.

Every page was written, reviewed, and rewritten by multiple teachers until my teenage son could read it and understand it completely on his own.

Sixty-six pages. One page per book. Four months of combined decades of study distilled into plain language any believer could work through on their own.

No pastor required.

When we finished, I brought a copy to Sarah.

She called me four days later. "I finished Revelation last night. The whole book. For the first time in my life. And I was not afraid once."

I started passing copies to others in my church quietly. One at a time. Every single person said the same thing.

"This is the first time I have ever understood what I was reading."

Not because we are gifted teachers. But because we finally gave them what they actually needed.

The roots.

Did you know that when Jesus said "It is finished," the Greek word tetelestai was the same word stamped on receipts in the Roman Empire to mean "paid in full"? His final breath was not a cry of defeat. It was a declaration of completion.

Did you know that the prophet Hosea, writing eight centuries before the empty tomb, wrote "After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live before Him"? The resurrection timeline was planted in the Old Testament hundreds of years before it happened.

Context changes everything. Every single time.

I call it The 66 Roots Journey. It has 66 pages. One for every book of the Bible. Each page gives you what you need before you open to the first verse. Who wrote it. When. Why. What was happening. The key themes. The symbolism. And how it connects to your actual life today.

Written in plain language. No seminary terms. No complicated theology.

Just the roots that make everything you have already read suddenly land with the full weight God intended.

Revelation was not written as a puzzle for scholars to decode in the distant future. It was written as a letter to frightened believers in seven real cities who needed to know that their suffering was seen, their faithfulness mattered, and their King was coming.

Two thousand years later, those cities are still there. The archaeology confirms every detail. And the letter still says the same thing it said the day it was written.

Hold on. It is going to be worth it.

If you have ever skipped the last book of your Bible because someone told you it was too complex or too frightening.

If you have ever read a verse you have heard your whole life and wondered what it actually meant to the people who first received it.

If you have ever wondered what you would find in God's Word if someone just gave you the context first.

This is what you have been looking for.

Get closer to God by actually understanding His Word.

Not just the familiar parts. All of it. The whole story.

That is what The 66 Roots Journey was created for.

And you can start yours today. I'll link it right down below.

God bless you and your journey through His Word. 🤍
