I never had luck with girls, until the sexiest one fell into my lap. Just that she was not an ordinary girl, but a dragon princess. And her dragon daddy wants me to marry her or he would kill me…

Chapter 1 - Rescuing A Stranger
It was mid-afternoon and Jacob was busy reading under his favourite cherry tree in the orchard. He lived with his grandmother in a town in Wisconsin and reading was his favourite pastime in between classes. The weather was sunny all morning but it kept growing darker and cloudier by afternoon. Soon enough, dark clouds covered the entire sky and pressed down towards the ground. The noise of thunder and lightning startled Jacob and he felt annoyed that he would now have to go back inside.
Thunder noises resonated in the sky as lightning flashed. It felt like the lightning was ready to dash through the clouds and break the sky into pieces. 
"Damn it!" exclaimed Jacob. He looked at the bad weather and sighed; he knew that a storm was approaching. He breathed in the moist air as he paced himself towards the corner store that was about 300 meters away.
If the superstore in the dorm area wasn't under renovation, if he didn't use three consecutive scissors in the rock, paper, scissors match, he wouldn't be out here in his pajamas and slippers. He wanted to read a book, but his roommates wanted to play cards.
Boom! A loud thunder sounded, and Jacob started to run as he tried to avoid the storm.
"AHAH..."
Jacob was about to speed up, when he heard the scream of a girl from above.
He looked up in confusion. He was shocked by what he saw. A girl was falling from the sky!
That wasn't all. That girl was about to land on his head!
"Damn..." exclaimed Jacob. He took a step back and lowered his center of gravity. He then reached out his hands and went into a squat.
Bam!
The girl smashed into Jacob's chest, and that force made him lower his center of gravity by another 10 centimeters. The force was so strong that he almost collapsed.
This girl's head also smashed onto Jacob's lips, and that impact almost made Jacob lose a few teeth.
"Gulp..." swallowed Jacob. Something dropped out of the girl's mouth, and it smoothly went down Jacob's throat since his mouth was still wide open due to the initial surprise.
Sweet, smooth, and small... Before Jacob could react, this candy-like object was already in his stomach.
However, Jacob didn't focus on that as he felt the weight of the girl on his body and felt that his hands were getting numb. He looked down at the girl in his arms.
Long black lashes, short pony-tail, snow-white hair, youthful figure, and the blue school uniform with the Cherry Grove High School badge. She seemed like a senior in high school and looked pretty. Jacob couldn’t seem to take his eyes off her.
"Ah..." the girl woke up in pain. It took her a few seconds to finally realize what had happened. She screamed as she opened her blue eyes. She looked at Jacob and suddenly tried to stand back up on her own.
Though the girl did not weigh as much, the impact of her fall made Jacob’s legs numb and now that she was finally awake, he couldn’t help but wonder about her fall. There weren’t any buildings around and she certainly fell from a height way above the trees. Where did she come from after all?
The girl stood up, touched her body and then rubbed her lips that felt a little swollen. After she saw the red mark on Jacob's lips, she blushed and hit Jacob's neck.
"Hey... I saved you..." Before Jacob could finish his sentence, the girl already ran off.
"Girls nowadays are really tough... She seems fine after falling from such a height." Jacob rubbed his neck as he watched the girl running away. "It's not too bad. She didn't hit me too hard. Thankfully, she didn't hit my face or break my neck."
He then rubbed his lips. While he remembered the girl’s lips coming down on his, he somehow didn’t feel like he kissed her. It wasn’t the kind of warmth you would feel when you kissed a girl. Not that Jacob or his friends had any luck with girls so far in their 20 years of existence. 
He was already a second-year university student, but he still didn't have a girlfriend. 
"I'm such a loser..."
Jacob thought as he patted his thighs and stood up. He looked up at the sky and suddenly found that the dark clouds were all gone and even the sun had come out.
"Damn this weather; I thought there was going to be a huge storm."
Jacob murmured to himself; he didn't want to get too hung up on what just happened. He quickly got to the corner store and bought two decks of cards. After that, he promptly returned to his dorm that was located in the south end of the campus.
As soon as he entered, his roommate Sam spoke up, "What took you so long? Quick, we are all waiting!" 
Jacob’s three roommates were waiting for him.
Jacob threw the two decks of cards onto the table and said, "You guys can play, I'm not in the mood."
"What’s up? You look grim!" Sam, who was wearing a white t-shirt, asked, "Didn't we agree that whoever lost would go and buy cards? What’s the point of being mad about that now?”
"I'm just a little dizzy..." Jacob said as he crawled up to the top of the bunk bed that belonged to him.
"Hey! We agreed on playing cards today!" Sam wasn't too happy.
"Are you ok?" asked another roommate. He was worried about Jacob.
"Not sure, I'm just not feeling too well." Jacob rubbed his chest as he responded. "Did my organs get injured from the impact when I caught that girl?" he thought to himself.
"Should we... take you to the infirmary?" Sam also got serious as he saw Jacob's face.
"It's fine. I fell by accident on my way to the corner store." Jacob pointed at his chin that swelled a little. It was hit by that girl's head but he didn’t bother telling his friends about the strange encounter.
"Then get some rest. Since it’s not raining, we’re going to the cafe," said the third roommate.
"Yeah, you guys go ahead." Jacob waved at them. He wasn't feeling up for anything but some sleep.
Sam was still a little worried. "Just call me if you need anything," he said.
"Ok." Jacob took off his slippers and got in his comfortable, cozy little bed.
The four of them were all single. Except for gaming and playing cards, they didn't have any other passion. Jacob sighed as he fell asleep; he was exhausted for some reason.
When he woke up, it was already 6 in the evening. There was a box of takeout food on the table; it was the dinner that the three of his roommates got for him.
Through the doors, Jacob heard the noise of his roommates playing cards in the dorm room next to his. They were afraid of being loud and waking up Jacob so they were playing next door.
"Real brothers" smiled Jacob. He scratched his head as climbed down from his bed to get the food.
When he stretched out his hand to open the parcel, he was shocked! His body froze in place. In the dark room, he saw a circle of green skin on his right wrist!
Jacob felt like his heart had stopped beating for five seconds. He drew the curtains so that he could see his arm better.
A green fish scale-like tattoo covered his right arm from wrist to shoulder!
Jacob felt like he was hallucinating. He rubbed his eyes, and the green skin was still there. He then tried to smear this green matter off of his body, but it didn't work.
Jacob felt a chill down his spine. He quickly undressed and stood in front of the full-length mirror. He wanted to see if there was anything like this on other parts of his body but there was nothing. He got dressed again and began to eat his food. After about half an hour his roommates came back and asked Jacob if he was feeling any better. Jacob said that he wasn’t sure. His roommates offered to take him to the infirmary but he refused.
The truth was that Jacob was himself puzzled with the day. A girl that fell from the sky and into his lap out of nowhere... the foreboding of a storm… the green scaly skin on his arm. He touched his wrist once again and made sure it was hidden from his roommates. He didn’t want to freak them out till he found out the truth about the strange events of the day. But how will he find out? Will these scaly marks disappear or would he have to live with them forever? Who was that mysterious girl?

Chapter 2 - We Meet Again

Just as Sam and the others in the dorm were discussing Jacob's strange behavior and the scab on his chin, Jacob had left the dorm frantically. He waved down a taxi and was on his way to the hospital that had the best department of dermatology - Bellin Memorial Hospital.
Once there, Jacob was made to go through a number of cumbersome administrative procedures and tiresome checkups. After going through a pile of reports, the dermatologist finally told Jacob that the streaks on his arm were caused by a type of dye. It was probably a discoloration from some bad quality bed sheets.
According to the reports, there was no mutation of cells in his body. All the results from the various tests had indicated no abnormalities. Moreover, the green color was not a result of pigmentation. As for the scaly patterns, it was only accidental - the color happened to spread out in a relatively regular pattern. Most importantly, it was definitely not contagious.
Although unconvincing, this explanation was enough to assure Jacob and calm him down for the time being.
Clutching his reports, Jacob left the hospital and returned to his dorm room. He began scrubbing his arm with soap, he noticed that the color did seem to lighten a bit. He heaved a sigh of relief. After an afternoon of such terrifying events, he could finally get some rest. Now he was finding his panic a bit silly and chuckled. He changed his bedsheet into a clean one and quietly climbed into his bed. He tiptoed so that his roommates wouldn’t wake up, and slept as soon as his head hit the pillow.
The Saturday afternoon sun shone brightly through the curtains and the sunlight was directly falling on Jacob’s face. But he was sleeping like a log.
"Jacob! Jacob!"
Someone banged the dorm room with loud thuds calling out Jacob’s name frantically.
"Heck! Who is it!?" Sam, who was sleeping on the bed below Jacob's, threw a pillow at the door in anger.
"Jacob, there is a cute girl waiting for you!" It was one of their classmates on the door.
"Cute girl? Cute girl!" As confused and dazed as he was, Sam abruptly woke up from his dream and rose to an upright position. Ever since Sam was rejected by the most popular girl at the university, he had lost the courage to pursue a relationship. However, he secretly wished that he had a girlfriend.
"Jacob, get up! I’ve to come and get you and take you to the cute girl waiting for you outside. There are so many people already gathered around the entrance of our cafeteria because they can’t believe that a girl is looking for you! You have quite an audience!" the classmate kept on banging at the door.
"What the hell are you talking about?" Jacob shouted. He was finally up and gently rubbing his slightly aching stomach, Jacob remembered something. As he raised his arm, the trace of the winding green marks came into sight. It did not fade away, but it did not expand either. He felt a little relieved.
Thump, thump, thump! The knocking persisted.
"I'm coming! I'm coming!" Jacob jumped off the bed and went to get the door.
By this time, Sam who was sitting on his bed listening to the commotion knew that he could not sleep anymore and rose from his bed grudgingly. On the other hand, upon hearing the words 
"cute girl", Sam began to dress excitedly.
"So many people have surrounded the entrance of our cafeteria. My roommate and I were on our way to get food and thought there was a fight or something. We went over to take a look and found that it was a pretty girl waiting for someone,” the classmate started talking without a pause as soon as Jacob opened the door to his dorm.
"That doesn't necessarily mean she is waiting for me, does it? Particularly if a good looking girl is in question. Why don’t you ask Sam to talk to her? I'm not interested." Jacob glared at his classmate in annoyance. He had a sound sleep but upon waking, his entire body felt uneasy and his muscles ached. Being woken up by this meaningless commotion had only irked him more.
"Let me finish!" The classmate grabbed Jacob’s shoulders excitedly. "That pretty girl had a poster in her hands, and it is totally you! She said that whoever brings you to her would get awarded 500 dollars!"
"Me?" Jacob looked lost. He looked at his classmate sternly, "You are here for the 500 dollars, aren't you?"
"Heehee…" his classmate’s smile was a little too bright. “I’m here for the drama too!”
Jacob heard a growing commotion and it felt like a crowd was approaching the outside of his dorm building. Jacob walked over to the balcony and saw a big group of students, mostly boys he was acquainted with running wildly towards his dorm room. He could tell that they were all coming after him because of the reward. He rushed inside his room and quickly threw on some clothes and shoes and followed his classmate down the stairs.
As the dorm captain, Sam worried about any unexpected mishaps, plus he also wanted to see the girl. He rushed outside too, closing the dorm room shut. Sam was Jacob’s closest friend. Even though he was usually foul-mouthed and liked to bug Jacob a lot, he was also the one who cared about Jacob the most.
The dorm building was situated outside the campus and as the trio walked along the entrance and entered the campus, they saw posters with Jacob’s picture and the words WANTED in bold pinned up on the bulletin boards. Underneath the posters, written in a large font were the words, "500 Dollars reward for bringing the above person to me - come to claim your reward by the entrance of the cafeteria!"
Going by the number of bulletin boards there were in the school, there had to be at least a few hundreds of these posters. This was no less than the scale of being wanted nationally!
"What did you do to that girl to make her come all the way to our college to make you a wanted man," Sam asked Jacob curiously as he anticipated in enthusiasm.
"How am I supposed to know? I don't even know who she is!" Jacob responded impatiently.
Escorted by the big crowd, Jacob unwillingly walked towards the cafeteria.
"He's coming. He's coming!" Seeing that the wanted person had appeared, some students started calling out to Jacob.
The crowd was now making way for Jacob to pass through. 
Under the curious gaze of at least a hundred students, Jacob awkwardly walked towards the door of the cafeteria, and stopped dead in his tracks. It was the girl from yesterday, the one who fell out of nowhere and seemed to be falling from the sky.
She was wearing a white shirt and a pair of washed-out jeans. It was a very common outfit; yet, it looked outstanding on her. Strands of her hair were drifting in the wind. However, underneath the fluttering hair, there was an angry face.
"Ohhh… Ohhhh…"
Someone started jeering.
"Such a pretty girl," Sam, whispered into Jacob's ear.
"When did you meet such a beautiful girl? Give us an introduction!" Sam turned around and winked at Jacob as he said that. He was itching to have another shot with a girl.
Seeing that Jacob finally showed up, the girl pursed her lips.
Suppressing the awkwardness he felt, he walked up and asked under the many piercing glances, "I heard you were looking for me?"
"Did you take something from me yesterday?" Staring right into Jacob's eyes, the girl questioned unflinchingly.
"What? What thing?" Jacob was not expecting this from her. He felt surprised and confused.
Now that they had started their conversation, the classmate who fetched Jacob from his dorm quickly came forward and interrupted them. Rubbing his hands, he said, "Well…"
The girl glanced over at him and drew out her wallet. From the purse, she took out 500 dollars and handed it to the boy.
"So she’s a rich girl. Well, it seems her arrogance comes from money then,” thought Jacob.
"You! Did you take something from me yesterday?" The pretty girl continued to question Jacob.
"What thing?" Jacob stared at her with eyes filled with anger.
"It was a bead, a blue bead." she replied.
"I didn't see it. You must have dropped it somewhere in the orchard," Jacob answered without thinking.
The audience was a little disappointed by their conversation. They felt that the girl had been bullied in some way and had come to seek revenge. The fact that she was only looking to recover a lost item was hardly entertaining to them.
"That bead is soft and bouncy." the girl explained, "I'll give you two more minutes, think harder."
"Can we talk somewhere else?" Jacob felt the crowd’s eyes on them and felt uncomfortable.
"Just give her back whatever you took from her! How shameless are you to steal from a girl," one of the students yelled at Jacob.
"Shut up! You have no right to comment on this," the girl was enraged at the crowd.
"The show’s over, guys! Go away already…... Go!" Sam quickly addressed the crowd and they slowly scattered away.
The girl quickly resumed the topic, "That bead is of great importance, so I was hoping you could give it back to me."
"But I don't know what you're talking about…" Before he could finish, the girl put out her hand and covered his mouth. Jacob caught a whiff of her scent and felt the softness of her palm on his lips.
"I can feel it here, right here," she slowly moved her palm from his lips down to his neck and placed it on his stomach. Jacob had goosebumps by now and Sam was just staring in complete shock.
Jacob slowly caught her hand to remove it from his stomach but the girl quickly caught hold of his wrist instead and rolled up his sleeve - the green colored dragon-like tattoo was revealed to the three of them. 
“If you don’t have my bead, how do you explain this?” The girl asked to which Jacob had no answer and was staring at her in complete shock. 

Chapter 3 - The Stubborn Girl

Not wanting to disclose the strange tattoo on him to others, Jacob immediately yanked his wrist away from the girl and covered his arm with his shirt sleeve.
The girl stretched out her hand and placed it on Jacob's stomach as if she was trying to feel something.
"We are in public, is it really necessary for you to be touching my stomach?" Jacob felt helpless and smacked her hand off.
Unfortunately for Jacob, the crowd had not completely vanished yet. Many were still waiting for more drama to unfold. A high school girl demanding something from a college man was something entirely unusual for the campus. Who would want to miss this scene?
"You two, whatever your problem is, resolve it somewhere else," since he was unable to fully break up the crowd, Sam was trying to find another way to help Jacob out. "Listen now,” Sam addressed the girl. “You’ve found Jacob now, he is a good man. I’m sure whatever is going on between the two of you can be solved privately. What’s your name, girl?"
"First off, do not call me girl! And humph, you call him a good person? I don't think he looks like a good person one bit!" The girl was glaring at Jacob. "You're not leaving until you give me back what is mine," she demanded from Jacob.
"Fine, fine. Let's talk somewhere else!" Jacob grabbed the girl by her wrist and rushed towards the college building.
Since the excitement and interest had died down, no one tried to go after them. After a short while of jogging, Jacob let go of the girl's delicate wrist and said, "Why did you have to cause such a big commotion? I really didn't take anything from you."
"Who are you trying to fool? How do you explain the patterns on your wrist then," she glared at Jacob. It looked like she wasn’t going to give up.
"First, I did not take anything of yours. Second, I saved your life yesterday - not only were you not grateful, you hit me. Third, you alarmed the whole college and caused an uproar to find me, just how am I supposed to go here after this?" Jacob argued.
"Just give that bead back to me and all of this will go away," she continued to stare at Jacob and there was stubbornness in her voice.
Her continually demanding something Jacob had no clue about was driving him insane.
"Ay… whatever. I am going to go eat," deserting the girl, Jacob turned around to go to the cafeteria inside the campus.
However, the girl followed him closely and maintained her persistent expression.
On entering the cafeteria, Jacob stood in line to buy food. And yet, the girl was stuck onto him like a nougat, following his every step.
Even when Jacob took out his cafeteria card to order, her eyes were glued to him.
"I really don't know what to do with you…" swiping his card for the second time, Jacob sighed, "one more order of the meatloaf, please."
As he carried his tray of food to the table, the girl also carried her tray and followed right behind him.
As he sat down, she sat down right across from him.
She was now copying his every move. She would take a bite of the food if he did; and when he stopped eating, so did she.
"Look,” Jacob said in a pleading tone. “I really, really did not take anything from you.” he couldn't help but look at her helplessly. He certainly did not expect so much trouble when he went ahead to save a life.
"Your tattoo is saying otherwise. It is the clear proof for what you took." she insisted and refused to take her eyes off Jacob for even a second.
"And why is that?" Jacob asked.
"Well, I can't reason with you... Anyway, I know for a fact that you have my bead. Which pocket did you put it in? It should be close to your stomach, right? Humph, you'd better not make me search you." She asserted.
"Search me,” Jacob thought to himself. “Why is this girl acting so stubborn? And so brazen in front of a strange man..." Jacob shot her a glance and carried on with his meal.
It seemed that she had starved herself all morning waiting for Jacob because she devoured her meal at a superfast speed.
Seizing the chance, Jacob raised his head and observed her quietly. He found that the white shirt she was wearing was not a common white shirt. Even though the shirt indicated the vigorous spirit of a high school girl overall, it was more of a retro style shirt. The lace knot on her chest was butterfly-like and adorned her petite body perfectly.
Also, the bottom of her shirt was tucked into her jeans, displaying a nice contour of her slim waist. Along with her idyllic style floral patterned wooden sandals, Jacob was convinced that this girl must have come from a reputed family.
Particularly, for someone who was at the age of a high-school girl, her casual gesture of throwing out 500 dollars so carelessly was definitely not common.
At this moment, the girl abruptly lifted her head. She seemed to have noticed that Jacob was observing her. To conceal his interest and thoughts, Jacob quickly put his head down.
Needless to say, the appearance of such an adorable girl in a university cafeteria had attracted attention from many of the university students.
"Ay, they must just think this is my sister…" Jacob reassured himself.
"You'd better leave as soon as you finish eating. Since you came all the way here by yourself, your parents must be worried," Jacob said to her.
"As long as you return to me what is mine, I will be able to go home with ease. I'm warning you, if my parents find out what I have lost and decide to come to you for it themselves, you will be in very serious trouble." With her eyes on Jacob, she suddenly spoke in a calm and mellow manner.
Nonetheless, her words obviously hinted at the underlying threat.
This time, her remarks caught Jacob’s complete attention. He honestly had no clue what she was talking about. "Kids at this age, whatever small matters they run into, always like to involve their parents so they could just conveniently hide behind them. With that being said, if her parents do get involved, this would become a very sticky business for me." Thoughts were running wild in his head.
Yet, Jacob still didn't think that he had taken anything that was hers. He came out with nothing on him yesterday. After the encounter with her, all he brought back to the dorm were two decks of cards.
As for the bead that she kept on babbling about, Jacob was wearing pocketless pyjamas and a pair of slippers at the time. How could he have possibly brought anything away with him? She must have dropped it somewhere else.
As for the green pattern on his skin, they were a reaction of the discoloration from his bed sheet according to the doctor.
However, judging from her stubborn character, he was afraid that her family would also believe that he had taken something from her. If it reaches that point, there would be no way for him to explain himself anymore. As he thought long and hard, Jacob felt that he was developing a mild headache over the trouble he got himself into from trying to save someone.
"Stop following me. I said I didn't take anything from you, and that means I didn't take anything from you. Even if you get your parents to come with you, I would still say the same thing," Jacob declared as he stood up and grabbed his tray.
After that, he returned the tray to the cafeteria counter and walked out of the door. When he turned his head around, he found that the girl was still following him.
Jacob decided to stop paying attention to her and walked right into the library building while drawing out his student ID.
[SFX] Beeeeeep.
The card was approved by the card reader and the door to the library opened.
She wanted to follow him inside but was denied access and the door began to close.
Standing on the other side, Jacob gave her a small wave and walked into the lobby of the library without any hesitation. He was relieved that he finally got rid of her.
"You will come to me yourself," she said as the door closed on her and Jacob walked away.

Chapter 1
Mira's POV
Two months ago, Jason Reed was my boyfriend. Now he had his tongue down my sister's throat, and she wanted me to watch.
I stood in the doorway of the classroom, bag over one shoulder, and waited for the twist in my stomach to pass. It didn't.
Jason saw me and pulled back, and the tips of his ears went red the way they always did when he felt bad about something.
"Mira." He cleared his throat. "Hey."
Alyssa turned slowly, like she was surprised to find me there.
"Oh." She pressed two fingers to her lips. "I'm sorry you had to see that. We just can't help ourselves." Her smile sharpened. "You understand, though. When it's your fated mate, you can't fight the bond."
"I get it. Totally." I walked to my seat three rows back and dropped my bag on the desk. My hands were steady. I made sure of that.
I'd managed to avoid them all day. First day back after winter break, and I'd mapped out every hallway, every stairwell, every route that didn't cross Alyssa's path. Survived the entire day. Then walked straight into her in the last class.
Alyssa had been doing this since the mating ceremony during the winter break. Every corner I turned — there she was, draped over Jason, making sure I knew Jason was fated to her now.
I couldn't really blame anyone.
The last full moon of December is the wolves' mating ceremony. Everyone who turns eighteen that year does their first shift, and somewhere in the howling and the moonlight, they find the fate mate the moongoddess picked for them. Their fated mate. The one your wolf knows before your head does.
I'd waited my whole life for that night. Jason and I had dated for three years. We were so sure we were fated mates. Jason never cared that I was the orphan, the baby found abandoned in the forest and handed to Alyssa's family to raise. He liked that I was a strong girl that didn't feel sorry for myself.
However, I never shifted into my wolf that night.
I stood there in my dress while wolves howled around me. My bones didn't crack. My skin didn't ripple. Nothing happened. I just stood there, human-shaped and wrong, while the world celebrated without me.
And Jason — my Jason — walked past me without a word. Crossed the clearing to where Alyssa stood in her new wolf form, sleek and silver, and when she shifted back, he kissed her. In front of the whole pack. In front of me.
You don't say no to your fated mate. The mate bond was the strongest force among wolf shifters. When you found your fated mate, your wolf chose for you — body, heart, instincts, all of it locked onto one person. Fighting it was pointless.
I had to let him go.
Plus, Alyssa never liked me because I was adopted. And as our beta family's real daughter, she had hated me since the day I started dating Jason. She always thought she was supposed to date the Alpha's son and I stole her thunder.
That was two months ago. I shoved the memory down and did what I always did. Smiled. Breathed. Moved on.
"So." Alyssa dropped into the seat across from mine, Jason trailing after her. "It's Valentine's Day. Last class of the day, then freedom." She tilted her head. "You and your mystery mate have plans tonight?"
My pulse ticked up. "Yep. Big plans."
That was a lie. There was no mystery mate.
After the ceremony, the whispers started — is she human? did she even try to shift?
Humans were known to be extinct for a while. The weakest species of all.
If I was considered a weak human orphan, I would be soon kicked out of my pack the next day.
So I did what I do best under pressure: I lied. I told everyone I'd felt a connection with someone that night. A mate bond, still forming, because I was a late shifter.
Late shifters were rare, but they existed. And a potential mate bond meant I was definitely a wolf, definitely one of them, definitely not a human.
The girl next to Alyssa leaned in. Piper, from one of the southern packs. She collected gossip the way some people collected coins.
"Wait, you found a mate too?" Piper's eyes lit up. "Who was he?"
Alyssa gave me a pointed look. “She’s been very mysterious about him.”
“I'm a late shifter. We just suddenly felt the mate-bond pull after the mating ceremony day and just started dating,” I said, trying to sound casual. “We’ve just started seeing each other, so we’re not really ready to tell everyone yet.”
Piper grinned, like this was the juiciest news she’d heard all week.
“Fine. Then just tell me what pack he’s from. I can figure out the rest myself.” She started counting on her fingers. “Is it Garrett? No, he’s mated. The Hale cousin—the tall one? One of the Voss-pack twins?”
"No," I said. "None of them."
"Huh." Piper frowned. "I thought I knew every unmated wolf nearby. Unless he's not a wolf." She gasped, delighted. "Oh my Goddess. Is he a different kind of shifter? I heard a vixen mated a wolf last year. Or a bear?"
"It's not — " My face was getting hot. "It's nothing like that."
Alyssa hadn't said anything in a while. She was watching me the way she watched me when she thought she'd caught something.
Piper's voice dropped, like she'd just thought of the most dangerous thing in the world.
"Mira." She grinned. "He can't be one of the vampires, is he?"
And that was the exact moment the door opened. The room went dead silent.
The vampires entered.
Damon Voss walked in first. He was tall, almost a full head taller than an Alpha son like Jason. His skin was pale but luminous, like porcelain catching the light, and his dark hair fell just enough across his forehead to look effortless. With his high and precise cheekbones, a strong jaw and a broad shoulder and chest, his presence made the air around him feel heavier.
Two more vampires followed behind him, boots clicking on the tile floor, spreading to their seats without a word.
Everyone knew who Damon Voss was. Son of Lord Alaric Voss, the vampire heir who would rule the world one day. Damon's friends had a reputation for bullying shifters. No one dared to cross them on campus.
Nobody looked at their way. Nobody spoke. Piper pressed her lips shut so fast it was almost funny.
But I looked.
I always looked at Damon Voss, and I never understood why. For some reason, something about him felt familiar. Not safe. Not warm. Just known, in a way I couldn't explain.
His gaze swept the room。
Then they found mine.
Chapter 2
Mira's POV
He looked away first.
Damon Voss turned his gaze back to the front of the room like I was a wall he'd glanced at by accident. He then sat down in the back row with his two friends.
I forced myself to look at my desk. My heart was doing something strange. Not fear. Something else. Something I didn't have a name for.
Piper leaned into me, her voice barely a breath.
"Mira." Her eyes were huge. "You're not really dating one of the vampires, are you?"
"No," I said. Too fast. "No. He's just — he's not a vampire. I told you. I'm just not ready to say who it is yet."
"Then why was he looking at you like that?"
"He wasn't looking at me."
He was. I knew he always was. I just didn't know why.

By lunch it was worse. People I'd never spoken to came up to my table in the cafeteria. Is it true? You and Voss? Since when? How did it happen?
I tried to leave with an awkward smile that I always wore.
Then Alyssa was there. Planting both hands flat on my table, leaning in with that face she got when she knew she'd cornered something.
Kissing Damon Voss must have been a bigger mistake than I expected. Alyssa had always hated it when I got more attention than she did—but now, everyone’s eyes are on me, and she looked furious and so determined to take me down.
"I was there last night," she said. Loud enough for the nearest tables to hear. "At the café. And you know what I noticed? Damon Voss never actually said you were his girlfriend. Not once. You said it. He just stood there."
People were listening now. A circle was forming — not obviously, not crowding in, but chairs turning, forks going down, conversations dying mid-sentence.
"I think you made it all up." Her voice climbed. "The mate. The boyfriend. All of it. I think there's no mate bond, there's no fated connection, and you're just a girl who can't shift because she's not actually a wolf."
"Alyssa — "
"So tell them." She straightened up and gestured at the gathering crowd. "Tell everyone, right now. Is Damon Voss really your boyfriend? Yes or no?"
The cafeteria had gone quiet. Faces everywhere, all turned to me, all waiting. I could feel my pulse in my ears.
I was so tired. Tired of running, tired of lying, tired of the lie getting bigger every single day until I couldn't see over the top of it. Maybe it was time to just stop. Tell the truth. Take whatever came next.
I opened my mouth to say no.
An arm settled across my shoulders. Heavy and Certain.
"Of course it's true," Damon said.

bodyText:
Three months after my husband died, I was invited to dinner only to be told by my best friends I was excluded from our annual couples trip.

"We gave your spot to someone else.

You don't speak the language over there.

You have to understand."

I smiled.

I understand.

For twelve years, my husband Tom and I cruised the Mediterranean every September with the same three couples.

It was our thing.

We'd plan it together over wine in January, book by March, and spend all summer looking forward to it.

I researched the ports.

Found the excursions.

Booked the restaurants.

Tom was the one who talked to people.

He picked up languages the way some men pick up bar tabs.

Enough Italian to charm a waiter.

Enough Spanish to haggle at a market.

Enough French to make a maître d' smile.

Everyone said he was a natural.

Tom died fourteen months ago.

Pancreatic cancer.

He was 61.

After the funeral, the calls came constantly.

Cassie checking in.

Pam dropping off casseroles.

Everyone saying "let us know if you need anything."

By month three, the calls slowed down.

By month six, they stopped.

Then I open Instagram on a Tuesday morning.

And there they are.

All six of them.

At a café in Florence.

Cassie's holding a glass of wine and grinning.

The caption: "The crew does Italy! 🇮🇹✈️"

The crew.

Without me.

I called Cassie that afternoon.

"Oh, Susan."

That voice.

The one that sounds like warmth but lands like a verdict.

"We didn't want to upset you.

It was sort of last-minute.

And honestly, we didn't think you'd be up for it.

You know, with everything you've been going through."

She kept going.

"And Italy is impossible if you don't speak the language.

The restaurants, the trains, the locals.

Tom always handled that for you.

He was the one who talked to everyone.

Without him, we just didn't think you could manage over there."

I sat there and listened.

"It was for your own good, Susan.

We didn't want you to be overwhelmed."

Two weeks later, they're all back.

Tanned.

Full of stories.

And Cassie calls me.

"Susan, I have exciting news.

We're doing our annual cruise in September.

Mediterranean.

And we'd love for you to help plan the itinerary.

You always find those incredible hidden restaurants and those excursions nobody else knows about.

You're so good at organizing."

So let me get this straight.

I'm not good enough to ATTEND the Italy trip.

But I'm good enough to PLAN the cruise.

I'm the free travel agent for the friends who left me behind.

I said, "Sure, Cassie.

I'll put something together."

Then I hung up and sat in the kitchen for an hour.

That's when something clicked.

They didn't just exclude me from Italy.

They excluded me because they decided, without asking, that I couldn't handle it.

That without Tom, I was a liability.

That without the man who spoke to waiters and taxi drivers and hotel staff for me, I was helpless in a foreign country.

But my port research?

My restaurant reservations?

My excursion finds?

Those they still wanted.

Because apparently I'm capable enough to find a private lemon grove tour in a blog written in Italian.

Just not capable enough to stand in the grove and understand the owner when she speaks.

I started planning the cruise.

Spent weeks on it.

Found the lemon grove tour on the Amalfi Coast that wasn't in any guidebook.

Booked a sunset dinner reservation at a cliffside restaurant in Positano with a three-month waitlist.

Mapped out walking routes through Cinque Terre that avoided the tourist crush.

Sent it all to the group chat.

Cassie replied: "Susan, this is INCREDIBLE.

You're amazing.

This is going to be the best one yet!! 💕"

Then I booked my own cabin on the same sailing.

Same ship.

Same dates.

Upgraded.

Balcony suite.

And I told no one.

A week later, Cassie invited me to dinner at her house.

"Just a little get-together," she said.

"Nothing fancy."

I showed up at six.

The good china was out.

Candles lit.

All three couples were already seated.

They were exchanging looks when I walked in.

The kind where everyone knows something you don't.

I thought someone was sick.

After dinner, Cassie cleared her throat.

"Susan, we need to talk about the cruise."

My stomach dropped.

"We've been talking, all of us, and we think it would be better if Lauren took your cabin this year."

Lauren.

Tom's replacement.

I mean, Mike's new girlfriend.

She was 34.

She'd been in the group for eight months.

"Lauren speaks conversational Italian," Cassie continued.

"She studied abroad in Rome.

And honestly, we think the trip will just flow better with someone who can help us communicate over there."

I looked around the table.

Six faces.

Not one of them surprised.

They'd already decided.

The dinner wasn't a discussion.

It was a notification.

Greg leaned forward.

"Susan, I'm going to say what everyone's been thinking."

Everyone.

"Last September in Dubrovnik, you couldn't understand the taxi driver.

Tom had to negotiate the fare while we all waited.

In Split, you held up the restaurant line for ten minutes because you were fumbling with Google Translate trying to ask where the bathroom was.

You ordered the wrong dish at every dinner because you couldn't read the menus."

He wasn't done.

"We missed the shuttle to dinner in Kotor because the port announcements were in Croatian and you couldn't understand which dock we needed.

Dave had to find someone who spoke English to help us.

That was forty-five minutes, Susan."

He had dates.

He had details.

He'd been keeping score the entire time Tom was alive.

Cassie put her hand on Greg's arm.

Not to stop him.

To transition.

She turned to me.

That voice again.

"Susan, we love you.

You know that.

But ever since Tom passed, the language barrier has been impossible.

Tom was the one who talked to everyone.

He ordered for you.

He navigated for you.

He translated everything.

And without him..."

She looked around the table.

Like she was checking that everyone still agreed.

They did.

"We just think it's better this way.

Lauren offered to step in so nobody has to worry about the language thing.

You have to understand."

You have to understand.

Translation: Without your husband's languages, you're a burden.

And we found someone who speaks Italian.

I looked at Cassie.

At this woman whose cliffside dinner reservation in Positano I'd spent forty-five minutes on hold to get.

Whose lemon grove tour I'd found in a blog written in Italian that I ran through Google Translate three times.

I picked up my wine glass.

Took a sip.

"I understand," I said.

I drove home.

I didn't cry.

I was past that.

I sat in the kitchen with the lights off.

They didn't know I already had a cabin booked on their ship.

Balcony suite, one deck above theirs.

Paid for with the trip money Tom and I had been saving.

I'd booked it the night Cassie asked me to plan their itinerary.

Before the dinner.

Before Greg's speech.

Before Lauren's name was even mentioned.

I was going to surprise them.

Show up and let them realize they should've invited me.

But now it was different.

Now I wasn't surprising anyone.

I was proving something.

But I needed to show up right.

The next morning, I called Karen.

Tom's younger sister.

She'd been a flight attendant for twenty-two years.

International routes.

Tokyo, São Paulo, Rome.

She's landed in countries where she didn't speak a word of the language more times than Cassie has left her zip code.

I told her everything.

The Italy photos.

The "you're so good at organizing" call.

The dinner.

Greg's speech.

Cassie's voice.

"Ever since Tom passed."

Karen was quiet for a long time.

Then she said: "What are you planning to do about the language?"

"I don't know.

Download Google Translate?

Buy a phrasebook?"

"No.

No apps.

No phrasebooks.

No holding up your phone to a waiter while everyone behind you waits."

She told me about a pair of earbuds half her crew had been using on international routes for the past year.

The flight attendants who flew Rome, Seoul, São Paulo.

The ones who landed in countries where they didn't speak a word and needed to communicate with ground crews, hotel staff, medical personnel.

"They're called Vylaras," she said.

"Military-grade neural processing.

The same AI translation technology NATO forces used in Afghanistan and Iraq when understanding every word meant the difference between life and death."

"Karen, I can barely work my phone."

"One button.

That's it.

You put them in like hearing aids.

Nobody can tell.

You press one button and you understand every word anyone says to you in any language.

128 languages.

Under 0.3 seconds.

No internet.

No phone.

No app.

Works completely offline.

72-hour battery on a single charge."

"What if Cassie sees them at embarkation?"

Karen didn't hesitate.

"They look like hearing aids, Susan.

On a cruise ship full of people our age, nobody looks twice.

That's the point."

She mentioned that big tech companies are trying to buy the technology and lock it behind their subscription apps.

That once the deal goes through, the standalone offline version gets pulled from the market.

"Order tonight," she said.

"My whole crew group chat has been scrambling to get them before that happens.

Don't wait."

I ordered them that night.

The earbuds arrived six days later.

I sat at the kitchen table with the charging case.

Small.

Discreet.

They looked exactly like the hearing aids my mother wore.

I put them in and checked the bathroom mirror.

You couldn't tell.

I pressed the one button.

I turned on the Italian radio station I'd been using to research restaurants for Cassie's itinerary.

A man was describing a local festival.

Rapid.

Excited.

Full of slang and regional expressions.

I understood every word.

Not fragments.

Not a rough translation on a screen.

Every word, clear as English, whispered directly in my ear before the man even finished his sentence.

I switched to a Spanish news broadcast.

Understood every word.

French cooking show.

Every word.

Croatian travel podcast.

Every word.

I sat at that kitchen table for an hour.

The same table where I'd read Cassie's text asking me to plan the itinerary.

The same table where I'd sat in the dark after the dinner.

Six languages in one evening.

Tom picked up languages over decades.

Charming, but incomplete.

Enough to get by.

Never fluent.

These earbuds gave me 128 languages in one button press.

Every accent.

Every dialect.

Every fast-talking local Tom would've smiled through and hoped for the best.

I held Tom's watch in my other hand.

The silver one with the scratch across the face from the cabin door frame on our first Mediterranean cruise together, thirteen years ago.

He'd caught it reaching for the doorway and laughed and said, "Well, that one's yours now."

I put it in my travel wallet.

Before anything else.

Embarkation day.

Barcelona cruise terminal.

I arrived early.

Earbuds in.

Nobody noticed.

The Spanish port crew were directing passengers toward different gangways.

Rapid.

Loud.

Entirely in Spanish.

I understood every word.

Deck assignments.

Boarding groups.

Which entrance for balcony suites.

Four minutes.

Through security.

On the ship.

I was on the Lido Deck with a glass of prosecco when I saw them arrive below at the general embarkation line.

All six of them.

And Lauren.

The Spanish crew member at the check-in desk was explaining something.

Speaking fast.

Gesturing.

Cassie was holding up her phone.

Google Translate.

The app was buffering against the port wifi.

Greg was jabbing at his screen.

"Why isn't this working?

Can anyone get a signal?"

Lauren, the woman who "speaks conversational Italian," was staring at the Spanish crew member.

Her study abroad was in Rome.

Spanish wasn't Italian.

She understood about every fifth word.

Mike was trying a different app.

It translated the crew member's instructions as "your ship enters by the shrimp door."

"What is the shrimp door?" Cassie said.

I sipped my prosecco.

Twenty minutes later, Cassie appeared on deck.

Flushed.

Irritated.

She froze when she saw me.

"Susan?"

She blinked.

"What are you doing here?"

"Same cruise.

Same sailing."

She stared at me.

"But you don't speak the language.

Any of the languages.

How did you even get through the terminal?"

"I asked."

"Asked who?

In what language?"

"The crew member explained everything.

In Spanish."

She looked at me like I'd just said something in a language she didn't understand.

Which, in about twelve hours, would be every language.

"Well.

If you get confused about anything on board, Lauren speaks Italian, so just find us."

"That's sweet, Cassie.

I'm all set."

She walked toward her cabin.

I didn't move.

I had nowhere to be.

And a very good glass of prosecco.

First port.

Cinque Terre.

If you've never been, the villages are stacked on cliffs connected by narrow stone paths.

No cars.

No elevators.

Just ancient stairs and alleyways barely wide enough for two people.

At the top of the stairs, there was a small café tucked into the cliffside.

No English menu.

No tourist signs.

Just an old man behind the counter and a chalkboard written entirely in Italian.

Cassie pulled out her phone.

She needed wifi for the translation app.

There was no wifi.

Greg was jabbing at his screen.

"Why does nothing work in this country?"

Lauren squinted at the chalkboard.

Her conversational Italian from study abroad was twelve years old.

She recognized "caffè" and "gelato." That was about it.

"I think that one is some kind of fish thing?" she said, pointing.

I walked up to the counter.

The old man smiled and said something in Italian.

I understood every word.

He was telling me the daily special was a lemon granita made from lemons in his garden.

He asked if I wanted it with or without cream.

I ordered without cream.

I sat at a table on the cliff edge, eating lemon granita and watching the boats, while the six of them stood at the counter pointing at the chalkboard and hoping for the best.

Lauren ended up ordering what she thought was a cappuccino.

It was a cup of hot lemon water.

The old man had tried to tell her, but she couldn't understand him.

Cassie saw me sitting there.

"You seem comfortable."

"I am."

She didn't say anything else.

That afternoon, I walked the coastal route through Monterosso.

The one I'd mapped for their group.

Halfway along the path, I stopped at a small wine shop.

The owner was standing outside.

He started talking to me in Italian.

About the vineyard behind his house.

About how his grandfather planted the first vines.

About a wine he only sold to people who asked, because tourists just grab the cheapest bottle and leave.

I understood every word.

I bought the bottle he recommended.

I was sitting at the viewpoint I'd starred on their map, drinking wine from a cup the shopkeeper had given me, when I heard voices below.

Cassie and Lauren.

Cassie was holding a printed copy of my itinerary.

My itinerary.

Lauren said, "Whoever planned this route really knew what they were doing."

Cassie didn't respond.

Day three.

Amalfi Coast.

The lemon grove tour.

The one I'd found in a blog written in Italian.

Private.

Twelve people max.

I'd booked one spot for myself.

The group had taken the rest, because I'd put it in their itinerary.

I arrived first.

The grove owner, Signora Rossi, walked me through the terraced gardens above the coast.

She spoke entirely in Italian.

The history of the grove.

Three generations of her family.

How they wrap the lemons in cloth to protect them through winter.

How her grandmother could tell which lemons were ready by smell alone.

I understood every word.

Twenty minutes later, the group arrived.

Signora Rossi began the tour.

In Italian.

Lauren was supposed to translate.

She caught fragments.

"Lemons."

"Family."

"Grandmother."

She missed the story about how the grove nearly closed during the war.

She missed the part about the cloth wrapping technique that's been passed down for a hundred years.

She missed the grandmother's smell test.

She missed everything that made it special.

I didn't miss a word.

Greg saw me nodding along to Signora Rossi's story and stopped.

"Susan?

You understand what she's saying?"

"Every word."

He looked at Cassie.

Cassie adjusted her sunglasses and said nothing.

That evening, Dave walked over to my lounger at the pool bar.

Dave had always been the quietest of the husbands.

He sat down on the edge of the lounger next to mine.

"Susan, I need to say something."

I put down my book.

"That lemon grove today.

The walking route yesterday.

The fact that you understood everything the grove owner said while Lauren was guessing at every third word."

He paused.

"You planned every good thing that's happened on this trip.

And you're the one who wasn't supposed to be here."

He looked back toward the bar where Cassie and Greg were ordering drinks.

"Greg knows it too.

He just won't say it."

He got up and walked back to the group.

I picked up my book.

But I didn't read.

I sat there for a long time thinking about what Dave said.

That I'd planned every good thing on this trip.

And I was the one who wasn't supposed to be here.

Tom would've loved that.

Night four.

Captain's dinner.

I put on my black dress.

Tom's watch on my wrist.

The scratch caught the light from the porthole.

I walked into the dining room.

The Italian waiter arrived.

He described the specials.

Entirely in Italian.

Rapid.

Warm.

A thick southern accent.

The kind of Italian that makes translation apps crash.

Lauren held up her phone.

The app caught fragments.

It converted "branzino al sale" to "bronze at salt."

"I think it's some kind of fish?" she said.

Greg looked at his phone.

His app had translated the risotto special as "rice with bone water."

"What is bone water?" Cassie asked the table.

The waiter turned to me.

He described a local fish preparation his mother used to make.

Branzino baked in a salt crust.

The fish came from the boats at the port that morning.

He recommended it with the white wine from a vineyard twenty minutes up the coast because the minerality matched the crust.

I understood every word.

"I'll have the branzino," I said.

"And the white wine."

The waiter smiled.

He said, quietly, in Italian, "Finally, an American at this table who understands me."

I understood that too.

Six faces staring at me.

Lauren's phone still showing "bronze at salt."

After the first course, a woman at the next table leaned over.

Mid-fifties.

Elegant.

Small leather journal next to her plate, pen clipped to it.

"Excuse me," she said.

"I'm sorry to interrupt.

But did you just understand everything that waiter said?

In Italian?

With that accent?"

"Every word."

She leaned in.

"I write for a travel magazine.

I'm reviewing this sailing.

I've been watching you all evening.

Everyone else at your table is staring at their phones.

You're the only one who understood a single word.

What's your secret?"

"Translation earbuds," I said.

"Military-grade.

128 languages.

No internet.

No phone.

One button."

She put her hand on her chest.

"The ones that use NATO technology?

Every editor I know wants a pair."

"A friend of mine has been a flight attendant for twenty-two years.

She told me about them."

She leaned closer.

"Do they really work without internet?

Even with that accent he had?"

"We're on a cruise ship in the middle of the Mediterranean.

I haven't had wifi since Barcelona.

And that waiter had one of the thickest accents I've heard all week."

"May I write about this?

For the piece?"

"Of course."

A man two seats down, ship's officer, three stripes on his sleeve, looked over.

"Is that the device my wife keeps telling me about?

She's cabin crew.

She says every flight attendant she knows is trying to get a pair."

"They're selling the last batch," I said.

"Big tech companies are trying to buy the technology and lock it behind their subscription apps.

Once the deal goes through, the standalone version is done."

He shook his head.

"That's what my wife keeps saying."

Cassie watched all of it.

The travel writer.

The ship's officer.

The photographs of my ears that nobody had noticed until I pointed.

She picked up her wine glass.

Took a long sip.

Set it down.

Looked straight ahead.

Lauren had stopped looking at her phone.

Positano.

Day seven.

The sunset dinner at the cliffside restaurant.

The one with the three-month waitlist.

The one I'd booked.

I'd kept the reservation when they gave my spot to Lauren.

One table.

One person.

The waiter spoke entirely in Italian.

He described the tasting menu.

Seven courses.

The history of each dish.

Where the fish came from that morning.

The name of the farmer who grew the tomatoes.

I understood every word.

Tom's watch was on the table next to my wine glass.

The scratch caught the last light over the Amalfi Coast.

I didn't check my phone.

I just ate slowly.

Ordered dessert.

Had a conversation with the couple at the next table.

Italian.

They told me about their granddaughter's wedding next month.

I understood every word and told them it sounded beautiful.

When I got back to the ship, Cassie was in the atrium bar.

Tired.

"Where did you eat?" she asked.

I told her.

"We tried to get in there," she said.

"They told us it was fully booked.

Lauren tried to explain we were a group of seven but the host only spoke Italian and Lauren's phone app translated 'party of seven' as 'celebration at seven o'clock.' He thought we were asking about an event."

"It was lovely," I said.

Cassie looked at me for a long time.

"You understood the whole dinner?

In Italian?"

"Every course.

Every story."

"How, Susan?

You've never spoken Italian.

In twelve years of traveling with us, you never understood a word."

"I never needed to.

Tom was there."

Silence.

"Tom's not here anymore.

So I found a better way."

She didn't ask what the better way was.

Not yet.

Last night on the ship.

Farewell dinner.

Cassie found me on the upper deck afterward.

Ocean black.

Stars everywhere.

She sat down.

We were quiet for a while.

"Lauren's app told a waiter she was allergic to 'the table' yesterday," she said.

"He brought her a different chair."

"That must have been frustrating."

"And at the port today, Greg's phone died and he couldn't ask anyone where the shuttle was.

He stood there for twenty minutes pointing at a map until a teenager who spoke English walked by."

She was quiet again.

"You never pulled out your phone once.

The whole trip.

Not once."

"No."

"The lemon grove.

The waiter.

The wine shop.

That couple in Positano.

You understood everyone."

"I did."

Silence.

"What are they, Susan?"

I looked at her.

"They're called Vylaras," I said.

"Military-grade neural processing.

128 languages.

One button.

They look like hearing aids."

"Where do I get them?"

"Big tech companies are trying to buy the technology and lock it behind their subscription apps.

If the deal goes through, the standalone offline version gets pulled from the market."

She looked down at her hands.

"Of course."

"If the acquisition goes through, the only version left will be locked inside their apps.

Fewer languages.

Required internet.

Monthly subscription fees."

She nodded.

The way you nod at news you've already missed.

I stood up.

"Safe travels home, Cassie."

I walked back to my cabin without looking back.

Here's what I learned.

For twelve years, Tom and I cruised with these couples.

I researched every port.

Found every restaurant.

Planned every excursion.

After he died, they went to Italy without me.

Posted about it on Instagram.

Then called me to plan their next trip.

Because apparently I'm capable enough to find a private lemon grove in a blog written in Italian.

Just not capable enough to stand in the grove and understand the owner when she speaks.

Then they invited me to dinner.

Good china.

Candles.

Six faces that already knew.

Greg said: "You held up the restaurant line fumbling with Google Translate."

Cassie said: "Tom was the one who talked to everyone.

Without him..."

They gave my spot to a 34-year-old who studied abroad twelve years ago.

Then used the itinerary I built for them to enjoy every stop on the trip.

So when I showed up on that same ship, I had two choices.

Show up fumbling with translation apps, pointing at menus, proving them right.

Or show up understanding every word in every language at every port, proving I never needed anyone to translate the world for me.

The earbuds didn't make me capable.

But they proved I always was.

Cassie watched me sip prosecco on the Lido Deck while Greg jabbed at a translation app in the Barcelona terminal.

She watched Lauren order hot lemon water because she couldn't understand the old man in Cinque Terre while I sat at the cliff edge eating granita I'd ordered in Italian.

She watched a travel magazine writer photograph my ears at the captain's dinner while Lauren's app gave the table "bronze at salt" and "bone water."

And on the last night, she asked where to get them.

By the time she asked, big tech was already circling.

Karen's entire flight crew has been scrambling to order before the acquisition goes through.

Once the deal closes, the standalone offline version is gone.

If someone has excluded you and then asked you to do the work anyway.

If they've replaced you with someone younger who speaks "conversational Italian" and then handed you the planning.

If they think losing your husband means you lost your voice.

You need these earbuds.

Not because the technology is impressive.

Though it is.

But because sitting at a cliffside restaurant in Positano understanding every word the Italian waiter says, while the woman who took your spot can't tell the difference between "party of seven" and "celebration at seven o'clock"?

That's not petty.

That's just accurate.

One button.

128 languages.

Zero apps.

Zero internet.

Zero help from anyone.

Cassie asked where I got them.

I told her big tech is buying them out.

She's waiting for whatever version they decide to sell her.

Fewer languages.

Required wifi.

Monthly fees.

I was already home.

Already understanding.

Already planning Christmas in Paris.

Your move.

Everyone thinks Noah took 2 of every animal. He only took 2 of the ones the Nephilim had touched.

Genesis 6:4 says the Nephilim were on the earth in the days of Noah, and also afterward. Before the flood, the earth had become hell.

Genesis says the whole earth was filled with violence, and the blood of the innocent soaked so deep into the ground that it cried out to God. The wickedness sank into the soil until the earth itself was sick.

It corrupted the trees, it turned the animals into beasts, and it poisoned every living thing that walked or grew on the face of the earth.

So what made the world so wicked that God had to drown it? It started with a group of angels called the Watchers.

They looked down from heaven, lusted after the daughters of men, and gave up eternity to have them. And when those angels bred with human women, they created something that was never meant to exist.

The Nephilim.

But the Watchers did something even worse. The Book of Enoch records that they handed their children forbidden knowledge.

They had stood in the presence of God, they knew the secrets of heaven, how God formed every living thing and how the unseen world moves behind the one we see. That knowledge was never meant to leave heaven, but the Watchers dragged it down to earth, twisted it, and taught their children how to rule with it.

They taught men warfare, sorcery, astrology and blood magic.

The Nephilim were born with their fathers’ hatred for God. They hunted people, devoured them and drank their blood, chasing the power the forbidden knowledge had promised them.

And when that wasn’t enough, they turned on everything else God had made. The cattle, the birds, every creature that crawled on the ground, they twisted what God had written into them until they became things God never made.

Trees grew to monstrous size. Animals stopped looking like animals and turned into beasts.

And men were mixed with the Nephilim bloodline, creating abominations God never created. Genesis 6:6 says it grieved God to His heart that He had made man.

Not only because men sinned, but because what He made was no longer what He made.

Human blood was no longer fully human, and men no longer carried the image of God. The flood wasn’t just punishment.

It was God erasing what the Nephilim corrupted, so humanity could be human again.

But before the rain came, God gave Noah the strangest command in all of scripture. He told Noah to bring 7 pairs of every clean animal, and 1 pair of every unclean animal, onto the ark.

It’s right there in Genesis 7:2.

Unclean meant corrupted, touched by what the Nephilim had done to God’s creation. And God told Noah to bring them on board anyway.

Noah didn’t just carry God’s creation through the flood. He carried the Nephilim’s too.

That’s how the bloodline survived. Within a few generations the giants were back, the spies Moses sent into the promised land came home saying they looked like grasshoppers next to them, and David stood in front of one of them, a giant named Goliath who defied the armies of the living God.

But the bloodline wasn’t the most dangerous thing that survived the flood. The water drowned the bodies of the Nephilim, but it couldn’t drown what was inside them.

The Book of Enoch says that when the giants died, their spirits came out of their bodies as evil spirits. Heaven was never made for them, so they stayed here on the earth, restless and hungry, looking for someone to torment.

And the first family they came after was Noah’s. But Noah was an old man by then.

He had built the ark with his own hands, listened to the screaming outside the door as the water rose, and carried his sons and their wives through the end of the world. And when the ground finally dried and his sons had children of their own, he watched those spirits come for his grandchildren.

The Book of Jubilees says they began leading Noah’s grandchildren astray, to make them stumble and to destroy them. The first children born into the world God had just washed clean were being dragged into the same darkness He had just drowned.

Noah fell before God and begged Him. He reminded God what the Watchers, the fathers of these spirits, had done in his day, and he cried out for God not to let wicked spirits rule over his grandchildren and wipe them off the earth.

And God heard him. He commanded His angels to bind every one of those spirits.

But the chief of the spirits begged God to leave him some, and God let 1 out of every 10 stay on the earth.

That 1 in 10 never left.

So God sent His angels to Noah to teach him how to stand against them. They showed Noah how the spirits deceive, and how to heal the sickness they bring with what God planted in the earth.

And Noah wrote every word down in a book, so his grandchildren, and their grandchildren after them, would never stand defenseless again. But here’s what almost nobody has ever told you.

Every family alive today comes from Noah’s grandchildren.

Genesis 9:19 says that from Noah’s 3 sons the whole earth was filled. Then Genesis 10 names their children one by one, and closes by saying that from these families the nations were divided in the earth after the flood.

Every nation, every family line, every one of us traces back to the grandchildren Noah prayed over. That means you are Noah’s grandchild.

The same spirits that came for his family are still here, and they’re coming for you. But they don’t start with the people who are asleep.

They start with the ones who see it coming.

You’ve felt it. The closer you get to God, the harder something pushes back.

The heaviness that settles over the house the moment you sit down to pray. The thoughts that come out of nowhere in the middle of the night.

The prayers you pour your whole heart into that seem to hit the ceiling and fall right back down. And you look around at a world that laughs at the Bible like it’s a children’s story, the same way they laughed at Noah while he built the ark, and every year you feel a little more alone in your faith.

Noah felt that too.

He preached while he built, and they mocked him right up until the day the water came. When God shut the door, only 8 people were inside.

You were never crazy for seeing what you see, and it was never that you didn’t pray hard enough. You were standing against the 1 in 10 without the book God gave Noah to stand with.

But for centuries, the early church read these books as scripture. Jesus told His disciples the end would look just like the days of Noah.

His own brother Jude quotes the Book of Enoch word for word in the New Testament. And Peter writes about the spirits in prison who disobeyed in the days of Noah.

But slowly, church leaders began calling these books dangerous. One council at a time, they were pulled out, burned, and called heretical for exposing too much.

And the Bible got smaller and smaller, until most believers grew up never knowing the prayer Noah prayed over them. That’s why so many passages in your Bible point to something that isn’t there.

And none of it was an accident.

Because a believer who knows how the enemy works, who prays what Noah prayed, and who can see the attack coming before it reaches the house is a believer the enemy can’t touch. So those books were stripped out, and God’s people were left fighting a war they were never allowed to understand.

But God never loses. And the way He protected Noah’s book was hidden in Genesis the whole time.

Open your Bible to Genesis 10. Noah’s son Ham had a son named Cush.

Cush was Noah’s grandson, one of the very grandchildren Noah fell on his face and prayed over. Now turn back to Genesis 2:13 in your King James.

The river that flowed out of Eden ran around the whole land of Ethiopia.

In the Hebrew, that land is called Cush. Every time your King James Old Testament says Ethiopia, the word underneath it is Cush, the land of Noah’s grandson.

And once you see it, you see it everywhere. Moses married a woman of Cush, and when his own brother and sister turned on him for it, God Himself defended him.

When Jeremiah was thrown into a pit of mud to die, the man who pulled him out was from Cush. The Psalms promise that Ethiopia will soon stretch out her hands to God.

And in Acts 8, God sent His messenger running down a desert road to one man, an Ethiopian riding home reading the prophet Isaiah. Ethiopia was never a random nation.

It’s the land of Noah’s grandson, and God wove it through your Bible from the Garden of Eden to the Book of Acts.

So when the rest of the world cut Noah’s story out of its Bibles, the land of Cush kept it. The only complete copies of the Book of Enoch and the Book of Jubilees left anywhere on earth survived in Ethiopia, written in Ethiopia’s ancient language.

Everywhere else they were burned, banned or lost. Think about what that means.

The prayer Noah prayed to protect his grandchildren was kept safe for thousands of years by the family of the grandchild it protected.

And because you are Noah’s grandchild too, that prayer was prayed over you. Ethiopia is the only nation in Africa that was never colonized.

No empire ever ruled it, so no one could ever reach inside their churches and cut a single page from their Bible.

That’s why Ethiopia has the biggest Bible in the world, with 88 books. The same 66 books you were given, plus the 22 the rest of the world took out.

They even kept God’s name. Where your Bible says Lord, theirs says Yahweh.

The Book of Enoch is there, with the full story of the Watchers and what happened to the spirits of their children. The Book of Jubilees is there, with the prayer Noah prayed over his grandchildren, the 1 in 10 that were left behind, and what God’s angels taught Noah to do about them.

Enoch names the archangels who stand before God and what each one watches over, and he wrote his warnings for a generation far in the future, the generation that would see the end. And that’s the generation Jesus said would look just like the days of Noah.

A small group of believers set out to put that Bible back in the hands of every family.

They gave themselves a name, The Faith Made, and they had one mission, to put all 88 books Ethiopia kept into one Bible, in plain English, with nothing left out. Over 200,000 Christians are reading it now, and they’re sharing testimony after testimony of what God is doing in their homes.

Some of them write in tears that the heaviness finally left the house, that their prayers finally feel like they reach God, and that for the first time in their lives the Bible makes sense from Genesis to Revelation.

But The Faith Made is small. They print in batches, and when a batch sells out it can be weeks before the next one.

If the link below still works, they still have copies. And there’s no risk in trying it.

The Faith Made gives you a full 365 day guarantee.

That’s a full year to pray what Noah prayed over his grandchildren, to read what the angels taught him, and to read the whole story the enemy tried to bury. And if it’s not what you expected, send it back for a full refund, no questions asked.

God shut the door of the ark to carry Noah’s family through the flood, and He carried Noah’s book through thousands of years in the land of Noah’s own grandson. Now it’s waiting for you, his grandchild.

Get the complete Bible, the link is right below. 👉 https://thefaithmade.com/pages/6-ways P.S. If you’re afraid these books go against the Bible you already have, they don’t.

The 88 don’t contradict the 66, they complete them, and every book you already love is still there word for word. It’s printed on full 8.5 by 11 inch pages, so you’ll never have to squint at a single verse.
