bodyText:
C.S. Lewis called himself "the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England."
 
He didn't feel his way into Christianity. He argued his way in.

Before he wrote The Chronicles of Narnia, C.S. Lewis was a committed atheist teaching at Oxford.

And he wasn't a casual one.

When Lewis was 9, his mother was dying of cancer. He prayed for her to be healed.

She died in August 1908.

As a teenager at boarding school, he quietly let go of the faith he'd been raised in. By his twenties, he was sure the universe was too cruel to have been made by a good God.

As he later put it: "My argument against God was that the universe seemed so cruel and unjust."

He fought in the trenches of World War I and was wounded in 1918. Nothing he saw there changed his mind.

He went on to teach at Oxford, surrounded by some of the brightest minds in England. He was quick, widely read and very hard to win an argument against.

Years later, he admitted something revealing about those years.

"I maintained that God did not exist. I was also very angry with God for not existing."

That's the part most people miss about Lewis. He wasn't indifferent to God.

He had questions, real ones. And for more than 15 years, nobody gave him answers strong enough to take seriously.

Then something strange started happening.

The arguments that had held his atheism together began to come apart, one at a time. He kept noticing that the writers he respected most, the ones who seemed to see life most clearly, were believers.

He later joked, "A young man who wishes to remain a sound Atheist cannot be too careful of his reading."

Around 1930, he gave in and admitted that God exists. He called himself "the most dejected and reluctant convert in all England."

But believing in God wasn't the same as believing in Jesus. That step still felt impossible.

On the evening of September 19, 1931, Lewis had dinner at Magdalen College with two friends.

One was Hugo Dyson. The other was a professor of Anglo-Saxon named J.R.R. Tolkien.

After dinner, the three men walked along Addison's Walk, a path by the river. They talked about myth, metaphor and the story of Christ.

Lewis had a specific objection. He loved ancient myths about a god who dies and comes back to life, but when he read the same idea in the Gospels, it felt like just another myth.

Tolkien pushed back. What if the story of Christ was a myth that actually happened?

They kept going for hours. Tolkien went home around 3 a.m., and Lewis and Dyson kept talking until 4.

A few weeks later, Lewis wrote to his closest friend: "Now the story of Christ is simply a true myth."

On September 28, 1931, eight days after that walk, his brother drove him to Whipsnade Zoo in a motorcycle sidecar.

Lewis later wrote, "When we set out I did not believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and when we reached the zoo I did."

Here's what makes that so remarkable.

Lewis didn't feel his way into Christianity. He argued his way in.

He tested his faith against every hard question he had, and it held. That's why he could later defend it so well.

A decade later, during World War II, the BBC asked him to explain Christianity on the radio to a country at war. Those talks became Mere Christianity, one of the most widely read Christian books of the 20th century.

The man who spent years without good answers spent the rest of his life giving them to others.

Now compare that to how most of us came to faith.

We were raised in it. We heard the stories, sang the songs and memorized the verses.

That's a beautiful gift. But it means most of us have never tested our faith the way Lewis did.

We have what you could call an untested faith. It works perfectly inside church, where nobody challenges it.

Then someone outside church asks a real question.

A coworker asks how you can trust a book written 2,000 years ago. A relative at dinner says evolution disproved Genesis.

A friend going through a loss asks how a good God could allow this.

And an untested faith freezes. Not because the answers don't exist, but because we've never practiced giving them.

Here are 8 signs your faith has never really been tested:

→ You believe the Bible is true, but couldn't explain why to a skeptic

→ You change the subject when faith comes up at work

→ You've never read a serious argument against Christianity

→ You'd struggle to explain why a good God allows suffering

→ You assume science and faith are on opposite sides

→ You can't name any evidence for the resurrection outside the Bible itself

→ You feel a little anxious when a smart person says they don't believe

→ Your strongest answer to "Why do you believe?" is "I just do"

None of this means your faith is weak. It means it's untested, and that can change.

So where do you start?

→ Many systematic theology books run close to 1,000 pages. They're brilliant, and most end up half-read on a shelf.

→ Sermons are built to encourage you, not to prepare you for a debate.

→ Apologetics podcasts are interesting, but you forget most of an episode by the next week.

→ YouTube debates are entertaining. Watching someone else argue isn't the same as being able to do it yourself.

→ Seminary courses go deep, but they can cost hundreds of dollars a class and take years.

→ Most church Bible studies teach what to believe. Very few spend time on why.

What Lewis had, and what most of us never get, is practice facing hard questions with real evidence.

That's the idea behind the Systematic Theology 52 Week Workbook for Adults from Valorrea.

It takes one hard question a week, the kind Lewis wrestled with: Does God exist? Can we trust the Bible? What about evolution? Why is there suffering? Aren't all religions the same?

Each week has three pages, and each lesson takes about 10 minutes.

First comes the Evidence: biblical, philosophical, scientific and historical. Then comes the Defense, where you face the strongest objections skeptics raise and practice answering them.

Last comes Reflection, where you put it all in your own words.

That middle step is what makes it different. You don't just read the answer; you rehearse it, so you're ready when someone actually asks.

You don't need a theology background, and you don't need to prepare anything. It works on your own, with your spouse, or in a small group.

It's also grounded in historic Christian belief: the inspired, inerrant Word of God, one God in three persons, and salvation by grace alone, through faith alone, in Christ alone.

Don't expect to feel like Lewis in week 1. The first few lessons will probably raise as many questions as they answer.

That's how testing works. Week by week, the answers stop being something you've heard and become something you can explain.

Samantha B. put it simply: "Six months ago I would have frozen." When a coworker asked her why she believes the Bible is reliable, this time she had an actual answer.

More than 60,000 believers have used it. In a survey three months after purchase, 96% said they can now explain why they believe, not just recite verses.

94% said they now confidently answer questions that used to stump them. And 91% said they became more excited about their faith after working through the evidence themselves.

These aren't miracles. It's 10 minutes a week of doing what Lewis did: taking the hard questions seriously.

And there's a 90-day money-back guarantee. If you don't grow in your ability to explain what you believe, you get your money back.

Think like a detective. Defend what you believe.

You can see the workbook here: https://valorrea.com/products/systematic-theology-52-week-workbook-for-adults

P.S. Someone will ask you a hard question about your faith this year. Start this week, and by then you'll have worked through the answer instead of searching for one on the spot.

P.P.S. Lewis spent more than 15 years without good answers. You don't have to spend another one.

bodyText:
In 1969 I kept a 21-year-old cowboy alive for 31 hours, and he swore he'd dance with me for it. For four reunions I sat at the table while the band played, and watched him dance with every other woman in the room.

Every one of those nights, when the first song started, he crossed the floor and held out his hand. Every one of those nights I had a reason ready. New shoes. A bad knee. Somebody had to watch the purses. Not one of those reasons was the truth.

Last Veterans Day, I flew to Denver for the reunion again, and for once I was the one waiting on him.

I sat down at a round table near the dance floor and put my hand on the empty chair beside me. A young Navy corpsman in dress blues, one of the volunteers they send over every year, stopped with a tray of ginger ale and asked me who I was saving it for.

"A man who's late," I said. "About 56 years late."

He sat down. So I took him back to the sand at Chu Lai, and I told him.

He was maybe 22. He had the same short haircut and the same careful manners as the boys I used to wash and shave, and he called me ma'am every other sentence. I liked him right away.

Two widows at my table quit pretending to read the program. A drummer from the band came down off the stage with his coffee. People started dragging chairs over from the other tables, the way you do at a wedding when somebody's telling a good one. By the time Bill Hargrove walked into that ballroom, there were sixteen chairs pulled in around me.

I've told that story one time in my life, to sixteen people in a hotel ballroom. I'm writing it down now because I think somebody else needs it.

My name is Peggy Wu. Back then it was Peggy Chan. I'm 79. My father ran a grocery on King Street in Seattle's Chinatown, and I was raised in the rooms above it. I joined the Army Nurse Corps at 21 because my brother Henry got drafted and I wasn't about to let him go over there without somebody who knew how to stop bleeding.

Henry came home fine, by the way, and complained about the Army food for 50 years.

In January of 1969 the Army flew me to Chu Lai. An evacuation hospital made of Quonset huts on the sand, the South China Sea on one side and the helicopter pad on the other.

You learned fast at Chu Lai. You learned to tell how bad a night was going to be by how many rotors you could hear at once.

The wards were long tin tubes with plywood floors, forty beds to a side, fans that pushed the heat around without ever moving it out. We wore fatigues and jungle boots and worked twelve hours on and twelve off, which mostly meant twelve hours on and then however many more the helicopters said.

Bill Hargrove came in on one of those helicopters in March. Twenty-one years old. Six foot four. Boots longer than my forearm. A ranch kid from outside Billings, Montana, and before I'd finished cutting his shirt off he'd told me about his horse.

He was my patient for 23 days. Seven days in, I could have told you his mother was Arlene, his horse was Duster, and he'd never seen the ocean until he flew over it on his way to the war.

But the first night was the one that counted. Fourteen helicopters in two hours. Bill came out of surgery with a hole through his belly and another in his chest, and a little before midnight his pressure started to fall.

Our head nurse was Major Ruth Calloway. Thirty-four years old, from Muncie, Indiana, with a back as straight as a tent pole. She looked at the ward. She looked at him. She looked at me.

"Lieutenant Chan, that bed is yours. You don't leave it."

I didn't leave it for 31 hours. I took his pressure every 15 minutes and wrote it on a white index card clipped to the head of his bed. I hung blood and squeezed it in by hand. I talked to him when he couldn't hear me, and when he could.

Ruth ran that ward all night like a train station. She never raised her voice. She'd walk the aisle between the beds with a flashlight in her teeth and a clipboard under her arm, and every time she passed his bed she'd look at my card, then at me, and keep walking. That was how you knew you were doing it right. She didn't stop.

Here's what I remember most. He took hold of the bed rail with his right hand and my wrist with his left, and he did not let go. Not when he was out cold. Not when they took him back to surgery at hour nine and brought him back. Somewhere around hour 18 my legs quit, and I sat down on the plywood floor next to his bed with my arm still up in his hand. I sat down again at hour 26. He never let go of that rail. I sat down twice.

At hour 20, Ruth Calloway knelt down on that floor beside me in her fatigues and put a canteen cup of coffee in my free hand.

"Steady hands, Chan," she said. "He's watching your face, not his own."

By morning of the third day his pressure held. By the fifth he was cussing the orderlies. By the second week he was trying to get out of bed without asking anybody.

The doctors said later that he shouldn't have made it, that the bleeding was too much and too long. I don't know about that. I know he squeezed my wrist every time I said his name, and for 31 hours I said it about every two minutes.

Now. My mother. My mother believed there was nothing in this world a pot of tea couldn't put right, and she mailed oolong to me at that hospital every two weeks, my name brushed on the brown paper in Chinese. Tight little dark curls of leaf, from the herb shop on Jackson Street.

I'd switched to coffee at 14 to be American. I called it my mother's weeds, and I gave every single parcel away.

The first one went to Bill. He was sitting up by then. He dropped a pinch of it into a clear water glass from the mess hall, poured hot water over it from the coffee urn, and held it up to the window.

"Look at that, Lieutenant," he said. "Opens up like a hand."

He drank it. He made a face like I'd given him castor oil. "Boiled saddle," he said. And he finished every drop.

After that, every parcel that came while he was there went to Bill's bed. Every time, he held a glass out to me. "I'd rather drink the IV bag," I'd say. "Boiled saddle," he'd say, and drink it himself. By the end of the month the whole ward was saying it. Boiled saddle. I can still hear twenty boys saying it in the dark.

In April the Viet Cong put rockets into the compound one night. A piece of one opened Ruth Calloway's shoulder from the collarbone down. They stitched her up in the next hut, and two days later she was back on the ward with her arm in a sling, straight as a tent pole, telling the orderlies the floor was a disgrace.

On day 23 they flew Bill out to Japan. I walked with them to the pad. He was thin and yellow and grinning, and he pushed the last parcel of my mother's tea back into my hands.

"When we dance, Lieutenant, you're drinking a glass of this."

"When we what?"

"When I'm home," he said, "I'll dance with you. A real dance. A whole song, start to finish."

"You'll walk first, Hargrove," I said. "That's an order."

"Yes ma'am, Lieutenant."

He's answered me that way on every phone call for 56 years. That night, when I went to clip a fresh card on his bed for the next boy, I found the card from that first night was gone from his folder. He'd taken the index card with my handwriting on it.

I came home in January of 1970. I married Tom Wu, a machinist at Boeing, in 1972, and I worked 33 years of nights in an intensive care unit on First Hill. Bill went home to Montana and broke colts and fixed fence on one ranch outside Billings for 50 years, and he wrote me a letter every Christmas. He never once mentioned the dance. He never once had to.

The Chu Lai nurses started holding a reunion in the 1980s. Every year on Veterans Day, a hotel in Denver, a banquet, and a band. Ruth came every single year in her dress uniform, with the shoulder she said still told her the weather. She gave the toast. She was the last one off the dance floor.

I went to every one of them. I'd sit with the girls from my ward and we'd laugh about things nobody else on earth would laugh at. The rats in the supply hut. The chaplain who couldn't swim. The night the generator died in the middle of a surgery and six of us held flashlights over the table for an hour and a half.

Bill found us in 2021. His granddaughter found the reunion online and drove him down from Billings. For four years after that, he danced with every nurse in the room. Except one.

By then Ruth's cholesterol had gone bad, and I'd watched it take her apart one reunion at a time.

2001, a statin. 2010, they doubled it. 2017, an injection every two weeks. After the toast she'd excuse herself to the ladies' room with her purse, and come back with her sleeve buttoned at the wrist.

"My numbers are right where they should be, Peggy," she told me that year, with her napkin folded in her lap. "My doctor's thrilled with me."

2018, two stents. 2020, a small stroke, and a cane, and her hands shook so bad on her coffee cup she drank it through a straw. Ruth Calloway, who once stitched a boy's scalp by flashlight. 2022, she came in a wheelchair and sat at the end of the head table, and her numbers were still right where they should be.

In August of 2023 the phone rang before the sun was up. It was Ruth's husband, Gordon, and he skipped every word you'd normally start with.

"She doesn't know me anymore, Peggy."

The big stroke. A memory-care home in Tacoma.

That's the part I could never get past. A rocket couldn't put Ruth Calloway down in 1969. Fifty-four years later her own arteries did it, and left her alive to not know it.

Gordon died just after New Year's. The memorial was set for a Saturday in January, in a little Lutheran chapel in Tacoma. Ruth's daughter Janet called me that week. She wanted Mom's girls up front for "Abide With Me". All four verses, standing, the way Ruth would have wanted.

"Would you stand with them, Peggy?"

The yes was right there in my throat, waiting to come out.

But by then my own cholesterol had been climbing for a long time. I'd been on atorvastatin since 2013, and my LDL went up a little at every checkup anyway. And the last few years, my calves knotted up on the Seattle hills and my chest went tight on my own stairs.

I pictured that chapel. Four verses on my feet at the front of the room. The cramp climbing my legs by the second verse. Going down in front of Ruth's wheelchair, in front of every nurse I'd ever served with, in front of her grandchildren in the second row.

I'd sat down twice on a plywood floor in 1969. I wasn't going to fold up in front of Ruth.

"I'll be there, Janet," I said. "But I'll be sitting down."

She was too polite to ask me why.

So that Saturday I sat in the front pew with five purses in my lap, while five old nurses, not one of them under 75, stood up front and sang.

Bill had flown in from Billings. 76 years old, a gray suit he'd bought for the occasion, and his boots. He walked those old women up the aisle one on each arm, three trips, as easy as feeding horses. Then he stood behind Ruth's wheelchair with his hands on the grips through all four verses, and he never once shifted his feet.

Same monsoon. Same ward. Same year.

He was a boy with a hole through him on a plywood floor. I was the one who knew how to keep him alive. Fifty-six years later he was the one standing.

And he stood up there holding her chair while I sat in the pew holding the purses.

Afterward, in the fellowship hall, he found me by the cookie table.

"You doing all right, Lieutenant?"

"I'm fine."

He studied my face the way I used to study a monitor. Then he let it go.

"Come to Denver this year," he said. "And this time you dance with me. You still owe me one."

Four reunions. Four first songs. Four times he'd crossed that floor with his hand out, and four times I'd found a reason. The shoes. The knee. The purses. "I don't dance to this one."

The first year it might even have been the shoes. After that it never was. It was my legs, and it was my breath, and I was not going to let the boy I'd kept alive watch me need a chair halfway through a song.

"I'll think about it," I said.

He took the memorial program out of his jacket, wrote on the back with a pencil stub, and handed it to me.

"Nov 11. Denver. First song."

I took it home to Seattle and put it in the little velvet box where I keep my Army Nurse Corps pin.

I let the story rest there and lifted my eyes. I was back at the round table in Denver, and the band was tuning. The corpsman hadn't touched his ginger ale. One of the widows, a little woman named Dottie whose husband had been a surgeon at Qui Nhon, had turned her chair all the way around to face me.

"Is he coming, honey?" she asked.

"He said he was."

I looked at the ballroom doors. No Bill yet. So I picked the story up again at the winter after the memorial.

By February my calves were knotting on the hill up from the bus stop on Queen Anne. Halfway up, every time, I'd have to stop and hold on to the same lamppost and pretend I was looking at the view.

Then I started stopping on my own stairs. Twenty-two of them up to our apartment, and I'd stop on the landing with my hand on the rail. My chest went tight carrying groceries. I wore wool socks to bed and my toes stayed like ice. And by 7:30 the news was watching me instead of the other way round, my chin on my chest.

I told myself that's 78. I'd written those exact words in a hundred charts about other people, and I'd never once believed them.

Then came the night in March.

A little after 3, I woke up with my chest in a band and my left leg locked up like a fist. I made it to the bathroom doorway, and my legs folded and put me on the tile.

That's where Tom found me. On the bathroom floor in my nightgown, two fingers on my own wrist, counting.

He had 911 half dialed before I could even lift my head.

"I'm counting, Tom. Let me count."

"You're counting your own pulse on the bathroom floor."

"It's coming down now."

He pulled me up by both hands and walked me out to the kitchen. He put the kettle on, because neither one of us was going back to bed, and when he sat down across from me his hand shook on his mug.

"Fifty years," he said. "Fifty years you've told every man on your floor to go in. You'd chart this on anybody else in five seconds. You're going in."

He said it evenly. The mug said otherwise. I'd only seen that hand shake once before, at the airport in 1969, and he wasn't even my husband yet.

"You win," I said.

He was on the phone to the VA the minute they opened, and he stayed on hold 50 minutes rather than hang up.

Tom isn't a talker. He was a machinist for 38 years and he says about as many words a day as a lathe does. When Tom makes a speech at 3 in the morning, you listen.

The VA clinic is on Beacon Hill. A waiting room full of old men in ball caps, and one television nobody was watching.

Dr. Sundquist. Young, tall, tired. He was eating a granola bar between patients, and he finished it while he read my file.

They took four tubes of blood. The results were in by Friday, and so was I.

He swung the laptop around so I could see the screen, as if a retired nurse might not know how to read a lipid panel. I knew. That was the trouble.

"Mrs. Wu, your LDL is 169. Your blood pressure's up too."

I didn't give him a word back.

"Twelve years on atorvastatin, and every panel's been higher than the one before. After that business on your bathroom floor, I'm putting you on forty milligrams instead of twenty."

Then he said something kinder than I expected.

"Hear me on this: you didn't bring this on yourself. Your father had a heart attack at 61. That's genes. And you worked thirty-three years of nights and ate out of hospital cafeterias. That's not a moral failing, Mrs. Wu. That's a job."

I thought about my father, face down behind the counter between the rice sacks and the soy sauce, and my mother screaming for somebody to call the ambulance in two languages.

"If it's the genes and the job," I said, "then explain Bill Hargrove to me."

"And who would that be?"

I gave him the short version. Same ward, same year. Fifty years of ranch beef and fried eggs and no doctor if he could help it. Never once on a pill. And he'd walked five old women up a chapel aisle in January without breathing hard.

Dr. Sundquist shrugged.

"Some people just get lucky, Mrs. Wu."

Then he scrolled down.

"One more thing. In October I want your LDL below 100. If it isn't, you go to the injection clinic. A shot every two weeks."

I didn't hear much after that. The injection clinic was Ruth excusing herself after the toast. It was her sleeve buttoned at the wrist. It was a cane, and a straw, and a wheelchair at the end of the head table. It was Gordon's voice on the phone before sunrise.

The girl at the front desk handed me a card. Fasting lipid panel. Tuesday, October 21.

Dr. Sundquist leaned out of his door as I went. "Get me under a hundred, Mrs. Wu, and we'll talk."

When I got home I opened the velvet box and put the card in it, on top of a memorial program with "Nov 11. Denver. First song." written on the back.

One date to keep a needle out of my arm. One date to keep a promise I'd made on a helicopter pad.

In May I took the bus downtown to meet my granddaughter for lunch. On the Harbor Steps my left leg locked and I sat down on a step, and I couldn't get back up.

A teenage boy with a skateboard under his arm hauled me up by both elbows while a tour group off a cruise ship stood there and watched.

"You okay, grandma?"

I told him I was fine. I'd been telling everybody I was fine all year.

I rode the bus home with my hands in my lap so nobody would see them shaking. My granddaughter had waited at the restaurant forty minutes. I told her the bus was late.

That night I took both cards out of the velvet box and laid them side by side on my dresser, under the pin.

One said October 21. One said November 11. And I knew how both of them ended if nothing changed.

I wasn't going to fly to Denver and sit at that table a fifth time while Bill stood alone on the floor with his hand out. He'd walked every old nurse in Tacoma up an aisle. He was not going to walk me.

So I nursed myself. I'm a nurse. It's the one thing I know how to do. I gave up the roast duck skin from King Street and the Sunday bacon. Oatmeal every morning. Egg whites. I walked the Queen Anne hill twice a day, lamppost and all. I took the doubled pill every night. And I bought a fingerstick cholesterol tester off the drugstore shelf on Queen Anne Avenue and wrote every number in a little spiral notebook, like a chart.

Six weeks of that. My home meter said 172.

Higher than April. I'd done every single thing I would have told a patient to do, and the number went the wrong way.

I checked the meter against the strip lot number. I checked it against Tom. His was fine. Tom eats like a teenager and his was fine. Mine was the one going the wrong way.

The June check. Dr. Sundquist read my spiral notebook for a long time before he looked up at me.

"One sixty-six," he said. "Better than nothing. Not enough. October stays."

"I'll take your pill," I said. "I'm not going to the injection clinic."

He shut the laptop lid with one finger.

"Then I'm out of ideas, Mrs. Wu."

I sat in the car in the VA lot with the engine off until the windows fogged. Then I called Billings.

"Bill. I can't dance with you. My legs won't hold me through a song. They haven't for years. And my cholesterol won't come down. If it isn't under 100 by October 21, they send me to the injection clinic."

There was nothing on the line. Nothing for so long I checked the screen to see if the call had died.

"Yes ma'am, Lieutenant," he said. And he hung up.

Ten days later a box came from Billings. A boot box, taped shut three times around, with my address in that square handwriting. Inside, wrapped in an old canvas ranch jacket that smelled like horse, was a cassette player, one tape, and a note on a feed-store receipt. PEGGY. PLAY ALL OF IT.

At the round table in Denver, the other widow touched my sleeve. Marlene Kovach. She'd lost her first husband in 1968, she said, and married Frank in '74.

"My Frank says he's fine," she said. "He won't dance anymore. He's upstairs right now with the TV on."

Nobody at the table said anything to that. Dottie patted her hand.

The corpsman leaned in. "What was on the tape, ma'am?"

I pushed play at my kitchen table, with Tom across from me. There was Bill, slow, a screen door banging somewhere behind him.

"You never told me, Lieutenant. All this time. I watched you sit for that hymn in January and I knew something was wrong. I didn't know what till you called."

"You're going to call me a dumb cowboy when you hear the answer. You already know it. You handed it to me in a mess-hall glass. But first you have to understand what's making your number climb."

"After Gordon called about Ruth, I couldn't make it add up. So I spent two winters at the library in Billings, and my daughter's a pharmacist, so I made her read along. And you know what Ruth's numbers were the week of her stroke? Gordon read me her chart. Right where they should be. The pills got her number down. The stroke came anyway."

"Here's what I learned, Peggy. High cholesterol isn't really a cholesterol problem. The high LDL number is the symptom. The real problem is what happens to that cholesterol once it's in your bloodstream."

"After years of chronic inflammation from modern processed food, and constant exposure to free radicals, some of that LDL gets into your artery walls and gets held there."

"Then it gets oxidized. It turns sticky. And once it's sticky, it starts forming plaque. Your arteries start filling up with oxidized cholesterol that was never supposed to be there."

"And once that LDL is in the wall and oxidized, your immune system answers it like damage. More plaque forms. With every heartbeat your vessels stiffen and keep closing, and one day the plaque ruptures into the heart attack that kills you. Or the stroke that takes your name."

"Ruth's stents. Ruth's stroke. Your legs on that hill. Your chest on your stairs. That's not four things, Lieutenant. It's one. Oxidized LDL is what causes every one of them. Not the total number. The oxidized cholesterol your body can't clear."

"Now the statin. The statin lowers your LDL. Fine. But it does nothing to stop the cholesterol you've still got from oxidizing. Lowering the supply doesn't stop the oxidation. It just lowers the number on the chart, while the cholesterol you still have keeps turning dangerous underneath."

"That's why you gave up the duck skin and walked that hill and the number didn't care. You were working the supply. Nothing in your whole day was touching the oxidation."

"A chart number's a head count, Peggy. It tells you how many head are in the pen. It doesn't tell you how many of them are sick. Ruth's head count was right where it should be the whole way down."

"And it feeds itself. Oxidized cholesterol, damage, more plaque, a stiffer vessel, more cholesterol held in the wall, more of it oxidized. Every heartbeat, another turn. And a pill that only lowers the head count can't stop it turning."

"Now here's what nobody at that clinic is going to tell you. Same ward. Same monsoon. Same powdered eggs. Any doctor in that ward would have bet you'd outlive the boy with the hole in his belly by twenty years. Look at us. I've eaten beef every day for fifty years, and I've never taken a pill for anything but a hangover. In March my doctor sent me for a scan of the arteries in my heart, and he came out and said he'd never seen a rancher's that clean. Luck had nothing to do with it."

"There's exactly one thing I did every day for 56 years that you didn't. Your mother's tea."

"You gave away every parcel. I drank every glass. Boiled saddle, and I never once stopped. When I got home and the parcels quit, I wrote to your mother off the return address on the paper. Mrs. Chan, King Street, Seattle. She mailed me a tin every month until 1994. You didn't know that, did you."

I didn't. My mother never said one word. Tom stopped the tape for me, and I sat there a minute. Dumb cowboy, he'd said I'd call him. I was the dumb one.

I thought about her at the kitchen table on King Street, writing a man's name in English letters she'd practiced on the back of a grocery bag, wrapping a tin in newspaper for a cowboy in Montana she'd never meet. For twenty-five years. While her own daughter drank coffee.

"When she passed, the tins stopped. I bought every oolong in Billings. Not one of them opened in the glass. I wrote to shops in Chinatowns all over the country till I found whole leaf again, and I've had a cup every morning since. Every morning, Peggy. Calving season. Blizzards. The morning my wife died. Every morning."

"There's a class of compounds in oolong called polyphenols. Powerful antioxidants. They're concentrated in oolong, and they neutralize the free radicals responsible for oxidizing LDL cholesterol."

"Researchers in Japan took human LDL and added oolong to it, and it held out almost twice as long before it oxidized. Then in a second test, the oolong neutralized the free radicals themselves."

"Once the oxidation stops, the cholesterol in your blood stays in its normal, harmless form, and your body processes it through the liver the way it was designed to. But those polyphenols leave your blood within a day. So it's a cup every morning, Lieutenant. Not when you remember. Every morning. The cholesterol is not the enemy. The oxidation is."

"Your mother mailed you the answer every two weeks for a year, and you handed it to a ranch kid with a hole in his belly. I've been drinking your share for 56 years."

"Now listen, because you're cheap and I know it. The word oolong on a grocery box is a category name and nothing more. Nobody's promising you a gram of leaf. Nobody's promising you a thing about what ends up in your glass. Your average grocery-store oolong puts around 12 milligrams of EGCG in a cup. EGCG's the strongest of the polyphenols, and 12 is next to nothing."

"What your mother sent was whole leaf. You put it in a clear glass and it opens up like a hand. That's leaf that still has the polyphenols in it."

"Most of what's in a bag on the shelf is dust. Chopped and ground because it's cheaper. Put it in a clear glass and it clouds the water and sits on the bottom like silt."

There was a long pause on the tape there. I could hear him breathing, and a horse somewhere, and the screen door again. When he came back his voice was different.

"Look in the jacket pocket," he said.

I did. There was an index card, soft as cloth and yellow as an old tooth. On the front, in blue ballpoint, in my own handwriting: Hargrove, W. PFC. BP q15min. Then line after line of numbers, 15 minutes apart, so small I needed my glasses. He'd kept it 56 years. On the back, in pencil, in his: READ THE GLASS, NOT THE BOX. 1. Whole leaf, not dust. 2. Every bag weighs the same. 3. They measure the polyphenols in the tea you actually drink. 4. One way to make it, every morning, even half asleep.

Under that, smaller: Steep one bag in a clear drinking glass. Whole leaf opens back into leaves. Dust clouds the glass. A number like yours takes weeks, not days.

On the tape he said, "A hot cup of anything feels good going down, Lieutenant. Don't let a good feeling fool you. Look in the glass. Look at what's printed on the bag."

The last line on the card was squeezed in at the bottom edge: Under 100, you come to Denver. First song's mine.

In July I walked down to the big supermarket on Mercer Street and bought the store-brand oolong. Forty bags for $3.49. Never turned the box over. Never did the glass. I grabbed the cheapest thing on the shelf, the way I had my whole life.

I'll be honest with you. Part of me was glad it was cheap. Part of me still didn't want to be drinking my mother's weeds at all, at 78, because a cowboy told me to on a cassette tape.

It was nice enough. A hot cup in the morning. I felt a little better and told myself that was it working. Two weeks later my home meter said 168.

Only then did I follow the card. One bag in a clear drinking glass. The water went the color of a mud puddle in about ten seconds, and when I tipped the glass, a brown silt slid along the bottom. Not one leaf. After that I turned the box over and read every word on it. It didn't meet a single one of the four rules.

Thirty-one hours I sat with that man, and he still knew I'd reach for the bottom-dollar box. I'd been grabbing the cheapest everything since I was stocking cans in my father's store.

The next morning I walked to the branch library on Queen Anne. A librarian about my granddaughter's age sat me down at a computer and made the letters big enough to read without my glasses, and she never once rushed me. I went back three days running. I read up on every brand of oolong the library's computer would show me. And I looked up the oxidation work Bill had talked about, because I'm a nurse and I don't take anybody's word for anything, not even a cowboy's. It was real.

I crossed them off on the back of the supermarket receipt, one after another. The dust bags. The "blends". The fancy loose tins that never say how much leaf you're getting. Every box that didn't say one word about what's in the cup.

Every one of them said oolong. That was the whole trouble. Bill was right. It was a category name, and most of them were hiding behind it. Some had pretty pictures of mountains. Some had a little gold dragon. Not one in ten said how much leaf was in a bag, and almost none said anything at all about what ends up in the cup you drink.

One was left. PiPi Tea.

Whole-leaf oolong. Every bag weighs the same. 340 milligrams of total polyphenols in the brewed cup, including 187 milligrams of EGCG, tested by Light Labs. More than fifteen times the supermarket cup. One bag with breakfast, made the same way every morning. 4 for 4.

Their page explained why. PiPi Tea's cup is the strong one for three reasons.

The plants are grown above 4,500 feet in Pu'er, Yunnan. High altitude, strong sun and slow growth push the young leaf to make more of these compounds than lowland leaf grown for a factory.

They only take the tip. The bud and the first leaves hold most of the EGCG. The older leaves hold less. The stem holds the least. A picker taking the tip by hand leaves the weak parts on the bush.

A machine taking the same top growth can't do that. It cuts the tip, the stem and the lower leaves in one pass, and all of it goes into the same batch because it's cheaper. Then it's ground up into dust.

That's why when you open a supermarket bag, it's dust. And when you open a PiPi Tea bag, it's whole leaf.

Whole leaf. The leaf Bill held up to the window in 1969.

It cost more than $3.49. I paid for it out of my Army pension and didn't think twice. I've spent more on worse for less reason.

The PiPi Tea pouch was on the doormat the following Thursday. I put one bag in a clear glass on the kitchen counter, poured the water over it, and stood there and watched. The little dark curls loosened. Then they opened. Whole green leaves, edges and all, turning slowly in the glass. Like a hand. Exactly the way he'd said it in 1969.

I drank it with breakfast. And somewhere in the middle of the dishes I noticed I was humming. Standing at the sink, humming, the way I used to on the ward at 4 in the morning when the boys were finally asleep. I hadn't hummed in a year. Tom came in from the other room to see who'd turned the radio on.

That wasn't the cholesterol moving. Bill's card had been plain about that: a number like mine takes weeks.

Day 5, I walked up from the bus stop, past my lamppost, all the way to the top without stopping. Day 10, with Tom out at the hardware store, I put "Moon River" on the record player and danced the kitchen with a dish towel. One whole verse. I sat down after. But I'd done a verse.

I wanted to call Bill so bad my hands itched. I didn't. Under 100, you come to Denver. The number had to come first.

Week 2, the 7:30 slump didn't come. I watched the whole news and then read in bed till 10. I took all twenty-two stairs without stopping on the landing.

Week 3 I walked down to the Harbor Steps by myself on a Saturday, and I went up them, all of them, slow, with my hand an inch off the rail and not on it. A man selling flowers at the top clapped for me. I don't think he knew why. I didn't tell him.

The tea didn't do every bit of it, and I won't pretend it did. I walked that hill all summer. I took the doubled pill. But I'd been doing all that since May, and the number had gone up.

Week 5, I slept without the wool socks for the first time since winter. Week 8, on a Monday morning, my home meter said 117. I sat down on the edge of the tub and looked at it for a long time.

Tuesday, October 21 came.

I got to the VA an hour early, went down to the cafeteria, and ordered bacon and eggs. The same breakfast the Chu Lai cooks used to make us after a bad night, the only real bacon in all of I Corps. Two strips, two eggs, buttered toast. I ate every bite of it before a fasting draw.

The phlebotomist saw the toast crumbs on my sweater.

"Mrs. Wu, you know this is a fasting panel."

"Honey, I was drawing fasting panels before your mother was born. Draw it."

She drew it. She shook her head the whole time.

Dr. Sundquist came in with the printout an hour later, frowning at it like it was in the wrong language. He had them stick me again for a fresh tube. Then he dialed the lab from the wall phone, standing up, while I sat there with a cotton ball taped in my elbow.

"You're sure that's Wu," he said into the phone. "W, U. Margaret Wu. Date of birth 1946."

He hung up and sat down on his stool.

"Mrs. Wu. Your LDL is 91."

From 169.

"I don't know what you've been up to," he said, "but don't stop. The injection clinic can have somebody else. And your atorvastatin goes back to 20 milligrams, starting tonight." He typed it in while I watched. "I guess some people do get lucky."

"Luck had nothing to do with it," I said.

The appointment card from the velvet box was in my purse. I slid it across his desk. He turned it over once, read his own clinic's printing, and let it fall into the wastebasket under the desk.

Tom was waiting in the car. When I told him, he put both hands over his face and sat like that for a while.

"Go call your cowboy, Peg."

Same car. Same lot. Same phone.

"Bill," I said. "What's the band playing first this year?"

Nothing. Then he laughed until he was coughing, and through the coughing he said, "You know what they're playing, Lieutenant."

That was the end of the story. I looked up from the table. Sixteen chairs. Marlene had her phone out with Frank's room number on the screen. The bandleader had run the first bars of "Moon River" for the sound check and then held the song. It was 7:40, and still no Bill.

Marlene leaned over to me. "Next year," she said. "Tell your Bill to come up to 614 and make my Frank come down."

Dottie had a tissue out. The drummer had gone back up on the stage and was looking over at our table instead of at his bandleader. The corpsman kept looking at the doors, then at me, then at the doors, like he could make a man from Montana walk through them by staring.

I touched my collar. The appointment card wasn't in the velvet box anymore. The pin was on my dress.

When I looked up from it, a tall man in a silverbelly Stetson was coming across the dance floor from the elevators, a thermos under one arm and snow still on his shoulders. Billings had been socked in all afternoon.

He stopped at the table. He looked at my legs, and then he looked at me.

I got to my feet. Nothing on the table under my hand. Nothing on the chair-back.

"You're late, Hargrove," I said.

"Yes ma'am, Lieutenant."

And then two old people pushing 160 years between them stood in front of sixteen strangers and held on to each other, and neither one of us said anything for a while.

He put his right hand flat on my back and took my right hand in his left, the same hand that had held my wrist for 31 hours, and it was just as strong. I could feel every one of those sixteen chairs watching. I didn't look down at my feet once. I looked at his face, like Ruth told me to.

We danced "Moon River". The whole song, every bar, start to finish. When it ended the band went straight into the next one, and I didn't sit down for that one either.

Ruth wasn't there. She's in Tacoma, in a room with a window, and she doesn't know either of our names. But halfway through that first song my right leg gave a little warning, and I heard her as clear as 1969. Steady hands, Chan. I kept my feet.

In January I sat in a pew with five purses in my lap and couldn't stand for one hymn. In November I danced two songs with the man who held my wrist for 31 hours.

Back at the table, Bill twisted the cap off his thermos and filled a clear hotel water glass. The leaves turned over in it. He held it up to the chandelier, and then he held it out to me, the way he had a hundred times on that ward.

I took it. I drank the whole glass in front of sixteen people.

"Boiled saddle," I said.

He laughed till his hat came off and he had to grab a chair. I stayed on my feet.

I'm writing this because I came very close to sitting out that dance too.

Ruth's chart said right where it should be, every year, right up until the year she didn't know her own husband. The doctor reads the chart. A nurse watches the patient. Be the nurse.

So watch. Yourself, or the one who shares your kitchen with you. Stopping on the stairs. Holding a lamppost and pretending to look at the view. Icy toes under the covers. Asleep in the chair before the news is over. Sitting out the dance and blaming the shoes.

Nobody's going to put those things on a chart. Nobody's going to circle them. Your number can sit right where it should be while you stop going places, one by one, and nobody notices but your own family. And sometimes not even them, because you're good at hiding it. I was the best there was.

If a doctor is booking you into an injection clinic, and something in you says no because you sat beside somebody you loved all the way down that path, you're not being difficult. You're paying attention.

bodyText:
A Jewish billionaire told my pastor two years ago in Zurich: 'The same Bible that told you Israel would one day become a nation again also describes a day when the ships stop moving, the merchants stand far off, and everything downstream starts running out.'

My pastor didn't believe him. He thought it was financial paranoia. Until he saw the maps they don't put on television with his own eyes.

Then last Tuesday, a box showed up on my porch with no letter inside it.

Just seeds, and one sheet of paper with four biblical passages written on it in handwriting I have known for thirty years.

The man who mailed it was my pastor.

Nobody at our church had heard from him in two years.

I am writing this down because of what he said when he finally answered the phone, and because everything he described is in the news right now.

Let me say one thing before I go further.

I am not one of those end times people. I have never once stood in a grocery store and thought about the book of Revelation. I am a grandmother who has read her Bible her whole life and who mostly reads the Psalms.

So you can take this or leave it. I only want to tell you what happened.

Pastor Wendell came to our church in 1994.

He married my daughter Rachel. He buried my mother. He baptized both of my grandchildren, one of them in a pond because the baptistry was being repaired that spring.

I need you to understand what kind of man he is, because it matters to everything that comes after.

In thirty years in that pulpit I never heard him preach one sermon about the end of the world.

Not one. He thought it made people strange. He used to say that the Lord gave us Tuesday to be faithful in and we should start there.

He went on a mission trip in the spring of 2024.

He came back different.

Quiet in a way he had not been. Short with people. He preached three Sundays in a row on the same passage in Genesis, which he had never done before in his life.

By that fall he had stepped down, sold his house, and moved to Montana.

He did not send a letter. He did not do a farewell dinner. He answered his phone for about a month and then he stopped answering it at all.

Our church decided he had burned out. A few people said breakdown. One man said he thought Wendell had lost his faith over there and was too proud to say so.

I want to be honest with you. I was relieved to have an explanation. I told Rachel he had probably seen too much poverty and it had broken something in him.

She said, "Mom, he went off the deep end."

And I let that be the answer for two years.

Then last Tuesday there was a box on my porch.

Inside it was a sealed vault of seeds, heavier than I expected. Under the lid was a piece of notebook paper folded in half.

No letter. No explanation. Four verses in his handwriting.

Revelation 6:5 and 6. Matthew 20:2. Genesis 1:11. Matthew 24.

I sat on my porch step and read that paper probably ten times.

Then I called the only number I have for him.

He did not answer Tuesday. He did not answer Wednesday.

He answered Thursday afternoon.

The first thing he said was, "I wondered if you would call."

I asked him what the box was.

He said, "Did you read the paper?"

I said I read it and I did not understand it.

And he said, "Then let me tell you where I have been, and you can decide what you think of me after."

I want to give you what he said the way he said it, because I wrote it down that night while I still had it.

The trip was supposed to be two weeks. It turned into most of a summer, across three places, and he said he did not understand what he was looking at until he had seen the third one.

The first was Sri Lanka.

He said the government there banned chemical fertilizer. Not because of a war. Not because of weather. A decision, on paper, announced with good reasons attached to it.

The next harvest came in short. A country that had been feeding itself started buying rice from other countries instead, and the price of food went up so fast that people who had been fine the year before were standing in line.

He said, "Nobody was punished for that decision. Nobody resigned. It was just a policy, and then there was no food."

The second was Venezuela.

He said the shortage there did not look like a famine in a photograph. It looked like paperwork.

Ration cards. A limit on what one person could buy. Days of the week assigned to you by the last number on your identification card, so you could not simply go when you needed to.

He said the part he could not get out of his head was how normal everyone acted about it. Mothers standing in line on their assigned day, checking their phones, waiting their turn to be handed what they were allowed to have.

The third was Nigeria.

He said that one showed him the piece he had been missing, which is what happens when the ships stop.

Imports got restricted. A city that ate rice that came in on boats did not suddenly grow its own. Prices in the market doubled in a matter of weeks, and then doubled again, and the people who got through it were the ones with something growing in the dirt behind the house.

Then he said the thing that made me sit down.

He said, "Three countries. Fertilizer in the first one. Rationing in the second one. Shipping in the third one. Not one of the three started with a drought. Every one of them started with a decision made by somebody who was never going to stand in that line."

I asked him what any of that had to do with him quitting.

He said, "Because on the way home, I stopped in Zurich. I was invited to a private logistics roundtable by a prominent Jewish commodities investor whose family has financed shipping fleets for three generations."

"I sat in that conference room in Switzerland and watched hedge fund managers and shipping executives pull up satellite tracking maps of the Persian Gulf. They weren't talking about politics. They were tracking the Strait of Hormuz."

"That billionaire looked at me across the table, tapped a map showing twenty percent of the world's petroleum bottlenecked in a twenty-mile stretch of water, and said:

'Pastor, you preach Revelation 18 like it's a metaphor. The merchants standing far off while the ships stop moving isn't poetry. It's supply-chain math. And when those tankers halt, it's not just a problem for the Middle East. That reaches America.'"

He said the chill went right through his bones.

"On the flight home, I opened Matthew twenty-four and noticed the word order for the first time in my life. I realized I had spent thirty years picturing the wrong part."

He asked me to go get my Bible and read it out loud to him, and I did, standing in my kitchen.

"And ye shall hear of wars and rumours of wars."

"For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines."

He said, "Wars first. Then famine. Not at the same time. After."

He said he had preached that chapter for thirty years as something that happens later, to somebody else, in a time none of us would live to see, and he had never once read it as an order of events with a place in it where we are standing right now.

I said the news has been nothing but talks and deals for months. Every week they say they are close to something.

And he said, "Read First Thessalonians five, three."

I looked it up.

"For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them."

He said, "Count how many times you have heard the word peace this year. That verse is not a prediction about some future broadcast. It is a description of the sound it makes right before."

Then he told me to turn to Revelation 6, which is the verse on the paper, and read the third seal.

"And I beheld, and lo a black horse; and he that sat on him had a pair of balances in his hand."

He asked me what balances are.

I said scales.

He said, "Right. And what do people use scales for."

I said weighing things.

He said, "You weigh what is short. Nobody weighs what there is plenty of."

Then he had me read the next line.

"A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine."

He said, "Now read Matthew twenty, two. The second verse on that paper."

It is the parable of the men hired to work in the vineyard. The owner agrees with them for a penny a day.

A penny was a day of work.

And a measure of wheat was a penny.

He did not explain it to me. He let me sit there with my finger on the page and work out that a man was going to labor from morning until night for one measure of wheat, and go home with nothing else.

I said, "That is groceries."

He said, "That is groceries."

Then he said, "There is a second half of that verse that nobody ever quotes. Hurt not the oil and the wine. The bread gets weighed. The expensive things are left alone. When it starts here, the flour and the rice will have a limit sign on the shelf and the specialty aisle will be full."

He said I had already seen a version of it in 2020, and that I had told myself it was temporary, and that I would tell myself the same thing again.

I did not have an answer for that, because he was right. I did tell myself that.

He asked if I wanted him to stop. I said no.

So he told me to read Ezekiel four, sixteen, which is not a verse I had ever read in my life.

"They shall eat bread by weight, and with care."

Bread by weight.

That is a limit per customer. That is a sign taped to an empty shelf. Written down thousands of years before anybody built a grocery store.

Then he said, "Now let me tell you what I think about the water everybody is watching on the news."

He said the strait they keep showing on the map is not only about gasoline. Fertilizer moves through that same water. The stuff that makes food grow in the quantities this country eats comes in on ships.

He told me to read Revelation 18.

The chapter lists what stops. Wheat is on the list, right there in the merchandise.

And then this.

"Every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off."

And, "For in one hour so great riches is come to nought."

He said, "Sailors standing off at a distance watching it come to nothing. That is not a modern idea. Somebody wrote that down when the biggest ship on earth had oars."

Then he said, "Now go to the last verse on the paper, and this is the one I mailed you a box about."

Genesis 1:11.

"And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself."

Whose seed is in itself.

He said, "Eleven verses into the Bible, every plant on this earth is given the next plant inside it. That is the design. A seed makes a plant and the plant makes seeds and it never has to ask anybody for permission."

Then he asked me if I had a grape in the house.

I said I did.

He said, "Go cut one open. I will wait."

I put the phone on speaker and set it on the counter and cut one of my grapes in half with a paring knife.

Nothing.

I cut another one. Nothing.

I went and got the watermelon out of the refrigerator, the one I had cut for my grandson on Sunday, and there was not a seed in it.

The mandarins. Nothing.

I stood in my own kitchen with a knife in my hand and I could not find a seed in any fruit I owned.

He said, "I spat watermelon seeds off my grandmother's porch every summer of my childhood. So did you."

I said my grandchildren have never done that once.

He said, "It took about twenty years and nobody announced it. And there is a patent, and you can look it up tonight, for seed engineered to go sterile after one season. Seed built to die."

He let that sit.

Then he said, "Somebody spent money to undo the eleventh verse of the Bible, and they did it while we were all arguing about other things."

I asked him who he meant by somebody.

He said he was not going to give me a theory, and that he had stopped doing that when he stopped preaching. He said he would rather I read a document.

Then he asked me a question.

He said, "Have you ever heard of Agenda 2030?"

I said I had heard the name somewhere and had no idea what it was.

He said, "Everybody has heard the name. Almost nobody has read it. And your fruit bowl is a page out of it."

Here is what he told me it is, and I have since read it myself, so I am not repeating a rumor.

Agenda 2030 is a real United Nations document. Not a video somebody made. Not a theory off the internet. It is published on the United Nations' own website, it was agreed to by the member nations, and the full name of it is Transforming Our World: the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.

The deadline is in the title. 2030.

And running all the way through it is food. Remaking food systems. Who grows food, how it gets grown, what gets planted, what gets phased out.

He said, "They did not hide any of it. They printed it, they put a date on it, and they assumed nobody would read it. They were mostly right."

Then he said, "Now do the arithmetic that matters. Count the growing seasons between this fall and 2030."

I counted them on my kitchen calendar while he waited.

There are three.

He said, "Three springs. That is not a long time to learn something you have never done."

He told me one more thing about it that I did not want to hear. He said Sri Lanka did not ban that fertilizer out of nowhere. It was done in the name of the same kind of targets that document is built on, and announced as progress, and the people who made that decision were not the ones who stood in the rice line afterward.

He said one more verse about that and then he let it go.

Revelation 17. The kings of the earth have one mind, and give their power and their strength to the same thing.

He said, "You do not need a villain. You need to notice that nations making the same decision at the same time is in the book, and that it is happening on a schedule somebody published."

Then he said the part that I think about the most.

He said, "Look around your kitchen. Everything in it needed somebody's permission to be there. Somebody's truck, somebody's store, somebody's payment system, somebody's policy. And Revelation thirteen says the day comes when no man might buy or sell without permission."

He said, "Seed in a closet is the one thing in your house that does not need anyone's approval next spring."

I asked him what he wanted me to do about any of it.

And he said, "What Joseph did."

He said Joseph was not a prophet in that chapter. He was an administrator who believed a warning and filled the storehouses while there was still grain to put in them, in the years when it was easy and nobody thanked him for it.

Then he said, "Read Genesis forty one, thirty. All the plenty shall be forgotten. That is the part people miss. It gets forgotten. Nobody can remember afterward that it was ever easy."

Then he said it plainer than he had said anything else that night.

He said, "I am going to tell you exactly what I am doing, and I want you to do the same thing. Grow your own food. Start this season. Not the one after it."

I told him I did not know how to answer that. I am sixty nine years old and the only thing I have ever kept alive is a peace lily on the hall table.

He said, "I know. That is why I mailed you the box instead of a letter."

He walked me through it like he was reading me a recipe.

He said, "Open it. Do not plant all of it. That is the first thing people get wrong."

He said the vault is meant to sit sealed in a cool dark closet and keep for years, so that whenever the day comes that you need it, it is already in the house. That is the whole reason it exists. It is not groceries. It is the ability to make groceries.

Then he said, "But plant a little of it this season anyway."

I asked him why, if the point is to have it stored.

He said, "Because you do not want the first time you ever grow food to be the year you have to."

He said pick three easy things. Lettuce. Green beans. Tomatoes. Put them in this year while the stores are still full and nothing depends on it, kill some of them, learn what your window looks like, and then you will know what you are doing when it matters.

I said, "Wendell, I do not have a garden. I have a back yard the size of a parking space."

He said, "Then use pots. Every single thing in that box will grow in a five gallon bucket with a hole drilled in the bottom. I have people in an apartment in Billings growing tomatoes and lettuce on a concrete step that gets four hours of sun."

He said potting soil out of a bag. Water. Sunlight. Three things.

He said the seeds come up in a few days and the first time you see them come up you will understand why he could not stop talking about the eleventh verse.

I told him about my back, because I cannot kneel on the ground anymore and I have not been able to for four years.

He said, "Set the buckets on a table. Waist height. You will never bend over once. And let your grandchildren do the planting, they are better at it than we are and they will remember doing it for the rest of their lives."

I asked him what happens if I kill all of them.

He said, "Then you will have killed a couple of dollars of seed in a year when it did not cost you anything to learn. That is the cheapest lesson available to a person right now."

And I asked him the question I really wanted to ask, which is what if none of this ever happens.

He said, "Then you will have a box of seed in a closet that cost you less than a tank of gas and one shelf of space, and I will look like a man who moved to Montana for no reason. I have made peace with that."

Then he stopped being gentle about it, and this is the only time in the whole call that he did.

He said, "But if it does happen, and you have not done this, you are going to be standing in a line on your assigned day with a card in your hand, holding what somebody decided to give you. I watched thousands of mothers do exactly that. I am not willing to picture you in it."

He said, "Seed is not a hobby. It is the difference between waiting to be fed and feeding yourself."

I did not say anything for a minute.

Then he said, "One more thing, and this is the part where most people get taken."

He said the seed has to be heirloom.

He said hybrid seed is what most companies sell, and hybrid seed comes back weak the second year or does not come back at all, which means you are buying it again every spring on somebody else's terms.

He said, "Heirloom means the harvest gives you next year's seed for free. One box, and you are never buying seed again. That is the eleventh verse working the way it was set up to work, and it is the only kind worth putting in a closet."

I asked him why nobody at church was talking about any of this.

He said, "Matthew twenty four, thirty eight. They were eating and drinking and marrying, and knew not until the flood came. It does not say they were wicked. It says they did not know. That is all. They were busy."

Then he said, "And that is why I am not angry at any of you for what you decided about me."

I told him what Rachel had said about the deep end.

He laughed for the first time in the whole call and said, "She is not wrong to be careful. Tell her a prudent man foreseeth the evil. Proverbs twenty two, three. And tell her the rest of it, because the rest of it is the part that ought to worry a person. The simple pass on, and are punished."

I asked him why he mailed the box now.

He bought his own two years ago, when he got home, before any of this was on the news.

He said, "Because they are getting hard to get."

He told me most of the outfits that were selling heirloom seed a few years ago are not selling it anymore, one way or another, but that the one he uses is still shipping.

I asked him what he meant by one way or another.

He said, "someone doesn't want us to have these."

And he left it there, and I did not ask again.

Then he said something a preacher raising money would never say.

He said, "Do not take my word for one thing I have told you. Most of what gets sold to people who are worried is junk. Do not buy anything because I said it."

He told me to do four things instead.

One. Read Revelation six, five and six. Then read Matthew twenty, two. Work out on paper what a penny bought and what a penny paid for a day of work.

Two. Cut a grape open. Then read Genesis one, eleven.

Three. Look up that plan on the site of the people who published it and count the growing seasons left.

Four. Read Matthew twenty four, and then watch the evening news, and decide for yourself which part of the order we are standing in.

He said, "If all four of those come back the way I think they will, then get seed. Not because of me. Because you checked."

He asked me not to tell anyone he called.

I have not, until this.

Here is what I did over the next three days.

I read the two verses at my kitchen table with a pencil and did the arithmetic and it came out exactly the way he said it would.

I found that document on the website of the people who wrote it. The year is right there in the title.

I counted the growing seasons left on my kitchen calendar, and it is not very many.

And Friday night I sat down in front of the news with my husband and heard a man in a suit say the word peace twice in one segment, and for the first time in my life it did not sound like good news to me.

My husband told me Thursday that I was being dramatic.

He read the paper out of the box himself on Saturday morning. Not the verses, the handwriting. He knows that handwriting too. Wendell married us.

He did not say anything for a long time.

Then he went out to the garage and came back and asked me where the seeds were going to go, because the closet in the hall gets warm in the summer.

That is what agreement looks like in this house. No conversation. He just started solving it.

I ordered one vault for our house, one for Rachel, one for my son Kevin, and one for my sister Jo Ann.

That is when I understood why he mailed boxes to families he baptized instead of quietly keeping his seed in a closet in Montana.

First Timothy five, eight. If any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith.

He was not being generous. He believed he was under an obligation.

Then I did the thing I feel worst about.

I waited three days before I told anybody outside my family, because I did not want to be the woman at church who sends everybody links.

When I finally sent it to the fourteen women in my Sunday school class, eleven of them wrote back within the hour that it was out of stock.

I checked it myself and it was.

It came back Tuesday morning. I do not know for how long and neither does anybody else.

I sat at my table feeling like a fool for waiting three days to tell people I have sat beside for twenty years.

The vault he sent me is made by a company called Nuvera. They sell it directly on their own site, not in stores and not on Amazon. Over sixteen thousand seeds, thirty five garden varieties, mostly vegetables, sealed so it keeps for years in a cool dark closet.

It is under forty dollars, and if you do not want it they take it back.

Wendell told me plainly that it is forty dollars of seed and a job to do, not a miracle. Most of it stays sealed in the closet. A little of it goes in a bucket on my back step this month so that I know what I am doing before I have to know what I am doing.

That is all he asked of me, and it is all I am asking of you.

A prudent man foreseeth the evil.

The simple pass on.

P.S. On the stock, because eleven women from my class could not get one this week. It goes in and out, and it has been doing that since the spring, and it moves every time something new happens in the news. Check whether they actually have them before you decide anything. And understand what late costs on this one. Being early costs forty dollars. Being late costs a growing season, and there is nobody on this earth who can sell you a season back.

P.P.S. Rachel called me Sunday night. She had cut a grape open in her own kitchen with her daughter standing there. She did not apologize for what she said about him and I did not ask her to. She ordered two, one for her house and one for her husband's mother.

P.P.P.S. What is actually in it. Over sixteen thousand heirloom seeds. Thirty five varieties, mostly vegetables. Sealed for long storage in a cool dark closet. Set the buckets on a table if you cannot kneel, the way I cannot. Wendell has people doing this on an apartment step in Billings. You are not being asked to become a farmer. P.P.P.P.P.S. If you are thinking you will just buy canned goods instead, I thought that too. Wendell's answer was one sentence. Cans are a number that only goes down.
