bodyText:
Billy Graham's best friend walked away from God. It took one photograph.

This is not a rumor.

It's in the history books. It's in his own book. You can look it up tonight.

His name was Charles Templeton.

In the late 1940s, Templeton and a young Billy Graham were close friends and preaching partners. Two young evangelists traveling, preaching, filling halls. Some who heard them both thought Templeton was the more gifted preacher of the two.

If you'd asked anyone back then which one would change the world, a lot of them would have said Templeton.

Then the doubts came.

And he did something Billy Graham never did.

He walked away.

Templeton left the ministry. He became a novelist and a news commentator. And years later he wrote a book with a title that should stop every Christian parent cold.

Farewell to God.

He even tried to talk Billy Graham into leaving too. When Graham wouldn't, Templeton decided his old friend had "committed intellectual suicide by closing his mind."

Two best friends. Same pulpits. Same crowds. Same Bible.

One became the most famous evangelist in history.

The other said goodbye to God.

So what happened?

What was the one thing that broke Charles Templeton's faith?

It wasn't a scandal. It wasn't a woman. It wasn't money.

It was a photograph.

Years later, the journalist Lee Strobel sat down with Templeton for his book The Case for Faith. Templeton was 83 by then, and sick with Alzheimer's. And he told Strobel what started it all.

A photo in a magazine. A mother in Africa, during a drought, holding the body of her dead baby. Looking up at the sky.

Templeton looked at that picture and asked himself one question.

How can a loving God let this happen?

He couldn't answer it.

Nobody had ever taught him how.

And he decided that it simply wasn't possible for an intelligent person to believe in a God who loves.

One photograph. One question. One of the most gifted preachers of his generation, gone.

But here's the part of the story that broke my heart. And I think it will break yours.

At the end of that interview, Strobel asked Templeton what he thought of Jesus.

And the old man softened. He said Jesus was the most important person who ever lived. He said everything good he knew, he learned from Jesus.

And then he said three words.

"I miss Him."

And he started to cry.

He never came back. He died in 2001.

Think about that. A man who loved Jesus. Who missed Jesus. Who walked away anyway, because of one question about suffering that nobody ever helped him answer.

Now here's why a mom in 2026 should care about a preacher from the 1940s.

Because your child is going to see that photograph.

Not the same one. But one just like it.

It might be a news clip. A war somewhere. A kid her age in a hospital bed. A TikTok of a mother screaming over a stretcher.

And it will be on a screen in her hand. At night. In her room. With nobody next to her.

And she's going to ask Templeton's question.

How can a good God let this happen?

The only thing you get to decide is whether she's heard an answer before that moment.

Or whether it's the first time.

I didn't know any of this a year ago.

A year ago I was just a mom watching her daughter's faith get quieter, and telling myself it was a phase.

Let me tell you how it happened.

Hannah was 11. My oldest. The kid who used to make me pull over the car so she could pray for a dead squirrel on the side of the road. That's who she was. Tender. Believing. The first one up at the altar on kids' Sunday.

Then one night in March, she came downstairs at 10PM. She was supposed to be asleep.

Her face was white.

She had her phone in her hand. She'd been watching videos about a war overseas. One of them was a mother holding her little boy. He wasn't moving.

Hannah sat down on the stairs and said, "Mom. Why didn't God stop that?"

I hugged her. I said, "Oh, sweetie. God has a plan. We can't always understand it."

She said, "But He could have stopped it. Right? He's God."

I said, "He'll make everything right in heaven, honey. Let's go to bed."

She went to bed.

And I stood in the kitchen and realized I had just done exactly what everyone did to Charles Templeton.

I handed her a sentence instead of an answer.

I didn't know that was what I'd done yet. I just knew something had shifted.

Because after that night, Hannah stopped singing in church.

She still went. She still stood up when everyone stood up. But her mouth didn't move during the worship songs. She just watched.

Then she stopped praying at bedtime. She said she was "too tired." Every night. For weeks.

Then one Sunday on the way home she said, "I don't think prayer really does anything. If it did, all those people would have been okay."

My husband Dan looked at me in the rearview mirror.

Neither of us said a word.

Then the questions got harder.

"How do we know God is even real?"

"Why does God let little kids get cancer?"

"If God loves everybody, why does He let people go to hell?"

She'd ask at dinner. At bedtime. In the car. And every time I'd reach for something, and every time it came out the same.

"We just have to trust Him."

"Some things we won't understand until heaven."

"That's a good question for your Sunday school teacher."

She stopped asking me.

That's the part that scared me most. Not the questions. The silence after them.

Because I knew where the questions go when a child stops bringing them to you.

They go to the phone.

I did what every Christian mom does. I tried everything.

I talked to her Sunday school teacher. She was lovely. She said, "Oh, Hannah's a sweetheart. Kids this age go through this. Just keep bringing her."

I watched what they did in that class one Sunday. A Bible story. A craft. A snack. A song with hand motions. Eleven year olds gluing cotton balls on paper sheep.

Hannah was too old for it and she knew it.

I bought her a children's devotional with a pretty pink cover. She read two pages.

I bought her a "tough questions for kids" book. It had a one-paragraph answer to suffering that basically said God is sad too. She read it, closed it and said, "That's not an answer."

She was right.

I signed her up for a Christian girls' summer camp. $950. She came home with a bracelet and a sunburn. Three weeks later she still wasn't singing.

I made us do family devotions after dinner. Dan read a verse. We prayed. Hannah stared at her plate.

I asked our pastor to talk to her. He was kind. He told her that God works all things together for good. She nodded politely and later told me, "He didn't really answer it either."

I spent more than $1,500 that year on books and camps and curriculum.

None of it touched the actual question.

Because I didn't understand what the actual question was.

I thought it was a phase. Or hormones. Or the phone. Or the news. Or maybe I'd sheltered her too much. Or not enough.

I blamed myself a lot.

Dan grew up in church like I did. When Hannah asked him why God allows suffering, he said, "Because people sin, sweetheart." She said, "That baby didn't sin." He went quiet.

Two lifelong Christians. And our eleven year old had asked a question neither of us could answer.

And I had a son coming up behind her. Owen was 7. Still praying for every dog he met. Still asking if Jesus could hear him through the ceiling.

I'd tuck him in and think, four years. In four years he's going to see his own photograph.

And I'm going to say "God has a plan" again.

That's where I was.

Then one night in October, Hannah left her phone on the couch, and I saw her search history.

I wasn't snooping. It was just open.

"Is God real"

"How can God be good if bad things happen"

"Why I stopped believing in God"

There was a video in there. A young woman, maybe 22, sitting on her bed with a ring light, telling her "deconversion story." Raised in church. Youth group. Purity ring. All of it.

And then one day she saw something terrible on the news and asked how God could allow it, and nobody had an answer except "God has a plan."

That was the moment, she said. That's when she started to let go.

Hannah had watched it three times.

I sat on that couch and felt my whole body go cold.

Because I had said "God has a plan."

On the stairs. In March. To my daughter. Word for word.

I didn't sleep that night.

At 1AM I went down a rabbit hole I'll never forget.

I typed "why do kids leave the church" and I found the numbers.

LifeWay Research surveyed 2,002 young adults who attended a Protestant church regularly as teenagers. 66% of them stopped attending for at least a year between the ages of 18 and 22. Barna Group found 64% of 18 to 29 year olds who grew up in church dropped out.

Two out of three.

Then I found why.

When Barna asked young adults why they left, 36% said they couldn't ask their most pressing life questions in church. 35% said Christians act like they know all the answers. 23% said they had serious intellectual doubts about their faith.

Questions.

Questions like Hannah's.

And then, around 2AM, I found Charles Templeton.

Billy Graham's best friend. The photograph. The mother and her baby. The question nobody answered. Farewell to God.

And "I miss Him."

I read that part out loud in the dark kitchen and started crying so hard I had to put my hand over my mouth so I wouldn't wake Dan.

Because I could see it.

I could see Hannah at 83. Missing Jesus. Saying goodbye to Him anyway. Because of a question her mom answered with a sentence on the stairs when she was 11.

And then I found the other half of the story.

The half that saved me.

Because Templeton's questions didn't just go to Templeton. He asked Billy Graham the same kind of hard questions. And Graham had to wrestle with them too.

Graham later wrote that one night in 1949, after hearing Templeton's arguments, he walked into the woods at a retreat center called Forest Home. He set his Bible on a tree stump and decided to trust it as God's Word, even though he couldn't answer every question.

Same questions. Two men. Two different endings.

The difference wasn't that one of them was smarter.

The difference was what each of them did with the question.

One let it fester alone until it ate his faith.

One brought it out into the open and wrestled it all the way to the ground.

And I realized, that's the choice I have with Hannah.

Not whether she'll ask. She already has.

Whether she'll wrestle it with me. Or alone, at night, with a stranger on a ring light.

Nothing was wrong with my daughter.

Something was missing.

Nobody had ever given her the reasons. Not her Sunday school. Not her camp. Not her devotional with the pink cover.

Not me.

Somewhere around 3AM I typed one more search.

"Teaching kids why God allows suffering."

That's how I found the Systematic Theology 52 Week Workbook for Kids, from Valorrea.

I almost scrolled past. I'd bought so many things that year.

But I clicked, and I read the whole page.

It isn't a Bible storybook. It's apologetics. That's just an old word for giving reasons. It's what Peter told every believer to do: always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for the reason for the hope that is in you.

Everyone who asks.

Including an 11 year old on the stairs at 10PM.

Here's how it works.

Once a week, for 52 weeks, you sit down with your child for about 10 minutes.

Every lesson starts with a real hard question. How do we know God exists? Can we really trust the Bible? What about evolution? Why does God allow suffering?

When I saw that last one, I put my phone down on the counter and just stood there.

There it was. Templeton's question. Hannah's question. My question. In a kids' workbook. Not hidden in the back. Out in the open, where it belongs.

Then your kid becomes a detective. You look at three pieces of evidence together. You weigh it. You work through it. And then they practice saying the answer out loud, in their own words, like a friend just asked them at school.

That's the part that got me.

Templeton had his question for years and never once said an answer out loud that he believed.

This was the opposite. Question. Evidence. Then your child says it, in her own words, at your own table.

No prep. No seminary degree. Ten minutes.

Ages 6 to 14. Which meant Owen too. Before his photograph ever came.

$35.90 in their Fall Faith Sale. A 90 day money back guarantee.

After $1,500 that year, I thought, this is the last thing I try.

I ordered two at 3:22AM.

Week 1.

Hannah was not excited.

I put it on the table after Sunday lunch. "Ten minutes," I said. "That's it."

She rolled her eyes. But she sat down.

Owen thought being a detective was the greatest thing that had ever happened. He wore Dan's reading glasses "for clues."

The first question was how we know God exists. Three pieces of evidence.

Hannah did it. Barely. But she did it.

Week 2.

She read the question out loud before I could.

I didn't make a big deal of it. Inside, I was doing cartwheels.

Week 3.

The lesson was about whether the Bible can be trusted.

Hannah pushed back on the first piece of evidence. Hard. She had something from one of her videos.

And the workbook had an answer back. Not "just trust God." An actual reason. Something she could weigh.

She went quiet. Then she said, "Okay. That's kind of a good point."

I went to refill my coffee so she wouldn't see my face.

Week 5.

She started finishing the lesson before Owen.

Week 6.

Dan sat in. For the first time in his life he heard a real answer to a question he'd been asked since he was a kid himself.

He kept saying, "Huh. I never knew that."

Hannah grinned at him. "Dad, you're worse at this than me."

He laughed. "Yeah, honey. I think I am."

Week 8.

We got to the lesson on suffering.

Hannah read the question out loud. Then she stopped and looked at me.

"Mom. This is what I asked you on the stairs."

I said, "I know, sweetheart. I'm sorry I said God has a plan and sent you to bed. Let's actually look at it this time."

And we did.

For forty-five minutes. Way past the ten.

We didn't solve it. I'm not going to pretend we did. People have wrestled with that question for thousands of years.

But we wrestled with it. Together. Out loud. With reasons on the table instead of a sentence on the stairs.

At the end she sat back and said, "So God doesn't just not care."

I said, "No, honey. He doesn't just not care."

She nodded slowly. Like something heavy had been set down.

Week 10.

Hannah came home from school and said, without me asking, "Ava says she doesn't believe in God because of all the bad stuff in the world."

My stomach dropped.

Then she said, "So I told her what we talked about. She actually listened."

She grabbed a snack and went upstairs like it was nothing.

I stood in the kitchen with a dish towel in my hand for a full minute.

Week 12.

Her search history changed.

Still some hard questions. But now next to them were searches like "evidence for the resurrection" and "Christian answers about suffering."

She wasn't hiding from the questions anymore.

She was looking for the other side.

Week 14.

Sunday morning. Third song.

I glanced over.

Her mouth was moving.

Quietly. But she was singing.

I had to look straight ahead at the projector screen and blink a lot.

I'm not going to tell you my daughter has every answer now. She doesn't. Neither do I.

She still has questions. She always will. She's my tender girl who prayed for squirrels. She feels everything.

But now she brings the questions to me.

And she knows I'm not afraid of them.

That's the whole difference.

That's the difference between Charles Templeton and Billy Graham.

Not who had questions. They both did.

Who wrestled them in the open, and who carried them alone.

I think about Templeton a lot now.

About that photograph. About a man who missed Jesus and walked away anyway.

And I think about how close my daughter came to the same road. At 11. On the stairs.

I can't go back and answer Charles Templeton.

But I could answer Hannah.

And you can answer your child.

Before the photograph comes.

And you take no risk trying.

It's $35.90 right now in Valorrea's Fall Faith Sale. It arrives in 3 to 5 business days, with tracking.

That's less than one day of the camp that didn't work.

Your child gets roughly 30 hours a week of school. A lot of kids get 20 or more on screens. Every hour of it, somebody is teaching them what to think about the world.

And somewhere on that screen, the photograph is waiting.

How many minutes a week is anyone preparing them for it?

A 6 year old who starts this week has twelve years before they leave home. An 11 year old like Hannah has seven.

Every week you wait is another question they'll face alone, at night, in their room, for the first time.

Nothing is wrong with your kid.

Billy Graham's best friend had every gift in the world except one.

bodyText:
The demons that met Jesus were not afraid to die. They were afraid of one place. 

Luke 8:31 reads: “And they begged Jesus repeatedly not to order them to go into the Abyss.”

Those are demons speaking. A legion of them, standing in front of Jesus. And they are not begging for their lives. They are begging Him not to be sent to one place.
 
The King James calls that place “the deep.” The Greek word is abyssos. The Abyss.
 
So here is a question almost no Christian alive can answer. What is the Abyss? What is this one place, so terrible that a legion of demons would rather be sent anywhere else on earth than go there?
 
And the second you start pulling on that thread, a bigger question opens up underneath it. Where did these things even come from in the first place?
 
The answer to both questions was written down. Not in some fringe scroll that nobody trusted.
 
The book that holds it was treated as scripture by the men who walked with Jesus. Jude, the brother of Jesus, quotes it by name and calls it prophecy. Jude 1:14, sitting in the New Testament right now. Peter points at it when he writes, in 1 Peter 3:19, that Jesus preached to spirits held in prison from the days of Noah. And centuries later, copies of it were pulled from the Dead Sea Scrolls, in the original ancient Aramaic, pre-Christian and authentic.
 
Every mark of real scripture is on it. And it was still erased from your Bible.
 
That book is the Book of Enoch.
 
And it walks straight back into that scene and shows you what was really standing in front of Jesus.
 
It tells you where they came from. Enoch chapter 6, verse 6. Two hundred angels called the Watchers came down in the days before the flood. They took human wives. Their children were the Nephilim, the giants. And when the flood destroyed the bodies of the Nephilim, their spirits did not die with their bodies.
 
Enoch chapter 15, verse 8, says it in plain words. Those spirits became the evil spirits on the earth. They afflict, they oppress, they torment mankind, and they will keep doing it until the day of the final judgment.
 
That is what a demon is. Enoch says it. Your Bible never does.
 
The Book of Jubilees, chapter 10, verse 9, finishes the picture. After the flood these spirits went after humanity so fast that Noah cried out to God. God ordered them bound. But their prince begged that a tenth of them be left loose, to test and afflict mankind. And that tenth was permitted to remain.
 
A remnant of them. Still loose on the earth. Right now.
 
But none of that was what they feared most. That was the Abyss.
 
Enoch does not leave it vague. In chapter 21, verse 7, he is taken there and shown it with his own eyes. He describes a place beyond the edge of everything, with no heaven above it and no ground beneath it. A pit of fire and darkness with no bottom to it. And chained inside it are the Watchers who fell. The two hundred who came down. The ones who fathered the Nephilim. Bound there in the dark, held for the day of judgment, waiting.
 
And the ones who put them there were the archangels. Enoch chapter 10, verse 12, records the command. Michael. Raphael. The same seven that were cut out of your Bible. They are the ones who dragged the fallen down into that pit and sealed it over them.
 
That is why a legion of demons dropped to the ground and begged. The Abyss is not just any prison. It is the prison where their own fathers are held in chains. It is the one place in all creation built for their kind. And they know that on the last day, it is where they are going.
 
Now look at the scene again, and it stands all the way up.
 
A man had been living out among the tombs. No chain could hold him. He cried out through the night, and not one person alive could help him. Then he saw Jesus. And the thing inside him knew Him on sight, before a single human in that story did, and screamed it out loud. Son of the Most High God.
 
They knew Him because they had been at war with His side since before the flood. They had watched the archangels chain their fathers in the dark. And now the one Person with the authority to open that pit and throw them into it was standing on the shore, looking straight at them.
 
That is why they were not begging for their lives. They already knew how this ends. They were begging for time. Anywhere but the Abyss. Not yet.
 
And the Book of Enoch does not just expose the enemy. It shows you who fights for you. Your Bible names two angels. Michael and Gabriel. Enoch chapter 20 names all seven archangels and what each one is assigned to do. The same archangels who chained the Watchers in the Abyss in the first place. The Book of Tobit shows one of them, the angel Raphael, walking beside a young man, guarding him, and in chapter 8, verse 3, driving a demon off him. These were the names the early church prayed with. The West cut them out and told believers to make peace with vagueness.
 
And they cut out something heavier still. What Jesus Himself said about all of this. Your own Bible tells you that after He rose from the dead, He did not leave right away. He stayed and taught for forty more days. Acts 1:3. Forty days of teaching from the risen Christ. And your Bible records almost none of what He said in them.
 
But it survived. It is called the Book of the Covenant. In those pages the risen Jesus does not speak as a gentle teacher. He speaks as the King of heaven and earth. He warns His followers what is coming. He teaches them about the powers of darkness, and how a believer is meant to stand against them. The very instructions the West left on the floor.
 
And in that same teaching, He said something about authority that the powerful have never wanted repeated.
 
He warned that a day would come when people would seize His name and use it for their own gain. They would shout it in the streets. They would build kingdoms and cathedrals in it. They would wear His name like a badge while their hearts stayed far from Him. Your own Bible says the same thing, in Matthew 15:8. These people honor me with their lips, but their hearts are far from me.
 
And Jesus said plainly that He does not hand His authority to them. Not to the loud. Not to the powerful. Not to the ones who wear His name for profit. He trusts it to one kind of person only. The one who believes in Him deep in their heart. The humble. The overlooked. The ones the world never bothers to notice.
 
Because real authority was never a title or a robe. It was a fire, and it only burns in a believer who actually knows what he is carrying.
 
The early church knew it. They walked into rooms and sickness fled. They spoke His name over a tormented man and the thing inside him came out screaming. In Luke 10:19 Jesus had told them plainly, I have given you authority to trample on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy. They did not read that as poetry. They used it. And it worked, because they held the complete word, with the whole map of the enemy open in their hands.
 
Then the books were cut. And the church slowly forgot the authority it once carried. It kept the buildings and lost the fire.
 
Here is the part that should make every believer sit up. The bloodline the Watchers left behind did not drown in the flood. Enoch already told you what happened to it. The spirits of the dead Nephilim are still here, still roaming, still doing the one thing Enoch said they would do. They afflict. They oppress. They torment.
 
They are the reason for the heaviness that will not lift. The dread that has no cause. The war going on around a believer that no one else can see. It is not new and it is not random. It is the same enemy that has been working since before the flood, and it has never once stopped.
 
And it has help. The people who long ago made their peace with that darkness, who traded the truth for power and built the kingdoms of this world on it, are still here too. They sit on thrones and behind pulpits. They shout His name the loudest of anyone. They keep the world loud and distracted and unarmed. And yet they hold no authority over the darkness at all, because they never truly believed in the first place.
 
The authority they perform for the cameras was never theirs to hold. It was always meant for the believer who reads the whole word and believes it down in his bones.
 
But the believers that authority was meant for are the very ones who were robbed of it.
 
They lie awake at three in the morning, certain the room has gone wrong, certain they are not alone in it. And everyone around them has an easy answer for it. It is the job. It is the stress. It is just the weight of ordinary life catching up. Sleep it off.
 
But it gets worse the harder they try to get close to God. Every time they decide to pray more, read more, actually walk with Him, something pushes back. The dreams get darker. The pressure gets heavier. The closer they move toward the light, the deeper something drags them the other way.
 
They carry it to the people who are supposed to help, and they are told their faith is weak, or it is only anxiety, take something for it. So they start to wonder if they are simply broken. Or worse, if they are cursed. Their prayers feel like they hit the ceiling and slide back down, like they are talking to no one.
 
Nobody can tell them what they are actually dealing with.
 
The book that was cut out of their Bible can. What has been finding them in the dark is not weak faith and it is not imagination. It is real. It has a name. It has an origin. It has an expiration date and a prison already built for it. And every word of it was written down in a book that was taken out of the Bible before they were ever born.
 
Which is the question that should stop every Christian cold. If Jude quoted Enoch as scripture, if Jesus spoke as though His followers had read it, if the answer to what demons are and where they are held was sitting right there, how did it ever get out of your Bible.
 
Somebody made that decision.
 
The original King James Bible, printed in 1611, had 80 books. Not 66. The extra books sat in the middle of it for over two hundred years. Then in 1826 a British printing society made a business decision. Cut the extra books, or lose their funding. They cut them. To save on ink.
 
And in 1947 a shepherd boy threw a rock into a cave and found the oldest Bible manuscripts on earth. The Dead Sea Scrolls. Among them, copies of the Book of Enoch that had sat there since before Christ walked. They did not match the 66-book Protestant Bible. They matched the Ethiopian one.
 
One country never made the cut. The first Christian nation on earth. The only nation in Africa that never bowed to a colonial ruler. The country that still claims to guard the Ark of the Covenant in a chapel in Axum. Ethiopia kept the Book of Enoch. Kept Jubilees. Kept the full 88 books while the West trimmed the rest down to what was cheap to print.
 
Ethiopia did not add books. Everyone else removed them.
 
Say it plainly, because the comments will twist it. This is not a claim that your Bible is wrong. Every word in it is true and it is still His. The complete Bible does not change a single book you already own. It gives back the 22 that were taken out. The 22 that happen to hold the entire map of what has been fighting you in the dark.
 
This is not replacement. This is restoration.
 
And that map is what finally lets a believer sleep through the night.
 
When you finally know what you are up against, and Who is standing between you and it, the fear breaks.
 
You stop lying there as a victim of something you cannot name. Faith comes from hearing the word of God. They cut that hearing in half, and then the church told you the fear was your fault. It was never your fault. You were sent into a real fight with half the map missing.
 
The heaviness may still visit some nights. The difference is you know exactly what it is now. Where it came from. Whose chains it is running out of time before it returns to. And Who holds the key to that prison. You stop being a scared Christian. You become a Christian who has finally read the whole book.
 
Now here is the hard part. And this is where I have to tell you how I found all of this out.
 
I went looking for a real, complete Ethiopian Bible myself. And I learned fast how hard that is. Since Enoch started trending, Amazon filled up with counterfeits that call themselves complete and quietly leave books out. Chapters missing. Passages softened. I bought one, and then another, and then another. I lost almost four hundred dollars before I realized every copy I could get my hands on was still censored.
 
I had nearly given up. Then I found a small group of believers in America who could not let it go either. They had done the thing nobody else was willing to do. They flew to Ethiopia. Straight to the source. The one place that never changed a word. And they brought the complete Bible home in English. Word for word. Nothing softened. Nothing left out.
 
They call it Faith Made.
 
The full 88 books. The Book of Enoch. The Book of Jubilees. The Wisdom of Solomon. And every other ancient scripture the Western church carved away.
 
Because most Christians have never seen these books in their lives, every printed copy ships with a free audiobook that walks through every one of them. By the time you finish, you will understand what you are fighting, and Who fights for you, better than most pastors who have preached for thirty years.
 
Most stores that sell the Ethiopian Bible charge close to a hundred dollars. Faith Made put the whole thing together for under fifty.
 
And there is no risk in seeing it for yourself. They give you 30 days. 30 days to read what the Abyss actually is. 30 days to finally know the name of the thing that has been finding people in the dark. And if it does not change the way you pray, the way you read your Bible, or the way you sleep at night, send it back for every penny returned. No questions asked.

bodyText:
I'm a single dad. Last Thursday I found out my 10-year-old autistic son had been getting bullied every single day since September. His school knew. 

Nobody called me.

Seven months.
Seven months of him getting torn apart every day, and I had no idea.

My name's Luis. I run a body shop. It's me and Mateo. His mom's not in the picture.

Mateo's 10.

He's autistic. Level 1, they call it.

Which means he looks like every other kid in the hallway, right up until somebody says something with two meanings.

I thought I was doing everything right.

IEP in place. OT on Tuesdays. Social skills group on Thursdays.

I read every book. I know his triggers. I know his sounds. There's a pair of headphones in his backpack and a spare pair in my truck.

I became an expert on my kid.

But I missed it.

For seven straight months.

Mateo stopped asking to go to the skate park.

He used to beg every Saturday.

Then nothing.

I thought: "Good. He's pacing himself. He knows his limits."

He started wearing the same gray hoodie every day.

Even dirty. Even when it was 85 out.

I thought: "Sensory thing. Totally normal for him."

He'd come home and go straight to his room.

No snack. No decompressing on the couch. Door shut, Minecraft with the sound off.

I thought: "That's how he comes down. Leave him be."

Every Sunday night, a meltdown about nothing.

Every Monday morning, he wouldn't put his shoes on. Just sat on the floor rocking.

I thought: "Transitions are hard. School's hard for him."

Seven months of signs yelling at me.

And I had an autism explanation for every one.

Because with an autistic kid, everything looks like a sensory thing.

Everything looks like regulation.

Everything looks like just another autism thing.

Until it's not.

Last Thursday the school called at 11:20.

Mateo had gone into the library at the start of lunch and wouldn't come out.

Two hours.

Wouldn't talk. Wouldn't move.

When I got there, the vice principal, the counselor and his case manager were standing outside the library door.

Talking about him like he wasn't on the other side of it.

"He's probably overstimulated."

"He does this."

"We've tried everything."

He doesn't do this.

I walked past them and went in.

Mateo was on the carpet between the shelves in the back. Knees up. Headphones on. Rocking.

Not crying.

Just gone.

I sat down next to him. Didn't touch him. Didn't say anything.

After about ten minutes he slid one headphone off.

"Dad, why does everybody hate me?"

My stomach dropped.

"Who hates you, bud?"

"Everyone. The kids in my class. They do my voice. They ask me stuff with a trick in it and laugh when I answer. Dylan filmed me flapping in the lunch line and now it's on everybody's phone."

He pulled his knees in tighter.

"They call me Robot. They bump me in the hall and say it was an accident."

"Mateo. How long has this been going on?"

He looked at his shoelaces.

"Since September."

It was April.

Seven months.

"Why didn't you tell me?"

"Because you'd call a meeting. And then the teachers would talk to them. And then it gets worse."

He looked at me with these flat, tired eyes.

"Dad. Every time you help, it gets worse."

That night I didn't sleep.

I kept going back through every meeting I'd sat in.

Every time I pushed for something.

Every time I thought I was fixing it.

And I landed on something I hated.

He was right.

That whole system is built for kids who aren't him.

A regular kid gets bullied, there's a playbook. Tell the teacher. Write it down. Sit everybody in a room and talk it out.

For a kid like Mateo, that playbook is a trap.

He can't always explain what happened.

He can't read the setup until he's already in it.

He can't tell teasing from cruelty until it's over.

And a mediation?

You're putting an autistic kid in a room with the kids who hurt him, telling him to make eye contact and explain his feelings.

Everything that's already the hardest thing in the world for him.

So the bullies learn exactly what gets to him.

And do it quieter next time.

Friday morning I went in and asked for a meeting.

Six adults at a table.

"How does nobody notice this for seven months?"

The vice principal: "Mr. Soto, we have 540 students."

The counselor: "Mateo never reported anything."

His teacher: "He seems fine in class."

I said, "He spent two hours on the library floor yesterday."

Nobody said anything.

Then the school psychologist said the thing I'll never forget.

"Have you considered that Mateo might do better in a smaller setting?"

She wasn't talking about fixing it.

She was talking about moving him.

Making him somebody else's problem.

I looked around that table.

Six adults. All paid to look after kids.

Not one of them had anything.

I got up and left.

That weekend I was stuck.

I can't homeschool. I've got a shop and eleven guys who need me there at 7.

I can't afford private.

I can't quit.

But I couldn't send him back to that place either.

Sunday I called my sister Carmen.

She's a speech therapist. Twelve years in a middle school.

I told her all of it.

She was quiet for a long time.

Then she said, "Luis, the school can't fix this."

"What do you mean they can't fix it, it's their building."

"They're trying to fix the room. The room isn't the problem."

"Then what is?"

"Every other kid in that building learned the rules by watching. Who you can joke with. What a trick question sounds like. When somebody's testing you. Nobody ever wrote any of that down for Mateo. So every single one of those tests feels like hate to him."

I didn't say anything.

"They don't hate him, Luis. They're checking who gets upset. And he gets upset every time. So they keep going."

"He's been in social skills group for two years, Carmen."

"Keep him in it. It teaches him how to start a conversation. Nobody in that room teaches him what to do when a kid wants a show."

"So what does?"

"Somebody wrote the unwritten rules down."

"What?"

"There's a comic. The Street Smart Kid Survival Guide. 150 situations. A kid asks you a trick question. A kid films you. A kid says it was an accident. You see what the other kid is actually thinking, in the bubble over his head. Then you see what makes it worse and what makes it stop."

"Carmen, he's 10. He's not going to sit and read a..."

"Luis. He can see what they're thinking. That's the whole thing for our kids. My students with autism finish it in a weekend. For once nobody's hinting at them."

I ordered it that night.

When it came I didn't make a thing of it.

Left it on the kitchen table next to his fidget cube.

Saturday morning he came down, saw it, flipped it open standing up.

Sat down.

Two hours later he was still sitting there. Hadn't looked up.

By Sunday night he'd read half.

Monday after school he came in the door.

Didn't go to his room.

Sat down at the table and said, flat as anything:

"Dad. I figured something out."

"Yeah?"

"They don't hate me. They're checking who gets upset. I get upset every time. So they keep doing it."

I just looked at him.

"Where'd you get that?"

He held up the comic.

"It's in here. It's not because I'm weird. It's because I react."

He went to get a snack.

Week two.

He came home and told me about lunch.

Dylan did his voice in the line. Loud. Everybody waiting for Mateo to go off.

Mateo said: "Okay."

And kept walking.

Dylan stood there.

"He looked confused, Dad. Then he looked bored."

I had to go out to the truck for a minute.

Week four.

His teacher emailed me. I hadn't told her anything.

She said Mateo seemed more settled. Was talking in class. "Whatever changed at home, keep going."

Week six.

"Dad, can Owen come over Friday?"

First time he'd said another kid's name in six months.

Owen came over. They built something in Minecraft with the sound on.

I stood in the kitchen listening to my son laugh.

And I got it.

I didn't fix this.

The school didn't fix this.

A comic book gave him the thing everybody else got for free.

The rules.

Not in therapy words.

Not "use your words, buddy."

Just, here's what that kid is doing, here's what he wants, here's what happens when you don't give it to him.

Mateo read it in a week.

Then read it again.

Now he talks about it like a manual.

Not because he's pretending to be like them.

He's not masking. He's not hiding who he is.

He just finally got the rulebook everybody else was born holding.

Last week we were at the skate park.

A kid from his class rolled past. Said something to his buddy. They both laughed.

I waited for Mateo to shut down.

Headphones on. Rocking. Gone.

Instead he looked up and said, "That's Brayden. He used to mess with me every day."

"Does he still?"

"No. He got bored like a month ago."

And went back to his board.

Like Brayden was a bird.

I sat on that bench not moving.

Because two months ago, that kid was the reason Mateo was on a library floor.

Now he's background noise.

Here's what I need you to hear.

If your autistic kid stopped talking at dinner.

If the meltdowns are up for no reason.

If Sunday nights are a war.

If he won't put his shoes on Monday.

He's not "struggling with transitions."

He's not "having a hard time with the social demands."

He's getting taken apart by kids who figured out exactly where to push.

And the school can't stop it.

A meeting doesn't stop a hallway bump.

An IEP doesn't stop a video in a group chat.

Thursday group doesn't teach him what to do when a kid wants a reaction.

This does.

It gives autistic kids the rules the other kids got by osmosis.

Mateo still has hard days.

But he doesn't hide anymore.

He doesn't shut down when somebody's mean.

He doesn't think they hate him.

He knows what they're doing.

And once you know what they're doing, it stops being scary.

Last night at dinner he said something I didn't see coming.

"Dad, I'm kind of glad my brain works like this."

I put my fork down.

"Yeah?"

"Yeah. I had to learn the rules on purpose. So now I actually know them. Most kids just guess."

For the first time in seven months, my kid felt strong.

If you're a single parent.

If your kid's autistic or ADHD or just wired different.

If the school keeps having meetings and nothing changes.

If you feel like you're failing because you can't fix it.

You're not failing.

The system is.

But you can fix the part that matters at your kitchen table.

Before middle school.

Before he stops trusting you.

Before he believes the thing they're telling him about himself.

Mateo's 10.

Eight years before he's out in the world.

Eight years to use what he knows now.

I almost pulled him out of school.

I almost gave up.

A comic book did what seven months of meetings couldn't.

Over 100,000 parents have bought it. One mom wrote that her autistic son told her, "Mom, I desperately needed this."

Mine didn't say that. He just said he's glad his brain works like this.

I'll take it.

Click below. Read how it works. See if it's right for your kid.

bodyText:
Ten years of abuse taught Odessa to hide every bruise. One brutal night taught her to stop hiding. She photographed the evidence, saved her own money, and planned her escape. Hector thinks she is trapped. He has no idea she is already taking back her life. 👑⚡
Chapter 1: Odessa's Escape- Chapter 1
Odessa's POV-

Consciousness came back in pieces.

First, pain. Thick, hot, and everywhere.

Then my own rough breath, followed by a low sound I couldn’t stop from pushing past my mouth. I opened my eyes a little, then squeezed them shut again when my left side screamed at me.

Birds chattered somewhere outside. A few bikes growled past on the road, loud enough to yank me the rest of the way out of sleep.

My eyes flew open.

For one frozen second, I forgot where I was. Then the cracked dash, the cold steering wheel, and the cramped angle of my body reminded me.

My truck.

I jerked my gaze around the parking lot, praying no one had spotted me curled up in here overnight. If anyone from school found out I had slept in my truck, it would be everywhere before first period.

Then another thought hit me harder.

Shit. School.

I snatched up my phone and jabbed the power button, waiting for the screen to wake. Even before it fully loaded, I checked the time. My pulse slowed a fraction.

I wasn’t late yet.

Not if I moved.

I twisted toward the back seat for my duffle bag and instantly regretted it. Fire shot up my left side, sharp enough to tear a cry from me. I eased back into the driver’s seat one careful inch at a time, breathing through my teeth until the worst of it passed.

Hector had really gone all in last night.

Hector Jacobs is my stepfather. He has been in my life since I was born, which is why I still carry his last name. That does not make him my dad. He lost any chance at that word a long time ago.

Since I was eight, he has treated me like something built to absorb his fists.

One more month. That was all I had been telling myself. One more month, then I turn eighteen. After that, I can walk away, disappear, and never set foot in that house again.

But after last night, a month suddenly felt dangerous. Too long. Maybe long enough for him to finish what he has been starting for years.

And now I had proof. Real proof. I didn’t think anyone could stop me from leaving if I showed what he had done.

I had never seen Hector as bad as he was last night. He lost some major business deal, came home furious, and used me to bleed off the rage. At least one rib had to be broken. My face hurt in too many places, and my neck felt tender beneath the collar of my hoodie.

I flipped the visor down and stared into the little mirror.

Yeah. Fantastic.

A black eye. Bruising along my cheek. More color blooming near my jaw and across my lip. The eye itself wasn’t swollen, thank God, only darkened, so my bright green iris still showed clearly.

The cold weather helped. A turtleneck sweater would hide my neck. My face, though, was a separate problem.

Good thing I had learned makeup young.

I worked quickly, dabbing and blending until the damage looked less like a crime scene and more like a bad night’s sleep. Once my face was covered, I headed for the public restroom.

I had driven to the lake after running from the house. The lot was tucked away, quiet, and not the kind of place Hector would ever bother checking. Better yet, the bathroom stayed open all night. It gave me somewhere to brush my teeth, clean up, wrap whatever needed wrapping, and get dressed for school like everything was normal.

Normal. Right.

I climbed out of my battered black truck, shut the door, and pulled open the back to grab my duffle from the seat.

The truck was ugly because it had been the first vehicle I bought with money I’d earned myself. Some of it came from my part-time job. The rest came from work my parents knew nothing about.

I could have bought something much nicer with that second income, but nicer would raise questions. Questions led to attention, and attention was the last thing I needed at home.

After locking the truck, I crossed to the restroom.

Inside, I went straight to the stall I always used. It had a mirror and enough room to change without bumping into every wall. Jeans and underwear came first because I knew that would hurt less than dragging my shirt and bra over my ribs.

The bra might have to stay on. Bandages first, then survival.

I shoved my feet into my sneakers, then started working my T-shirt up. Every inch was a negotiation. I paused, winced, breathed, and tried again until I finally got it off.

The bruising looked worse without fabric hiding it.

For a moment, all I could do was stare.

Then I wiped away the makeup I had already put on and took pictures. Every mark. Every ugly patch of purple, blue, and yellow spread across my skin. If I had to prove this, I was going to prove all of it.

After that, I wrapped my ribs tight. If I didn’t support them, I might actually puncture a lung before the day was over.

I had almost finished winding the bandage around myself when my phone started ringing again.

Again, because it had been going off since I turned it back on. I had ignored every call. I also hadn’t really looked at the mountain of missed texts and notifications that had piled up while the phone had been off overnight.

With one hand holding the bandage in place, I picked up the phone.

Missed calls filled the screen. My mum. Brandon. Maya. Over and over.

A few messages from Hector sat in the list too, each one sounding more threatening than the last.

The incoming call was Maya.

She was my best friend, and if she was calling, Brandon was probably right there with her. Those two belonged together so obviously it was almost painful, not that either one of them would ever admit it. Brandon was my friend too.

I answered before grabbing my cami.

“Hey,” I said, trying for casual and landing nowhere near it. “Why is everyone blowing up my phone?”

“Why is everyone blowing up your phone?” Maya repeated, her voice pitching higher. “Seriously? Your mum called me and Brandon all night trying to figure out where you were. Where are you? What happened? She wouldn’t tell us anything, because of course she wouldn’t, and don’t you dare try to brush this off anymore.”

My mouth opened, but nothing came out.

What was I supposed to say? I had never told them the truth. Part of me had always been terrified they would look at me differently. Or worse, leave because being near me was too much trouble.

Muffled voices shifted on the other end. I caught pieces, then Maya snapping at Brandon, then Brandon snapping back. Typical. A few seconds later, the phone must have changed hands.

Brandon's voice came through, lower and steadier.

“Are you still coming to school?” he asked. “I think I already know some of what’s happening, but Odessa, you have to tell us. Let us help. You’re our best friend. That doesn’t stop because things are bad.”

My throat tightened.

He was right. I did need help. I definitely needed help.

I just didn’t want them getting hurt because of me.

I had handled Hector alone for almost ten years. Maybe that had been stupid. Maybe it was finally time to trust the people who had been trying to stand beside me all along.

A long breath left me.

“Meet me in the school parking lot in fifteen minutes,” I said. “I’ll tell you both everything. It’s time you know, because I need to get out of here.”

I ended the call before either of them could ask another question.

This was not a conversation for the phone. Words wouldn’t be enough anyway. It would be easier, and worse, to show them.

I pulled on the cami, then took my sweater and eased it over my head with more care than I had ever given a piece of clothing. Pain still stabbed through me, but I got it on.

At the sink, I brushed my teeth. Then I dragged a brush through my long black hair and tied it high in a ponytail. Once my face was covered again and the evidence was hidden as well as I could hide it, I repacked the duffle and headed back out to my truck.

The second I stepped outside, the feeling hit me.

Someone was watching.

I stopped near the restroom door and scanned the area. The lot looked empty, but out on the main road, a motorbike sat in view.

I could have sworn it belonged to Chaos.

Declan Pierce. Chaos. The biker boy I had been crushing on for longer than I wanted to admit.

Not that I ever would admit it. He was best friends with Miles Easton, and Miles was dating Sienna. Sienna, the queen of popularity, had also been my personal bully since I started high school.

That wasn’t the only reason I had never said a word to Declan. There was a bigger one.

He was the son of a Pyre Kingsman.

The Pyra Kingsmen MC were known all over the country. Around here, people talked about them like they were violence on wheels. At the same time, everyone also knew they donated obscene amounts of money and did serious charity work for homeless people, battered women, and abused kids.

The police didn’t touch them. Rumor said the cops even worked with them sometimes.

There had been an Assistant District Attorney once who made a lot of noise about taking the Kingsmen down. A week later, the ADA was disbarred for misconduct. That was the official version, anyway.

Nobody believed it was the whole truth.

Either way, boys were not allowed in my life. Dating was not allowed. A boy connected to an MC? Hector would have killed me for that alone.

He hadn’t even liked me playing games with neighborhood boys when I was little. Brandon was the only guy friend I had, and Hector didn’t know he existed. Hector didn’t care enough to track my friendships. He cared about my grades and almost nothing else.

God help me if I brought home a B in any class.

The one time it happened, it was because I had missed school after one of his beatings. His response to that grade had been another beating.

I let out a tired breath and climbed into the truck.

If the bike really was Declan's, what was I supposed to do about it? Nothing. Later, I would probably hear about it from Sienna after he told Miles and she overheard.

Today was shaping up beautifully.

*Sigh*

I had five minutes left to get to school. If I pushed the speed a little, I could make the drive in three.

I started the engine and pulled out of the lot, hoping the day ahead wouldn’t turn out as bad as I was afraid it would be.

============================================================

Chapter 2: Bruises and Backup
Odessa's POV-

By the time I pulled into my regular space at school, Brandon and Maya were already waiting beside it.

Chaos was there too.

Of course he was.

He had parked his bike where he could see me, his attention fixed on me the way it always seemed to be. I still have not figured out why he watches me so closely, or why he does it like he is waiting for something to go wrong.

I lifted a hand, motioning for Brandon and Maya to get in. Then I shut off the engine. Whatever I was about to say, I didn’t want it drifting across the parking lot.

Maya climbed into the front passenger seat first. Brandon folded himself into the back. The second Maya's door clicked shut, she faced me with her arms locked over her chest and anger written all over her face.

“Okay, explain. What the hell is happening with you? Why are you talking about running?”

I leaned back against my seat, then regretted it when pain bit through my ribs. Before answering, I scanned the area around my truck, making sure no one was close enough to overhear.

Brandon's voice came from behind me. “Odessa, what is it? Why are you acting like we’re being watched?”

“Because I don’t need the whole school knowing what I’ve been living through for the last ten years.”

My fingers shook as I reached for the hem of my sweater and the cami beneath it. Carefully, I lifted both just enough to expose the bruises spreading across my ribs.

Maya sucked in a sharp breath. Brandon swore under his breath.

I dropped the fabric fast, covering myself again before anyone outside could catch a glimpse.

Maya's anger collapsed into horror. “Why didn’t you tell us before now?”

“You know what Hector is like.” My voice came out quieter than I wanted. “He tells anyone who will listen that he took me in, gave me his last name, raised me like I was his own even though I wasn’t. Everyone thinks he’s this decent man. He performs it so well that people believe him.”

I swallowed, but my throat hurt. “Who would have believed me? After last night, though, I know I have to get out before he kills me. I just don’t know how anyone is supposed to help.”

Brandon shifted forward, elbows on his knees. “What about your real dad? Your biological one. Couldn’t he do something? You’ve never really talked about him.”

“My mum always said he was some one-night stand and that she doesn’t even remember his name.” I stared at the steering wheel. “I’m starting to think that was just another lie. I have tried looking for him, but if he has no idea I exist, he wouldn’t be searching for me.”

Brandon gave a slow nod. “So what’s your plan?”

“I have enough money to leave.” The words should have made me feel stronger. They didn’t. “But I think that means dropping out of school, and that was never what I wanted. I wanted college. I wanted to build my own accounting firm from nothing.”

A bitter breath slipped out of me. “With him the way he is, I don’t think I get to keep any of that. I think I just have to disappear.”

How was I supposed to feel anything but defeated? The man who should have kept me safe was the reason I was losing everything.

Maya moved before I could brace for it. She lunged across the space between us and wrapped her arms around me, crying hard.

Pain tore through me, and I couldn’t stop the loud wince that escaped.

She jerked back instantly, both hands hovering uselessly in the air. “Oh my God, I’m sorry. Did I make it worse?”

I shook my head. “I’m just really sore. I didn’t go home last night, so I couldn’t soak in a bath or do anything for the stiffness. And then I slept here, in this seat.” I tried to stretch and stopped almost immediately. “Everything hurts more than usual.”

This time, I reached for her first.

Maya came back carefully, like I was something cracked that might split apart in her hands. Brandon joined the hug from the back seat, and even that surprised me. He was usually the sort of guy who squeezed the air from your lungs without meaning to.

Now he was gentle.

Too gentle.

For a second, I wondered if he understood this kind of fear better than anyone else I knew.

Brandon pulled away first. “Do you need to start sneaking your stuff out of your parents’ house before you leave?”

I nodded. “Probably. And I’ll need another truck too. One they don’t recognize.”

“Buy one,” he said without hesitation. “We’ll keep it at my place. My mum won’t care. If you need help, she’ll help.”

I looked back at him. “Why would your mum help me? I’ve never even met her.”

I knew his dad wasn’t around, but that was about it.

Brandon's expression changed, not quite hard, not quite sad. “My dad isn’t in my life because he used to hurt my mum. When I was thirteen, I beat the shit out of him. Made enough noise that the police came, and they took him away.”

He glanced down. “He’s in prison now.”

That explained so much. Why he never mentioned his father. Why he spent so much time at the boxing gym. Brandon could fight; I had watched him spar before, and Maya had too. He must have started young because he had needed to protect his mother.

It also gave me one more reason to believe he would be good for Maya.

Not that either of them had admitted anything yet. But I had seen how they looked at each other.

“If I can hide a few things at your house over the next few days,” I said, “and maybe keep a new truck in your driveway until I’m ready to go, that would help more than you know. Thank you, Brandon.”

His answer came easily. “Anytime, Odessa. You’re basically my sister.”

Then his gaze slid to Maya, and his mouth curved. “Unlike this one.”

He said it like a joke, but the truth sat underneath it. Maya was definitely not a sister to him.

I turned my head toward the lot again. Chaos was still watching me from beside his bike, except now he was talking to Miles. I couldn’t hear a word from where we sat, but my stomach tightened anyway.

What were they discussing?

Behind me and beside me, Brandon and Maya started bickering, and despite everything, a laugh slipped out of me.

The laugh hurt.

I flinched, one hand going to my ribs. Both of them stopped instantly, worry sweeping over their faces. I forced a tiny smile and nodded so they would know I was okay, or at least as close to okay as I could manage.

Maya reached down and lifted a paper bag. “Come on. Let’s get you coffee. We brought you a croissant too, because we know you love them.”

She handed me the bag from our favorite bakery, the one I insisted had the best pastries in the entire country. I would defend that opinion to my grave.

“Thank you.” I took it and tried to smile properly.

Food didn’t interest me at the moment, so I tucked the bag into my smaller school bag. Maybe I would pick at it later if hunger showed up. Lately, my appetite had been disappearing under the pain. Swallowing was harder when every part of me ached, and today the bruising around my neck made it worse.

We got out of the truck wearing the kind of smiles people put on when they need the world to mind its own business.

Maya and Brandon fell into their usual teasing almost immediately. Within a minute, they were talking about the winter formal, and Maya was already bringing up shopping.

I looked between them and couldn’t help it. “You two should just start dating already.”

Maya's cheeks went pink.

Brandon smirked.

That was all the confirmation I needed.

My eyes widened. “Wait. Are you already dating?”

“I asked her out over the weekend,” Brandon said, dragging the words out while his smirk deepened. “And, well...”

“I said yes,” Maya finished, smiling now. “We wanted to tell you in person.”

I squealed and wrapped both of them in a hug, carefully enough not to destroy myself this time. “It is about bloody time. Seriously, how long have you liked each other?”

“Since we met,” Maya said.

Brandon nodded like that had never been in question.

He chuckled then, his attention turning back to me. “Maybe now you should tell him.”

My stomach dropped. “Tell who what?”

Please don’t let them know.

Maya leaned closer and lowered her voice. “Chaos.”

I shook my head at once. “If I have to leave, what would be the point? Telling him would only hurt both of us.”

“I don’t know,” she said, studying me. “I have a feeling things might change today.”

Before I could ask what that meant, she shifted topics. “Also, you never told us you had a birthmark.”

We started toward the school building and my locker. As we crossed the lot, Kelseiy walked past us, heading in the direction of her brother, Miles, and Chaos.

“My mum said my biological dad has the exact same birthmark in the exact same place.” I shrugged, then had to bite down on another wince because even that tugged at my ribs.

“Have you tried using that to find him?” Maya asked.

“It wouldn’t exactly be simple. My mother has barely told me anything useful about him.” I glanced toward the entrance. “And that’s before adding in how often she lies to me.”

Maya sighed. “Yeah. I can see how that would make it complicated.”

We let the subject fade after that. Assignments became safer ground, so we talked about schoolwork while we entered the building and made our way down the hall.

When we reached my locker, I noticed Chaos wasn’t far away.

Neither were Miles and his girlfriend, Sienna.

Worse, they were heading in our direction.

So much for a peaceful morning.

Part of me worried about what Chaos might have said to Miles. If Miles knew anything, he would probably tell Sienna, and Sienna never wasted a chance to use something against me.

I pulled in the deepest breath my ribs would allow, then another, trying to steady myself before whatever was coming landed at my feet.

Chapter 3: Lines Drawn
Declan's POV-

Over the last few weeks, Odessa has changed in ways I can’t ignore.

She has been easing herself out of everyone’s reach, bit by bit, so quietly most people would miss it. I haven’t. Even the way she moves has slowed, like every step costs her something. The more I watch, the more worried I get.

And yeah, I know why it hits me so hard.

I like her.

I have liked her since the first time I saw her during freshman year. Admitting that out loud, though? Not happening. Not yet. Maybe not ever, if I had my way.

My brothers in the club call me Chaos, and they didn’t pick the name because it sounded cool. When my temper snaps, things get wrecked. People get wrecked. I have caused enough damage for the name to stick.

One time, I picked up a bike and threw it. After that, one of the guys said they should have called me Hulk instead. He wasn’t completely wrong. I’m six-five, close to two hundred pounds, and most of that is muscle. I live in the gym, and I train harder than I work out.

That is what our club expects. For me, it is worse. My dad is the Vice-President, which means I don’t get to coast. I am supposed to become the future Vice-President of the mother chapter of the Pyra Kingsmen, and everyone knows it.

Because of that, I have always kept every feeling locked down where no one could touch it.

Odessa broke through anyway.

Those bright green eyes of hers grabbed me first. In the right light, they catch and flash like cut emeralds. Beautiful doesn’t even cover it. Still, that wasn’t what bothered me. The color itself felt familiar, like I had seen those eyes somewhere before, only I couldn’t drag the memory close enough to name it.

Then there was her hair. Odessa has this long raven-dark hair that looks unreal when it falls loose, though I like it best tied up the way she has it now. Her body is another problem entirely. The curve of her hips, the weight of her breasts, the shape of her ass—any guy with a pulse would notice.

I have gotten myself off too many times with the memory of her body in my head.

But she buries all of that under oversized clothes and too much make-up. Not in a careless way. In a hiding way. It keeps making me wonder what kind of hell might be waiting for her at home.

The club has helped enough abused women and kids that I know what some of the signs look like. Odessa shows too many of them for me to brush it off. Every instinct I have starts sharpening when I think about it.

I want to protect her.

More than that, I want to be the person she reaches for. I have never wanted to be anyone’s hero before her.

Seeing her walk into a public bathroom wearing one outfit and come out wearing another only made my suspicions dig deeper. Then she tried to casually show her friends something inside her truck, like she didn’t want anyone else to notice. Whatever it was, it made her best friend, Maya, sob.

That was the moment I knew I couldn’t keep pretending this wasn’t my business.

Bro code or not, screw it.

The problem is Miles. He is my best friend, and one day he will be president of the club. He is also dating Sienna, whose little group has made bullying Odessa one of their favorite habits.

I hate watching it. I have swallowed my words again and again because of Miles, but the silence has been eating holes through our friendship. I don’t talk to him the way I used to. I don’t tell him things. He has noticed, even if he hasn’t figured out why.

“Okay, man, what the hell is going on with you?” Miles demanded. “You bailed like that without a word. You know that breaks biker code.”

He meant earlier, when I had stopped after spotting Odessa's truck and hadn’t explained myself.

“Sorry, Miles. I just…”

“You just what?” His voice dropped into a growl.

My eyes stayed on Odessa. “I think something is wrong with her. I saw her over in the parking lot by the lake.”

Miles followed my stare. “Dude, you are always looking at her. What, do you like her or something?”

Right then, the truth was the last thing I wanted out in the open. I didn’t want anyone knowing. Not yet, at least.

I let out a breath. “I don’t know. There’s just this familiar feeling I can’t place. Her eyes especially. It’s like I have seen them before.”

“On somebody else,” he said.

I nodded.

Odessa and her friends climbed out of her truck and started toward the school. A few seconds later, Sienna came our way too, her friends trailing along with her. She latched onto Miles the second she reached him, same as always.

Sienna was a rich daddy’s girl playing rebel by dating a biker. That was her whole personality half the time. Her friend Daphne, all bones and attitude, slid up beside me and pressed herself against my arm.

I stepped away immediately.

Daphne wore barely enough clothing to count and flirted with anything that inhaled. She had slept with almost every guy at school, except Miles and me. Miles had Sienna, which meant Daphne had apparently decided I was the next prize.

“Come on, Chaos,” Daphne said, trying to make her voice sound sultry. “I promise I’d be worth your time.”

I rolled my eyes and ignored her. My attention had already shifted back to Odessa and where she had gone. Just before Odessa and her friends entered the building, I noticed Kelseiy, Miles's little sister, pass by them.

Maybe I should talk to her. She might be more useful than her brother right now.

Daphne huffed. “Why are you always staring at Odessa? Don’t act like I haven’t seen you watching that geeky little nerd.”

Sienna's high-pitched voice cut in before I could tell Daphne to shut up. “She’s probably a total slut. She won’t change in front of the rest of us for gym, and she never showers afterward. Makes you wonder what she’s hiding.”

Daphne's eyes lit up with gossip. “Did you see the way her friends hugged her? Maybe she’s pregnant.”

Heat detonated in my veins.

I didn’t believe that was what was going on, but a rumor like that could shred Odessa. She looked too sweet, too innocent, and I had never seen her around any guy except Brandon. Brandon was obviously into Maya anyway.

Part of me, a selfish part I didn’t like admitting existed, wanted to be all of Odessa's firsts. Every single one. But for anything to ever happen, this needed to stop, and I needed to get close enough for Odessa to trust me.

My voice came out rough. “Do either of you ever shut up about her? She’s better than both of you. You two are the sluts.”

Miles stiffened beside Sienna, but I wasn’t done.

“You’re my best friend, Miles, but I am done standing here while your idiot girlfriend and her squeaky voice team up with her trashy friend to bully people. Seriously, man, you must be fucking tone-deaf.”

Miles's fists curled first. Then confusion flickered over his face, like he couldn’t decide if he had heard me right. Anger followed fast.

I understood why. I had never spoken to him that way before.

There is a first time for everything.

Whatever had shifted in me today, after seeing Odessa and seeing where she had been, wasn’t shifting back. I was finished pretending I could stomach it.

I grabbed my backpack, turned away from all of them, and started walking.

“What the fuck is your problem, Chaos?” Miles shouted after me.

“The bitches you keep around,” I yelled without slowing down.

“Where are you going?” he called.

I didn’t answer.

“Talk to me, Chaos!” he tried again.

I kept moving.

If I hurried, I might still catch Kelseiy before class. Maybe she could help me understand why Odessa's eyes kept pulling at a memory I couldn’t reach. Or maybe she would tell me I was letting my feelings twist my head around. Either way, I had a better shot with her than I did with Miles right now.

I headed the way I had seen Kelseiy go.

There was one spot near the side of the school building where she liked to hide when she wanted to smoke without her brother finding out. I cut around that corner, expecting to find her there.

I did.

She was with her friends, and there was a boy beside her. His arm was around her shoulders until he noticed me.

Then every bit of color drained out of his face.

It was almost funny.

Chapter 4: Smoke and Questions
Declan's POV-
I posted myself against the wall beside Kelseiy and dug my cigarettes from my pocket. Whatever came next, I already knew I would need nicotine to get through it.

A hard breath left me as I stared down her little circle of friends. If they had any survival instinct, they would read my face and scatter.

Kelseiy made a sound of pure irritation at my side. “What are you doing here? Did my brother put you up to this?”

I answered with a shake of my head and a low laugh, then fished my lighter from my jacket. The flame caught, the cigarette burned, and I let the silence stretch long enough to make every one of her friends twitchy. None of them liked Miles. They liked me even less.

Kelseiy finally huffed. “You all should go. I’ll catch up with you in class.”

They obeyed fast. Even the guy who had been standing there with his arm draped around her took the hint and hurried away.

Smoke curled from my mouth as I watched him leave. “So what is he to you?”

Her eyes narrowed. “Someone who’s actually interested in me. You’re not going to tell Miles, right?” She turned toward me while I lifted the cigarette again and pulled in a deep drag.

Once the smoke settled in my lungs, I lowered it. “No. Not if you help me with something. And for now, it stays between us.”

Her expression shifted. “Help you with what?”

I had never asked Kelseiy for anything before. Shock was a fair response.

“Odessa,” I said quietly.

Her face lit up like she had just won a bet. “I knew it. You like her. I can tell by the way you watch her, even if my clueless brother can’t.” She smiled wide, bright with satisfaction. Kelseiy hated Sienna and Daphne for the way they went after Odessa, and she never had a problem saying so to Miles’s face.

I let my mouth curve and gave her a small nod.

She sucked in a dramatic gasp. “You smiled. Holy crap, I didn’t know your face could do that.” Then she sobered a little. “What do you need from me?”

“This morning, I saw her by the lake parking lot. It looked like she had slept in her car. She went into the public bathroom wearing one set of clothes and came out in another.” My voice dropped lower. “I think something bad is happening at home. Abuse, maybe. I want to help her, but I don’t know how to bring it up without making everything worse.”

Kelseiy’s teasing disappeared. “I overheard a little of what she and her friends were saying earlier. Did you know the man who raised her—the one married to her mom—isn’t her biological father?”

Surprise hit before I could hide it. Odessa almost never talked about home, so maybe I should not have been caught off guard. Still, that did not make the idea of abuse feel any less likely.

“They were talking about looking for her real father,” Kelseiy went on. “Something about a birthmark they both have.”

“I was going to ask if her eyes seem familiar to you.” I frowned through the smoke. “There’s something about them I know, but I can’t place it.”

“Rule,” she said immediately. “His eyes and hers are almost the exact same shade of green. You seriously never noticed?”

I stopped and thought about it. Staring into the eyes of a ranked brother was not exactly a habit of mine. That would have been weird.

Rule was the club treasurer. He owned a massive company worth billions, and when he first made serious money, the first thing he bought had been a gold bike. That was how he had earned the road name Rule. And yes, his eyes were green. The same green that kept pulling at my memory whenever I looked at Odessa.

“He has a birthmark on his lower back,” I said slowly, “right above his hip. I remember seeing it when we sparred.” The thought formed before I could stop it. “You don’t think…?”

“I’ve caught a glimpse of his birthmark too, and I remember the shape.” Kelseiy leaned back against the wall. “He had been with a woman for years. From what I heard, they were serious. Then one day she just left. Nobody ever explained why, at least not to me. So yeah, it could fit.”

“How are we supposed to find out? And even if we do, how do we prove it?”

“Let me stay close to her for a while,” she said. “I’ll see what I can pick up, and I’ll try to confirm whether she’s being hurt at home too. If I learn anything, I’ll come find you.”

The tightness in my chest loosened a fraction. “Thank you. It matters.”

Kelseiy studied me with a softer kind of amusement. “You really care about her, don’t you? Not just want-to-date-her care. Old lady care.”

A laugh escaped me. “You see too much. You’re like the irritating little sister I never asked for.”

“Well, she might already belong to our world and not even know it.” Kelseiy pushed away from the wall, a sharp little smirk spreading across her mouth. “I’ll start digging. You should go find my brother. I heard the fight, by the way. Can’t say I blame you. Those bitches have earned everything coming their way.”

I knew that smirk. I had seen it enough times to recognize danger tucked behind it. She had a plan—or she had already acted on one.

“What did you do?” I asked.

“She may need new tires,” Kelseiy said, flicking her cigarette away, “and probably a new paint job.”

Then she walked off, fingers wiggling over her shoulder like she had done nothing more serious than borrow a pen.

Her father and brother both acted like she would never survive the Kingsmen life, but they were wrong. Kelseiy had the blood for it. She was too much like them in all the ways they refused to admit. They just wanted her somewhere normal, somewhere far from the Pyra Kingsmen.

I understood why.

A few years earlier, every Kingsman over fifteen had been called in when war broke out between us and another rival biker crew. Miles and Kelseiy lost their mother during it. Lost was the only word we had, because she had not been found dead. She had vanished. All anyone knew was that there had been a struggle, and two Kingsmen had been killed. CB—Cipher Brimstone—was still trying to track even the smallest trace of her.

Since then, Miles’s dad, Pres, had rebuilt security from the ground up. The clubhouse was basically a fortress now, and every house on club-owned land had been built and owned by the club. From far enough away, the whole place could pass for a gated community.

I rest my head back against the wall and stare up at the sky. Heavy boots scuff toward me at an unhurried pace, and when I look over, Demon is coming my way. He signs, “Saw you go at Miles and that girl of his.”

I roll my eyes.

For someone so deadly and cold when he kills—and, honestly, in almost every part of his life—Demon had earned his name early. He was nineteen and had been held back a year because he kept missing school or getting into fights. Pres had been the one who pulled him out of whatever mess he had been drowning in and brought him into the club when he was twelve.

Demon adds, “You ripped into him. That isn’t your usual style. But I know what’s sitting in your head.”

“You do?” I ask.

He nods once. “Odessa. She’s the one on your mind. You look at her the way I look at Pyra.”

Pyra is his girlfriend, and I swear I have never seen two people more violently in love than those two.

She had been a runaway. At sixteen, Pyra had fled her foster parents and crossed to the other side of the country. She had been granted the age of majority, cutting legal ties so she could live on her own without guardians controlling her. When we found her, she had been fighting underground. She is probably the strongest female fighter I have ever seen. She and Demon clicked immediately, and they have been glued together ever since. Both of them go to school here with Miles, Kelseiy, and Odessa.

I give a quiet laugh. “Yeah. She’s on my mind. I don’t understand how Miles hasn’t figured that out.”

“He’s too busy getting his dick wet with that dumb girlfriend,” Demon says. “So no, he won’t notice. We’re men. Needs get handled.”

“Class is about to start,” I say, tossing my cigarette butt aside. “If we’re late, Pres will stick us on gate duty.”

Demon nods, and together we head into the school to find our crew. Knowing Miles, his skank, Kelseiy, and Pyra, they will already be somewhere inside, waiting for the two of us to show before the bell rings.
