bodyText:
In 1969 I kept a 21-year-old cowboy alive for 31 hours, and he swore he'd dance with me for it. For four reunions I sat at the table while the band played, and watched him dance with every other woman in the room.

Every one of those nights, when the first song started, he crossed the floor and held out his hand. Every one of those nights I had a reason ready. New shoes. A bad knee. Somebody had to watch the purses. Not one of those reasons was the truth.

Last Veterans Day, I flew to Denver for the reunion again, and for once I was the one waiting on him.

I sat down at a round table near the dance floor and put my hand on the empty chair beside me. A young Navy corpsman in dress blues, one of the volunteers they send over every year, stopped with a tray of ginger ale and asked me who I was saving it for.

"A man who's late," I said. "About 56 years late."

He sat down. So I took him back to the sand at Chu Lai, and I told him.

He was maybe 22. He had the same short haircut and the same careful manners as the boys I used to wash and shave, and he called me ma'am every other sentence. I liked him right away.

Two widows at my table quit pretending to read the program. A drummer from the band came down off the stage with his coffee. People started dragging chairs over from the other tables, the way you do at a wedding when somebody's telling a good one. By the time Bill Hargrove walked into that ballroom, there were sixteen chairs pulled in around me.

I've told that story one time in my life, to sixteen people in a hotel ballroom. I'm writing it down now because I think somebody else needs it.

My name is Peggy Wu. Back then it was Peggy Chan. I'm 79. My father ran a grocery on King Street in Seattle's Chinatown, and I was raised in the rooms above it. I joined the Army Nurse Corps at 21 because my brother Henry got drafted and I wasn't about to let him go over there without somebody who knew how to stop bleeding.

Henry came home fine, by the way, and complained about the Army food for 50 years.

In January of 1969 the Army flew me to Chu Lai. An evacuation hospital made of Quonset huts on the sand, the South China Sea on one side and the helicopter pad on the other.

You learned fast at Chu Lai. You learned to tell how bad a night was going to be by how many rotors you could hear at once.

The wards were long tin tubes with plywood floors, forty beds to a side, fans that pushed the heat around without ever moving it out. We wore fatigues and jungle boots and worked twelve hours on and twelve off, which mostly meant twelve hours on and then however many more the helicopters said.

Bill Hargrove came in on one of those helicopters in March. Twenty-one years old. Six foot four. Boots longer than my forearm. A ranch kid from outside Billings, Montana, and before I'd finished cutting his shirt off he'd told me about his horse.

He was my patient for 23 days. Seven days in, I could have told you his mother was Arlene, his horse was Duster, and he'd never seen the ocean until he flew over it on his way to the war.

But the first night was the one that counted. Fourteen helicopters in two hours. Bill came out of surgery with a hole through his belly and another in his chest, and a little before midnight his pressure started to fall.

Our head nurse was Major Ruth Calloway. Thirty-four years old, from Muncie, Indiana, with a back as straight as a tent pole. She looked at the ward. She looked at him. She looked at me.

"Lieutenant Chan, that bed is yours. You don't leave it."

I didn't leave it for 31 hours. I took his pressure every 15 minutes and wrote it on a white index card clipped to the head of his bed. I hung blood and squeezed it in by hand. I talked to him when he couldn't hear me, and when he could.

Ruth ran that ward all night like a train station. She never raised her voice. She'd walk the aisle between the beds with a flashlight in her teeth and a clipboard under her arm, and every time she passed his bed she'd look at my card, then at me, and keep walking. That was how you knew you were doing it right. She didn't stop.

Here's what I remember most. He took hold of the bed rail with his right hand and my wrist with his left, and he did not let go. Not when he was out cold. Not when they took him back to surgery at hour nine and brought him back. Somewhere around hour 18 my legs quit, and I sat down on the plywood floor next to his bed with my arm still up in his hand. I sat down again at hour 26. He never let go of that rail. I sat down twice.

At hour 20, Ruth Calloway knelt down on that floor beside me in her fatigues and put a canteen cup of coffee in my free hand.

"Steady hands, Chan," she said. "He's watching your face, not his own."

By morning of the third day his pressure held. By the fifth he was cussing the orderlies. By the second week he was trying to get out of bed without asking anybody.

The doctors said later that he shouldn't have made it, that the bleeding was too much and too long. I don't know about that. I know he squeezed my wrist every time I said his name, and for 31 hours I said it about every two minutes.

Now. My mother. My mother believed there was nothing in this world a pot of tea couldn't put right, and she mailed oolong to me at that hospital every two weeks, my name brushed on the brown paper in Chinese. Tight little dark curls of leaf, from the herb shop on Jackson Street.

I'd switched to coffee at 14 to be American. I called it my mother's weeds, and I gave every single parcel away.

The first one went to Bill. He was sitting up by then. He dropped a pinch of it into a clear water glass from the mess hall, poured hot water over it from the coffee urn, and held it up to the window.

"Look at that, Lieutenant," he said. "Opens up like a hand."

He drank it. He made a face like I'd given him castor oil. "Boiled saddle," he said. And he finished every drop.

After that, every parcel that came while he was there went to Bill's bed. Every time, he held a glass out to me. "I'd rather drink the IV bag," I'd say. "Boiled saddle," he'd say, and drink it himself. By the end of the month the whole ward was saying it. Boiled saddle. I can still hear twenty boys saying it in the dark.

In April the Viet Cong put rockets into the compound one night. A piece of one opened Ruth Calloway's shoulder from the collarbone down. They stitched her up in the next hut, and two days later she was back on the ward with her arm in a sling, straight as a tent pole, telling the orderlies the floor was a disgrace.

On day 23 they flew Bill out to Japan. I walked with them to the pad. He was thin and yellow and grinning, and he pushed the last parcel of my mother's tea back into my hands.

"When we dance, Lieutenant, you're drinking a glass of this."

"When we what?"

"When I'm home," he said, "I'll dance with you. A real dance. A whole song, start to finish."

"You'll walk first, Hargrove," I said. "That's an order."

"Yes ma'am, Lieutenant."

He's answered me that way on every phone call for 56 years. That night, when I went to clip a fresh card on his bed for the next boy, I found the card from that first night was gone from his folder. He'd taken the index card with my handwriting on it.

I came home in January of 1970. I married Tom Wu, a machinist at Boeing, in 1972, and I worked 33 years of nights in an intensive care unit on First Hill. Bill went home to Montana and broke colts and fixed fence on one ranch outside Billings for 50 years, and he wrote me a letter every Christmas. He never once mentioned the dance. He never once had to.

The Chu Lai nurses started holding a reunion in the 1980s. Every year on Veterans Day, a hotel in Denver, a banquet, and a band. Ruth came every single year in her dress uniform, with the shoulder she said still told her the weather. She gave the toast. She was the last one off the dance floor.

I went to every one of them. I'd sit with the girls from my ward and we'd laugh about things nobody else on earth would laugh at. The rats in the supply hut. The chaplain who couldn't swim. The night the generator died in the middle of a surgery and six of us held flashlights over the table for an hour and a half.

Bill found us in 2021. His granddaughter found the reunion online and drove him down from Billings. For four years after that, he danced with every nurse in the room. Except one.

By then Ruth's cholesterol had gone bad, and I'd watched it take her apart one reunion at a time.

2001, a statin. 2010, they doubled it. 2017, an injection every two weeks. After the toast she'd excuse herself to the ladies' room with her purse, and come back with her sleeve buttoned at the wrist.

"My numbers are right where they should be, Peggy," she told me that year, with her napkin folded in her lap. "My doctor's thrilled with me."

2018, two stents. 2020, a small stroke, and a cane, and her hands shook so bad on her coffee cup she drank it through a straw. Ruth Calloway, who once stitched a boy's scalp by flashlight. 2022, she came in a wheelchair and sat at the end of the head table, and her numbers were still right where they should be.

In August of 2023 the phone rang before the sun was up. It was Ruth's husband, Gordon, and he skipped every word you'd normally start with.

"She doesn't know me anymore, Peggy."

The big stroke. A memory-care home in Tacoma.

That's the part I could never get past. A rocket couldn't put Ruth Calloway down in 1969. Fifty-four years later her own arteries did it, and left her alive to not know it.

Gordon died just after New Year's. The memorial was set for a Saturday in January, in a little Lutheran chapel in Tacoma. Ruth's daughter Janet called me that week. She wanted Mom's girls up front for "Abide With Me". All four verses, standing, the way Ruth would have wanted.

"Would you stand with them, Peggy?"

The yes was right there in my throat, waiting to come out.

But by then my own cholesterol had been climbing for a long time. I'd been on atorvastatin since 2013, and my LDL went up a little at every checkup anyway. And the last few years, my calves knotted up on the Seattle hills and my chest went tight on my own stairs.

I pictured that chapel. Four verses on my feet at the front of the room. The cramp climbing my legs by the second verse. Going down in front of Ruth's wheelchair, in front of every nurse I'd ever served with, in front of her grandchildren in the second row.

I'd sat down twice on a plywood floor in 1969. I wasn't going to fold up in front of Ruth.

"I'll be there, Janet," I said. "But I'll be sitting down."

She was too polite to ask me why.

So that Saturday I sat in the front pew with five purses in my lap, while five old nurses, not one of them under 75, stood up front and sang.

Bill had flown in from Billings. 76 years old, a gray suit he'd bought for the occasion, and his boots. He walked those old women up the aisle one on each arm, three trips, as easy as feeding horses. Then he stood behind Ruth's wheelchair with his hands on the grips through all four verses, and he never once shifted his feet.

Same monsoon. Same ward. Same year.

He was a boy with a hole through him on a plywood floor. I was the one who knew how to keep him alive. Fifty-six years later he was the one standing.

And he stood up there holding her chair while I sat in the pew holding the purses.

Afterward, in the fellowship hall, he found me by the cookie table.

"You doing all right, Lieutenant?"

"I'm fine."

He studied my face the way I used to study a monitor. Then he let it go.

"Come to Denver this year," he said. "And this time you dance with me. You still owe me one."

Four reunions. Four first songs. Four times he'd crossed that floor with his hand out, and four times I'd found a reason. The shoes. The knee. The purses. "I don't dance to this one."

The first year it might even have been the shoes. After that it never was. It was my legs, and it was my breath, and I was not going to let the boy I'd kept alive watch me need a chair halfway through a song.

"I'll think about it," I said.

He took the memorial program out of his jacket, wrote on the back with a pencil stub, and handed it to me.

"Nov 11. Denver. First song."

I took it home to Seattle and put it in the little velvet box where I keep my Army Nurse Corps pin.

I let the story rest there and lifted my eyes. I was back at the round table in Denver, and the band was tuning. The corpsman hadn't touched his ginger ale. One of the widows, a little woman named Dottie whose husband had been a surgeon at Qui Nhon, had turned her chair all the way around to face me.

"Is he coming, honey?" she asked.

"He said he was."

I looked at the ballroom doors. No Bill yet. So I picked the story up again at the winter after the memorial.

By February my calves were knotting on the hill up from the bus stop on Queen Anne. Halfway up, every time, I'd have to stop and hold on to the same lamppost and pretend I was looking at the view.

Then I started stopping on my own stairs. Twenty-two of them up to our apartment, and I'd stop on the landing with my hand on the rail. My chest went tight carrying groceries. I wore wool socks to bed and my toes stayed like ice. And by 7:30 the news was watching me instead of the other way round, my chin on my chest.

I told myself that's 78. I'd written those exact words in a hundred charts about other people, and I'd never once believed them.

Then came the night in March.

A little after 3, I woke up with my chest in a band and my left leg locked up like a fist. I made it to the bathroom doorway, and my legs folded and put me on the tile.

That's where Tom found me. On the bathroom floor in my nightgown, two fingers on my own wrist, counting.

He had 911 half dialed before I could even lift my head.

"I'm counting, Tom. Let me count."

"You're counting your own pulse on the bathroom floor."

"It's coming down now."

He pulled me up by both hands and walked me out to the kitchen. He put the kettle on, because neither one of us was going back to bed, and when he sat down across from me his hand shook on his mug.

"Fifty years," he said. "Fifty years you've told every man on your floor to go in. You'd chart this on anybody else in five seconds. You're going in."

He said it evenly. The mug said otherwise. I'd only seen that hand shake once before, at the airport in 1969, and he wasn't even my husband yet.

"You win," I said.

He was on the phone to the VA the minute they opened, and he stayed on hold 50 minutes rather than hang up.

Tom isn't a talker. He was a machinist for 38 years and he says about as many words a day as a lathe does. When Tom makes a speech at 3 in the morning, you listen.

The VA clinic is on Beacon Hill. A waiting room full of old men in ball caps, and one television nobody was watching.

Dr. Sundquist. Young, tall, tired. He was eating a granola bar between patients, and he finished it while he read my file.

They took four tubes of blood. The results were in by Friday, and so was I.

He swung the laptop around so I could see the screen, as if a retired nurse might not know how to read a lipid panel. I knew. That was the trouble.

"Mrs. Wu, your LDL is 169. Your blood pressure's up too."

I didn't give him a word back.

"Twelve years on atorvastatin, and every panel's been higher than the one before. After that business on your bathroom floor, I'm putting you on forty milligrams instead of twenty."

Then he said something kinder than I expected.

"Hear me on this: you didn't bring this on yourself. Your father had a heart attack at 61. That's genes. And you worked thirty-three years of nights and ate out of hospital cafeterias. That's not a moral failing, Mrs. Wu. That's a job."

I thought about my father, face down behind the counter between the rice sacks and the soy sauce, and my mother screaming for somebody to call the ambulance in two languages.

"If it's the genes and the job," I said, "then explain Bill Hargrove to me."

"And who would that be?"

I gave him the short version. Same ward, same year. Fifty years of ranch beef and fried eggs and no doctor if he could help it. Never once on a pill. And he'd walked five old women up a chapel aisle in January without breathing hard.

Dr. Sundquist shrugged.

"Some people just get lucky, Mrs. Wu."

Then he scrolled down.

"One more thing. In October I want your LDL below 100. If it isn't, you go to the injection clinic. A shot every two weeks."

I didn't hear much after that. The injection clinic was Ruth excusing herself after the toast. It was her sleeve buttoned at the wrist. It was a cane, and a straw, and a wheelchair at the end of the head table. It was Gordon's voice on the phone before sunrise.

The girl at the front desk handed me a card. Fasting lipid panel. Tuesday, October 21.

Dr. Sundquist leaned out of his door as I went. "Get me under a hundred, Mrs. Wu, and we'll talk."

When I got home I opened the velvet box and put the card in it, on top of a memorial program with "Nov 11. Denver. First song." written on the back.

One date to keep a needle out of my arm. One date to keep a promise I'd made on a helicopter pad.

In May I took the bus downtown to meet my granddaughter for lunch. On the Harbor Steps my left leg locked and I sat down on a step, and I couldn't get back up.

A teenage boy with a skateboard under his arm hauled me up by both elbows while a tour group off a cruise ship stood there and watched.

"You okay, grandma?"

I told him I was fine. I'd been telling everybody I was fine all year.

I rode the bus home with my hands in my lap so nobody would see them shaking. My granddaughter had waited at the restaurant forty minutes. I told her the bus was late.

That night I took both cards out of the velvet box and laid them side by side on my dresser, under the pin.

One said October 21. One said November 11. And I knew how both of them ended if nothing changed.

I wasn't going to fly to Denver and sit at that table a fifth time while Bill stood alone on the floor with his hand out. He'd walked every old nurse in Tacoma up an aisle. He was not going to walk me.

So I nursed myself. I'm a nurse. It's the one thing I know how to do. I gave up the roast duck skin from King Street and the Sunday bacon. Oatmeal every morning. Egg whites. I walked the Queen Anne hill twice a day, lamppost and all. I took the doubled pill every night. And I bought a fingerstick cholesterol tester off the drugstore shelf on Queen Anne Avenue and wrote every number in a little spiral notebook, like a chart.

Six weeks of that. My home meter said 172.

Higher than April. I'd done every single thing I would have told a patient to do, and the number went the wrong way.

I checked the meter against the strip lot number. I checked it against Tom. His was fine. Tom eats like a teenager and his was fine. Mine was the one going the wrong way.

The June check. Dr. Sundquist read my spiral notebook for a long time before he looked up at me.

"One sixty-six," he said. "Better than nothing. Not enough. October stays."

"I'll take your pill," I said. "I'm not going to the injection clinic."

He shut the laptop lid with one finger.

"Then I'm out of ideas, Mrs. Wu."

I sat in the car in the VA lot with the engine off until the windows fogged. Then I called Billings.

"Bill. I can't dance with you. My legs won't hold me through a song. They haven't for years. And my cholesterol won't come down. If it isn't under 100 by October 21, they send me to the injection clinic."

There was nothing on the line. Nothing for so long I checked the screen to see if the call had died.

"Yes ma'am, Lieutenant," he said. And he hung up.

Ten days later a box came from Billings. A boot box, taped shut three times around, with my address in that square handwriting. Inside, wrapped in an old canvas ranch jacket that smelled like horse, was a cassette player, one tape, and a note on a feed-store receipt. PEGGY. PLAY ALL OF IT.

At the round table in Denver, the other widow touched my sleeve. Marlene Kovach. She'd lost her first husband in 1968, she said, and married Frank in '74.

"My Frank says he's fine," she said. "He won't dance anymore. He's upstairs right now with the TV on."

Nobody at the table said anything to that. Dottie patted her hand.

The corpsman leaned in. "What was on the tape, ma'am?"

I pushed play at my kitchen table, with Tom across from me. There was Bill, slow, a screen door banging somewhere behind him.

"You never told me, Lieutenant. All this time. I watched you sit for that hymn in January and I knew something was wrong. I didn't know what till you called."

"You're going to call me a dumb cowboy when you hear the answer. You already know it. You handed it to me in a mess-hall glass. But first you have to understand what's making your number climb."

"After Gordon called about Ruth, I couldn't make it add up. So I spent two winters at the library in Billings, and my daughter's a pharmacist, so I made her read along. And you know what Ruth's numbers were the week of her stroke? Gordon read me her chart. Right where they should be. The pills got her number down. The stroke came anyway."

"Here's what I learned, Peggy. High cholesterol isn't really a cholesterol problem. The high LDL number is the symptom. The real problem is what happens to that cholesterol once it's in your bloodstream."

"After years of chronic inflammation from modern processed food, and constant exposure to free radicals, some of that LDL gets into your artery walls and gets held there."

"Then it gets oxidized. It turns sticky. And once it's sticky, it starts forming plaque. Your arteries start filling up with oxidized cholesterol that was never supposed to be there."

"And once that LDL is in the wall and oxidized, your immune system answers it like damage. More plaque forms. With every heartbeat your vessels stiffen and keep closing, and one day the plaque ruptures into the heart attack that kills you. Or the stroke that takes your name."

"Ruth's stents. Ruth's stroke. Your legs on that hill. Your chest on your stairs. That's not four things, Lieutenant. It's one. Oxidized LDL is what causes every one of them. Not the total number. The oxidized cholesterol your body can't clear."

"Now the statin. The statin lowers your LDL. Fine. But it does nothing to stop the cholesterol you've still got from oxidizing. Lowering the supply doesn't stop the oxidation. It just lowers the number on the chart, while the cholesterol you still have keeps turning dangerous underneath."

"That's why you gave up the duck skin and walked that hill and the number didn't care. You were working the supply. Nothing in your whole day was touching the oxidation."

"A chart number's a head count, Peggy. It tells you how many head are in the pen. It doesn't tell you how many of them are sick. Ruth's head count was right where it should be the whole way down."

"And it feeds itself. Oxidized cholesterol, damage, more plaque, a stiffer vessel, more cholesterol held in the wall, more of it oxidized. Every heartbeat, another turn. And a pill that only lowers the head count can't stop it turning."

"Now here's what nobody at that clinic is going to tell you. Same ward. Same monsoon. Same powdered eggs. Any doctor in that ward would have bet you'd outlive the boy with the hole in his belly by twenty years. Look at us. I've eaten beef every day for fifty years, and I've never taken a pill for anything but a hangover. In March my doctor sent me for a scan of the arteries in my heart, and he came out and said he'd never seen a rancher's that clean. Luck had nothing to do with it."

"There's exactly one thing I did every day for 56 years that you didn't. Your mother's tea."

"You gave away every parcel. I drank every glass. Boiled saddle, and I never once stopped. When I got home and the parcels quit, I wrote to your mother off the return address on the paper. Mrs. Chan, King Street, Seattle. She mailed me a tin every month until 1994. You didn't know that, did you."

I didn't. My mother never said one word. Tom stopped the tape for me, and I sat there a minute. Dumb cowboy, he'd said I'd call him. I was the dumb one.

I thought about her at the kitchen table on King Street, writing a man's name in English letters she'd practiced on the back of a grocery bag, wrapping a tin in newspaper for a cowboy in Montana she'd never meet. For twenty-five years. While her own daughter drank coffee.

"When she passed, the tins stopped. I bought every oolong in Billings. Not one of them opened in the glass. I wrote to shops in Chinatowns all over the country till I found whole leaf again, and I've had a cup every morning since. Every morning, Peggy. Calving season. Blizzards. The morning my wife died. Every morning."

"There's a class of compounds in oolong called polyphenols. Powerful antioxidants. They're concentrated in oolong, and they neutralize the free radicals responsible for oxidizing LDL cholesterol."

"Researchers in Japan took human LDL and added oolong to it, and it held out almost twice as long before it oxidized. Then in a second test, the oolong neutralized the free radicals themselves."

"Once the oxidation stops, the cholesterol in your blood stays in its normal, harmless form, and your body processes it through the liver the way it was designed to. But those polyphenols leave your blood within a day. So it's a cup every morning, Lieutenant. Not when you remember. Every morning. The cholesterol is not the enemy. The oxidation is."

"Your mother mailed you the answer every two weeks for a year, and you handed it to a ranch kid with a hole in his belly. I've been drinking your share for 56 years."

"Now listen, because you're cheap and I know it. The word oolong on a grocery box is a category name and nothing more. Nobody's promising you a gram of leaf. Nobody's promising you a thing about what ends up in your glass. Your average grocery-store oolong puts around 12 milligrams of EGCG in a cup. EGCG's the strongest of the polyphenols, and 12 is next to nothing."

"What your mother sent was whole leaf. You put it in a clear glass and it opens up like a hand. That's leaf that still has the polyphenols in it."

"Most of what's in a bag on the shelf is dust. Chopped and ground because it's cheaper. Put it in a clear glass and it clouds the water and sits on the bottom like silt."

There was a long pause on the tape there. I could hear him breathing, and a horse somewhere, and the screen door again. When he came back his voice was different.

"Look in the jacket pocket," he said.

I did. There was an index card, soft as cloth and yellow as an old tooth. On the front, in blue ballpoint, in my own handwriting: Hargrove, W. PFC. BP q15min. Then line after line of numbers, 15 minutes apart, so small I needed my glasses. He'd kept it 56 years. On the back, in pencil, in his: READ THE GLASS, NOT THE BOX. 1. Whole leaf, not dust. 2. Every bag weighs the same. 3. They measure the polyphenols in the tea you actually drink. 4. One way to make it, every morning, even half asleep.

Under that, smaller: Steep one bag in a clear drinking glass. Whole leaf opens back into leaves. Dust clouds the glass. A number like yours takes weeks, not days.

On the tape he said, "A hot cup of anything feels good going down, Lieutenant. Don't let a good feeling fool you. Look in the glass. Look at what's printed on the bag."

The last line on the card was squeezed in at the bottom edge: Under 100, you come to Denver. First song's mine.

In July I walked down to the big supermarket on Mercer Street and bought the store-brand oolong. Forty bags for $3.49. Never turned the box over. Never did the glass. I grabbed the cheapest thing on the shelf, the way I had my whole life.

I'll be honest with you. Part of me was glad it was cheap. Part of me still didn't want to be drinking my mother's weeds at all, at 78, because a cowboy told me to on a cassette tape.

It was nice enough. A hot cup in the morning. I felt a little better and told myself that was it working. Two weeks later my home meter said 168.

Only then did I follow the card. One bag in a clear drinking glass. The water went the color of a mud puddle in about ten seconds, and when I tipped the glass, a brown silt slid along the bottom. Not one leaf. After that I turned the box over and read every word on it. It didn't meet a single one of the four rules.

Thirty-one hours I sat with that man, and he still knew I'd reach for the bottom-dollar box. I'd been grabbing the cheapest everything since I was stocking cans in my father's store.

The next morning I walked to the branch library on Queen Anne. A librarian about my granddaughter's age sat me down at a computer and made the letters big enough to read without my glasses, and she never once rushed me. I went back three days running. I read up on every brand of oolong the library's computer would show me. And I looked up the oxidation work Bill had talked about, because I'm a nurse and I don't take anybody's word for anything, not even a cowboy's. It was real.

I crossed them off on the back of the supermarket receipt, one after another. The dust bags. The "blends". The fancy loose tins that never say how much leaf you're getting. Every box that didn't say one word about what's in the cup.

Every one of them said oolong. That was the whole trouble. Bill was right. It was a category name, and most of them were hiding behind it. Some had pretty pictures of mountains. Some had a little gold dragon. Not one in ten said how much leaf was in a bag, and almost none said anything at all about what ends up in the cup you drink.

One was left. PiPi Tea.

Whole-leaf oolong. Every bag weighs the same. 340 milligrams of total polyphenols in the brewed cup, including 187 milligrams of EGCG, tested by Light Labs. More than fifteen times the supermarket cup. One bag with breakfast, made the same way every morning. 4 for 4.

Their page explained why. PiPi Tea's cup is the strong one for three reasons.

The plants are grown above 4,500 feet in Pu'er, Yunnan. High altitude, strong sun and slow growth push the young leaf to make more of these compounds than lowland leaf grown for a factory.

They only take the tip. The bud and the first leaves hold most of the EGCG. The older leaves hold less. The stem holds the least. A picker taking the tip by hand leaves the weak parts on the bush.

A machine taking the same top growth can't do that. It cuts the tip, the stem and the lower leaves in one pass, and all of it goes into the same batch because it's cheaper. Then it's ground up into dust.

That's why when you open a supermarket bag, it's dust. And when you open a PiPi Tea bag, it's whole leaf.

Whole leaf. The leaf Bill held up to the window in 1969.

It cost more than $3.49. I paid for it out of my Army pension and didn't think twice. I've spent more on worse for less reason.

The PiPi Tea pouch was on the doormat the following Thursday. I put one bag in a clear glass on the kitchen counter, poured the water over it, and stood there and watched. The little dark curls loosened. Then they opened. Whole green leaves, edges and all, turning slowly in the glass. Like a hand. Exactly the way he'd said it in 1969.

I drank it with breakfast. And somewhere in the middle of the dishes I noticed I was humming. Standing at the sink, humming, the way I used to on the ward at 4 in the morning when the boys were finally asleep. I hadn't hummed in a year. Tom came in from the other room to see who'd turned the radio on.

That wasn't the cholesterol moving. Bill's card had been plain about that: a number like mine takes weeks.

Day 5, I walked up from the bus stop, past my lamppost, all the way to the top without stopping. Day 10, with Tom out at the hardware store, I put "Moon River" on the record player and danced the kitchen with a dish towel. One whole verse. I sat down after. But I'd done a verse.

I wanted to call Bill so bad my hands itched. I didn't. Under 100, you come to Denver. The number had to come first.

Week 2, the 7:30 slump didn't come. I watched the whole news and then read in bed till 10. I took all twenty-two stairs without stopping on the landing.

Week 3 I walked down to the Harbor Steps by myself on a Saturday, and I went up them, all of them, slow, with my hand an inch off the rail and not on it. A man selling flowers at the top clapped for me. I don't think he knew why. I didn't tell him.

The tea didn't do every bit of it, and I won't pretend it did. I walked that hill all summer. I took the doubled pill. But I'd been doing all that since May, and the number had gone up.

Week 5, I slept without the wool socks for the first time since winter. Week 8, on a Monday morning, my home meter said 117. I sat down on the edge of the tub and looked at it for a long time.

Tuesday, October 21 came.

I got to the VA an hour early, went down to the cafeteria, and ordered bacon and eggs. The same breakfast the Chu Lai cooks used to make us after a bad night, the only real bacon in all of I Corps. Two strips, two eggs, buttered toast. I ate every bite of it before a fasting draw.

The phlebotomist saw the toast crumbs on my sweater.

"Mrs. Wu, you know this is a fasting panel."

"Honey, I was drawing fasting panels before your mother was born. Draw it."

She drew it. She shook her head the whole time.

Dr. Sundquist came in with the printout an hour later, frowning at it like it was in the wrong language. He had them stick me again for a fresh tube. Then he dialed the lab from the wall phone, standing up, while I sat there with a cotton ball taped in my elbow.

"You're sure that's Wu," he said into the phone. "W, U. Margaret Wu. Date of birth 1946."

He hung up and sat down on his stool.

"Mrs. Wu. Your LDL is 91."

From 169.

"I don't know what you've been up to," he said, "but don't stop. The injection clinic can have somebody else. And your atorvastatin goes back to 20 milligrams, starting tonight." He typed it in while I watched. "I guess some people do get lucky."

"Luck had nothing to do with it," I said.

The appointment card from the velvet box was in my purse. I slid it across his desk. He turned it over once, read his own clinic's printing, and let it fall into the wastebasket under the desk.

Tom was waiting in the car. When I told him, he put both hands over his face and sat like that for a while.

"Go call your cowboy, Peg."

Same car. Same lot. Same phone.

"Bill," I said. "What's the band playing first this year?"

Nothing. Then he laughed until he was coughing, and through the coughing he said, "You know what they're playing, Lieutenant."

That was the end of the story. I looked up from the table. Sixteen chairs. Marlene had her phone out with Frank's room number on the screen. The bandleader had run the first bars of "Moon River" for the sound check and then held the song. It was 7:40, and still no Bill.

Marlene leaned over to me. "Next year," she said. "Tell your Bill to come up to 614 and make my Frank come down."

Dottie had a tissue out. The drummer had gone back up on the stage and was looking over at our table instead of at his bandleader. The corpsman kept looking at the doors, then at me, then at the doors, like he could make a man from Montana walk through them by staring.

I touched my collar. The appointment card wasn't in the velvet box anymore. The pin was on my dress.

When I looked up from it, a tall man in a silverbelly Stetson was coming across the dance floor from the elevators, a thermos under one arm and snow still on his shoulders. Billings had been socked in all afternoon.

He stopped at the table. He looked at my legs, and then he looked at me.

I got to my feet. Nothing on the table under my hand. Nothing on the chair-back.

"You're late, Hargrove," I said.

"Yes ma'am, Lieutenant."

And then two old people pushing 160 years between them stood in front of sixteen strangers and held on to each other, and neither one of us said anything for a while.

He put his right hand flat on my back and took my right hand in his left, the same hand that had held my wrist for 31 hours, and it was just as strong. I could feel every one of those sixteen chairs watching. I didn't look down at my feet once. I looked at his face, like Ruth told me to.

We danced "Moon River". The whole song, every bar, start to finish. When it ended the band went straight into the next one, and I didn't sit down for that one either.

Ruth wasn't there. She's in Tacoma, in a room with a window, and she doesn't know either of our names. But halfway through that first song my right leg gave a little warning, and I heard her as clear as 1969. Steady hands, Chan. I kept my feet.

In January I sat in a pew with five purses in my lap and couldn't stand for one hymn. In November I danced two songs with the man who held my wrist for 31 hours.

Back at the table, Bill twisted the cap off his thermos and filled a clear hotel water glass. The leaves turned over in it. He held it up to the chandelier, and then he held it out to me, the way he had a hundred times on that ward.

I took it. I drank the whole glass in front of sixteen people.

"Boiled saddle," I said.

He laughed till his hat came off and he had to grab a chair. I stayed on my feet.

I'm writing this because I came very close to sitting out that dance too.

Ruth's chart said right where it should be, every year, right up until the year she didn't know her own husband. The doctor reads the chart. A nurse watches the patient. Be the nurse.

So watch. Yourself, or the one who shares your kitchen with you. Stopping on the stairs. Holding a lamppost and pretending to look at the view. Icy toes under the covers. Asleep in the chair before the news is over. Sitting out the dance and blaming the shoes.

Nobody's going to put those things on a chart. Nobody's going to circle them. Your number can sit right where it should be while you stop going places, one by one, and nobody notices but your own family. And sometimes not even them, because you're good at hiding it. I was the best there was.

If a doctor is booking you into an injection clinic, and something in you says no because you sat beside somebody you loved all the way down that path, you're not being difficult. You're paying attention.

Bill drank his way past all of it for 56 years and never knew what he was doing. I caught up in eleven weeks.

PiPi Tea. One bag with breakfast. Whole leaf, the same in every bag, 340 milligrams of polyphenols in the cup. It's there to stop the cholesterol oxidation your medications were never designed to address. Stop the oxidation.

Do what Bill told me to do. When the pouch comes, steep one bag in a clear drinking glass. If the leaves open up like a hand, that's the tea he drank for 56 years.

Peggy Wu, 1st Lt., Army Nurse Corps (ret.), Seattle

P.S. You didn't read a letter this long by accident. Somewhere around the chapel, I'd bet you started seeing a particular chair. Somebody you love, sitting at the edge of things while the music plays. Go ask them to dance, and bring a glass.

P.P.S. Coming off the floor after the second song, Bill said, "Fifty years you nursed everybody in sight, Lieutenant, and you never once let anybody nurse you." Then he said, "Stop the oxidation." So I'm passing it on, and you've got nothing to lose trying. PiPi Tea's 90-day money-back guarantee: if you don't notice a difference, they'll refund you within 90 days of delivery, no questions asked.

P.P.P.S. With the first proper cup, you'll feel something before the dishes are done. Not a jolt. More like somebody opened a window in a stuffy room. The cholesterol takes weeks; Bill's card said so, and he was right. And if you're not sure which tea you've got, the glass will tell you the first morning.

P.P.P.P.S. Please don't stop your statin. I'm still on mine. Dr. Sundquist lowered the dose himself when my number earned it. That's his call and your doctor's call. Not yours, and not mine.

P.P.P.P.P.S. For Marlene, and for every woman whose husband says he's fine and stays upstairs when the music starts. Brew it in a clear glass, set it next to his eggs, and put on a record he used to dance to.

P.P.P.P.P.P.S. PiPi Tea is a small company. They buy tip-picked leaf from family farms above 4,500 feet, and a bush only grows so much tip in a season, so they do run out. bodyText:
Ten years of abuse taught Odessa to hide every bruise. One brutal night taught her to stop hiding. She photographed the evidence, saved her own money, and planned her escape. Hector thinks she is trapped. He has no idea she is already taking back her life. 👑⚡
Chapter 1: Odessa's Escape- Chapter 1
Odessa's POV-

Consciousness came back in pieces.

First, pain. Thick, hot, and everywhere.

Then my own rough breath, followed by a low sound I couldn’t stop from pushing past my mouth. I opened my eyes a little, then squeezed them shut again when my left side screamed at me.

Birds chattered somewhere outside. A few bikes growled past on the road, loud enough to yank me the rest of the way out of sleep.

My eyes flew open.

For one frozen second, I forgot where I was. Then the cracked dash, the cold steering wheel, and the cramped angle of my body reminded me.

My truck.

I jerked my gaze around the parking lot, praying no one had spotted me curled up in here overnight. If anyone from school found out I had slept in my truck, it would be everywhere before first period.

Then another thought hit me harder.

Shit. School.

I snatched up my phone and jabbed the power button, waiting for the screen to wake. Even before it fully loaded, I checked the time. My pulse slowed a fraction.

I wasn’t late yet.

Not if I moved.

I twisted toward the back seat for my duffle bag and instantly regretted it. Fire shot up my left side, sharp enough to tear a cry from me. I eased back into the driver’s seat one careful inch at a time, breathing through my teeth until the worst of it passed.

Hector had really gone all in last night.

Hector Jacobs is my stepfather. He has been in my life since I was born, which is why I still carry his last name. That does not make him my dad. He lost any chance at that word a long time ago.

Since I was eight, he has treated me like something built to absorb his fists.

One more month. That was all I had been telling myself. One more month, then I turn eighteen. After that, I can walk away, disappear, and never set foot in that house again.

But after last night, a month suddenly felt dangerous. Too long. Maybe long enough for him to finish what he has been starting for years.

And now I had proof. Real proof. I didn’t think anyone could stop me from leaving if I showed what he had done.

I had never seen Hector as bad as he was last night. He lost some major business deal, came home furious, and used me to bleed off the rage. At least one rib had to be broken. My face hurt in too many places, and my neck felt tender beneath the collar of my hoodie.

I flipped the visor down and stared into the little mirror.

Yeah. Fantastic.

A black eye. Bruising along my cheek. More color blooming near my jaw and across my lip. The eye itself wasn’t swollen, thank God, only darkened, so my bright green iris still showed clearly.

The cold weather helped. A turtleneck sweater would hide my neck. My face, though, was a separate problem.

Good thing I had learned makeup young.

I worked quickly, dabbing and blending until the damage looked less like a crime scene and more like a bad night’s sleep. Once my face was covered, I headed for the public restroom.

I had driven to the lake after running from the house. The lot was tucked away, quiet, and not the kind of place Hector would ever bother checking. Better yet, the bathroom stayed open all night. It gave me somewhere to brush my teeth, clean up, wrap whatever needed wrapping, and get dressed for school like everything was normal.

Normal. Right.

I climbed out of my battered black truck, shut the door, and pulled open the back to grab my duffle from the seat.

The truck was ugly because it had been the first vehicle I bought with money I’d earned myself. Some of it came from my part-time job. The rest came from work my parents knew nothing about.

I could have bought something much nicer with that second income, but nicer would raise questions. Questions led to attention, and attention was the last thing I needed at home.

After locking the truck, I crossed to the restroom.

Inside, I went straight to the stall I always used. It had a mirror and enough room to change without bumping into every wall. Jeans and underwear came first because I knew that would hurt less than dragging my shirt and bra over my ribs.

The bra might have to stay on. Bandages first, then survival.

I shoved my feet into my sneakers, then started working my T-shirt up. Every inch was a negotiation. I paused, winced, breathed, and tried again until I finally got it off.

The bruising looked worse without fabric hiding it.

For a moment, all I could do was stare.

Then I wiped away the makeup I had already put on and took pictures. Every mark. Every ugly patch of purple, blue, and yellow spread across my skin. If I had to prove this, I was going to prove all of it.

After that, I wrapped my ribs tight. If I didn’t support them, I might actually puncture a lung before the day was over.

I had almost finished winding the bandage around myself when my phone started ringing again.

Again, because it had been going off since I turned it back on. I had ignored every call. I also hadn’t really looked at the mountain of missed texts and notifications that had piled up while the phone had been off overnight.

With one hand holding the bandage in place, I picked up the phone.

Missed calls filled the screen. My mum. Brandon. Maya. Over and over.

A few messages from Hector sat in the list too, each one sounding more threatening than the last.

The incoming call was Maya.

She was my best friend, and if she was calling, Brandon was probably right there with her. Those two belonged together so obviously it was almost painful, not that either one of them would ever admit it. Brandon was my friend too.

I answered before grabbing my cami.

“Hey,” I said, trying for casual and landing nowhere near it. “Why is everyone blowing up my phone?”

“Why is everyone blowing up your phone?” Maya repeated, her voice pitching higher. “Seriously? Your mum called me and Brandon all night trying to figure out where you were. Where are you? What happened? She wouldn’t tell us anything, because of course she wouldn’t, and don’t you dare try to brush this off anymore.”

My mouth opened, but nothing came out.

What was I supposed to say? I had never told them the truth. Part of me had always been terrified they would look at me differently. Or worse, leave because being near me was too much trouble.

Muffled voices shifted on the other end. I caught pieces, then Maya snapping at Brandon, then Brandon snapping back. Typical. A few seconds later, the phone must have changed hands.

Brandon's voice came through, lower and steadier.

“Are you still coming to school?” he asked. “I think I already know some of what’s happening, but Odessa, you have to tell us. Let us help. You’re our best friend. That doesn’t stop because things are bad.”

My throat tightened.

He was right. I did need help. I definitely needed help.

I just didn’t want them getting hurt because of me.

I had handled Hector alone for almost ten years. Maybe that had been stupid. Maybe it was finally time to trust the people who had been trying to stand beside me all along.

A long breath left me.

“Meet me in the school parking lot in fifteen minutes,” I said. “I’ll tell you both everything. It’s time you know, because I need to get out of here.”

I ended the call before either of them could ask another question.

This was not a conversation for the phone. Words wouldn’t be enough anyway. It would be easier, and worse, to show them.

I pulled on the cami, then took my sweater and eased it over my head with more care than I had ever given a piece of clothing. Pain still stabbed through me, but I got it on.

At the sink, I brushed my teeth. Then I dragged a brush through my long black hair and tied it high in a ponytail. Once my face was covered again and the evidence was hidden as well as I could hide it, I repacked the duffle and headed back out to my truck.

The second I stepped outside, the feeling hit me.

Someone was watching.

I stopped near the restroom door and scanned the area. The lot looked empty, but out on the main road, a motorbike sat in view.

I could have sworn it belonged to Chaos.

Declan Pierce. Chaos. The biker boy I had been crushing on for longer than I wanted to admit.

Not that I ever would admit it. He was best friends with Miles Easton, and Miles was dating Sienna. Sienna, the queen of popularity, had also been my personal bully since I started high school.

That wasn’t the only reason I had never said a word to Declan. There was a bigger one.

He was the son of a Pyre Kingsman.

The Pyra Kingsmen MC were known all over the country. Around here, people talked about them like they were violence on wheels. At the same time, everyone also knew they donated obscene amounts of money and did serious charity work for homeless people, battered women, and abused kids.

The police didn’t touch them. Rumor said the cops even worked with them sometimes.

There had been an Assistant District Attorney once who made a lot of noise about taking the Kingsmen down. A week later, the ADA was disbarred for misconduct. That was the official version, anyway.

Nobody believed it was the whole truth.

Either way, boys were not allowed in my life. Dating was not allowed. A boy connected to an MC? Hector would have killed me for that alone.

He hadn’t even liked me playing games with neighborhood boys when I was little. Brandon was the only guy friend I had, and Hector didn’t know he existed. Hector didn’t care enough to track my friendships. He cared about my grades and almost nothing else.

God help me if I brought home a B in any class.

The one time it happened, it was because I had missed school after one of his beatings. His response to that grade had been another beating.

I let out a tired breath and climbed into the truck.

If the bike really was Declan's, what was I supposed to do about it? Nothing. Later, I would probably hear about it from Sienna after he told Miles and she overheard.

Today was shaping up beautifully.

*Sigh*

I had five minutes left to get to school. If I pushed the speed a little, I could make the drive in three.

I started the engine and pulled out of the lot, hoping the day ahead wouldn’t turn out as bad as I was afraid it would be.

============================================================

Chapter 2: Bruises and Backup
Odessa's POV-

By the time I pulled into my regular space at school, Brandon and Maya were already waiting beside it.

Chaos was there too.

Of course he was.

He had parked his bike where he could see me, his attention fixed on me the way it always seemed to be. I still have not figured out why he watches me so closely, or why he does it like he is waiting for something to go wrong.

I lifted a hand, motioning for Brandon and Maya to get in. Then I shut off the engine. Whatever I was about to say, I didn’t want it drifting across the parking lot.

Maya climbed into the front passenger seat first. Brandon folded himself into the back. The second Maya's door clicked shut, she faced me with her arms locked over her chest and anger written all over her face.

“Okay, explain. What the hell is happening with you? Why are you talking about running?”

I leaned back against my seat, then regretted it when pain bit through my ribs. Before answering, I scanned the area around my truck, making sure no one was close enough to overhear.

Brandon's voice came from behind me. “Odessa, what is it? Why are you acting like we’re being watched?”

“Because I don’t need the whole school knowing what I’ve been living through for the last ten years.”

My fingers shook as I reached for the hem of my sweater and the cami beneath it. Carefully, I lifted both just enough to expose the bruises spreading across my ribs.

Maya sucked in a sharp breath. Brandon swore under his breath.

I dropped the fabric fast, covering myself again before anyone outside could catch a glimpse.

Maya's anger collapsed into horror. “Why didn’t you tell us before now?”

“You know what Hector is like.” My voice came out quieter than I wanted. “He tells anyone who will listen that he took me in, gave me his last name, raised me like I was his own even though I wasn’t. Everyone thinks he’s this decent man. He performs it so well that people believe him.”

I swallowed, but my throat hurt. “Who would have believed me? After last night, though, I know I have to get out before he kills me. I just don’t know how anyone is supposed to help.”

Brandon shifted forward, elbows on his knees. “What about your real dad? Your biological one. Couldn’t he do something? You’ve never really talked about him.”

“My mum always said he was some one-night stand and that she doesn’t even remember his name.” I stared at the steering wheel. “I’m starting to think that was just another lie. I have tried looking for him, but if he has no idea I exist, he wouldn’t be searching for me.”

Brandon gave a slow nod. “So what’s your plan?”

“I have enough money to leave.” The words should have made me feel stronger. They didn’t. “But I think that means dropping out of school, and that was never what I wanted. I wanted college. I wanted to build my own accounting firm from nothing.”

A bitter breath slipped out of me. “With him the way he is, I don’t think I get to keep any of that. I think I just have to disappear.”

How was I supposed to feel anything but defeated? The man who should have kept me safe was the reason I was losing everything.

Maya moved before I could brace for it. She lunged across the space between us and wrapped her arms around me, crying hard.

Pain tore through me, and I couldn’t stop the loud wince that escaped.

She jerked back instantly, both hands hovering uselessly in the air. “Oh my God, I’m sorry. Did I make it worse?”

I shook my head. “I’m just really sore. I didn’t go home last night, so I couldn’t soak in a bath or do anything for the stiffness. And then I slept here, in this seat.” I tried to stretch and stopped almost immediately. “Everything hurts more than usual.”

This time, I reached for her first.

Maya came back carefully, like I was something cracked that might split apart in her hands. Brandon joined the hug from the back seat, and even that surprised me. He was usually the sort of guy who squeezed the air from your lungs without meaning to.

Now he was gentle.

Too gentle.

For a second, I wondered if he understood this kind of fear better than anyone else I knew.

Brandon pulled away first. “Do you need to start sneaking your stuff out of your parents’ house before you leave?”

I nodded. “Probably. And I’ll need another truck too. One they don’t recognize.”

“Buy one,” he said without hesitation. “We’ll keep it at my place. My mum won’t care. If you need help, she’ll help.”

I looked back at him. “Why would your mum help me? I’ve never even met her.”

I knew his dad wasn’t around, but that was about it.

Brandon's expression changed, not quite hard, not quite sad. “My dad isn’t in my life because he used to hurt my mum. When I was thirteen, I beat the shit out of him. Made enough noise that the police came, and they took him away.”

He glanced down. “He’s in prison now.”

That explained so much. Why he never mentioned his father. Why he spent so much time at the boxing gym. Brandon could fight; I had watched him spar before, and Maya had too. He must have started young because he had needed to protect his mother.

It also gave me one more reason to believe he would be good for Maya.

Not that either of them had admitted anything yet. But I had seen how they looked at each other.

“If I can hide a few things at your house over the next few days,” I said, “and maybe keep a new truck in your driveway until I’m ready to go, that would help more than you know. Thank you, Brandon.”

His answer came easily. “Anytime, Odessa. You’re basically my sister.”

Then his gaze slid to Maya, and his mouth curved. “Unlike this one.”

He said it like a joke, but the truth sat underneath it. Maya was definitely not a sister to him.

I turned my head toward the lot again. Chaos was still watching me from beside his bike, except now he was talking to Miles. I couldn’t hear a word from where we sat, but my stomach tightened anyway.

What were they discussing?

Behind me and beside me, Brandon and Maya started bickering, and despite everything, a laugh slipped out of me.

The laugh hurt.

I flinched, one hand going to my ribs. Both of them stopped instantly, worry sweeping over their faces. I forced a tiny smile and nodded so they would know I was okay, or at least as close to okay as I could manage.

Maya reached down and lifted a paper bag. “Come on. Let’s get you coffee. We brought you a croissant too, because we know you love them.”

She handed me the bag from our favorite bakery, the one I insisted had the best pastries in the entire country. I would defend that opinion to my grave.

“Thank you.” I took it and tried to smile properly.

Food didn’t interest me at the moment, so I tucked the bag into my smaller school bag. Maybe I would pick at it later if hunger showed up. Lately, my appetite had been disappearing under the pain. Swallowing was harder when every part of me ached, and today the bruising around my neck made it worse.

We got out of the truck wearing the kind of smiles people put on when they need the world to mind its own business.

Maya and Brandon fell into their usual teasing almost immediately. Within a minute, they were talking about the winter formal, and Maya was already bringing up shopping.

I looked between them and couldn’t help it. “You two should just start dating already.”

Maya's cheeks went pink.

Brandon smirked.

That was all the confirmation I needed.

My eyes widened. “Wait. Are you already dating?”

“I asked her out over the weekend,” Brandon said, dragging the words out while his smirk deepened. “And, well...”

“I said yes,” Maya finished, smiling now. “We wanted to tell you in person.”

I squealed and wrapped both of them in a hug, carefully enough not to destroy myself this time. “It is about bloody time. Seriously, how long have you liked each other?”

“Since we met,” Maya said.

Brandon nodded like that had never been in question.

He chuckled then, his attention turning back to me. “Maybe now you should tell him.”

My stomach dropped. “Tell who what?”

Please don’t let them know.

Maya leaned closer and lowered her voice. “Chaos.”

I shook my head at once. “If I have to leave, what would be the point? Telling him would only hurt both of us.”

“I don’t know,” she said, studying me. “I have a feeling things might change today.”

Before I could ask what that meant, she shifted topics. “Also, you never told us you had a birthmark.”

We started toward the school building and my locker. As we crossed the lot, Kelseiy walked past us, heading in the direction of her brother, Miles, and Chaos.

“My mum said my biological dad has the exact same birthmark in the exact same place.” I shrugged, then had to bite down on another wince because even that tugged at my ribs.

“Have you tried using that to find him?” Maya asked.

“It wouldn’t exactly be simple. My mother has barely told me anything useful about him.” I glanced toward the entrance. “And that’s before adding in how often she lies to me.”

Maya sighed. “Yeah. I can see how that would make it complicated.”

We let the subject fade after that. Assignments became safer ground, so we talked about schoolwork while we entered the building and made our way down the hall.

When we reached my locker, I noticed Chaos wasn’t far away.

Neither were Miles and his girlfriend, Sienna.

Worse, they were heading in our direction.

So much for a peaceful morning.

Part of me worried about what Chaos might have said to Miles. If Miles knew anything, he would probably tell Sienna, and Sienna never wasted a chance to use something against me.

I pulled in the deepest breath my ribs would allow, then another, trying to steady myself before whatever was coming landed at my feet.

Chapter 3: Lines Drawn
Declan's POV-

Over the last few weeks, Odessa has changed in ways I can’t ignore.

She has been easing herself out of everyone’s reach, bit by bit, so quietly most people would miss it. I haven’t. Even the way she moves has slowed, like every step costs her something. The more I watch, the more worried I get.

And yeah, I know why it hits me so hard.

I like her.

I have liked her since the first time I saw her during freshman year. Admitting that out loud, though? Not happening. Not yet. Maybe not ever, if I had my way.

My brothers in the club call me Chaos, and they didn’t pick the name because it sounded cool. When my temper snaps, things get wrecked. People get wrecked. I have caused enough damage for the name to stick.

One time, I picked up a bike and threw it. After that, one of the guys said they should have called me Hulk instead. He wasn’t completely wrong. I’m six-five, close to two hundred pounds, and most of that is muscle. I live in the gym, and I train harder than I work out.

That is what our club expects. For me, it is worse. My dad is the Vice-President, which means I don’t get to coast. I am supposed to become the future Vice-President of the mother chapter of the Pyra Kingsmen, and everyone knows it.

Because of that, I have always kept every feeling locked down where no one could touch it.

Odessa broke through anyway.

Those bright green eyes of hers grabbed me first. In the right light, they catch and flash like cut emeralds. Beautiful doesn’t even cover it. Still, that wasn’t what bothered me. The color itself felt familiar, like I had seen those eyes somewhere before, only I couldn’t drag the memory close enough to name it.

Then there was her hair. Odessa has this long raven-dark hair that looks unreal when it falls loose, though I like it best tied up the way she has it now. Her body is another problem entirely. The curve of her hips, the weight of her breasts, the shape of her ass—any guy with a pulse would notice.

I have gotten myself off too many times with the memory of her body in my head.

But she buries all of that under oversized clothes and too much make-up. Not in a careless way. In a hiding way. It keeps making me wonder what kind of hell might be waiting for her at home.

The club has helped enough abused women and kids that I know what some of the signs look like. Odessa shows too many of them for me to brush it off. Every instinct I have starts sharpening when I think about it.

I want to protect her.

More than that, I want to be the person she reaches for. I have never wanted to be anyone’s hero before her.

Seeing her walk into a public bathroom wearing one outfit and come out wearing another only made my suspicions dig deeper. Then she tried to casually show her friends something inside her truck, like she didn’t want anyone else to notice. Whatever it was, it made her best friend, Maya, sob.

That was the moment I knew I couldn’t keep pretending this wasn’t my business.

Bro code or not, screw it.

The problem is Miles. He is my best friend, and one day he will be president of the club. He is also dating Sienna, whose little group has made bullying Odessa one of their favorite habits.

I hate watching it. I have swallowed my words again and again because of Miles, but the silence has been eating holes through our friendship. I don’t talk to him the way I used to. I don’t tell him things. He has noticed, even if he hasn’t figured out why.

“Okay, man, what the hell is going on with you?” Miles demanded. “You bailed like that without a word. You know that breaks biker code.”

He meant earlier, when I had stopped after spotting Odessa's truck and hadn’t explained myself.

“Sorry, Miles. I just…”

“You just what?” His voice dropped into a growl.

My eyes stayed on Odessa. “I think something is wrong with her. I saw her over in the parking lot by the lake.”

Miles followed my stare. “Dude, you are always looking at her. What, do you like her or something?”

Right then, the truth was the last thing I wanted out in the open. I didn’t want anyone knowing. Not yet, at least.

I let out a breath. “I don’t know. There’s just this familiar feeling I can’t place. Her eyes especially. It’s like I have seen them before.”

“On somebody else,” he said.

I nodded.

Odessa and her friends climbed out of her truck and started toward the school. A few seconds later, Sienna came our way too, her friends trailing along with her. She latched onto Miles the second she reached him, same as always.

Sienna was a rich daddy’s girl playing rebel by dating a biker. That was her whole personality half the time. Her friend Daphne, all bones and attitude, slid up beside me and pressed herself against my arm.

I stepped away immediately.

Daphne wore barely enough clothing to count and flirted with anything that inhaled. She had slept with almost every guy at school, except Miles and me. Miles had Sienna, which meant Daphne had apparently decided I was the next prize.

“Come on, Chaos,” Daphne said, trying to make her voice sound sultry. “I promise I’d be worth your time.”

I rolled my eyes and ignored her. My attention had already shifted back to Odessa and where she had gone. Just before Odessa and her friends entered the building, I noticed Kelseiy, Miles's little sister, pass by them.

Maybe I should talk to her. She might be more useful than her brother right now.

Daphne huffed. “Why are you always staring at Odessa? Don’t act like I haven’t seen you watching that geeky little nerd.”

Sienna's high-pitched voice cut in before I could tell Daphne to shut up. “She’s probably a total slut. She won’t change in front of the rest of us for gym, and she never showers afterward. Makes you wonder what she’s hiding.”

Daphne's eyes lit up with gossip. “Did you see the way her friends hugged her? Maybe she’s pregnant.”

Heat detonated in my veins.

I didn’t believe that was what was going on, but a rumor like that could shred Odessa. She looked too sweet, too innocent, and I had never seen her around any guy except Brandon. Brandon was obviously into Maya anyway.

Part of me, a selfish part I didn’t like admitting existed, wanted to be all of Odessa's firsts. Every single one. But for anything to ever happen, this needed to stop, and I needed to get close enough for Odessa to trust me.

My voice came out rough. “Do either of you ever shut up about her? She’s better than both of you. You two are the sluts.”

Miles stiffened beside Sienna, but I wasn’t done.

“You’re my best friend, Miles, but I am done standing here while your idiot girlfriend and her squeaky voice team up with her trashy friend to bully people. Seriously, man, you must be fucking tone-deaf.”

Miles's fists curled first. Then confusion flickered over his face, like he couldn’t decide if he had heard me right. Anger followed fast.

I understood why. I had never spoken to him that way before.

There is a first time for everything.

Whatever had shifted in me today, after seeing Odessa and seeing where she had been, wasn’t shifting back. I was finished pretending I could stomach it.

I grabbed my backpack, turned away from all of them, and started walking.

“What the fuck is your problem, Chaos?” Miles shouted after me.

“The bitches you keep around,” I yelled without slowing down.

“Where are you going?” he called.

I didn’t answer.

“Talk to me, Chaos!” he tried again.

I kept moving.

If I hurried, I might still catch Kelseiy before class. Maybe she could help me understand why Odessa's eyes kept pulling at a memory I couldn’t reach. Or maybe she would tell me I was letting my feelings twist my head around. Either way, I had a better shot with her than I did with Miles right now.

I headed the way I had seen Kelseiy go.

There was one spot near the side of the school building where she liked to hide when she wanted to smoke without her brother finding out. I cut around that corner, expecting to find her there.

I did.

She was with her friends, and there was a boy beside her. His arm was around her shoulders until he noticed me.

Then every bit of color drained out of his face.

It was almost funny.

Chapter 4: Smoke and Questions
Declan's POV-
I posted myself against the wall beside Kelseiy and dug my cigarettes from my pocket. Whatever came next, I already knew I would need nicotine to get through it.

A hard breath left me as I stared down her little circle of friends. If they had any survival instinct, they would read my face and scatter.

Kelseiy made a sound of pure irritation at my side. “What are you doing here? Did my brother put you up to this?”

I answered with a shake of my head and a low laugh, then fished my lighter from my jacket. The flame caught, the cigarette burned, and I let the silence stretch long enough to make every one of her friends twitchy. None of them liked Miles. They liked me even less.

Kelseiy finally huffed. “You all should go. I’ll catch up with you in class.”

They obeyed fast. Even the guy who had been standing there with his arm draped around her took the hint and hurried away.

Smoke curled from my mouth as I watched him leave. “So what is he to you?”

Her eyes narrowed. “Someone who’s actually interested in me. You’re not going to tell Miles, right?” She turned toward me while I lifted the cigarette again and pulled in a deep drag.

Once the smoke settled in my lungs, I lowered it. “No. Not if you help me with something. And for now, it stays between us.”

Her expression shifted. “Help you with what?”

I had never asked Kelseiy for anything before. Shock was a fair response.

“Odessa,” I said quietly.

Her face lit up like she had just won a bet. “I knew it. You like her. I can tell by the way you watch her, even if my clueless brother can’t.” She smiled wide, bright with satisfaction. Kelseiy hated Sienna and Daphne for the way they went after Odessa, and she never had a problem saying so to Miles’s face.

I let my mouth curve and gave her a small nod.

She sucked in a dramatic gasp. “You smiled. Holy crap, I didn’t know your face could do that.” Then she sobered a little. “What do you need from me?”

“This morning, I saw her by the lake parking lot. It looked like she had slept in her car. She went into the public bathroom wearing one set of clothes and came out in another.” My voice dropped lower. “I think something bad is happening at home. Abuse, maybe. I want to help her, but I don’t know how to bring it up without making everything worse.”

Kelseiy’s teasing disappeared. “I overheard a little of what she and her friends were saying earlier. Did you know the man who raised her—the one married to her mom—isn’t her biological father?”

Surprise hit before I could hide it. Odessa almost never talked about home, so maybe I should not have been caught off guard. Still, that did not make the idea of abuse feel any less likely.

“They were talking about looking for her real father,” Kelseiy went on. “Something about a birthmark they both have.”

“I was going to ask if her eyes seem familiar to you.” I frowned through the smoke. “There’s something about them I know, but I can’t place it.”

“Rule,” she said immediately. “His eyes and hers are almost the exact same shade of green. You seriously never noticed?”

I stopped and thought about it. Staring into the eyes of a ranked brother was not exactly a habit of mine. That would have been weird.

Rule was the club treasurer. He owned a massive company worth billions, and when he first made serious money, the first thing he bought had been a gold bike. That was how he had earned the road name Rule. And yes, his eyes were green. The same green that kept pulling at my memory whenever I looked at Odessa.

“He has a birthmark on his lower back,” I said slowly, “right above his hip. I remember seeing it when we sparred.” The thought formed before I could stop it. “You don’t think…?”

“I’ve caught a glimpse of his birthmark too, and I remember the shape.” Kelseiy leaned back against the wall. “He had been with a woman for years. From what I heard, they were serious. Then one day she just left. Nobody ever explained why, at least not to me. So yeah, it could fit.”

“How are we supposed to find out? And even if we do, how do we prove it?”

“Let me stay close to her for a while,” she said. “I’ll see what I can pick up, and I’ll try to confirm whether she’s being hurt at home too. If I learn anything, I’ll come find you.”

The tightness in my chest loosened a fraction. “Thank you. It matters.”

Kelseiy studied me with a softer kind of amusement. “You really care about her, don’t you? Not just want-to-date-her care. Old lady care.”

A laugh escaped me. “You see too much. You’re like the irritating little sister I never asked for.”

“Well, she might already belong to our world and not even know it.” Kelseiy pushed away from the wall, a sharp little smirk spreading across her mouth. “I’ll start digging. You should go find my brother. I heard the fight, by the way. Can’t say I blame you. Those bitches have earned everything coming their way.”

I knew that smirk. I had seen it enough times to recognize danger tucked behind it. She had a plan—or she had already acted on one.

“What did you do?” I asked.

“She may need new tires,” Kelseiy said, flicking her cigarette away, “and probably a new paint job.”

Then she walked off, fingers wiggling over her shoulder like she had done nothing more serious than borrow a pen.

Her father and brother both acted like she would never survive the Kingsmen life, but they were wrong. Kelseiy had the blood for it. She was too much like them in all the ways they refused to admit. They just wanted her somewhere normal, somewhere far from the Pyra Kingsmen.

I understood why.

A few years earlier, every Kingsman over fifteen had been called in when war broke out between us and another rival biker crew. Miles and Kelseiy lost their mother during it. Lost was the only word we had, because she had not been found dead. She had vanished. All anyone knew was that there had been a struggle, and two Kingsmen had been killed. CB—Cipher Brimstone—was still trying to track even the smallest trace of her.

Since then, Miles’s dad, Pres, had rebuilt security from the ground up. The clubhouse was basically a fortress now, and every house on club-owned land had been built and owned by the club. From far enough away, the whole place could pass for a gated community.

I rest my head back against the wall and stare up at the sky. Heavy boots scuff toward me at an unhurried pace, and when I look over, Demon is coming my way. He signs, “Saw you go at Miles and that girl of his.”

I roll my eyes.

For someone so deadly and cold when he kills—and, honestly, in almost every part of his life—Demon had earned his name early. He was nineteen and had been held back a year because he kept missing school or getting into fights. Pres had been the one who pulled him out of whatever mess he had been drowning in and brought him into the club when he was twelve.

Demon adds, “You ripped into him. That isn’t your usual style. But I know what’s sitting in your head.”

“You do?” I ask.

He nods once. “Odessa. She’s the one on your mind. You look at her the way I look at Pyra.”

Pyra is his girlfriend, and I swear I have never seen two people more violently in love than those two.

She had been a runaway. At sixteen, Pyra had fled her foster parents and crossed to the other side of the country. She had been granted the age of majority, cutting legal ties so she could live on her own without guardians controlling her. When we found her, she had been fighting underground. She is probably the strongest female fighter I have ever seen. She and Demon clicked immediately, and they have been glued together ever since. Both of them go to school here with Miles, Kelseiy, and Odessa.

I give a quiet laugh. “Yeah. She’s on my mind. I don’t understand how Miles hasn’t figured that out.”

“He’s too busy getting his dick wet with that dumb girlfriend,” Demon says. “So no, he won’t notice. We’re men. Needs get handled.”

“Class is about to start,” I say, tossing my cigarette butt aside. “If we’re late, Pres will stick us on gate duty.”

Demon nods, and together we head into the school to find our crew. Knowing Miles, his skank, Kelseiy, and Pyra, they will already be somewhere inside, waiting for the two of us to show before the bell rings.
